But I got to meet a ton of people in the space — and like I said, it's not that big a space, so you really get to know all the executives. I got to build a whole bunch of new stuff and learn to build products from 0 to 1 and 1 to N. It was super super fun and super meaningful.

And the other thing I should say is: I met my co-founder.

Devon was the first engineer ever to work at Blend. The first week of my internship, I met him on a Friday. I remember this because he doesn't remember it at all. I remember thinking, "Wow, I came in with all the Blend propaganda in my mind — they had told me about how they left Palantir to start it as a mortgage company and they saw these problems." And Devon was like, "No, that's not true at all. When I first joined Blend, we weren't doing mortgages at all. We were doing some other crazy thing." I was like, "Wow, this guy's really cool. He really knows what's going on." And he was like, "This is just some intern kid who doesn't know anything" — and he didn't remember me.

But we worked together really closely starting about six months into my time at Blend. So I also had the great fortune of meeting Devon there, and of course we knew we wanted to do something together afterwards. Which is how we end up where we are today.

Kimberly: Great. So what does Vesta do?

What Vesta Does

Mike: Vesta is also in the mortgage software space. Vesta provides what you can think of as the core system of record and back office capability for all these mortgage lenders.

If someone wants to originate a mortgage, they often have people spending 45 days just manually reading documents. They probably called the borrower and asked for the same document three times. Someone has to actually underwrite the loan. It's got to connect to all the other systems in the ecosystem, including the government, including regulatory checks. It's got to generate all the disclosures. So there's a ton of back office work.

Vesta is basically the single system that you take out your existing legacy system, and then we provide the system of record that underlies all the compliance, all the rules and workflow, all the integrations — and then AI agents that basically replace the work that all those people are doing for the lender.

Why Replace the System of Record?

Kimberly: I think one of the really interesting things about Vesta — and you and I worked together now for five plus years — is that you always had the vision in the early days that you wanted to automate a mortgage end-to-end. The exact mechanism by which one would do that was a little bit less clear, but you knew the mortgage space better than anyone else. You knew that it had to be a modern system of record. I'm first curious why you set out to do what I think a lot of people told you was a really really hard idea — ripping out a core system of record is very difficult. And then also I think one of the most amazing things is it's a very good market for AI agents actually. I think that was not as obvious in 2021 even if your end vision was clear, but it's much more obvious now. I'd love to learn how you made that transition.

Mike: In 2021 it wasn't obvious because there weren't even AI agents. But we were always very bullish on technology — it has just gotten better inevitably over the last 30 years. And we were really starting to see signs of life in computer vision. 2020 was not really a time when we were like, "Oh yeah, LLMs are going to eat the world." But it was quite clear that the developments being made in computer vision were very significant. You had the self-driving car era. You had a bunch of these companies doing OCR and doc extraction. And it turns out a huge percentage of mortgage origination is just reading the borrower's documents and figuring out what's on them and triangulating that against everything else in the file.

So the bull case even pre-agents was: you could probably automate 80% of the work if you just combined classical rules, a lot of workflow configuration, and some variant of document extraction. We had always designed the system with in mind that even if the document extraction wasn't good enough for the mortgage lenders to trust today — "I'm going to underwrite this $800,000 loan based on what the AI says" — that somehow, someway it would get good enough.

Of course, to your point, we got the best tailwind of all time: somebody figured out that you actually don't need to build any specialized models. We'll just build you one amazing model that's as smart as a human, and it can power everything that you do. So we've been able to make much faster leaps towards that vision of 80%, then 95%, then eventual 100% automation of this back office sloggy work of reading documents and moving stuff around.

But we did redesign the system of record to be positioned for this idea that eventually all the work could have this interchange and handoff between humans and software. We're pretty agnostic to what kind of software was doing the work.

To the first part of your question about the system of record — everyone said you shouldn't do it, everyone said it was too hard. Honestly, I think you told me quite a few times, "Why don't you just figure out some other clever wedge and figure out how to do it later?"

Kimberly: Yeah, because I think ripping a core system of record for an industry as complicated as mortgages, something that underpins the economy as much as mortgages do — it's very very difficult. If Vesta goes down, your customer goes down. So it's mission critical work. You could just build an AI agent that sits on top of the existing system of record, or wedge in some other way. Like, why do you have to do the whole thing?

The Data Architecture Argument

Mike: We were very convicted from day one. If you had told me how hard it was actually going to be to get all these big lenders to be like, "You know what, yeah, we're going to bet our entire business on the guys who have two customers" (now we have way more than two customers, of course), I think maybe would have thought a little bit harder about it. There's something viscerally about how hard it is that you have to feel and understand to really be scared of it and respect it.

The other thing is: we saw that in many ways Blend was the pinnacle. It built the best and most prolific piece of software that sat on top of these core systems. And we felt very strongly there were just limits to how much of the workflow you could change and how much automation you could drive.

I was talking to the CTO of Jack Henry, and he said something really smart: "If you're going to replace a core system of record, you better have a belief that goes all the way down to the data architecture as to why it's broken. Because everything that's not the data architecture, you can replace by integrating the system of record. You can replace the UI by putting UI on top of it. You can replace the automation by building some sidecar automation. If the data architecture is messed up, then you have no choice but to replace the data architecture — and that's a new system of record."

In the incumbent's data architecture, there are a few things particularly difficult. One is that the data modeling is just really hard, especially in today's world of AI agents and their ability to understand the semantic data model. The incumbent has 30,000 fields, and it's a flat file database — so there's no relationships, no relational SQL on the back. It's a flat file. And then they have a bunch of redundant fields because it's actually such an old Windows app that the fields map directly to the screens. So if you want the same field on two different screens, you need to replicate the field. That is a really hard way to drive reasonable automation, whether it's classical rules or AI agents. So we felt like the data model was just not going to be tenable to build a lot of automation on top of.

The other problem with the data architecture is that flat file database is single-writer. You can only write to the entire loan file — one person has to overwrite the entire loan file in one go. What that effectively ends up meaning is you can only have one thing with write access to the loan file at any given time.

If you want to run a bunch of AI agents, like a swarm of agents, to automate your loan origination process — you probably want a different agent calculating the income and a different one calculating the assets and a different one looking at the purchase contract and making sure it all matches. And you cannot parallelize any of that work. Which is a big latency problem, especially with the pace at which agents are working today. That also made that kind of not work.

So if you go all the way down to the database level, there are these two constraints. And that meant you have no choice but to totally rip out the system of record and start over if you really want to automate this thing.

Were Customers Really Ready to Rip and Replace?

Kimberly: Sometimes in Silicon Valley we're like, "Hey, this should be automated. This is a very inefficient way of doing work. There's a much better solution." And sometimes you go to your customers and customers are like, "We're actually kind of happy with the way things are going." How did you decide that customers were not happy with this, and that they were willing to undergo the extreme pain of ripping out their system of record?

Mike: It helps a ton to have been at Blend and in the industry. You have to viscerally feel it. I often say — as someone who's out there ripping and replacing a system of record — that all these people trying to rip and replace Salesforce, I think, is probably not correct.

Kimberly: Why?

Mike: Everyone complains about Salesforce, but you actually don't see that much migration off of Salesforce historically. One big thing that told me people were willing to do it: they would migrate from the legacy system built in the '80s to the legacy system built in the '90s. And other ones would migrate from the legacy system built in the '90s to the legacy system built in the '80s. If they're doing an 18-month project to go from one thing to the other, and then literally five years later sometimes going back — that tells you that the hatred of the incumbent systems is so visceral that there is opportunity if there's something better.

From the business perspective — mortgage is a little bit of a commodity business. Everyone kind of originates the same 30-year product. It's government-backed. The prices — I mean, CNBC has a mortgage price tracker. If that doesn't mean your price is commodity, I don't know what does. So it was very clear the structure of the industry is in a commodity, the cost to manufacture really, really matters. We were hearing from lenders at Blend all the time: "Okay, but how are you helping my cost to manufacture? I know I have a bunch of people in the back office doing all this stuff. And when I look at what they're doing, it is super clear that technology can do this. Can you help me automate that? Can you help me lower my cost to manufacture?"

Between those two things — that visceral focus on cost to manufacture, and the clear "people making changes and I was like, why are you even doing that, the thing you're getting on the other side is the same" — it felt like there was a unique opportunity here that I just think isn't there in a lot of other system-of-record businesses.

Macro View on Interest Rates

Kimberly: As part of building this business, I know you and I talk about rates a lot of the time, because obviously a mortgage rate is a derivative of any sort of core rate out there. I'd love to just get your macro take on interest rates. We read all the time about the AI capex build, the implication on rates. You follow this day-to-day in your business. What's your macro take?

Mike: Mortgage people are eternal optimists, is what we joke. Every mortgage person says six months from now rates are going to be lower and we're going to get a refi boom. I would say for the last three or four years, I've been pretty bearish on that take. I really think we have to build the business assuming we are not going to get some rate boom and some refi boom. Honestly, a refi boom at this point would be pretty insane for our revenue. But you shouldn't expect it.

There are three big things that I think drive up the long end of the curve no matter what.

(1) The national debt is a very real thing, and it is especially problematic for mortgages because mortgages are government-backed. The correlation between treasuries and 30-year MBS is way higher than the correlation between treasuries and lots of other things, because the credit risk of the 30-year MBS is also the credit risk of the 10-year Treasury in some ways.

(2) The AI capex buildup — there's just very competing demand for capital that has very high yield and return in theory. People are willing to borrow money at higher rates for it. That structurally drives interest rates up.

(3) I like to say that long-term interest rates are reflective of the average of every person on Earth's discount rate — their personal discount rate.

Kimberly: What do you mean by that?

Mike: If you have a dollar today, or if you could take money from the future and have a dollar today, how much money would you give up next year? For a lot of people it's like $1.15 or $1.10. In college, we always had this thing — for me it was like $3 because we're all going to make way more money after college.

Kimberly: It's why Mike has no savings.

Mike: Yeah, it was very controversial in our friend group actually. I was like, "I'm not going to put any money in my 401k." One thing I am going to say: post-college, all of our friends basically told me I was right. They were like, "You were actually right in college. You spent all your money in college, and as soon as they graduated, they made way more money." Your discount rate is just what's your money worth today to you, what's it worth tomorrow to you? That affects how you spend and how you save.

In many ways the long-term interest rate curve is just a function of everyone on Earth's average discount rate. The problem is everyone's discount rate is probably significantly higher today than it was 5 to 10 years ago, for a few reasons:

  • There's a lot more volatility in the world. You have two significant wars going on, which make people uneasy.
  • There's this AI thing — if AI is really great, you'd rather spend all your dollars today because you're not going to need dollars in the future, you're going to have utopia. If AI is really horrible, you'd rather spend them all today because you might be dead or something.

I don't necessarily think either of those are high probability, to be clear. But if you underwrite the probabilities, just the increased volatility means that I think people's discount rates naturally have gone up, and that is going to get manifested in higher interest rates.

Running the Business in a High-Rate World

Kimberly: How much of this thinking informs how you run the business? What changes do you have to make if you think rates are going to be higher versus lower? Most enterprise software companies don't really care in a very direct sense about what the interest rate is.

Mike: There are a few things. One: there's a tendency by mortgage lenders — and accordingly a lot of mortgage software businesses that are rate sensitive — to forecast and plan cash assuming whatever the Mortgage Bankers Association forecasts. Which is a terrible practice, by the way, because as I said, mortgage people are optimistic. It is much better to be conservative and run your business assuming volumes are going to stay pretty conservative and pretty purchase-oriented. The number of homes bought in this country — and accordingly the number of purchase mortgages — does fluctuate with rates a little bit, but not that much. It's really the refinances that go crazy. So you have to forecast conservatively.

The other thing: while rates are high and volumes are low, it's actually really good for us to be extra aggressive in sales. Lenders are struggling a little bit more than when rates are good and they're making a lot more money. They accordingly need our partnership more. But they also have more time. These businesses are very capacity constrained — and the capacity is very human.

Kimberly: Sorry, what do you mean by that?

Mike: They have all these people who spend all their time originating mortgages. If rates drop 75 bips and volume goes up 25%, you can't just instantly hire people to make all those mortgages. What people actually do: they'll go and take people off their technology project team and be like, "Today you're processing the mortgages for the next month." This actually happens.

So when rates are really good and volumes are really good, it's actually really hard to get a mortgage company to make big change, implement new technology, etc. This is a nice window for us to go in and get a lot of market share, roll out a lot of customers, make them successful. There are going to be a lot of mortgages in this country no matter what — maybe not 2021 numbers, but even the baseline is trillions of dollars in volume and a lot of units. It's a really good opportunity to sign up a bunch of customers and get them implemented. If rates drop even a little bit, you get some nice volume pickup. But I think we're not going to see a big drop for several years, is my personal opinion.

The SaaS Apocalypse Debate

Kimberly: You're now at a point where you've built enough product, you have early referenceable very large customers, and you want to scale the go-to-market. At the same time, you're doing this against the backdrop of what we affectionately term the "SaaS-pocalypse" — where SaaS companies are just getting destroyed in the public markets right now. How do you think about that? Because you are at your core still an enterprise software company. Do you think the SaaS apocalypse is fair?

Mike: If I thought the SaaS apocalypse was real, I would really have to question what I was doing here. I also will remind everybody that all these AI agent companies that we know and love also happen to be enterprise software companies. They're also just writing code and delivering it to customers.

Kimberly: So you think it's just a false dichotomy.

Mike: I think it is a false dichotomy. There are a few things that are true. The fundamental SaaS business model is: if you build the software one time, you can amortize that building across 100 or 1,000 or 100,000 customers. The alternative is for each of them to build it 100 times.

Even if you take the cost of software building and divide it by 10 (and I don't think anyone has really managed to divide it by 10 yet) — let's say you can divide by 10 or by 100 — it's still going to make sense for 100 people to pool and have one company do it, and buy it from that company at a fraction of what they would pay to build it, than for them all to build it themselves.

Now there's some other stuff: do they all actually want the same product? How similar is that product overlap? This makes me more bullish on vertical than horizontal. In vertical, your customers usually do have very similar needs, so they're using all the software you build.

Kimberly: Define the difference between vertical and horizontal.

Mike: Vertical is like us — we only serve the mortgage industry. Veeva is vertical because they do life sciences. Salesforce is horizontal because literally anyone can use Salesforce in some way.

The problem with horizontal SaaS that makes it harder: your customers are often only using 10% of what you build. You're paying the price for 100% to develop it, you're charging them for 100%, and they're only getting 10% of the value. That's a case where they might think about building the much narrower thing than your product themselves.

But if your customer is using 100% of what you're building, and you've built it and are selling it to other customers — how can you possibly charge them more than it would cost them to build it themselves?

As the cost of building software goes down — does that mean your prices have to go down? Does that mean you have to build 10x more functionality to maintain the same price? Maybe. But you also should be able to build 10x more functionality. Every time a lender is like, "Well, can I use Claude Code to build an LOS?" — I'm like, "What do you think I'm doing? Do you think I just have a bunch of engineers typing the code by hand?"

The SaaS business model is not about how high the cost is to make technology. It really is about this pooling and specialization — which I think will remain very true.

If you're a vertically entrenched software company in a highly regulated space, we're probably going to be fine. And if we're not going to be fine — there are worlds where you should always underwrite the possibility that Anthropic is the only company remaining. That would be bad for me. But I don't know what anyone is supposed to do about that. I don't really spend that much time worrying about it.

The Jane Street Influence

Kimberly: How much of your thinking is informed by your time at Jane Street? From this conversation, you're obviously thinking in terms of probabilities, discount factors, etc.

Mike: Jane Street was extremely formative for how I think. I also think I kind of thought quite similar to this before I went to Jane Street — which is why I had so much fun there and I think they liked me quite a lot. But I definitely really think about the world in this very probabilistic sense. It just has always made sense to be that way, I guess.

Tokens, Margins, and the Inference Economy

Kimberly: One of the differences for the SaaS business model versus a more AI agent business model is: there's a cost to serve each individual AI agent in a way that there's not a cost to serve an additional instance of an enterprise SaaS product. Do you think margins for SaaS companies layering on AI are just going to structurally be lower?

Mike: As we are seeing already — GPT 6 Luna came out today and they're charging 10 cents per million input tokens, and 6 Luna is pretty good. We're already seeing enough competition in the model layer that we're going to see inference costs fall pretty significantly.

I don't know exactly what the world looked like in 1995 when people were doing dot-com and building their own data centers. But if I had to guess, the early providers of software like Salesforce back in the day maybe would go to the customer and be like, "Look, it actually costs us a lot of money to serve this stuff because we have all the data centers and all the capex, and running the software is actually not that cheap."

There's this common thing people say: "Oh yeah, running the infrastructure is free but the tokens are really expensive for us." The infrastructure is also expensive, and the tokens are actually not that expensive, because we don't necessarily need the most frontier intelligence to do a lot of these mortgage tasks.

Margins are going to be much more about the things that margins are always about in software: how good are you at managing your costs, how lean of a business can you run, how important is your thing to your customers. We'll converge to that place. This "token being — are you doing a 20% markup on tokens, or your customers thinking about how many tokens they're buying from you" — I think that's not really going to make sense in 5 years. Like, no one asked me, "What was your AWS bill? I only want you to make a 20% margin on your AWS bill." But that's literally how all the coding providers seem to be going around selling tokens today.

Kimberly: Do you think that's sustainable in the future?

Mike: Probably not. Over time, the question is going to be: what value do you provide to these companies? What is their alternative cost to build it themselves? You have to give them a positive ROI, and you have to be cheaper than building it themselves. Your margins are probably a function of those two things more than literally what the tokens are.

Becoming AI-Native: The Devin Story

Kimberly: Listening to you talk — you did study AI and CS in college, so you weren't AI illiterate at the start of this AI wave. But you've definitely gotten a lot more AI-native over time as you started to layer on those products into your own company. How did that happen? How did you have to refound yourself as a CEO to be like, "We are an AI-native business"?

Mike: A couple things. I love to make this joke about product people — everyone's like, "Oh, how do I become a good product person?" And the meme for so long in Silicon Valley was: "Just use a lot of products." I think that's actually very true — and yet no one follows this advice.

In this new world, so much of it is: use a lot of AI products. You just have to try everything new that comes out. You have to try all the dumb form factors. You have to play with stuff. Some of these products are bad. You have to connect your personal email and have some burner email to connect it to all these things that you have no idea if they're secure. A lot of it really is just playing with the products — you kind of crowdsource everyone else's thinking about how this technology is going to evolve and what the models can do. You get the distillation of everyone's best thinking in their products.

We were very lucky to be super early to Devin by Cognition — which was, in many ways, the first real agent product that unlocked a lot of the way we thought about that. We spent a ton of time using Devin. It was horrible, by the way. When they did the whole launch video and everyone was like, "Oh, this thing is like, you know, whatever, whatever" — we actually got pretty early access maybe that summer. They were building a coding agent with GPT-4.

Kimberly: This is summer 2024?

Mike: Summer of 2024, yeah. They were building a coding agent with GPT-4, which, by the way — the reason no one had agents is because GPT-4 was not smart enough to build an agent. But you could kind of see it, and see the glimmer of the future. That was the first time I looked at it and was like, "Holy crap, this is AGI."

Kimberly: I remember this — because everyone on the internet was like, "Devin doesn't work. This is all fake." And you were like, "No, this actually really does work. And we use it a lot, but it's really hard to figure out how to get it to work."

Mike: Getting it to work was super difficult. We went to school with Russell, so Russell and I are very close. He got me early access, and we spent a lot of time talking about how to make it work. We really got it to work when — I think Sonnet 3.6 was the big unlock, when the thing really could do meaningful work. But even with GPT-4 you could get it to hack out little things. It was more a toy at that point.

That's a good example of just using all these products and getting to understand them early. It gives you much better intuition for how you should work with these agents. The number of people at Vesta who have turned around and taught, "No, the way you should think about this agent is: if you told a person to do this, they also wouldn't know what to do. So why are you telling an agent to do this?"

People are hyped about understanding exactly what the quirks of the various models are, and you get some of that too. But really understanding the different form factors and how they express that intelligence is super super important. That has helped a ton, and my relationship with that company has continued to help a lot as well.

Kimberly: What is your relationship with that company?

Mike: I advise them on product. I'll try, when I'm in SF, to go into the office on Sundays and hang out with the guys and try all the newest stuff and give them advice on whatever. I don't know — is my advice any good? We'll see. But it gives you a lot of access to how those guys think. Seeing how they actually build software, seeing that they'll work on Sundays — we do not actively make Sunday an on-day workday — but seeing the way they're developing software and using their own product is obviously super instructive. The way they think about the capabilities of the new models — they often have a really good sense for "all right, now we feel like computer use is good enough that you can actually test in an economic way."

Getting to outsource where the new models are really good is a super big advantage for me. I don't have time to spend 10 hours playing with every single model that drops — they dropped three today, you know, for God's sake. So spending a lot of time with them has been really helpful just in understanding how you build an AI-native company and how to build a great agent product. So much of that stuff they actually innovated on, and I've been lucky enough to learn a lot.

Tactical: Event-Driven Agents at Vesta

Kimberly: Let's make this a little bit more tactical. Your original core business still is the system of record — you are the system upon which mortgage lenders originate their mortgages. That's relatively easy to understand. I think we've been a little bit theoretical about what the AI agent thing you were doing on top of that is. Let's take the learnings from your time advising Cognition — what have you actually tactically taken from that and put into your own product?

Mike: Vesta was actually very early to the idea that you should use automation to orchestrate these agents. A lot of agents were still kind of copilot — we all say it's an agent, but some human still goes and types the thing in.

I remember — this is maybe Q3 last year, around September — when Stephen How at Cognition started talking a lot about how agents are going to be event-driven. "It's going to just be like you have some bug report and it's going to fire, and the models are now smart enough that the agent will just go do whatever." I was like, "Well, if the agent can be event-driven, it also can just know when to step in on the loan, and you just write some classical rules to kick off the agent on the loan."

Very concretely: when you sign your disclosure at most Vesta customers today, it will flow through to Vesta to the loan origination system. It'll mark "Hey, Mike gave intent to proceed with this loan." We'll kick off a bunch of classical automation — order flood, order fraud, order the appraisal — but we'll also kick off a bunch of agents.

Rather than waiting for a processor to get to the computer and prompt the agent and tell the agent what to do, you basically let the mortgage lender hard-code a prompt: "You need to go through the purchase contract and make sure all the terms are in line with what we disclosed, that the dates are set correctly, mark the loan's priority accordingly, and check that the house is within 50 miles of the employer." That's a horrible prompt, but you just feed it, and every single loan that goes through that stage at Vesta will automatically spin up an agent to go do exactly that work.

That was a huge unlock for us because our customers often don't let us let individual users prompt the agent as the primary use case. They want a lot more control. They maybe don't trust all of their operations people quite as much. A lot of these guys have a lot of offshore. This whole orchestrated agent scenario really was inspired by those guys talking about how it was all going to be like Datadog-driven and Sentry-driven. I was like, "How come no one else does this?"

I think a lot of the reason people didn't do it much prior to that was the models actually. You couldn't trust the models enough to give them that hands-off of a result in many cases. But that's both the very tactical learning and also how most of the agents at Vesta get manifested today.

Automation Progress: 2024 → 2026

Kimberly: So, 2024 — what was the automation rate of a mortgage, or the time-to-close that you were able to reduce it by? What did that look like in 2025 into 2026? Where do you think the long-term trajectory of a mortgage origination is headed with Vesta?

Mike: In 2024 we probably had not made that much progress towards actual automation. 2024 we were just getting our first customers live. Building the core system of record is a two-year journey to even get one loan done.

Kimberly: Why is that?

Mike: A lot of it is how complicated the data model is, how complicated the regulatory requirements are. Mortgage is just fundamentally so much more complicated than a lot of other things because of the political sensitivity and the accordingly resulting regulatory environment and investor environment.

It turns out some other companies that have been trying to build a new loan origination system for mortgages — they've been at it like five years and they haven't funded a loan. I actually think I heard one funded their first loan a few months ago, and that was six years in. We did it in two years, which was on one hand a really long time, and on the other hand remarkably short. By the way, this was before we had AI to assist us. So you type that code by hand.

Kimberly: You typed all that code yourself.

Mike: Yeah. It did take a really long time. So 2024 was pretty flat. The industry was closing in 45 days — it was probably the same. 2025 we really started to see meaningful automation increases. You probably had automations firing across our customer base, automating something like an average of 15-20%. That doesn't always straight up result in time taken off because you have appraisal delays, and wall clock time is a little bit different from human manufacturing time.

At the beginning of this year, PennyMac went on their earnings and said they had taken 25% of the operating cost out — and that was before we deployed the AI agents. We've now deployed a ton of AI agents with them.

Kimberly: PennyMac is a top five lender.

Mike: PennyMac is depending on the quarter, the first or second normally biggest lender in the country. That was a very good thing for us when they went on and said, "Yeah, we just took out 25% back office efficiency improvement."

So we are well on our way, but so much of getting the adoption in production — the hard part is really getting people to trust AI agents. You can roll out a bunch of AI agents, and there are definitely lenders that will still have people look at every single agent run and they're like, "Well, it's faster because I didn't have to click anything, I just read this long chain of thought." It's like, "Maybe a little bit, but why are you reading the chain of thought?"

The diffusion of technology takes longer. From a "what you can automate" perspective, we're probably around 75% of the way there. The last parts are usually the hardest. One very specific difficult thing for us: we will have to figure out how to get the VA to allow lenders to use a system account to access their online portal to get their certificate of eligibility for a VA loan.

Kimberly: I probably don't need to ask you what that even means, but...

Mike: Basically — a veteran's loan requires you to go to the Department of Veteran Affairs website to get the certificate to confirm that they're eligible. That website does not have a way to log in with a system account. You have to use a user account, and that user has to have a social, and you are not allowed to scrape the website. So you cannot automate that until the VA says, "We will figure out how to let you do it." The last 5% is definitely going to be the hardest. But 75% is probably my guess from a product perspective where we are.

The Regulatory Landscape: Why Mortgages Are Uniquely Complicated

Kimberly: You talked a little bit about why mortgages are even more complicated than a lot of traditional financial services, because it's basically a government program. Can you talk about that regulatory landscape? Are you even allowed to automate a mortgage end-to-end? Is that legal?

Mike: Let me give a little bit of context first. I don't think FDR was making a strategic bet, but in some ways the US made this overall bet that no other country really made: we're going to have 30-year fixed rate mortgages. I think Denmark might have them, but other than that, no other country in the world has a 30-year fixed rate mortgage.

Why is that important? In a lot of other countries — Canada, for example — it's a 5-year mortgage. 25-year amortization, but at year five you have to refi, or that whole balance becomes due, or you have to move out of your house. You can imagine that changes the risk profile. In 2023 everyone's freaking out that rates are up a lot. If you were in Canada and 2023 happened to be year five of your mortgage, you had to figure out how to make a payment of twice the size.

So the US made this decision over FDR, over the course after World War II, that we were going to have 30-year fixed mortgages. That's great. I think that's been really good for the American middle class, good for American prosperity and stability.

It comes with a downside: how on earth do you underwrite somebody for 30 years of fixed payments at a fixed rate? You're taking on a ton of duration risk. Why do some of the banks holding mortgages — like SVB — become a big problem? Because you have this insane duration risk. You're taking on 30 years of credit risk. I don't know anybody in my life who I can be like, "Oh yeah, I'm sure they're going to be making money" 30 years from now — you might be retired, I hope you're retired actually.

You take on meaningful duration risk and interest rate risk. You take on credit risk. And you take on macro risk, which is pretty correlated with credit risk. Mortgages are quite macro-sensitive — when there's a recession, mortgage delinquencies go way up.

That combination is just fundamentally really hard to underwrite. I don't know how any capital market investor is supposed to get comfortable with a 30-year fixed payment thing. So what do you look at instead? The US government backs them. And the US government is going to back this super complicated thing.

There's a lot of political stuff around mortgages and home ownership. Before the midterms, I go on these mortgage podcasts and people are like, "What do you think Trump is going to do so he can improve affordability before the midterms?" It's actually a very common topic in mortgage circles now.

You end up with something very politicized, very bureaucratic. Ignore the regulations for a second — when you sell a mortgage to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, they have rules you have to meet. Underwriting criteria, debt-to-income, things like that. Those are government-sponsored enterprises. How do you think they make rules? They write us a sheet of a 1,100-page PDF of the rules. And they add rules a lot. Subtracting rules is very rare.

Then apart from that, you have the regulators — the CFPB, the OCC if you're a bank. It's a very politically charged topic because of the historical issues in this country with redlining and racial home ownership stuff. And then you have 50 states that all have regulators — that's how you get licensed at the state level for these independent mortgage banks.

So there's a huge patchwork of everybody adding rules. Almost no one ever subtracts rules. A ton of these rules date back to 2010-2015 after the Great Financial Crisis, when mortgages basically tanked the economy. People are very conservative in the space, and that leads to an insane gamut of rules. You get new rules every month from at least 10 different entities.

The mortgage lenders are always in this game of managing risk and managing compliance. From a "can you automate a mortgage" standpoint — the good thing about this underwriting decision being so rules-based and from the government: they have these government systems called automated underwriting systems that you have to integrate to. Integrating them is also really hard as a startup, but you have to integrate to them, and they really decision whether the loan is acceptable or not.

What you're really doing as a mortgage lender is massaging the loan: making sure all the docs check out, nothing's fraudulent, everything triangulates, the borrower is getting the right disclosures and information, and then fitting it into the box so you can run the automated underwriting system. The AUS is making the credit decision.

A lot of fair lending stuff — as long as all the AI is doing is moving data around, taking data off documents, and structuring stuff, and the AUS is making the decision — that removes a lot of the compliance risk. People still have concerns with "can the salesperson who has a license be replaced by an AI voice agent" — we're still very very early in that game because the regulatory guidance is quite unclear. Different lenders have different risk appetites on the back office — but the back office we find much less resistance because so much of it is just AUS-driven.

Getting the First Loan Originated

Kimberly: As you describe that, it almost seems like a miracle that you were able to originate one loan at all. The company was founded in 2020. When did you originate your first loan? Can you talk about the journey to getting the dominoes of this customer base — admittedly smaller, more constrained — to fall?

Mike: We originated our first loan on December 21st, 2022. I would not recommend launching your brand new software that does this very compliance-sensitive thing in a very complicated way during Christmas. That's not a good idea, but that's what we did.

We started as just Devon and I, trying to figure out what to do — building the database, modeling data. We raised a bunch of money.

Kimberly: You were founded November 2020, so almost exactly two years.

Mike: Almost exactly two years. Then we had to build a team and bring on all these engineers. A few things were really hard about getting started.

(1) The data model. So many of these vertical software plays — the only reason you should do a full-blown system of record replacement is you have to go rewrite the data architecture. Yes, we knew their data model was messed up. What the correct data model is, is still a very hard problem to get right. It helps a ton to have all the industry experience we did. It helps a ton to have integrated to a bunch of these existing systems to understand the rules and regulations. We still got a few things wrong — we fixed them, but each took like 3 months to fix. Once you're in production, changing the schema of a system of record meaningfully is pretty hard.

(2) Integrations. To originate a loan, you have to integrate to a ton of stuff. The most notoriously difficult from a BD and partnerships perspective were the automated underwriting systems. I knew lots of the senior execs at both Fannie and Freddie because in my time at Blend I had really spent a lot of time with them. So I thought it would be hard — I underestimated how hard it would be still.

I knew a guy at Fannie named Steve Pilaski. I called him and he was like, "Yeah, we want to help, but the problem is we have a policy — you have to have a big lender already signed up to do this in order for us to spend the resources to let you integrate to Desktop Underwriter." We were like, "Well, we don't have any customers yet. How are you supposed to get a customer if you can't use the AUS? It's not clear how this works."

After we had raised a bunch of money and partnered with you guys, we're like, "Can we pay you for the resources?" He was like, "That makes sense to me. I'll look into it, but this is kind of a new revenue stream for the US Treasury, so we have to do a bunch of paperwork to figure out what it would look like to open a program so you can wire us some money so we can do your integration." It was a solid two months — huge credit to him, he really pulled for us. They had to figure out how to account for this revenue stream that flows from us into Fannie Mae, and the GSEs' profits go straight to the Treasury.

(3) Document generation systems. There are 3,000+ counties in this country, all with different recording offices. The county record is hopefully digitized, sometimes paper. There's a note — a mortgage note that is a lien on that property — and you have to record it with the county. Every county has different formats for what's acceptable on the note, what font can they use, what the margins look like. Fortunately, there are incumbent systems that generate all this stuff — basically they maintain it. Every county changes the rules once in a while, and all they do is read the letters and update this stuff.

Integrating to those things is also really hard — their data models are hundreds of thousands of fields. I had a lot of weekends of my life where I would sit there with the state of New Hampshire's custom fields and look at the Vesta data model with its 30,000-row spreadsheet and go, "I think we have this field that's this. I think we have this field that's this." We weren't using LLMs back then.

Kimberly: You were the LLM.

Mike: Yeah. And then someone had to type that code by hand too. His name is Connor. He was our first engineer. He's amazing.

A lot of the integrations make it really hard. Getting the partners to spend time with you is a big problem. Docutech was the first document generation engine we integrated to. There was a lot of, "Hey guys, lots of people come and tell us they're going to build a new LOS. We spent a bunch of time supporting them and showing them our data model, and they pretty much never finish." We had to convince them, "No no no, we're going to finish."

And then finally you have to get your first customer. Our first customer — I'm eternally grateful to those guys, and I think they're kind of crazy — because if I ran a mortgage business and someone's like, "Hey, you're going to move all your origination to me. If our system doesn't work, you literally will not be able to make a loan, and no one else has done it before. But this is going to be great." They took a crazy bet on us. We had many sleepless nights figuring out how to make the software work for them.

Why Not Just Vibe-Code an LOS?

Kimberly: I can see why you're so bearish on the ability to vibe-code basically an LOS.

Mike: A lot of the stuff isn't written down anywhere. It's not like you can just go to Claude and be like, "Hey, go on the internet and figure out how to build an LOS." A lot of these details — it is tribal knowledge. Lots of these industries have embedded tribal knowledge where people talk about it, people understand "this is the convention of how things are done" — they're just not that well documented.

I know all these process-mining companies want to go videotape everyone who's ever originated a mortgage and record their screens. I think that's pretty lossy. We've spent a lot of time just sitting on Zooms watching people do stuff. It's still pretty hard to figure out what they do. And we're not Fable, but we're not dumb. There's a lot of context out there.

The big question is going to be: all right, when somebody is so good at vibe-coding that they can figure this out — are they going to go do the context extraction to build this, or are they just going to buy Vesta? I think most of them are going to choose to buy Vesta.

Post-AGI: Why Does Vesta Still Exist?

Kimberly: Some people say we have AGI now. Some people will say five years we'll have AGI. 10 years, whatever. At some point there will be more consensus about when AGI happens. When that happens, why does Vesta still exist?

Mike: Well, I think it's happened already, so that helps.

A few things. Especially in these verticals, there is this big transformation component. Yes, we build an amazing software product. Yes, we build AI agents. So much of our work is actually educating lenders and helping them implement these AI agents and understand what that means for their business. What do the processors do now? How do you talk about this with your regulators, or with the investors? So much of it is like this almost-consulting transformation motion that really matters to help people embrace AI.

Enterprise diffusion is going to take a long time. I'm a big believer we've had AGI for quite a while actually.

Kimberly: Why do you think that?

Mike: It depends on your definition of AGI, obviously. Someone made a joke: if in 2018 you asked, "Do we have AGI?" everyone would have said no. 2020 everyone would have said no. 2022 people said no. Starting in 2024-2025 if you asked, people were like, "Well, it depends — you have to define AGI. What does that really mean?"

That means we have AGI, and no one's ego wants to admit they're not as smart as the model anymore. Probably the best models are smarter than us. People are like, "Oh, is AGI — now there's recursive self-improvement and there's ASI." Everyone wants to invent some new term for the thing that we don't have yet, so that (a) they feel like there's something to work on, and (b) they feel like there's still use for people.

By the way, I don't think AI will mean there's no use for people. But the enterprise diffusion for all this AI is going to take a long time, and our job is to deliver that to our customers. 10 or 20 years from now, it's very hard to underwrite what the world's going to look like. To me, the question isn't "is Vesta around?" I think the question is "do we have money?" Do we have mortgages? Or does everyone just have a house that is generated for them by robots? I don't know. There are lots of very interesting future-looking questions that I just don't think it's correct to underwrite to. The world's going to come as it comes.

What Keeps Mike Motivated

Kimberly: We're now many years into this journey of building Vesta, as well as several years into this AGI journey. A lot of people nowadays are like, "Oh, should I even get a job? Should I just work at the labs? Are they the last companies that exist?" Maybe the only companies that aren't the labs that also exist are the coding companies. What keeps you motivated to work on mortgages? I made a joke in the very beginning — if 20-year-old Mike was like, "I'm going to spend my whole life on mortgages," you might have actually been like, "Yeah, I will." But it's definitely not the most typical path for somebody like you.

Mike: Everyone who knew us at Stanford would have been shocked if they knew that was going to happen.

A few thoughts. The mortgage industry is really important in this country. People can talk about the whole emotional home-ownership component, which is true. My Jane Street brain doesn't think as much about that part. I'm much more in the "I think structurally a lot of the success of America relative to other countries is quite middle-class driven" camp. Most politicians would say that. We're actually in a time when wealth inequality is a big problem, there's general unrest, people are worried about the degradation of the middle class.

One of the main things that has propped up the middle class for the last 50 years in this country is that we have 30-year mortgages. The downside is the mortgage industry in this country is super messed up and complicated. Taking all the friction out of that, making it just work, lowering the barrier around that being a successful product that we continue to offer and bet on — and taking the cost out of that — is a very worthwhile thing to do.

If we don't do it, I don't think anyone else is going to do it. Maybe I'm not smart enough to get a job at Anthropic — but yeah, you can go work at Anthropic. The problem is Anthropic already has hundreds of people who are really smart. I don't think if I went to Anthropic, it's going to make the difference between them winning and not. That would be an insanely arrogant thing to believe.

But I do think that Vesta is going to be the company that delivers AI to all of these mortgage lenders, and it's going to make this process work finally. There are a lot of people on the Vesta team who are really great, who could get jobs at these places. It does resonate with a certain group of people — you do want to put your dent in the universe, and you do want to do something where a competitor wouldn't do it if you didn't do it, where the team wouldn't be able to do it without you. That continues to be a really important motivator for me and for a lot of the team.

Team, Remote Culture, Series B

Kimberly: How big is the team today?

Mike: Almost 100 now. Like 95.

Kimberly: And where are they based?

Mike: We are remote. Everyone's in the US because our customers are pretty sensitive to that, but we are a distributed team.

Kimberly: You were founded in 2020, so on one hand it's COVID — therefore remote. Why have you maintained a remote culture?

Mike: Two things. One: we have a really high retention. A lot of people have been with us four or five years. Pretty much everyone who was with us in 2021 — maybe three or so people are not here anymore. We hired this team when we were fully remote, and we retained them. Them being with us a long time means (a) we really want to keep them, and (b) they already have a lot of the trust and context. It makes it easier to be remote when people have worked together for a long time.

The other: conditional on keeping those people, people are like, "Well, why don't you start moving to offices?" I'm a big believer in focus. One place where it's really important to focus: you have a People team who thinks about the culture and helps people collaborate. You want them thinking all day long about how do I make this remote thing work — not splitting their focus between running the office and figuring out how to include the remote people.

Kimberly: So you're 100 people now. You just raised a Series B. What do you want to use the proceeds for? Who are you trying to hire for?

Mike: A ton of it is scaling. We've gotten this thing to work. You spend so many years making the software work, making the product work, taking your first customers live, taking one of the three biggest lenders in the country live. They go on their earnings and they just rave about it. It turns out that if you cross that really hard chasm, it leads to a lot of demand. With a lot of demand does come a lot of work.

We're scaling really aggressively, especially in implementations, especially in engineering — making the product scale. There's an endless amount of stuff to build. Every mortgage lender uses 50 pieces of software, and we are their favorite one by a very large margin. So they ask us to build new stuff all the time. We try to stay focused, not go around building all our partner stuff. But there's an endless amount of stuff to build. And a lot of customers to implement — we're up 12x year over year on revenue. Our contracted is up like 3x. The pipeline is up probably 5x. Everything is really blowing up, so you have to raise the money to bring in the right people.

We're also at the stage where I'm really interested in finding early-career people who are going to grow a lot here. It's a very good time to join — similar to when I joined Blend. You've gotten the thing working. You've proven it. Now there's a bunch of scaling to do, which means a bunch of learning opportunities and growth. Really ambitious, smart people thrive in that environment. It's relatively derisked — when I joined Blend, I was pretty sure it was going to go somewhere, we had signed Wells Fargo. But it's still early enough that you get to have a lot of ownership and grow a lot.

That profile is something we didn't focus on as much a couple years ago, because we were so single-focused as a company: "We have to make this PennyMac project work. We have to make this AI thing work" — in that order. I was very involved in both those things. But now we actually have so many things going on that the opportunities for ownership are a lot more, and you need a lot of people to do that too.

Kimberly: So you'd be willing to hire college-intern Mike now.

Mike: I would definitely be willing to hire college-new-grad Mike. Intern Mike — if intern Mike did as good a job as I did getting into Vesta, they probably would get in here.

The Changing Role of Product

Kimberly: Maybe one last thing: I actually think the role of product has changed a lot. I've never really known exactly how you would define PM anyway, but it's definitely changed since 2020 or 2019 or whenever you were doing that. What do you actually think is the role of a really good product person today? And as a corollary — because you are still the main product person at Vesta — how does your job change as a result?

Mike: I just want to pause for a second — aren't your three best friends all product people?

Kimberly: Uh — no. Is that true?

Mike: I think so. I'm pretty sure.

Product fundamentally in my mind has almost always been about — this sounds really kind of bad — but I've always said product is just about being right. You do have to figure out a bunch of trade-offs and prioritization and what to build, but at the end of the day you've got to be right. You've got to be very correct and precise in exactly what you specify. You've got to be correct in how you think about the problem. You better be correct in what solution you come up with. You better be correct in where that fits in priority.

Then there's a bunch of other stuff layered on top: convincing people that you're right, stakeholder management, all sorts of stuff — which fortunately, when you're CEO, you have a pretty big advantage when you do those things.

Being right about what the priorities are and what the customer actually wants, and then very precisely conveying that context — is more important than ever, not less important. You probably don't need as many product people, because product people spend a lot of time doing stakeholder management and paper-pushing, which AI can do a lot of. But the fundamental craft — understanding the problem, designing the solution, prioritizing against everything else you need to do, then making it so that other people can do that by explaining it very precisely — that will might be one of the last things to go away. Because somehow you've got to tell the model what to do, right?

Closing

Kimberly: Got it. Okay, cool. Well, thank you so much for joining us, Mike. It was really great to have you here and really great to hear the journey of you from 2020 up until now.

Mike: Yeah, thanks for having me.

item.description:
## 一、数据架构才是AI代理的"隐秘天花板"——而非模型能力
全场最反直觉的观察藏在一个几乎没人谈论的技术细节里：Vesta不得不彻底替换系统核心的真正原因，不是UI丑、不是规则复杂，而是**那个80年代Windows应用的"平面文件数据库"是"单写入者"结构**——整个贷款文件任何时刻只能由一个进程写入。这意味着你永远不可能同时跑一个"收入代理"、一个"资产代理"、一个"购房合同代理"去并行审核同一笔贷款。
这是一个被业界严重低估的真相：**AI代理群的瓶颈往往不在模型层，而在被冻结了的历史工程决策层**。它就像现代集装箱船的尺寸被1914年巴拿马运河闸门的宽度规定了整整一个世纪——未来的技术形态，被过去某个工程师的权宜之计悄悄殖民。所以AGI到来的真实限速因素，可能不是GPU产能，也不是算法突破，而是全世界遗留系统的数据库schema什么时候愿意被重写。
## 二、长期利率是"全人类主观时间折扣率"的统计平均——微观心理与宏观金融的同构桥
Mike一句看似随口的话其实非常深刻：**长期利率本质上是地球上每一个人个人折扣率的加权平均**。他把宏观金融还原为集体心理学——10

item.title: [Odds on Open] Ex-Goldman MD: "Credit Markets Move in Step Functions"
item.dc:creator: Odds on Open
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、信贷市场的"阶跃函数"：被忽视的物理学直觉

Jeff 作为哥伦比亚物理系出身的人，用"step function"（阶跃函数）形容信贷市场的运行方式——这不是随口的比喻，而是一种相变思维。信贷市场平时像临界态的沙堆，看起来稳定，但压力积累到某个阈值时会瞬间崩塌、重新组织。这与自组织临界性（Self-Organized Criticality）惊人地吻合：地震、森林火灾、神经元雪崩、心脏骤停，背后都是同一种数学。

令人意外的观察：Jeff 的整个职业生涯其实是在"反物理直觉"中前行——物理学家接受训练去寻找平滑的微分方程，但他真正发家的洞见却是识别"不连续点"。2007 年 Valentine's Day 的 ABX 从 8bp 到 12bp 看似渐进，但他回看时意识到那只是雪崩前最后一粒沙。真正的信贷 PM 不是在预测价格，而是在识别系统已经进入"自组织临界态"的信号。他现在反复提到美国财政赤字、民粹主义时的焦虑，就是同一种直觉：系统已经临界，只是不知道哪粒沙是最后一粒。

二、"末期分布"：CMBS 的衰老生物学

Jeff 对商业地产贷款的描述里，藏着一个被所有人低估的洞见：一笔 10 年期 CMBS 贷款的 50%–75% 的生命里"相当无聊"，但最后 25% 决定一切。这不就是人类寿命的"压缩发病率"（compressed morbidity）吗？——Gompertz 曲线告诉我们，死亡率在生命末期指数级攀升。老年病学家 James Fries 发现，大多数人一生的医疗费用集中在最后两年；而 Jeff 的整个基金策略，本质上就是做"CMBS 的老年病医生"：别人想在壮年时赚利差，他专门在债券的"临终阶段"进场提供流动性。

跨领域连接：这个"末期集中"模式还出现在：企业并购（估值溢价集中在 earn-out 期）、政治任期（跛脚鸭现象）、恒星演化（主序星平稳 90 亿年，然后在最后几百万年里把所有有趣的事都干完）。他真正的 edge 不是信贷专业知识，而是选择了一个"末期回报极度非对称"的生态位——而大型 PE 基金的组织结构根本无法在印第安纳波利斯的 3000 万美元贷款上部署高带宽注意力。这是一个被大基金的"规模诅咒"系统性让出的生态位。

三、"不要搞砸"文化 vs. "100 个 no 里有 1 个 yes"：两套截然不同的效用函数

Jeff 对高盛经验最诚实的描述是："the mentality is don't screw up"（心态就是别搞砸）。然后他离开后发现，LP 融资的世界是"99 个 no 中找 1 个 yes"。这不是风格差异，而是两套根本不同的效用函数：高盛是左偏（避免负尾），创业是右偏（追求正尾）。

让你意外的观察：Jeff 没意识到他自己身上这两种 DNA 的冲突，正好塑造了他基金的奇怪定位——他想用"右偏创业者"的身份，运行一个"左偏高盛人"的产品。他反复强调"低方差 + 高均值"、"80–90% 把握才下注"、"仓位不超过 50–100 bp"——这些都是左偏思维。他的基金本质上是用创业者的勇气去兜售机构投资者需要的低方差回报。这个张力既是他的护城河（大机构没有创业勇气，小基金没有机构级风控），也是他的天花板（Brad Gerstner 那种"幂律思维"的回报，他结构上永远拿不到）。

四、被所有人忽略的 AI 盲点：带宽，不是智力

当所有人在讨论 AI 如何颠覆投资时，Jeff 讲了一句极度非共识的话："Put all relevant information in front of me, then upload into my brain"——LLM 对他而言是带宽放大器，不是决策者。他的论点隐含着一个被忽视的真相：AI 让分析变便宜，但没让"责任承担"变便宜。他基金的护城河正是基于"没人愿意把一个 3000 万美元印第安纳波利斯贷款的决策权，放进一个千亿美元 PE 的决策链里"——这是组织学问题，不是技术问题。

跨领域连接：这与医疗 AI 的困境高度相似。影像 AI 已经比放射科医生准，但谁敢让 AI 签字负责？Jeff 的生意本质上是在"决策不可外包"的裂缝中套利——AI 让分析平民化，反而让"愿意亲自看那栋楼"的人更稀缺、更值钱。

五、他没明说的最大赌注：政治是慢速阶跃函数

Jeff 在访谈末尾吐露的真正焦虑不是信贷技术，而是"没有稳定剂的政治系统"——左右两极都在走极端，没有温和派。他把这当成最大的隐性宏观风险，但没明说的是：这与他 2007 年亲历的 AAA 系统崩塌是完全同构的现象。当年的 CDO 系统也没有稳定剂——所有参与方都在同一方向下注，没有真正的空头提供负反馈。生态学里，没有顶级捕食者的系统会周期性崩溃；今天的美国政治，就是一个"去除了温和派捕食者"的生态系统。

他真正在做的事：买"末日保险"（rates optionality），但方式极其高盛式——"如果保险太贵，说明我漏了风险因子"。这是我在整段访谈里看到最具物理学家气质的句子：价格异常本身就是信息。他把 Fama 的有效市场假说倒过来用：不是"价格反映信息"，而是"价格的反常反映我的无知"。

Opening

Host: Jeff, thank you so much for coming on the pod.

Jeff: Thanks for having me.

Host: You were at Goldman in 2008. Walk me through the worst day.

2008 at Goldman: The Worst Days

Well, that was 18 years ago, so you know, I was thinking a little bit about this — and memories, you know, I have bits and pieces. Some of the most vivid memories I have is, you know, I had the benefit of being in the mortgage department throughout 2008. I moved into trading in 2005 when things were going really crazy.

I remember at one point — I mean, obviously with Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers — that was a crazy situation because that seemed to snowball from an area that we were involved in, in trading the product. So we had, you know, specific knowledge in terms of what was going on, and they had, you know, not great endings.

And then even at Goldman though, the stock was just totally crashing. And at the time I was a couple years out of college, so in hindsight my whole life was ahead of me, but at the time it was like, "Oh my god, I have this great job. I'm working in the mortgage department." And yeah, I mean I think we were a little bit concerned about what would happen to the company — not because we were having losses or otherwise, but I think every company and every investment bank was just too levered. And then there was uncertainty, and then that lack of trust spread.

The Berkshire Moment and Money Market Risk

So I remember one moment when we found out about the Berkshire investment — that helped. That was a preferred equity and a call option, or sorry, warrants, excuse me — as a bit of a stabilizing force. And then on top of that the Fed came in a little bit later, but it was still that moment of uncertainty in terms of "what's the outcome, could we be next" and otherwise.

Other moments, just in terms of the contagion: I still remember a senior person on the desk just walking around — there were so many issues with vehicles that had asset-liability mismatch. So all of a sudden money market funds were becoming a risk, and I still remember a senior person walking around and just saying: check all of the cash that you have in your PA and where it's sitting and otherwise.

And so those are things that you go from — out of college, "I'm working with neat products," to "wow, I'm in an interesting place and a lot's going on, I'm learning a lot, it's exciting." But I mean, obviously there's a lot of people losing money and making money, so the weight of that wasn't lost on me. But all of a sudden it's like, okay, it's here, and these things became very real.

Anyway, those were the memories I could think of in terms of worst moments, but overall it was a rewarding time. It was obviously a very challenging time for many people. I learned a ton. There were some very scary moments. But I guess that's a career in markets.

What Jeff Traded at Goldman

Host: Oh yeah. What sort of stuff were you trading at Goldman?

I had the benefit of being in a number of different roles. Initially out of college I was in a proprietary trading area that looked at CLOs and double-ATCs. So CLOs are securitizations of corporate levered loans. Double-ATCs are aircraft lease securitizations.

Then I moved into asset-backed finance where I was working on larger projects — we were setting up a monoline. I remember I went off and worked on something called a volumetric production payment, which was a securitization of natural gas cash flows, to credit card securitizations.

Mortgage Trading (2005)

But then in 2005 I moved into the mortgage trading business, and that was an interesting area because you had the housing boom. You had a lot of different products that were getting created, both in corporates — so credit derivatives, which were derivatives traded on credit, had been a hugely growing market in corporates — and with the growth in structured finance and mortgage-backed securities and otherwise. So that's securitizations backed by residential mortgages, commercial mortgages, student loan ABS, credit cards, and things like that. We had these new products and there are credit derivatives referencing those products.

So you had a market that was growing. There was more and more origination. There were more and more derivative products. And with my background — I mean, I was a physics major at Columbia. I may have been the only one that didn't get his PhD. For me, it was attractive because I could use the math side of my brain and maybe understand these funky products a little bit better than other people. I released it well enough to get a job and look at it.

The Valentine's Day Massacre and ABX

So I was there and I worked on structuring and trading synthetic structured products, CDOs. And then, as the market started to unravel, I was fortunate enough to be put in charge of a book that was trading tranches on ABX — which is a product called TABX. A lot of people still like to make fun of me because it launched on Valentine's Day of 2014 — sorry, not 2014, 2007 — which people call the Valentine's Day Massacre, because that was a period of tremendous... I'll come back to it a second.

So I was fortunate enough to trade that book for a while, and then I was trading asset-backeds — or sorry, ABS CDOs — as everything was unraveling. Then I moved over to CMBS trading, where I was for a number of years and co-ran that business before I left.

The AAA Illusion: How Insatiable Demand Fueled the Crisis

But in terms of the most interesting times, just stepping back: the period from 2005 to 2006 in hindsight was totally strange, in that you had all these products that were rated AAA, and there was insatiable demand coming from many different sources — some in Europe, some in the US and otherwise.

Because I still remember sayings like, "the loss rate on a structured finance AAA is almost..." — I mean, maybe it was one basis point or 10 basis points, but it was a very low historic number. And so, because of that, you had the products and said, "these products are great and these products have great ratings." And you had many different pools of capital.

The Super Senior Trade

And again, not to say that this is a holistic experience, but anecdotally, you had many different US and European banks that would take tens of billions of exposure to what was called "super senior" on ABS CDOs. Because not only was it a AAA, there was a AAA below it, right? That was there. So this had to be totally remote. And tens of billions of protection were sold on that for about one-tenth of 1% per year — so 10 basis points.

Why? Because that actually looked like a great return on historical losses. There's more to it than that, but that was the basic business model. And maybe that was quite smart. But as it continued to unfold and grow, the fact that that was there allowed so much origination — which put more and more money into the housing market. And there were a lot of bad incentives.

Again, I'm not trying to do everything, but ultimately you took something that was never ever supposed to take a loss, and that helped contribute to prices going up in housing markets and a lot of bad origination through the creation of credit. There wasn't as much alignment as you'd like.

When It Broke

But at the time, everything felt really good. It's like, "I don't know if this will ever move, because it feels like there's insatiable demand for this product. And what do I know? I'm, you know, three or four years out." I mean, I had some thoughts in terms of relative value and what looked rich or cheap, and we were market makers in the products we were doing — so we were trying to make money no matter what happened.

But it was a very stable environment with a lot getting done, and then all of a sudden it starts to break. And all of a sudden housing prices aren't going up and a lot of the mal-origination of the prior couple of years all of a sudden unravels.

So you go from those tranches — super senior off of ABS CDOs trading at 10 basis points — to, I remember in 2007, it's like, "Okay, this had been at eight basis points, now it's going out to 12 basis points." And remember, if you're talking about $50 billion on a book, an extra four bips is a lot of carry and a lot of mark-to-market. But then it's like, "Oh, but all the derivatives are trading off, so maybe this is like 35 basis points — and that's kind of like a crazy level, you're getting paid three times what it was." And then all of a sudden you go a little bit further and it's like, "Oh well, that's trading at five points up front" — so 5% upfront, 500 basis points.

And I think when you actually look back, the TABX product I was talking about as one example — not that this is a great product, but it was still a bellwether of the price discovery — I want to say that started trading when it launched in February of '07. Maybe it was five or 10 points up front, and then ultimately the recovery I think ended up being something between 10 and 30 on that tranche. And why? Because it was senior exposure, but it was senior exposure relative to a lot of very levered underlying bonds that wouldn't perform very well if there was something different than expected.

A Period of Regime Change

Anyway, that is a very long-winded answer, but I just go back to it: it was a period of tremendous shift from one regime and one sort of scenario of the world to something that's totally different. And so it was interesting along the way being in the middle, and "what is the price discovery? Who thinks what? What is right? What is wrong?"

By the way, as these things are moving in price, it's like, "are the products supposed to work if this all happens? Do the documents work? How do you price things at the losses or multiples of what would be expected? How do you compare a 2005 vintage from 2006 or 2007? What do the models look like?" And all that is against a backdrop where people are like, "I think this is rated now, it's been downgraded." How do we tear all this out and make markets along the way?

I look back, I learned a ton. It was a fascinating period. It was a challenging period. But again, back to my original comment: it was almost 20 years ago now.
