CMBS Trading at Goldman

Host: Talk to me about that later role you were doing in CMBS trading. What did that look like?

Sure. CMBS is commercial mortgage-backed securities, and it comes in more shapes and sizes today than it used to — well, maybe that's actually debatable. But the baseline product is called conduit CMBS, which is a securitization of maybe 30 to 90 underlying loans backed by commercial real estate. So that's multifamily, office, regional malls, strip centers, storage facilities — there are more and more types of properties that have come over time.

And when the loans are originated, they're 10-year loans. The properties are in different parts of the country. Like I said, some of them are malls — that's been a big headline over the last couple of decades. They get securitized, and so what that basically means is they all get pulled together and then the cash flows get split up, where at first they pay off also the "duper" or the super senior in the CMBS transaction. But that's actually backed by first mortgages, so those are generally very safe, all the way down to the bottom of the capital structure.

So they're sliced on a credit risk basis, where the last to get paid off is the most risky because you have exposure for all the different loans in terms of repayment. Although they also tend to not default immediately, so there's some protection that you have in the junior part of the capital stack, all the way up to the safest that I talked about.

Why CMBS Is Fascinating

I generally think — I mean, that also went through a little bit different than residential — but commercial mortgage origination also went through a tremendous cycle leading into the GFC, where there was a lot of pro forma underwriting and a lot of leverage that was ultimately provided. There I'd say the fundamentals of the properties were generally sound for the most part. The problem was there was just too much debt, and so it took a while to work through that, particularly as securitization and other markets froze up.

So that is the product. And what I still think — because that's actually one area that is our primary focus today — currently is really fascinating for a number of reasons.

The Cycles of Commercial Real Estate

One is: commercial real estate itself has all different types of cycles that happen organically. And so what do I mean by that? Well, sometimes you actually have demand shock in terms of tenants that want a lease. Ultimately most commercial spaces — whether it's you in your apartment, or TJ Maxx in a retail center — someone's paying rent, there's a market rent.

The Mall Cycle

What's interesting though is one cycle was: enclosed regional malls went from, when I was growing up, really great. I'd probably go every weekend and hang out with my friends and go shopping and whatever else. And I guess they're making a bit of a comeback now. But what was interesting is because you didn't have as much online from a retailer perspective, you really wanted to be in the mall. That was the best place to be. You're paying the highest rents. It's the most differentiated space and they could prosecute their business plan.

But with Amazon and online, that's one area that just went through a total cycle where all retailers really wanted to rationalize what is their footprint in any individual market — do they even want to have physical stores. That was something where rents dramatically shifted and many properties became obsolete that were great for a period of time just because you were overbuilt. So that's a cycle where there was a lot of noise for retail and the "retail apocalypse" or whatever people call it.

The Office Cycle Post-COVID

More recently, post-COVID you had office, and that's still something that's going through the cycle. It's amazing with COVID — people talk about New York and San Francisco as having totally come back in terms of office demand. Coming up here to 37th Street in New York, it feels just like it did in 2019 or earlier. There are a lot of other cities that haven't fully recovered. And you still have this mix where many tenants and office tenants — I think you're towards the end of this — but on average gave back 30 or 40% of their space. Now maybe that means some companies just closed down and went totally remote, some companies just said, "Okay, well, we can be remote sometimes, so we'll give back less space."

But overall, you're left in many markets today with 20 to 30% vacancies. And then you've also seen the critical mass shift around, where maybe what had been the CBD and the best place to work has all of a sudden moved to a second newer cooler area — maybe you could call it like a Hudson Yards in New York. But anyway, that's crazy for these assets that are super highly levered, to go for in aggregate 30% vacant. And they're super capital intensive, so you're going to have huge competition from buildings to hang on to tenants. There are only so many tenants and so much demand. So that's why you've seen such value destruction in office.

The Life Science Lab Cycle

So that's another cycle in terms of commercial real estate recently. But then you can go a step further and say, what happened to life science lab? That is an area that was the coolest, sexiest space — where you have like Alexandria Real Estate, which is a public REIT (its chart is an interesting thing to pull up), and there are a couple private entities that had most of the life science lab space in the country, and they did phenomenally well.

And then the classic problem is: post-COVID a ton got developed because more and more people said, "Oh this is great and it pencils really well, so let's build a lot of this." And like many things in commercial real estate that have long lead times to build and a lot of people doing development independently and maybe not keeping a good track of what's out there, you get over-supplied.

Geographies Matter Too

So maybe I'm getting a little bit too much in the weeds, but the asset class is interesting because you have that, you have geographies. Buffalo was a great market for a long period of time; it's really struggled over the last decade or two, or actually maybe even a little bit longer. People have left. Some West Coast cities I still look at — I mean, to me, the wealth tax in California is still just one of the crazy elements in terms of: do you have more markets and MSAs that are going to jeopardize business for populist and populist politics?

The End-of-Life Problem

But you put that all together and you say: you have 30 to 90 of these loans in all these different markets, of all these different property types, over 10 years. All this is going to happen over 10 years. The world changes, and so you get to the end of life and it's like, "Okay, this pool is totally different than 10 years ago when I underwrote it and everything was a brand new loan that looked clean."

And so it's a space where that's fascinating because 50 to 75% of this conduit bond's life it's pretty straightforward — it's the same tenants are in there, the cash flows are there or otherwise. You get to the end of the 10 years and it's all over the place. What's going to happen? Has value moved up or down? Does the owner care anymore? What is interest rates? And that's what creates this noise, and distress is fascinating because, unlike corporates, you're not looking at a capital stack with 20 billion outstanding where tons of people are going to cover it and know it and own its size. You might be dealing with a $30 million loan in Indianapolis on a retail center, and it's like, "what's the story there and how do you actually kind of get your arms around it?"

Goldman's Role

So back to Goldman: we were in the marketplace of having balance sheet, providing liquidity to our clients. We had a large origination business, which was valuable as well too. We had trade securities backed by governments, but a lot of this non-agency paper where we were taking this risk towards the middle and the end of securities' lives — that ultimately, there was a need for that, because they don't look squeaky clean, they don't have the same ratings, and you need balance sheet to take it.

Since then though, and post-GFC, it's gotten a lot trickier to basically run that risk in dealers. I'd say one consequence of the GFC is most dealers have very onerous capital treatment for most securitized product that was viewed as creating the crisis. So that's kind of moved outside of dealers and created opportunities for hedge funds and other forms of alternative capital to be the balance sheet that dealers used to be.

Leaving Goldman and Starting the Fund

Host: You leave Goldman, you start your fund. Could you explain to me and to our audience how you would describe what you do to someone who has no context and no understanding of credit trading?

Opportunistic Structured Finance

We take an opportunistic approach to structured finance investing. These markets have continued to grow and they provide a lot of credit and lending, both through but mostly outside the banking system. So originators can do what they do best and originate. And different investors like insurance companies or money managers can take exposure directly to different product types. One area there is a lot of the people I used to sit with at Goldman — billions of dollars — and they allocate at scale to those areas to provide the money that allows borrowers to borrow.

When I say our opportunistic approach, we tend to look for areas that, kind of in CMBS as I was alluding to, have some persistence in terms of opportunity set. We think that there's typically a need for end-of-life capital to come in with the expertise to understand the real estate, to understand the structured finance element, to understand everything else, to deploy capital and take the other side of the trade when people want to get out at the end of life.

Catalysts: COVID, 2023–24 Outflows, Residential Solar

Sometimes that's really exciting — like post-COVID there were a lot of bonds that were owned on repo and a lot of immediate distress, and so there was a ton of paper out there at attractive levels. We also saw in the backup of '23 and '24, there were a lot of outflows from money managers, so a lot of bonds were being sold and you can deploy a lot of capital there. But it's also persistent because even in the normal times you need eyeballs on products to get going.

In other spaces, we've been studying residential solar quite closely, and we think that that's another area that went through a boom-bust cycle where there were reasons to be excited. There was a lot of bad origination, there was a lot of bad originators — a few of whom have filed for bankruptcy. And you've also had policy noise where the "Big Beautiful Bill" pulled back and really changed a lot of the incentives to build residential solar. That's actually a fascinating space, both in terms of what are the existing products but what might a new product be. And then we have another area as well that focuses on a different geography that has another similar persistent opportunity to originate mortgages.

Picking the Right Poker Table

But coming back to your question: what we're trying to do on the opportunistic side is find spaces where us and our expertise, relative to the opportunity set, is going to be most attractive. Just going back to — on the podcast, a lot of people talk about what poker table are you sitting down at? Even though it might not be the... I mean, I guess a lot of stuff we look at is pretty complicated, but at the same time you can have complicated stuff, but if it's not at the right price, or if it gets competed away, or maybe we're not at the scale where we can actually be the dominant player — we want to shun those areas and go to: "why are we here? Do we understand why we're here? Do we think with our resources we are as knowledgeable as anyone else? Maybe better, maybe not, but at least we can compete."

And it's not that we have to be the absolute best. It just needs to be: are we understanding who we're buying bonds from, why, and can we explain why that jibes with fundamentals or otherwise.

So what do we do? It starts with what is the marketplace and what is the vertical that we want to spend our time and get up to speed and understand all those dynamics. What are the fundamentals? Maybe have some good sense of what we know, what we don't know. Use our judgment to figure out how that can impact cash flows and returns. But also experiment and say what sort of bonds are out there. What's slipping through the cracks? What is meaningful for us in terms of deployment? That's an area that we can focus in because it's underloved, or there's enough of an opportunity that we can look at it.

So it comes in all sorts of shapes and sizes. But it boils down to choosing the space, really rolling up our sleeves to understand, feeling comfortable that we're not getting adversely selected too — I mean, that's a part of the business but at an acceptable level that we can still deliver the returns.

How They Underwrite and Price a CMBS Bond

Host: Walk me through, in simple terms, let's say you identify a publicly listed credit product that you think you have expertise in that domain. How do you underwrite it, price it, figure out where it should be fairly valued, and then take a position in it? Can you walk me through that process?

Starting with the Real Estate

Sure. Maybe we'll use a CMBS example, just given I already babbled on about that for quite some time. So CMBS, we approach it as: you need to understand commercial real estate. Because a lot of the bonds we're looking at — they're securities, so you can trade them over the counter, but they come in varying degrees of liquidity. In some of the areas we traffic, there are probably 10 buyers or 15, there aren't a hundred overall.

Defensibility: Bandwidth

And what's also important about them, that we think is actually a defensibility in the space, is — especially with all the things in AI — there is real bandwidth associated with understanding any individual loan. So a lot of people come into the space and they're like, "I'm going to build an unbelievable credit model, I'll throw it in Astra, and it's going to come back and give me an answer." That's still very far... I mean, I use LLMs all the time, I'm obsessed with them. But I'd say it's more of: put all of the relevant information in front of me, and then that's going to upload into my brain, and I'll try to come up with some sort of sense of what's there. And by the way, maybe I need to go see the asset, maybe I need to do some extra work.

So it's loan-by-loan, and there are many different subtle things that we can look for that we're doing underwrite.

Fulcrum Loans vs. Safe Loans

The point being is that, given the liquidity profile, it starts with: how comfortable are we in the real estate? And with some loans you need to be insanely comfortable, because maybe it's a fulcrum loan where if it takes a 50% loss, maybe we don't get any of our money back. But if it gets paid back a hundred, we get all of our money back. And so we're looking at — well, as you can have other loans that maybe they're super low LTV, so maybe it's a hotel somewhere that I don't understand too well, but if it's a 99% chance that it's going to get refinanced, my margin of safety of "how well do I need to know this specific asset" is much lower.

So there's a sort of: what are the loans that matter that I really need to understand because they look close to the sun or they can swing things either way. And then an overlay of my general credit views on the space, and then my general credit views in the market. And sort of an interplay of what is my underwrite, what is my level of certainty on my underwrite. And by the way, they're always unknown unknowns — so we'll talk about sizing maybe later in the discussion, but that's a key feature. We're never going to know as much as the property owner. And maybe sometimes we know people in markets — not that they know the specific asset, but we know enough about a location or what's generally good and what's bad — and we do this underwrite.

Different Levels of the Capital Stack

For different levels of the cap stack, things matter differently. So if we're looking at a senior bond, there are times that we can sit there and say, "Hey, this is coming up to maturity and here's this building in a certain place, and maybe I feel so comfortable with the borrower's balance sheet and their tax basis and how they look at it, and I'm just like: there is no chance that this guy is not going to refinance this loan, even though he can actually probably ask for an extension and get more timing." So you can make a timing bet where we're looking at that and modeling out and saying: what is our level of conviction in terms of what this borrower is going to do at maturity? What is our downside if this does extend and we're wrong? How comfortable are we in this office building and the information we found out overall? And then what sorts of things can go wrong?

In that case, we love bonds like that — those are things that are quite, we think, quite cheap risk-reward relative to where a new loan with a similar risk profile would trade.

Low-Dollar-Price Bonds and Timing

In other parts of the stack, it might make a different decision. Going back to a timing story, we may have cases where you have bonds that are super low dollar price and they trade at five or 10 cents, and there it's a little bit of: maybe there's some chance that this thing gets some principal back and a good amount, and there could be leverage. What also matters is how much longer is it going to get its coupon.

I'm giving the bookends. There's also a lot of bonds at 70 and 50 where we can sit there and say, "Here's an office building that is in the right market in a certain NFL city that has been leased up recently, but is being valued at a horrific level that might be stale from two years ago, because that's lagging. And the reality is office buildings like that have improved a lot." And that could be the sort of thing where that is the exposure that I want, because I'm buying it at a fair price, I'm earning equity-like returns if the forward happens, and I feel really comfortable that this is sort of a stale valuation and we're coming out of a cycle.

The Liquidity Premium Discipline

So I'm just giving you a bit of a flavor. These things come in all shapes and sizes. And it's: how most importantly, are we comfortable with the cash flows and our underwrite? And then we could say, well, what sort of risk are we really taking?

Going back to my Goldman days when I was creating ABS CDOs — that product, after they broke, was quite simply: you had a bunch of different RMBS bonds that were packaged together, for all shapes and sizes, and then now you could buy the senior bonds at 30 cents. Now maybe the underlying assets were worth 35 or 37, and there's some assumptions you made, but it was always like: this is a less liquid product than all of the underlying cash flows. So by definition, if I'm selling the liquidity premium, I need to make sure that risk-adjusted returns are mapping to being cheaper.

So they're all different sorts of mappings, and we try to be super disciplined with that, because otherwise we should always go for the more liquid way to have that. But within that, we can do that, and then we can also create a very diversified portfolio so that there's some diversification benefit to the liquidity premium.

The 80/20 Rule

I would say that over time, based on the property type — because you have different tenants and some tenants are across the nation, and so you have a pretty good sense of what they're doing and tools to look at that. Sizing: 50–100 bps for Risky, 5% for Safest

So to your original point: what do our returns look like? Going back to how old I am, I've learned a lot of hard lessons, and I still think our approach — maybe it'll be right or wrong in hindsight — but our fund investors want stable returns and they want high returns, but I think overall for our business we want to build in a lot of diversification. So those unknown unknowns, where you can be as careful as possible — weird things still happen. Everything's based on public information.

Those positions where you can lose everything — I'd say we're generally not sizing more than 50 or 100 basis points now in a portfolio. I'd say what we view to be our safest positions, that have very low risk of principal loss, maybe some timing, maybe we take a little bit more credit risk — maybe we're talking about 5%. Now there's no way I'm nearly as scientific as most people on this podcast at looking at it, but those are sort of the heuristics where we're trying to optimize: what are the size of the opportunities relative to our capital? How do we build a pool where if we are targeting equity-like returns, we can get a few things wrong every... I mean, we hope we get more things right than wrong, but we can have a bad batting average on some of those risky positions in a year and it's not turning our performance from good to mediocre. Lower Variance Beats Higher Expected Returns

For an unlevered return, I think something that hopefully over time people find attractive. But yeah, I'd say, going back to the day, I'm sure many people in the Goldman floor — the position would walk around screaming "not big enough." Maybe not screaming, but thinking that. And I get that, and I've had exchanges with a buddy recently who's making the point about expected returns and Sharpe ratios and how things can be better.

You would almost always prefer the higher expected returns, but we're running a business. We're running a business for multiple investors. Maintaining their confidence in us is important. And as much as they know and like us, I think it's still easier to do with lower variance — high mean, but lower variance in return. So that's kind of how we think about the book. If there is a super compelling opportunity where things are totally mispriced, maybe we'll lean in, but the risk-reward needs to be there.

We spend a lot more time thinking about that than several years ago. I think we've improved there a lot, and it's obviously critical, especially as you're in a bit more illiquid securities.

Floating-Rate Hedges

And sorry, that's not to say that we don't have some five-year exposures, but we look at it a little bit differently in terms of what can we know at that point in time and what's the risk profile along the way. We have some derivative positions outside of just directly hedging rates that I think ironically do really well because they have floating-rate — or super levered to floating-rate — profiles. So when rates or short-term rates go up, they carry way better, but they reference fixed-rate collateral that might actually be around a lot longer in a higher-rate environment or slower-rate environment. So you can find some securities that are mispriced for some of those macro views too, that you put together in a portfolio and they look relatively nice. But that's maybe a little bit too into the weeds for here. You can find those things in structured finance.

How Political Risk Translates to Trading

Host: When you assess those different political risks associated with stuff including populism for different cities, how does that lead to a difference in the way you trade? Do you filter out those markets? Do you tread very carefully? Are there only particular sets of products you look at? How does it impact the book in actuality?

Real estate is very much about — I mean, the main governors are demographics for particular areas, and property taxes and taxes and business formation, whatever else goes into that. But as I alluded to before, there are other things that matter, like cycles, like are you overbuilding multifamily in the Sun Belt? So you can go through cycles. And interest rates matter.

Why Not Just Avoid the Risk?

I think — with the backdrop — we are opportunistic investors. So if I have the choice to not take that risk and find a similar return somewhere where I'm not taking that risk, then why would I take that risk?

And I think — that and the deficit — some of the best private equity investors or medium-to-long-term investors (I mean, Blackstone's obviously famous for "what are our secular tailwind beliefs," or I think they call it thematic investing). What are the mega-trends that they want to get right? That's really important. But I also think: what are the problems that you don't see getting better?

No Stabilizer in US Politics

It's kind of depressing, but with politics — and again, I'm not professional in sitting there — but obviously it's an overlay on trading views. The one objective truth in politics in the US: I've been trying to be a supporter of whatever moderate politics I could find anywhere for a long period of time. I like to think of myself as very down the middle, and what's practical and pragmatic.

And it seems to me as an objective truth that the right's going to the right — although maybe it's going a little bit less to the right than some things — but Trump's a populist. It's the party of Trump, and he came off of a week where he said he was going to give everyone $5,000. And then on the left, they're going far to the left. People talk about horseshoe theory. The depressing thing is I don't see what the stabilizer is. I don't see every moderate running for — maybe that's extreme — most moderates that you see running for any position have no chance. In the meantime, you're going to keep on racking up deficits.

Dalio and the Secular Headwind

There are a lot of people that sit here and say, "Hey, Ray Dalio doesn't know what he's talking about, just because he's studied all these things happening in the past. He's been growing for 30 years." And by the way, totally rational if you're trading liquid products to not account for that. Because I've heard people say, "Yeah, like how can you account for it? Just have stop losses on your positions." And so for liquid products, it's fine.

When you're trading something a little bit more in the medium term, that is like the reverse — like secular tailwind theme — where it's like, "okay, I don't see it getting better. I'm focused on it. What are the areas that it could impact the most? And am I protecting myself from that as much as possible? And maybe find a great way to hedge it at some point."

But that's not what we're doing. We're just trying to stay relatively short, stay in a space that we think has good risk-adjusted returns, and then have our views evolve. But not get caught surprised if this thing that we've been watching for a long time all of a sudden accelerates.

Final Question: The Biggest Mistake

Host: Final question. This is for other fixed income PMs out there, structured finance PMs, structured finance traders. What is the biggest mistake that one can make in trading these products? What makes an awful PM in the space?

Not Seeing the Step Functions

I'm — the older you get, the more battle wounds you have in terms of what can go wrong. And I know that cuts both ways because maybe that makes me and others at my age or older more risk-averse than they should be. So you want a bit of a hybrid.

But I think what I believe is fascinating overall is: we've been in a very benign general credit environment. And I know less about corporate credit, but I know defaults have historically been pretty low. Maybe we're looking at higher rates. We're looking at AI disruption, which maybe is nothing, and maybe is very consequential.

I maybe just go back to looking at the local situation and what is the current ecosystem and what's functioning and working — and not appreciating some of the step functions that can really change — and having an eye or a lens towards that.

Credit Blows Out, Then Comes Back to Tights

So to describe — I mean, I guess the worst one could be someone that just makes a lot of bad decisions, but I assume we're talking a little bit there. I'd say you can just have some people that, in terms of the current ecosystem is so narrow, that they can't imagine a different functioning. Because, you know, credit markets move in step functions. Some things can change dramatically.

I do think overall on the private sector balance sheets we're way more stable than we were when I started, because you have insurers and you have banks with low leverage, and insurers have termed out liabilities for the most part. So there's a lot of stability that goes in there.

But I don't know — could you have much higher rates? Could you have a totally different dollar or some of these themes that are starting to come through? Can that impact the zeitgeist and really create some fear in credit markets that maybe haven't existed?

Listen, maybe the systems are so good. But if you look at most charts of credit, they tend to blow out for a little while and there's no trust and everyone's like, "What the hell is going to happen?" And look at this — and then they come back down into the tights. And so we've been more or less at periods of tights for quite some time. It definitely got noisier during '22 and '23, where you move from insanely low rates to something higher.

But yeah — I think it's a bit of thinking through and really scenario-analyzing. Not just, "do I have diversification in my portfolio today?" but really thinking about some of what could happen, and do I want to be in this or not. Because things can go from liquid to illiquid — or in my case semi-liquid, semi-illiquid, to less so. So what do things look like, and how do you stress there? Most people run stress tests, but it's still difficult to think about until you've effectively seen it.

Closing

Host: I love it. Thank you so much for coming on the pod, Jeff. This was awesome.

Jeff: Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、信贷市场的"阶跃函数"：被忽视的物理学直觉
Jeff 作为哥伦比亚物理系出身的人，用"step function"（阶跃函数）形容信贷市场的运行方式——这不是随口的比喻，而是一种**相变思维**。信贷市场平时像临界态的沙堆，看起来稳定，但压力积累到某个阈值时会瞬间崩塌、重新组织。这与自组织临界性（Self-Organized Criticality）惊人地吻合：地震、森林火灾、神经元雪崩、心脏骤停，背后都是同一种数学。
**令人意外的观察**：Jeff 的整个职业生涯其实是在"反物理直觉"中前行——物理学家接受训练去寻找平滑的微分方程，但他真正发家的洞见却是识别"不连续点"。2007 年 Valentine's Day 的 ABX 从 8bp 到 12bp 看似渐进，但他回看时意识到那只是雪崩前最后一粒沙。**真正的信贷 PM 不是在预测价格，而是在识别系统已经进入"自组织临界态"的信号**。他现在反复提到美国财政赤字、民粹主义时的焦虑，就是同一种直觉：系统已经临界，只是不知道哪粒沙是最后一粒。
## 二、"末期分布"：CMBS 的衰老生物学
Jeff 对商业地产贷款

item.title: [Bits + Bips] Does Spousal Privilege Cover an AI That Knows You Better?
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"冷漠即隐私"——东西方的管辖权套利

这期节目最反直觉的一句话，是那位 OG 隐私专家说的：作为西方人，他反而更愿意把 prompt 交给中国的模型公司。表面上这是地缘政治笑话，但骨子里是一种深刻的制度套利——他要买的不是"加密"，而是对方的漠不关心。

这其实不是新东西。它是瑞士银行范式在 AI 时代的重生：历史上瑞士银行受欢迎，并非技术先进，而是因为它对客户的本国税务局"没兴趣"。同样的逻辑曾出现在德拉华州注册、加勒比海离岸信托、冷战时期的科学家互访。换言之：隐私的本质从来不是加密强度，而是"接收方的激励结构"。

有趣的结论是：AI 隐私的下一个护城河，可能不是密码学，而是外交孤立。谁最不想和你的国家合作，谁就最适合存你的秘密。这把"友岸外包"（friend-shoring）彻底倒过来了——我们正在走向"敌岸隐私"（enemy-shoring privacy）。

二、Flock 判决背后的"马赛克定理"——AI 其实已经触发了

Austin 提到的 Flock 摄像头案件（综合性监控≠偶然观察）听起来像一个技术小案子，但它其实是情报学里著名的 mosaic theory（马赛克理论） 在民事领域的首次正式落地：单独无害的数据碎片，当被聚合到某个阈值时，会相变为一种全新性质的侵害。

把这个框架套到 AI 上，一个让人脊背发凉的推论出现了——你和 LLM 的每一次对话单独看都平淡无奇，但你一年的 prompt 历史合起来，比你的配偶、律师、医生、心理治疗师加起来还更了解你。嘉宾半开玩笑问的"配偶豁免权是否该延伸到 AI"，在马赛克理论下其实不是玩笑：AI 甚至比配偶更有资格享有豁免，因为它掌握的 context 更深、更连续、更无防御。

跨领域连接：这个问题早在 1976 年由福柯在《规训与惩罚》里预言过——他说现代权力的本质是"可见性即陷阱"。他讲的是全景监狱里囚犯的身体，而我们正把自己的"思维过程"主动推进了全景监狱。而且这次不是国家强迫，是我们付费订阅进去的。

三、Honeypot 的奇点——为什么 AI 让"沉睡数据"全部复活为资产

Austin 那句"every pile of data sitting with internet access is now a honeypot"是整期最被低估的洞察。它暗示了一个相变：在前 AI 时代，陈旧数据的价值随时间衰减；在 AI 时代，它的价值随时间增值，因为未来的模型总能从中榨出更多关联。

这和核废料的处理困境结构完全同构——我们从未真正学会"处置"一种半衰期比我们文明还长的东西。核废料是物理的，数据废料是语义的，但两者共享一个诅咒：产生它比处置它便宜几个数量级。

而最反直觉的观察在最后：Rahm 说 Meta 擅长设计界面，而擅长设计界面的人正好也在为那些想方设法从用户身上榨取每一分钱的公司工作。这不是巧合——这是一种人才的因果囚徒困境：UX 领域最顶尖的人类学洞察力和心理学天赋，被结构性地吸附到最有动机背叛用户的雇主那里。所以说"便利"从来不是中性的，它是经过精心设计的、针对人类认知弱点的诱捕几何。

一个意外的推论：真正保护隐私的那一天，不会来自更好的加密技术，而是来自好 UX 设计师开始集体拒绝为监控资本主义工作——就像冷战期间核物理学家的良心运动。隐私最终是一个劳动力市场问题，不是技术问题。

📝 转录文本

开场与频道预告

If you've enjoyed Bits and Bips these last few years, be sure to subscribe to its dedicated channels. All Bits and Bips content has now moved to the Bits and Bips channel and no longer plays on Unchained. Search Bits plus sign BIPS wherever you listen and subscribe. We'll see you there.

一场正在到来的"算账"：模型公司如何使用你的 prompt

I also think soon we're going to be in for a reckoning going back to what these AGs are looking at — at how these model companies are using the prompts and using the data that they get from users.

And like, my favorite example of where this went horribly wrong was: I believe Anthropic had turned over data from somebody who was a fiction writer writing a novel with terrorist elements to the FBI, that led to somebody somewhere in the world getting a door knock on this exact topic. And it raised some interesting questions of privacy.

一个 OG 隐私专家的反直觉观点：我更信任中国模型

So, I've got a friend who's an OG privacy person, so I'm not going to dox him on here with the name. But he was talking to me over the weekend and saying:

"This will sound strange, but as somebody living in the West, in some ways, I feel more comfortable giving my prompts to the Chinese model companies."

And I'm like, "Why is that?"

And he's like, "Because they don't really particularly care about me in any way, and they're sure as hell not going to turn my stuff over to the authorities I care about where I live."

Right? Without naming the Western government, let's just say if they sent an MLAT treaty request to the PRC, the response would probably be like hilarious laughter for about five minutes.

And so he was making the point that the whole privacy framework is starting to like mutate because of the surface of where prompts are going and who cares. Because to give like an example that was raised, he's like: "If I'm talking about aggressively tax optimizing for my business, I might care if my local government gets a hold of that because they're going to be very upset about this. But do I care if the PRC sees that? This is so far below their level of relevance that…"

On-prem 的回归与 IP 盗窃的现实

This goes back to David's point on on-prem.

Yes, people will want on-prem solutions. That's why Nvidia has built a GPU box that you can purchase, deploy it on prem. So, we'll see more of that.

But if you're a technology company, you're not going to want to develop your valuable IP on China models because of IP theft. It's a very real thing. You go to China, they will find a way to work out your business model, IP, and replicate. This is a known thing.

Brave + Leo：被忽视的消费级隐私 AI 方案

The interesting part of this to me — you're both right about the on-prem part, but also there are going to be models of this coming forward that, as we have a data breach or two or disclosures like this, people are going to care about.

So one of the most interesting AI implementations to me that virtually nobody talks about right now — and guys, I love you, but it's because you market like engineers — is Brave, right? Where Leo in the browser has an AI implementation with many of the different models loaded in there, and they need to update a few of them, but there are a couple of the more modern ones in there like GLM. And they essentially take your prompt, run it through their models in a sandboxed AWS instance, immediately shred everything after returning the thing to you. So you've got it encrypted in your browser and nobody else has a hold of it.

每一个数据堆都成了蜜罐

I think even for consumers, because ironically of AI, those solutions are going to start getting more powerful. Because one of the things I think we're about to learn — and to bring it all the way back around that the Hugging Face incident has started to reveal — is that large piles of data that are just left sitting there with access to the internet are all honeypots now. Every single one of these has become a target.

And I would tell everybody: you should assume 100% of what you're putting into one of those will be compromised on some long enough time frame. Now, you may not care about that. If it's your credit card number and it gets compromised, great. Just cancel it, get another one. But there are probably a lot of private communications that you're not going to want being spilled out into the world.

Rahm, like you, business IP is a great example, right? That's one that clearly people have a privacy interest in and there's nothing malicious about it. But like, I don't want my internal deliberations of some great new technology suddenly showing up on the internet on Wednesday.

律师-当事人特权能否延伸到 LLM？

Well, yeah. I mean, you got to wonder: when do we see attorney-client privilege show up in LLM? Like, how do I get my lawyer in all the chats? Like that's going to be a nice unique value proposition to add out there, because people share their most intimate thoughts with AI.

Medical privacy is another kind of related one, right? Like — you know the most — yeah, it's a huge one.

Boy, all this stuff really — it makes it sound like it would be a great time for somebody to put some legislation together that we might actually be able to pass. But, boy, speaking of being in the land of fantasy…

— How about we live in the real world, David?

— Right. Like, you know, for example…

— Let's not go crazy.

配偶豁免权 vs AI、以及 Flock 判决的意义

Like in the common law, you can't deposition or force testimony from the spouse to divulge information. Does that extend to AI — arguably — who has a deeper context than your spouse?

I would also suggest there was a recent ruling in a federal district court about Flock where they basically said: no, this is a search. Right? Like the whole "hey, observing people in public is not a search" thing was predicated around those being individual and discrete observations. Like the police saw you walk into the doughnut shop — that's fine. But Flock cameras creating a comprehensive visual record of all public spaces at all times is the equivalent of following that person around. That is a very different sort of search than "oh, we were incidentally there and saw them."

Rahm, to your point, I feel like AI is posing a similar problem for the way the world is currently structured, which is: nobody really thought about what if there's a device with all these connectors that has all of your context about all things. Like, that is obviously much closer to somebody's papers and personal effects in like Fourth or Fifth Amendment terms in the United States.

自由与安全的权衡 + 本地化的重要性

Yeah. Well, it's a classic trade-off between security and liberty. And people historically have traded away liberty for convenience and security.

And you know, one of the remedies is: you make that as local as possible. You make that as — you attach it to the individual. And if you can't do that, you attach it to the municipality where there's more accountability on local elected leaders who are accessible, as opposed to say the federal government. So that's probably the right approach and balance to strike.

欧洲议会否决 Chat Control 2.0 + 悲观的商业模式分析

I would jump in there and just say a couple of things.

One is that on this subject, I hadn't heard about the Flock ruling, Austin, but that sounds very kind of positive to me from a civil liberties perspective. There had to be some reason this was not just normal.

At the same time, we also saw — I think it was maybe either yesterday or early today — the European Parliament has rejected what people have called Chat Control 2.0, which was legislation at that level to get enforcement of back doors for encryption on electronic applications.

But on a sort of more systematically pessimistic analysis of this question: the other thing to keep in mind is that none of these entities are going to willingly give up their ability to gather and surveil all of your data because that is a possible business model.

And so from that perspective, I think we do need to look for outside pressure. I mean, I won't — I'm a fan of federal power, but on a situational basis…

— You're a fan of federal power. Really?

— I mean, I'm going to — I think there sometimes needs to be some decisions made, and in this one…

— That's true.

We're also seeing stuff around gambling where maybe I could see some federal — anyway, for debate.

But the point being: I don't think these entities — I think there is some commercial pressure for entities like Brave to offer a more private option, and there will be an audience for those no doubt. But at a macro level, you talked about convenience, Rahm — I think that the business models feeding into the convenience factor…

I mean, one of the reasons Meta's Muse is such a big deal is because Meta is really good at designing interfaces. And those people who are really good at designing interfaces also work at companies that want to find every possible way to get money out of their users. So that dynamic, I think, demands some real scrutiny and perhaps enforcement.

节目尾声与赞助内容

If you like this segment, please like, subscribe, and tune in every Monday at 4:30 p.m. Eastern time. I'm Austin Campbell, the host of Bits and Bips, along with my friends Rahm Ahluwalia and Chris Perkins and our slate of exceptional guests. Every week we're going to discuss macro, crypto, and the collision of worlds — covering topics that move markets and shape the financial landscape.

One more thing: we've got a listener survey open. It takes just a few minutes. It's anonymous and it changes what we make next. Use the QR code on screen or go to unchainedcrypto.com/survey. The link is in the show notes.

赞助：1inch Aqua

$540 million — that's how much concentrated liquidity sat idle in a given week in the first half of this year. About 30% of the DeFi TVL, if you're wondering. That's according to Dune Research commissioned by 1inch.

But there's a solution: 1inch Aqua is the new shared liquidity platform. It lets LPs back multiple positions with the same token balance and keep their tokens in their wallet till a swap comes.

Why does that help? Because the LPs don't have to split their tokens across positions. They can cover more market conditions and pairs with their full balance. That means more activity across deeper liquidity.

See how it works at 1inch.com/aqua.

item.title: [Sequoia Capital] Luca Ferrari: The Operating System Behind Bending Spoons
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反常识的发现：Bending Spoons 的"操作系统"其实是一场"反向私募"

Luca 把公司定义为"永远持有、深度改造、合并进同一平台"——这乍听像 Berkshire 的变体，但真正的颠覆之处在于他主动放弃了一切"退出话术"。私募基金的全部治理技术，本质上是围绕"3-7 年卖出"这一节奏构建的：短期化的 KPI、财报美化、团队留存奖金、SPV 结构……当你从根上拿掉"卖出"这个选项，几乎所有传统 PE 的工具都失效了，但同时也消除了短期套利的激励扭曲。

这里有一个几乎没人谈到的隐藏结构："永不卖出"+"彻底改造"合在一起，让他可以做一件 Berkshire 做不到、PE 更做不到的事——把一家被收购公司的代码库、组织架构、云架构全部重写，因为他有 20 年时间去摊销这笔重投资。Berkshire 不改造（信托）、PE 不敢深改（周期），只有"永远持有+深改造"的组合才能解锁"把一群独立公司压缩成同一平台上的 app"这种操作。这不是运营效率的加法，而是时间尺度的套利。

二、跨领域连接：他的招聘团队运行的是一个"因子投资模型"，但更有意思的是信号背后的隐藏哲学

Luca 自己用了量化交易的比喻——评估数百个信号、测试与未来表现的相关性、迭代组合权重。但请注意他分享的那个"意外信号"：17 岁高度参政活跃、25 岁后退出政治的人表现最好；25 岁后仍在参政的人表现反而差。

这其实揭示了一个超越招聘的更深层模式——他在筛选"曾经燃烧过、但愿意切换燃烧对象的能量系统"。这跟宗教学里的"改宗者比原生信徒更虔诚"是同一个心理机制；也跟 Peter Thiel 偏爱"从数学奥赛转码农"的人、Jim Simons 偏爱转行物理学家的逻辑同构。他在找的不是"天赋"，而是可迁移的狂热（transferrable obsession）——一种曾被证明能对抗现状、但尚未被某个特定使命锁死的能量。

这解释了为什么他承认"Harvard/Stanford 预测力很弱"：名校筛选出的是顺从型高执行，而他要的是不顺从型但可引导的高能量，这两个群体的交集小得惊人。

三、最震撼的个人线索：他全部运营哲学的源头，是一次感情背叛后的羞愧

节目最后那段，他主动坦白：20 岁出头出轨了女友，被自己的羞愧击中，于是立下"永不说谎、永不省略重要信息"的终身誓言。然后他把这条个人誓言，一步步结构化为整个公司的操作系统：radical candor（即时当众反馈）、面试全程录音分离评估、burden of proof on complexity、不要高管团队……这些都是"反省略"的制度化表达。

这里有一个几乎没人意识到的递归：Bending Spoons 的运营优势，本质上是一个人把自己对自己说谎这件事的恐惧，外化为一整套防止组织对自己说谎的机制。所以当被收购公司的创始人反馈"Luca 诚信度极高"时，那不是性格的赞美，而是系统设计的必然输出——他建造的整个平台都是为了让谎言在其中无法生存，因为他自己无法再承担一次谎言。

这对任何想复制该模式的人都是一个残酷提示：你可以抄走他的组织架构、招聘漏斗、矩阵式管理，但如果你没有那种被自己背叛过一次、因而对"自我欺骗"产生过深层恐惧的内核，整个系统会在第一个利益冲突时松动。他的护城河不是流程——是一个 20 岁青年的羞愧。

四、一个让人头皮发麻的小矛盾

Luca 在同一段对话里说了两件互相拉扯的事： - "我把大部分时间都在找最顶尖的人；人才密度是一切。" - "好生意的定义是：即使管理层平庸也能跑得好。"

多数人会把这当成对不同层面的描述，但如果把两句叠加读，真正的意思是——他把 A+ 人才投放到了"不需要 A+ 人才就能跑的生意里"。这就是复利密码：别人用天才去救平庸生意（高风险、低回报），他用天才去放大本已坚固的生意（低风险、超额回报）。这是 Buffett 的"宁要七尺栏杆走过去"的工程化版本，只是 Buffett 不改造，他改造。
