The Model: an "operating system" for digital businesses

Host: I think by this point most of the listeners have heard of Bending Spoons, but I doubt they understand the model and what the magic is. If you wouldn't mind — two, three minutes on how it works and what's special about it.

Luca: Yeah, sure. The entire thesis on which the company is built is that if we can build a machine — a system — whereby we can operate digital technology businesses better than almost anybody else, then we are pretty much guaranteed to compound capital efficiently for a very long time through acquisitions.

The reason is: if a lot of businesses are better off once they're integrated into the system — what we call our platform — than being operated as standalone companies by someone else, then we should be able to offer prices to people that are appealing, and so they will sell their businesses to us, and we still deliver a high return for shareholders. That's the thinking behind it.

Of course, the difficult part is to build that system, that platform, so we can operate these businesses better than almost anybody else — and that's what we have poured our hearts and minds into for the past, well, 13 years technically. We have tried to have an amazing team of people, strong culture, powerful proprietary technologies, lots of proprietary data.

What we do: we buy these businesses, we integrate them very deeply into this platform. So we have a shared R&D, marketing, G&A team that can fluidly move across all of our businesses. We basically replatform the acquired businesses so that they're based on the same technological foundation. Some investor at some point called it an operating system. I think it's a pretty apt comparison or metaphor.

And then we transform them pretty deeply. So we can rebuild the org, rewrite big chunks of the codebase, re-architect cloud infrastructure, launch useful new features, fix bugs, improve performance, rethink monetization and marketing.

So there is a serial-acquirer component that you'll find in private equity, you'll find in companies like Berkshire Hathaway or TransDigm. The big difference — certainly vis-à-vis private equity — is that we are not a fund. We buy off our balance sheet, we've never sold a material business, we don't intend to sell one in the future. So we buy to hold and operate forever.

The other very big difference — vis-à-vis private equity but also the Berkshires of the world — is that we transform these businesses pretty deeply and we integrate them all together. They go from being a company to being a product installed on the same foundation, basically.

That's the model. I've been doing it for 13 years at this point.

Host: Yeah, it's going remarkably well. You went public — what's roughly the market cap?

Luca: At the time of IPO a few months ago, $18 billion I think, equity value.

Host: Congratulations. I'm a huge fan of the model — it's really unique. I was comparing it in my head to Berkshire Hathaway, but it reminds me of when I was in my 20s. I worked for a US tech company called PTC, and they moved me to Japan to set up Japanese operations. My office was inside Mitsubishi headquarters, and I dealt with Mitsubishi HQ people, across all the different divisions. It feels more like Mitsubishi or Samsung than it does like some big PE firm or Berkshire. Is that how you'd describe it?

Luca: I don't know those companies that well, so I can't say for sure. But again, the distinctive features are: we buy to hold and operate forever — so I think that kind of strikes out PE firms. And then, this very deep integration. Most companies that acquire other companies serially, in my experience, try to run them somewhat separately for the most part. We take the completely opposite approach, where we make sure they have the same technological foundation, broadly speaking the same core team that moves fluidly across to go after R&D opportunities and withdraws when those are exhausted. And a lot of serial acquirers keep these companies broadly speaking the same way they were before — we change them completely from the ground up. It's very time-consuming and challenging, but the bright side is we generally deliver very high returns.

I don't really know of any company that does it this way.

Host: It's kind of an n of one. Is the magic, Luca, in the picking or in the operating — and what percentage would you give it?

Luca: It's almost completely in the operating. Without the platform I described, we couldn't do what we do. I'd like to think we've gotten pretty good at selecting the right businesses, but it's relatively easy to deliver high returns if you have access to our platform.

For example, we have been enjoying an exceptional inflow of talent. We got 800,000 applications last year. We had hired fewer than 300 people. When you have amazing engineers, designers, product managers, general managers, it's much easier to take a business and rethink it from the ground up and run it much more successfully.

Anyone who's run a digital business for a sufficiently long period will tell you that headcount matters not a lot — it's just how good the people are and the culture you've established. When you have access to this caliber of people, you can run a business with 20 people that someone else would need 200 people for. That alone will give you both cost efficiencies and opportunity to innovate faster, improve monetization faster.

We have also invested a lot over the past decade in building powerful proprietary technologies to do pretty much everything across the board that you need to run a digital business. They're natively integrated with one another, and that makes everything so much more effective and faster. If I were to run one of these businesses on a standalone basis, I wouldn't have the resources to build these technologies — I wouldn't even know where to start. So that's also kind of a cheat code.

Definitely the operational part is far more important than the picking. But we try to pick well — why do it poorly if you can do it well?

Hiring: industrializing talent density

Host: Luca, let's click on the hiring. I spend most of my time with CEOs these days, and everyone talks about high talent density, being a talent magnet. A lot of them pull it off early, but as it scales it inevitably waters down. You seem to have almost industrialized this talent-density idea. You have unique ways of pulling in applications, pulling in interest, and qualifying the top of the funnel. Let's talk about that — and roll the clock back to when nobody had ever heard of you. You had no employer brand, no inbound interest. How did you get the talent flywheel rolling?

Luca: We basically believe that if you have a strategy that works, then almost all that matters is the talent you deploy toward the execution of that strategy and the culture — meaning the rules of the game, how people interact, what they choose to do and how. Those are the areas we've obsessed over pretty much since the beginning.

You start with nothing. That's what founders or early team members need to do well — basically punching above their weight. I remember early on spending at least 50% of my time, probably more for the first two or three years, on recruiting among other talent-related things. A couple of us managed to find lists of the best graduates from some of the best Italian universities — at the time we hired pretty much only in Italy, now we're international — and we kind of tracked them down. I remember calling hundreds of them, poorly harassing a few until they accepted to join us.

The quant-trader approach

Later, we built a pretty substantial talent team. These days we have scientists, researchers, and we treat the selection of talent within our pipeline similarly to how a quantitative trader would pick stocks. We look for all signals, then test signals against future performance to determine whether they're predictive, or what combinations of signals are predictive — and keep iterating. It's a very rigorous and sophisticated system. At this point we assess hundreds of signals in each application.

That helps you select potentially dramatically better given the same level of employer brand. And half the game is also attracting very good applications — because if only geniuses apply, it's easier to build a good team.

Why top talent self-selects into Bending Spoons

We have kind of an unfair advantage with our model. A lot of engineers, designers, product managers absolutely love the idea of working at a company where they can spend nine months helping rebuild Vimeo's video infrastructure, then six months rethinking advertising on AOL, then maybe a year building a platform technology — all with the same employer, the same colleagues, the same culture. The track record they're building does not get diluted when they change roles. When you change employer, a lot of that is lost — you have to re-establish credibility. So that's a very powerful point of attraction.

Because we've been systematic and uncompromising on extremely high levels of talent density pretty much from the beginning, once that's in place, it's a powerful means of retaining excellent performers and attracting more. When people love their colleagues, they never leave. We had 0.6% regrettable churn of "spooners" — the members of our core team — last year. And trust me, they get poaching attempts from big tech all the time. It's not for a lack of opportunities.

Equally, these people will tell their former fellow students, "Oh, it's amazing here, you should apply." It makes your life easier.

It's very difficult to get to a very high level of talent density late in a company's history. You need to establish it from the beginning and be completely obsessed with it, never giving up — even when it means hiring way fewer people than you'd like to for prolonged periods, and parting ways with people who are being helpful just because you think you have better people. It's quite painful: nobody's a sociopath here, you don't like to tell someone who's a perfectly good contributor that they should look for another job. And you're losing good capacity in the short term to look for amazing capacity down the line. Those are difficult things to do — but if you do them consistently, you develop a very powerful flywheel.

Signals: what the data science team actually looks for

Host: Sounds like you have a data-science-type team looking at all the inbound and hunting for signals. What are the signals most strongly correlated with success? And once you get beyond that, I assume there's a human interview. What are the questions that tease out what you're looking for that maybe aren't obvious?

Luca: We're fairly secretive about the details — I guess you'd get a similar answer from a quantitative trader. But I can share some.

Some obvious signals: GPA — not super strong but helpful. The university graduated from. I think people would be surprised by how poorly graduating from Harvard or Stanford predicts performance. All else being equal, someone from Harvard will do a little bit better than someone from a less well-known university — but not dramatically so. Often, people lose that potential raw-talent edge by being a bit more entitled and thinking too highly of themselves.

The teenage-activist signal

One I can share, that's relatively predictive — I was surprised when this came up: if someone is politically active as a teenager but ceases to be in their early 20s, that correlates highly with drive and an entrepreneurial mindset — qualities we highly value.

The way we've explained it: if you're 17 and school is not enough — you feel like you need to do more — that shows agency, productivity, not settling for the status quo. That's generally healthy. But if you still do that when you're 25, 26, 30, it means it's probably a life mission — perfectly fine, but likely incompatible with your job being top priority. Your job probably takes a backseat to your political aspirations.

Host: How do you find that signal? Do you ask them in an interview? Look through their old Instagram?

Luca: Thankfully, people think they need to include leadership experiences in their CVs because that gets them a job at a consulting company or something. So most people would include something significant in that area if they did it. In any case, we ask later in the process — whether an interview or written assessment — questions that would clearly lend themselves to people sharing this sort of thing.

Be proactive, not passive, about signals

You shouldn't be passive in accepting whatever signals are present in someone's application — you can be very proactive. A lot of the best signals in our case come from the practical tests we ask candidates to go through. You can elicit signals that way.

Interviews are the weakest predictor — unless you structure them

Interviews, of all the typical elements in a selection process, are the worst predictors. But you can make them decent if you give interviewers extremely precise questions they need to ask in exactly the same way, make sure the answers are recorded, and have them assessed separately. What's completely useless is having someone talk to someone else with no guidelines or just a high-level agenda, and then tell you, "I like the guy, I didn't like the guy." That's noise. If you structure it a lot and separate the conducting of the interview from the evaluation of the responses, it can be somewhat predictive.

Interlude: HubSpot's sales-hiring playbook

Host: Can I tell you about something HubSpot unlocked on the sales side? We scaled our inside sales from 10 to a thousand. It was harder to get into HubSpot than Harvard — we had lots of inbound. We'd look at resumes and look for people who went to a state school: University of Vermont, University of Wisconsin. Not Harvard, not MIT. We looked for people who had done a sport, who were athletic and competitive.

We didn't interview them in a standard way. We gave them half an hour with a person who'd set up a role play: I'd be the HubSpot employee, you'd be the potential — then I'd have you sell to me for 12 minutes. I'd give you objections. Then I'd give you feedback on how you did. Give you a minute to think about it. Then we'd do the exact same thing again. If the person absorbed the feedback and did a half-decent job the second time, we'd do a couple blind references — boom, we hired them.

That actually ended up scaling for us. We didn't do normal interviews on the sales side.

References — not blind, but structured

Host: The other thing I wanted to ask you about — blind references. Where is that in your signal?

Luca: We do that as the very last step. Well — no, we don't do blind references, we do references. We don't do blind references because they're illegal in Italy. So we figured, let's have a method that works across jurisdictions.

The candidate presents a few names. We try to guide it: give me people who had plenty of exposure. We try to get at least one person for the couple of biggest experiences someone had — ideally their manager, if possible — but ultimately it's their call.

We structure these interviews with references quite a lot. They can be predictive, but again, you need to be scientific. If you leave it to someone picking up the phone, almost always it's positive — very rarely do people give you names of people who will criticize them. So you need to be specific and ask for hard grading decisions.

For example: "Of the 20 people you've worked with the most, would you say this person is top 5?" Then a few follow-up questions to make sure there's substance. People who are enthusiastic will often say, "Well, it's above average." And you're like, hold on — it sounded like this person was a genius, and you're telling me they're ranked 8 out of 20? Which is nice, but… You can make it predictive, but you need to put in the effort and structure.

Host: I love that advice. I get a lot of blind references when people do that to me. "Is that the best person you've ever worked with?" — "Well, no." — "Why?" That opens things up.

Management styles: there is no common thread

Host: You're the 20th CEO I've interviewed. My thesis when I started this podcast was: I'm going to figure out the common thread, write it down, standardize it. The truth is there's no common thread. Everyone does it differently, and the playbooks are changing extra fast.

My last two interviews are emblematic: I interviewed TK from Kalshi — he and his co-founder have 200 employees, no levels of management, everyone reports to those two. He called it "management by chaos." Then I interviewed Ali from Databricks: eight direct reports, very structured, three meetings a week with his direct reports, QBR once a quarter, offsite strategy session once a quarter. Polar opposites, both doing extremely well. Where do you fit on that spectrum?

Luca: Probably somewhere in between. I think these more formal approaches to management are greatly overestimated in their impact on outcomes.

I always ask myself: a business is a good business if it would do well even if management was mediocre — maybe not awful, but mediocre. That's the first thing. The second thing that matters is talent levels and culture — culture meaning: how do you make decisions, what matters, what doesn't, what do we value, what do we not value.

Then everything else — reporting lines, OKRs vs. keeping it fluid and informal, span of control — does matter on the margin. Different solutions would be optimal depending on the people involved. But within reason, I'd say maybe plus-or-minus 10% impact. You're much better off obsessing over, first and foremost, strategy — then once that's in place, the quality of the people and the culture.

If a 200-person organization is chaotic but super high talent density, with a culture of business orientation, rationality, hard work — even if a little extra structure could theoretically help, talent and culture will mostly close the gap. Vice versa: a little more fluidity, if you have good people and a great culture, people won't get stuck because there's a little extra structure.

I'm convinced these things are not the most important in excelling in business.

Self-reflection: leader vs. manager

Host: When I was CEO, I tried to evolve as the business scaled. I got a lot of feedback. One piece I got a couple of times was: "Brian, you're a very good leader and a very bad manager." Where are you on that?

Luca: I don't know. I'm not sure if I'm a good leader or a good manager. I'm pretty privileged to work with very good people. I tend to be more self-conscious and question whether I'm doing enough and living up to expectations. So I tend to see the glass half-empty. My instinctual reaction would be: I'm probably not terrible at either. I'd rate myself okay at both, but not necessarily amazing.

Probably a better leader than manager. I've generally done okay at setting a vision that made sense and communicating it reasonably well. If I've succeeded as a leader, it's been mostly through what I'd call servant leadership — just working super hard and helping people as much as I could. I don't think I'm the William Wallace kind of leader making a grand speech. But when you work with someone who walks the talk and is in the trenches, you tend to be inspired. I try to be that kind of person. I don't think I'm the best at running one-on-ones.

Head in the clouds, feet on the ground

Host: I used to say to myself — I got this quote from Eleanor Roosevelt — "I wanted to keep my head in the clouds but my feet on the ground." I wanted to be a JV William Wallace, painting a picture of the future, but also in the ground: holy crap, we have a lot of problems. My glass was half empty, and I spent a lot of time negative, looking at problems. Where are you on the Eleanor Roosevelt quote?

Luca: I want to give myself a little pat on the shoulder. If there's one thing I tend to do reasonably well, it's seeing the big picture — "head in the clouds." I'm not the best at articulating it with a grand speech, but in substance I'm pretty good at understanding what matters, what doesn't, where the opportunity is, what logically we should be doing, and what's just noise.

I've historically been very hands-on in the details, in the trenches. It's a good quality for an entrepreneur and CEO — not super widespread in the population, but commonly found in entrepreneurs. It's quite powerful: if you don't have the big picture, you can't set a winning directional strategy — unless someone brings it to you, which is dicey. Hope is not a strategy. But if you're not in the details, feet firmly planted on the ground, you can't inform the big picture properly, you're unlikely to be inspiring to colleagues, and you can't assess or coach others because you don't really know anything about the work.

I find it's easier to sequence those activities than to run them in parallel. I try to have times where I'm very much in the clouds — "What are the big problems, the big opportunities? How should we go about them?" — being more of an architect. Then long stretches where I'm in execution mode, mud head to toe, just getting stuff done — blood, sweat, and tears. It's quite difficult to be both at the same time, but you can be both in sequence.

Coaching, experience vs. talent

Host: Let's talk about coaching. Similar to me — I'd never been CEO of a company with thousands of employees in public. Sometimes I didn't feel qualified to coach some of my executives. Do you ever have that feeling? And related: so many CEOs have a very talented person internally on their way up. Should they bet on that person, or find someone who's seen the movie before? That's happening everywhere across Silicon Valley.

Luca: On coaching — I'm certainly inadequate as a coach for people I work with. At Bending Spoons we work on the assumption that managers should always be capable of solving or advising on problems experienced by their direct reports. We think any one person may be able to coach any other person on some things, and they should do so regardless of reporting lines. A good manager would generally be very smart, a good problem solver, so at least they can provide generalist support. They should be emotionally supportive and ready to get their hands dirty. But being someone's manager doesn't mean you're always better positioned to solve a problem for them.

We don't value experience as much as most people

We do value experience, but a lot less than most. Being there, done that helps — but there are big "buts."

First: The world changes pretty fast. I'm not certain that someone who did something seven years ago still has advice that applies well. There's a huge risk that people will be blind to the new context because they did it that way before, and will paste whatever solution they applied. So you buy some good, but you also buy a lot of bad.

Second: We have such a distinctive culture that every time we've hired someone very experienced, they struggled to adapt. We're hands-on, no politics, radically candid, everybody needs to carry their own weight. Often, people successful at large tech companies have a different leadership style that may be optimal there, but not at Bending. We need to account for the cost of that cultural change — which sometimes doesn't even happen, and if it does, takes a long time.

Third — last but not least: Generally, people lose motivation as they gain experience. You need to consider whether it's better to have someone with 20 years of experience but 6-out-of-10 motivation, or someone with two years of experience and 10-out-of-10 motivation. I find the latter is often better.

Host: Has that changed as you've scaled?

Luca: No. And I may be wrong. We have hired experienced people with great success occasionally — we weren't completely close-minded. But we keep investing in students or new graduates, or people with a couple years of experience where we can help them mold their skill set and professional culture in the way we believe will best serve them and the company long-term. Also, in a competitive labor market there's a trade-off between talent and experience: experience we can provide, we just need to be a little patient; talent we can't. So we focus more on talent than experience.

We've encountered difficult situations — maybe a 25-year-old lead engineer showing up at an acquired company and essentially being the person in charge, and people with 20 years of experience thinking, "Does this guy even know what he's doing?" Our track record consistently shows that yes, he or she does. But I can see how it's a more difficult sale than if we had a 50-year-old with 30 years of experience say the same things.

The 25-year-olds running acquired companies

Host: I've spoken to a couple of founders of companies you acquired. One said the person who replaced them was 25; the other said 27. They didn't seem bothered. Let's say that 25-year-old takes over Meero or whatever company you're buying. What are you looking for in that person?

Luca: We wouldn't put someone in that position who we haven't tested in a smaller version — generally someone who led a team or a smaller business before. But yes, it could be someone with three or four years of experience.

On a high level we look for smart and what we call extreme ownership.

Smart: you learn very quickly, we have evidence of that, and you're consistently capable of high-quality reasoning. When you propose a solution or diagnose a problem, what you say or write makes a lot of sense. Not perfect answers to everything, but your analysis is always rational, accurate, logically sound. That works across the board.

Extreme ownership: you care tremendously about being or becoming the best in the world at your job, bringing the greatest possible contribution to your team and the company. Almost fanatical. So when you find an obstacle or identify a shortcoming in your skill set, you'll be hell-bent on overcoming that.

Then of course we look for more specific skills. But when those two qualities are in place in big ways, you're very likely to succeed — assuming you can communicate a little bit and you're not an a-hole. Those are hygienic factors. The core killer features are those two.

When it doesn't work

Host: And when it doesn't work — you put in the 25-year-old and there's an immune-system rejection, or they weren't up to it. What falls down?

Luca: That's happened very rarely — I can only think of one or two cases. When it happens, it's been primarily one of two things.

One: the person, while very good, we didn't pay enough attention to their ability to lead others — communication, common sense, empathy. They were incredibly smart problem solvers, moved 100 miles an hour, but failed to notice when someone was a little bit off, had an issue. They didn't say the right thing at the right time, and that created hostility or at least friction that ultimately made them untenable as leaders.

Two: enough people in the org felt more competent, and although this person was great and super nice and empathetic, these people couldn't get over the fact that "I'm so much more experienced, I cannot be led by this person, even just formally." Very rare — I can remember maybe one such case. And there, we can do one of two things: move or part ways with the people who reject leadership, or change the leader. Depends on context.

Developing people: deep end of the pool

Host: How do you develop these people? Do you train them, coach them? Or is it "they're smart, they'll figure it out, throw them in"?

Luca: We have training materials, but broadly, 90% of the outcome depends on throwing them into the deep end of the pool — giving them way more responsibility than seems reasonable — and surrounding them with amazing colleagues. We find that we learn primarily by working with amazing people. Almost invariably, some people around you will be better than you at some things; if you emulate those good traits, you'll learn. They'll also suck at some things, and if you notice the weaknesses, you can avoid falling into the same trap. Level of responsibility and level of talent around you are the two things that drive growth the most. A little formal training and active coaching adds 10–20% extra.

Feedback: radical candor and the "no" hat

Host: The one thing that helped me on my journey — we decided to do a 360-degree review on me. My co-founder volunteered, which was strange because he's really introverted. He thought, "How do I do this without talking to other homo sapiens?" So he did a Net Promoter survey. First question: on a scale of 1 to 10, how likely are you to recommend Brian as CEO of HubSpot? Second: why did you give that number? He sent it to 25 people — board, customers, employees — and people wrote freaking novels.

He correlated it, showed me the histogram. Then — clever — for each feature, he pulled direct quotes about that feature. In the first 10 pages I'm like, "Feature, feature — I've got this nailed." Page 11 is where the bugs started. The direct quotes were incredibly helpful. One of my ahas was that some of the features were bugs — people didn't like that I was really passionate and sometimes get really excited.

How do you personally go about getting feedback and getting better?

Luca: We're big on feedback. We have something called radical candor internally. The idea: you should always tell people when you see something good or bad — as long as you don't share it because you're venting but because you believe there's a chance they could improve or the team could benefit. Don't worry about the accuracy, the wording, whether you hurt feelings. Try to be nice if you can, but that's secondary to being honest.

We're not perfect — not everybody does it all the time — but we try to have an environment where opinions and observations flow very quickly and abundantly. That's a very good source of learning.

Host: Face to face? You make everyone do it face to face?

Luca: We try. Our recommendation: if it happens in person, say it immediately — even in front of everybody in a meeting. Don't delay. Respectfully, empathetically, but straight up. If it's something you notice through asynchronous communications like Slack, you can send a message — it's really secondary, as long as you do it and you're fully candid.

Once a year we have more structured feedback based on six to ten assessors depending on the person. That applies to me as well. Once a year I try to identify at least one major point of improvement. I went through exactly the same thing as you — I had five, then halfway through the year figured out it's too many. If they're challenging to improve, five is too many. So I try to have one per year that I try to get a lot better at.

Luca's current focus

Host: What's your one right now, Luca?

Luca: The quality of the people I get to work with is probably the greatest privilege I feel I have in my life — and I really mean it. I appreciate their skills, talents, contribution tremendously. I'm awful at saying that aloud. I'm very critical of myself too, to be clear. Generally at night when I call it a day, I'm disappointed in myself. So, same way toward myself as toward others — maybe more critical of myself.

Even people I hold in the highest esteem, I rarely tell them how amazing they are. So I decided I need to be better at telling them how much I appreciate them — in a fully honest way, not hypocritical, just voicing what I know unconsciously but don't really linger on. Half-success, half-failure, but an improvement.

Host: I had the exact same feedback pretty much every year. There's an old-school saying — five positives for every correction. I was definitely the opposite. "Let's use all six slots for corrections." I eventually put a 15-minute slot on Friday afternoon on my calendar: give compliments. I had to force myself.

No executive team

Host: A lot of CEOs get feedback that their trust circle is just small — they trust four people and run everything through them, and everyone else feels arms-length. Do you get that?

Luca: No, actually I haven't gotten this feedback. We're quite distributed. We don't even have an executive team or a leadership team. People could reconstruct one — "whoever leads product should be in there" — but we did have one many years ago, and we dropped it, because we found the precise definition of that group didn't help at all. It would lead to some people being involved in discussions who shouldn't be, just because they're on the executive team — and then some people missing from discussions because we needed to have it at the "executive team level." Now we just involve whoever needs to be involved, no matter the title or standing. We don't need an executive team.

Host: How is it organized? If you do a strategy offsite, who's there?

Luca: I'd invite people I think can contribute the most or take away the most. Sometimes I'd invite someone who in general won't contribute, but could learn something — we hate meetings and we hate big meetings, but inviting someone just so they feel good about themselves is never an option. It has to be useful. Depending on the precise angle, we invite different people.

An algorithmic org chart

Host: It doesn't sound like you have an org chart. More like Kalshi — no "I report to Luca."

Luca: No, we do have one. It's basically an algorithm — a matrix organization with functions and teams. Functions are in charge of how things are done — the hard skills. Teams are in charge of what we do — the objectives. Every person has a functional lead and a team lead, and it all flows to a single node — currently me. Whoever the CEO is at that point in time.

We use it to automate a lot of stuff, but we remind people that it's only useful to the extent that it's useful. They shouldn't feel limited by it — it's quite fluid. We've had many cases where someone is a lead for a while and then goes back to being an individual contributor.

"Whoever is the CEO at that point in time"

Host: You said something interesting — "whoever is the CEO at that point in time." I chatted with Jensen Huang a year ago. He's got 60 direct reports, gives direct feedback positive and negative in public, doesn't do one-on-ones. I asked him: when and if you retire, will the person who replaces you inherit that system? He said, "Oh, hell no. This is built for me specifically. Somebody else should come in and completely rewrite it." You said "as long as you're CEO" — what did you mean?

Luca: Absolutely agree. It's like coaching a sports team — you'd be a fool to say "the way to win is this, and that's the only way to win no matter the players." If and when we change our CEO, I'd encourage her or him to see whether any change is warranted. They don't have to change anything if they like it, but they should feel free to change things if they think it would improve things.

First principles and conventional wisdom

Host: You're a very first-principles person — big skepticism of conventional wisdom. I was sort of the same back in the day. What is conventional wisdom right about, that you do, where you maybe were like, "This is wrong, we'll rethink it," but… it's on wheels, we should just do what everyone else does?

Luca: We've tried to build this company from the ground up, questioning everything — not because we thought we knew better, but because we had this ambition of building one of the most successful companies of all time, knowing full well that we would very likely not succeed. If that's the bar, the only chance to achieve that level of ambition is to do something differently. If you emulate what everybody else is doing, you're guaranteed to be approximately mediocre.

We never even bothered understanding what conventional wisdom was. For each important problem, we just tried to find the optimal solution given our particular context and vision. I'm sure there are plenty of things in conventional wisdom that make sense — being nice to people, I guess I agree with that.

Radical simplification

Host: One thing people ask me about all the time: AI-native companies seem to be running differently than companies founded before ChatGPT. You're famous for simplifying things. A lot of people are doing a lot of stuff at once — year two they're going international, year three they're acquiring a business. Stuff that took HubSpot eight years, people are doing in the first couple of years.

At HubSpot, I was a big simplification guy. I even got myself a "no" hat.

Luca: Oh, that's awesome. 😄

Host: I'd go to a big meeting — the good thing about HubSpot was everyone always had great ideas. "We should do this! We should do that!" We were definitely a company much more likely to die of overeating than of starvation. So I bought everyone the "no" hat.

But things seem to be changing. I've noticed these companies are wearing "yes" hats, getting a lot done, pulling it off. What's your reaction?

Luca: It's really a winning strategy to be a radical simplifier. Complexity means costs, means being slower, being worse — generally speaking. But the perfect balance depends on your particular context. Obviously, building a business in the 1800s with no technology, no internet, a far less efficient labor market — you should have chosen to do a lot less than would have been reasonable in the 1990s. With modern technology, AI, and what we've learned, I'm not surprised we can do more given the same resources than we could in the past.

But as a general rule, leaning less rather than more is a very useful thing even in this day and age. The fact that some companies are pulling it off doesn't mean they've chosen the right path. We don't know how well they would have done had they done three rather than four things, dropping the smallest, least important one. Maybe the biggest, most important one would have been 35% better and bigger — maybe it's a net positive.

Burden of proof on complexity

We have a value, a quality, called relentless simplification. We measure ourselves against it and demand it.

Host: You measure yourself — that's fascinating.

Luca: Well, "assess" — frankly, it's not very quantifiable. But we want people, every time someone recommends we should add complexity — a step in a process, a feature, a team, headcount — the burden of proof is on those making the recommendation. Those who believe it's a bad idea don't need to bring any proof.

If we choose to go forward, there needs to be very clear proof that it makes sense, or it has to be revertible, and the people who drive the initiative need to then determine whether it was a clear success — and otherwise revert it pretty quickly.

The other part of the rule: we need to stay alert and question complexity that's been there for a while, because we become blind to it as human beings. Anyone who does that should always be applauded, even if it's a nuisance — "Oh my goodness, again, we're questioning this process or policy."

With better technology — AI is amazing — and, as someone who failed with an AI startup in 2010 (we started in 2010, failed in 2013), I obviously believe in the power of technology. I'm not surprised we can do a lot more today than 20 years ago.

Why Milan, not Silicon Valley

Host: You decided to base a company in Milan. We were based in Boston — I felt there were big pluses and big minuses to being in Boston. A lot of people think you can't create a great company outside Silicon Valley — that's obviously not me. Why Milan? What are the pluses and minuses? Do you perennially feel like you're not a cool kid because you're in Milan?

Luca: I actually couldn't care less about coolness. Someone who buys a company like AOL cannot possibly care about cool. 😄 If anything — or maybe I do care, but I think the uncool is cool. You choose, but it's one or the other.

Host: What are the pluses and minuses? My thesis: San Francisco is the best place in the world to start a company, but holy crap is it hard to scale there. It's so expensive — there's not a lot of loyalty — darn hard to scale. What's your thesis?

Luca: I haven't built a company in San Francisco, so I can't tell for sure. It does strike me as the place if you have the coolest, highest-potential, best-resourced company on the planet — that's where you want to build it. You can absorb the most talent the fastest there. If you're more of a mid-ling project — and by the way, mid-ling by Silicon Valley standards is a pretty high bar — it may be harder there than in many other locations.

We chose Italy, Milan. Today we're an international company — hiring way more people outside Italy than in Italy, including now more in the States. We'll probably open an office there in the next year. But yes, we started in Milan, on purpose. We'd actually been in Denmark with my co-founders, where we'd completed our engineering studies and launched and shut down our AI startup.

Two reasons for Italy

Reason one — commercial and selfish: Italy, 60 million people, excellent education, relatively few amazing companies — certainly very few up-and-coming tech companies. Could be a win-win in talent. We brought a lot of ambition, an idea that made sense, a project that was exciting — so a lot of people who would otherwise be relegated to joining an inferior business or moving abroad could stay with their families and have both an exciting job and that. We'd be able to build a better team for the same dollars — or an equally good team for cheaper. I think that has proven to be true, and it's a significant advantage.

Reason two — missionary: I believe, and my co-founders did too, and we certainly believe so today, that the world in general is a better place if knowledge, opportunity, and wealth are a little better distributed. I think it's totally fine — probably a good thing — that you have one or two hubs like Silicon Valley that are one notch above. The world probably needs that to achieve maximum prosperity. But if the gap becomes immense and essentially everything that matters happens in one or two places, it's a really big problem — including for the people who live in those places in the long run.

We wanted to do our part — "1%, make a 1% change" — by showing you can build a world-beating company with massive ambitions in an unlikely place. Italy being one of many clearly, but we're Italian, we understood the culture better. It was easy.

We don't regret it. You can never A/B test life — I can't definitively say we would have done less well in Silicon Valley — but I do suspect it was a better choice.

Integrity as a moral stance

Host: My last question. I called three of the founders of companies you acquired. All three said the same thing: you are exceptionally high integrity. I don't hear that a lot about CEOs, and I don't hear that a lot in preparation for these calls. Are there principles you live by? What can we borrow from you?

Luca: It's up to you to determine whether it's worth borrowing. But it's not a point of expedience — it's a moral point. Morality is very personal. I can be transparent about it.

At some point early in my adult life — in my early 20s — I cheated on my girlfriend at the time. I was so ashamed. Sometimes I think making a big mistake is a better way of learning than rationalizing how you should conduct yourself. I was so ashamed of myself that I made a promise to myself to never lie — but also never omit something important that people should know — even if it's to my detriment. I've tried to extend that to all aspects of my life.

I suspect that although it's sometimes costly in the short run, it tends to pay off in the long run. I'm very glad you shared that feedback — you just made my day. I didn't know you talked to them, but I'm glad they said that over praising my looks or something. 😄

No, jokes aside, it really matters to me. It's a life mission I set for myself — to be the kind of person you can trust is telling you things as they are. At least as I think they are.

I think it does pay off in the long run. When you're known as someone who can be trusted, it's easier to have a good life, make good friends, have relationships that last and matter. To do business — people come to you and say, "Okay, we're looking to sell. We believe you guys. Your word means something." But it doesn't come from a place of seeking expediency. It's really just a moral point for me. Very subjective.

Host: I love that. I'm going to leave it there. Congratulations on building something really special. Good luck on your journey to a trillion dollars, my friend. 😄

Luca: We'll do our best. Thank you — it's been a pleasure. Thank you for having me, Brian.

Host: Appreciate it.

Host's takeaways

Okay — I thought Luca was really interesting. His company's doing really well and the guy beats to his own drummer. Just to stick on the ending there: for CEOs, integrity is really an underrated thing. You are what your word is. You've got a great reputation probably — but you do one stupid thing and you can have that crash down.

I like that he said, "I never lie and I never omit important info." He could've just said that and I'd be like, "That's a bunch of BS" — but I had three of the companies he acquired kind of say the same thing. It reminds me of my last interview with Ali Ghodsi from Databricks, where he said the worst thing you can be as a CEO is conflict averse. If you're never going to admit important information, you're going to have conflict. That reinforces it in my mind.

Other things I thought were unique — the way he does hiring is really unique along a lot of different levels. He's conscious about the top of his funnel, how he brings people in, conscious about his employer brand. This rhymes with HubSpot — we had a woman named Katie Burke, a marketer actually, whom we moved into HR, and she was excellent at it. She treated it like marketing: how do we create a flywheel, pull people in, create a real employee brand? She's now COO at Harvey. I think that's really important for scaling companies — create a hiring brand, get very good at hiring.

He's got a whole data science team looking at hundreds or thousands of signals, trying to find the right candidates. One of the least interesting things he does is the interview itself — I kind of agree with that. Everyone's good at being interviewed now, so I discount that a little bit relative to other signals.

He's pretty obsessive on talent. He said it on this pod, and I've heard him say it elsewhere — you just can't drop the bar. As companies scale, they inevitably drop the bar. It sounds like he really hasn't — and it causes a lot of suffering, a lot of people working long hours. But he sticks with it.

He weighed in on the age-old battle: hire for experience, or slope? He's at a pretty big scale and he's still full-on slope over experience. His management teams, other than his founders, are all in their 20s and have high slope, and it's working for him. I'm not saying that's the answer. For some people experience matters. He also buys a lot of companies in the PLG type sales motion — not necessarily enterprise sales — where some experience might be useful. But that's where he comes down.

He talks so much about team-team-team — but then at one point he's like, "Actually, you can have a mediocre team if your strategy is really good." Which hurt my head a little. And he also talked about: when he buys a company, is it more picking or operating? Operating. He's a really good operator.

The reality is: you have to be really good at all of that stuff. You need a really compelling strategy, unique relative to competitors and compelling to potential customers. You need to be an amazing operator. You need an amazing team. There's not really any shortcut on any of that stuff.

Anyway — that's Luca. I thought he was really interesting and smart, and I hope you liked it.

item.description:
## 一、最反常识的发现：Bending Spoons 的"操作系统"其实是一场"反向私募"
Luca 把公司定义为"永远持有、深度改造、合并进同一平台"——这乍听像 Berkshire 的变体，但真正的颠覆之处在于**他主动放弃了一切"退出话术"**。私募基金的全部治理技术，本质上是围绕"3-7 年卖出"这一节奏构建的：短期化的 KPI、财报美化、团队留存奖金、SPV 结构……当你从根上拿掉"卖出"这个选项，几乎所有传统 PE 的工具都失效了，但同时也**消除了短期套利的激励扭曲**。
这里有一个几乎没人谈到的隐藏结构：**"永不卖出"+"彻底改造"**合在一起，让他可以做一件 Berkshire 做不到、PE 更做不到的事——把一家被收购公司的代码库、组织架构、云架构全部重写，因为他有 20 年时间去摊销这笔重投资。Berkshire 不改造（信托）、PE 不敢深改（周期），只有"永远持有+深改造"的组合才能解锁"把一群独立公司压缩成同一平台上的 app"这种操作。这不是运营效率的加法，而是**时间尺度的套利**。
