item.title: [Mercatus Center] Kishen Shastry on the Political Economy of Hindu Monastic Institutions (Mutts) in Karnataka
item.dc:creator: Mercatus Center
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意想不到的结构性发现：MUT 其实是"反瓦合夫（Waqf）"的罕见样本

真正令人震惊的，不是 MUT 推动了结构转型，而是它逃过了宗教资产的"僵化诅咒"。Timur Kuran 的经典论断是：伊斯兰世界之所以在现代化中落后，很大程度上来自瓦合夫——宗教信托一旦设立就无法随时代变更用途，1000 年前为抄经房准备的地产永远只能抄经。印度尼西亚 1960 年代的土改豁免瓦合夫，结果宗教资产沉淀最终催生了伊斯兰主义政治。

Karnataka 的 MUT 走出了完全相反的路径：1920 年代拿来办免费宿舍的那块地，2000 年代可以变成工程学院；明天还能变成医院或创投基金。关键不是"自由"二字本身，而是决策权交给一个独身、无子嗣继承、具有宗教威望的 Guru 个人——这个制度安排意外地解决了宗教资产的委托—代理与跨期灵活性问题。你会发现这个结构在跨领域中有一个精确对应物：现代主权财富基金的"独立治理 + 使命弹性"。挪威 GPFG、新加坡淡马锡追求的治理蓝图，Karnataka 的 Lingayat 其实在 400 年前就无意中达到了。

二、一个真正违反直觉的政治经济学观察：MUT 不是"票仓"，而是"摇摆制造机"

主流叙事（包括媒体和多数外部观察者的先验）会假设：宗教组织密集的地区 → 身份政治强化 → 选举竞争减弱、形成固定票仓。而 Kishen 的数据给出的方向完全反过来：MUT 曝光度越高的选区，1994 年之后胜负差反而缩小约 0.7 个百分点。

这个方向反转背后的机制非常漂亮，但很少被明说出来：MUT 的议价权正好来自"不承诺"。它从不绑死一个政党，每届都重新报价。这在博弈论上恰好等同于中央银行独立性的逻辑——一个无法被预先承诺收买的参与者，反而是定价能力最强的参与者。更妙的是，这跟 Thomas Schelling 讲的"烧船策略"是镜像结构：Schelling 说放弃选择权能提高议价；MUT 说定期续约选择权能提高议价。两种策略都对，但背景参数不同——前者适用于一次博弈，后者适用于无限重复博弈。Karnataka 政治恰恰是无限重复博弈。

另一个几乎没人提的观察：Karnataka 的 Guru 几乎从不亲自参选，而北印度（如 UP 的 Yogi 现象）宗教领袖直接下场。这不是风俗差异，这是信号成本的制度均衡差异：Karnataka 的 MUT 规模和跨代传承价值太高，Guru 一旦下场就"自我贬值"——这跟中世纪威尼斯禁止贵族单独经商、清代帝王表演节俭、现代最高法院大法官不发表政治意见，都是同一类"可信度资产"的保值机制。

三、藏在"教育—制造业"相关性之下的真正故事：MUT 是印度最早的"信息基础设施"

论文的表面结论是教育投资→人力资本→非农就业。但 Kishen 自己也承认数据不够：制造业的提升幅度超过了单纯教育通道能解释的部分。这里有一个跨领域连接，几乎没人注意：

MUT 本质上是印度前互联网时代的 LinkedIn + 征信局 + 商业仲裁庭的三合一。 - 它用种姓身份作为"实名认证" - 用 Guru 的宗教权威作为"信用背书中介" - 用定期聚集作为"信息匹配事件" - 用非正式仲裁作为"轻量法院"

这解释了为什么 1991 年去管制一到，这些地区的制造业滞后 10 年但突然起飞：10 年是教育周期，但同时也是信任网络被激活到足以支撑非血缘资本流动所需的时间。Avner Greif 讲的 Maghribi 商人联盟、Peter Leeson 讲的海盗章程、Elinor Ostrom 讲的共同池资源治理——这些"非正式制度降低交易成本"的全部文献，在 Karnataka 的 MUT 上找到了一个被完全忽视的印度样本。

一个让人起鸡皮疙瘩的推论：班加罗尔之所以成为班加罗尔，可能不只是因为英语和软件——还因为周边几百公里内早就有一个运行了四百年的信任与信息基础设施。班加罗尔不是建在空白地上的，它是建在 MUT 网络的社会操作系统之上的。印度要在其他邦复制班加罗尔的难点，可能根本不在技术园区政策，而在于——另一个邦没有 Lingayat。

四、一个被播客没问出来的、更深的监管反转

有一个法律层面的悖论值得特别指出：在印度，多数宗教（印度教）通常受到比少数宗教更深的国家干预（印度教寺庙被各邦接管管理）。但 MUT 被 Karnataka 立法明确豁免于 HRCE 法案——2013 年高等法院质疑这一豁免、立法会跨党派一致重新立法保留豁免。

这意味着：MUT 享受的是"少数宗教级别的自治权 + 多数宗教的规模优势"的罕见组合。类比到美国语境，这相当于一个基督教会同时获得了阿米什人的宗教豁免和主流新教的政治影响力。这种"结构性监管套利"产生的制度租金，才是 MUT 真正不可复制的护城河——不是神学、不是传统、不是种姓，而是一行写在州法第 1(4) 条上的例外条款。

📝 转录文本

Kishen Shastry on the Political Economy of Hindu Monastic Institutions (Mutts) in Karnataka

开场介绍

Welcome to Ideas of India, a podcast where we examine academic ideas that can propel India forward. My name is Shruti Rajagopalan and this is the 2026 job market series where I speak with young scholars entering the academic job market about their latest research on India.

I spoke with Kishan Shastri, who is a postdoctoral research associate at the Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance at Judge Business School. Before this, he received his PhD in Economics in 2026 at the University of Cambridge, where his research focus was the economics of religion and informal institutions.

We discussed his job market paper titled The Political Economy of Informal Institutions in India. We talked about the economics of religion, the role of long-standing monastic institutions in India (also known as Mutts), how Mutts are regulated by the state, and their impact on education, structural transformation and political competition in India — and much more.

For a full transcript of this conversation, including helpful links of all the references mentioned, click the link in the show notes or visit mercatus.org/podcasts.

一、论文核心发现概述

Shruti: Hi Kishan, welcome to the show, it's so great to have you here.

Kishan: Hi Shruti, thank you so much for having me today.

Shruti: Your paper is super super interesting, because the only context in which I ever hear about Hindu Mutts is when my parents or grandparents wanted me to visit one in the southern parts of India. So reading your paper is making my lived experience and my childhood come alive and clash with what I do for a living, which is economics and structural transformation.

In this paper, you ask whether Hindu Mutts — which are longstanding monastic institutions, in your instance you're looking at this in Karnataka — helped shape the structural transformation and political competition in Karnataka. More specifically, you're studying whether the 1991 reforms had a greater impact in those areas that had greater exposure to these Hindu Mutts, or greater proximity to these Hindu Mutts.

And when we're talking about reforms, you're looking at sort of two sets of major reforms that happened in India in the 90s. One is, of course, the 1991 reforms, which was delicensing, trade liberalization, getting out of license-permit Raj. But the second part of it is the political decentralization, which is the 73rd and 74th Amendment combined with the Panchayati Raj Act in the states — in your instance, in Karnataka in 1993.

And now within this world of before and after these reforms, you managed to construct a phenomenally new dataset of 253 Mutts, and you look across Karnataka at a district level: what is the exposure and proximity to these Mutts? And what is the impact? You look at the impact on very specific instances:

  1. Structural transformation — non-farm jobs versus farm jobs and how that changes.
  2. Secular education uptake — not just religious education.
  3. Political competition — specifically in assembly elections.

If I were to just give away the headline results:

  • Much exposure is associated with 10 additional non-farm jobs per thousand residents, roughly 15 to 20 percent relative to the 1990 baseline. Most of these gains are concentrated not in agriculture, but in manufacturing and services.
  • More exposed places also see about a 9% increase in secondary school (senior secondary and college education) per capita.
  • On the political side, when it comes to assembly elections, the margin of victory is narrowing by about 0.7 percentage points from 1994 onwards, because the Panchayati Raj Act kicks in in '93.

This is the overall picture. But these two things seem seemingly unconnected — that is, exposure to these kinds of monastic institutions (which we associate with very historical, long-run, sticky institutions) and what is happening with structural transformation today.

So first of all, did I get the paper right? And second, what made you write this paper and what were you really trying to look at?

二、为什么研究 Mutt？

Kishan: Thank you so much, Shruti. I think that was quite an accurate description of the entire work.

Generally, I find Mutts to be quite a fascinating institution. It has a long history, as you've mentioned. Some of the earlier Mutts, they go back to 8th century, 9th century. And then there has been consistent revolution in terms of how people think about religion. And Mutts became somewhat of a manifestation of this understanding of religious education overall.

I grew up in Bangalore, which is in Karnataka, and this is the main state that I take for studying. And as you know, economists are always interested in the tails of any kinds of distribution. In this case, it so happens that because these Hindu Mutts specifically exist at a scale and size not found elsewhere outside of Karnataka, it was a natural place for me to study Karnataka.

While I was growing up, of course, there's a lot of journalistic coverage on these Hindu Mutts, and predominantly of two types. One would mostly focus on the kind of political lobbying or liaisoning that the Mutts, Hindu Mutts would do. And this is just to flag to everybody — this is across party lines. It doesn't have to be just for a political party. And this gets an enormous amount of attention.

But the understated bit was how influenced and embedded they are within the society, particularly through their societal or rather philanthropic work that they conduct. And again, the scale and institutions that they generate is quite understated.

So I was very keen when I got into economics to try and put these two things together: the political aspect and perhaps the kind of developmental impact they may have, together. And I think this paper largely attempts to do the same.

It is a bit surprising to me that not many people have done this kind of work in the past. In fact, the only two large major works that exist on Hindu Mutts in Karnataka are either ethnographic accounts or by anthropologists — and we have to thank them a lot for giving us fantastic primary sources to rely on and define what a Mutt is, figure out the kind of model they think about, and then bring that to economics.

And as you put it together, I think the data set here is not the easiest thing to do. The interesting bit about Hindu Mutts is perhaps they're the only institution of Hinduism in the entire country that are fully autonomous — and this legal quandary in a way generates interesting incentives for us to study them.

三、什么是 Mutt？与其他宗教机构的对比

Shruti: Before we get into the legal incentives and how Mutts specifically were not treated the same as Hindu temples — for those who are unfamiliar with the institution, can you walk us through how this long-standing Hindu institution has functioned historically? What role did it play in the past, what is the role it plays today, and can you tell us something about its closest analogs from other religions?

Kishan: Absolutely. For those who are unfamiliar with Hinduism, oftentimes these Mutts get translated as "monastic institutions" — and that's what I've done — but they don't fully do justice to what they exactly perform as their duties. A description in the nature of monastic sort of gives a feeling that they are removed far from society. If anything, Mutts are opposite to that — they're deeply embedded, very active across different areas of the society.

Just to define them: the idea of a Hindu Mutt has to do with a monastery-like institution often led by a guru. And the way the guru is chosen is not through hereditary — as happens mostly in temples — but they're chosen to do this. And this guru is the prime renouncer of materialistic life.

But if you think about why this becomes important: each Hindu Mutt is generally associated with a caste, specifically in Karnataka. So if you have a pool of resources that a caste tries to either put to some sort of use or collects together, they would rather do it to the renouncer, because it's sort of a commitment device in terms of an economist's language. So this guru becomes the central aspect to these Mutts' organization, and of course he has tremendous autonomy to choose his team and run these organizations. And this is what makes the institution quite different from a temple.

In terms of how it is comparable — honestly, it's quite similar to how a Catholic missionary would work, in that the order has a strict hierarchy, the celibate life of the gurus is equivalent to the guru system there, and they run a large network, not for the state but for the community. So the design is very similar, but often the structure predates perhaps some of the other institutions before they even come to India.

The modern-day pioneer of the Mutt organization was initially laid in the 12th and 13th century by Basava. He's sort of the founder of the unique way of thinking of Lingayats. It's very similar, in my opinion, to how Martin Luther comes up with opposition to Rome's power — versus in this context, similar to opposing the Brahmin controlling of the institutions. And there, there was opposing Latin; here, in this case, it used to be the Sanskrit.

So there's striking similarities. And of course, economics of religion has done quite a bit of work on testing all of these hypotheses in the Christian world, and I try to do that for the Hindu world here.

四、经济学视角下的 Mutt：俱乐部物品与身份经济学

Shruti: Since you talk about the economics of religion, we've had a few economists like Karshria here, who's also from Cambridge like you, and Rohit Tiku and so on. But this is not an area too many people are familiar with. The way I think about economics of religion is it has a very strong literature on religious institutions providing club goods and solving very specific kinds of collective action problems.

Is this the way we should think about the Hindu Mutt in its modern-day context — not just about standing up to a particular kind of existing clergy or existing norms and institutions, not just about representing different castes or Vaishnavites versus Shaivites (which is also a major distinction in the different Mutts) — but what is a good way to think about how a Mutt operates today? What does it produce? Who produces it, and who are the chief consumers, or whose incentives should we account for?

Kishan: Absolutely. I think we have a long list of people to thank for in this subfield of economics of religion. Shriya here, who happens to be my supervisor, is one of them. But the tradition goes slightly longer. In fact, I think even Adam Smith began some of his work trying to explain the incentives of the church and why some churches don't do well. So it begins with the regulation of religious markets.

And Larry Iannaccone comes up with this superb set of papers in the 1990s, trying to explain —

Shruti: At George Mason University.

Kishan: Exactly, absolutely. I think it's been a fantastic home, the university. Larry Iannaccone comes up with this mechanism to explain why religion can be considered a club good. The basic framework is that these clubs produce goods that are useful for all the members, but it has to have a certain kind of strictness or sort of a cost to enter this club. His paper was wonderfully titled "Sacrifice and Stigma." That opens up the world of economics of religion, particularly looking at religion as a club good.

In terms of Mutts, I would say it is similar to club goods, but more so I would also pair this with the work that has been done in the economics of identity — particularly started by many in the field, including Akerlof and Kranton's 2001 paper on explaining the incentives of creation of identity. Another fantastic scholar, Jean-Paul Carvalho at Oxford, wrote a superb paper called Identity-Based Organizations. The idea here is: the identity of any organization — of the people who are part of that organization — is a co-creation process. In this paper, he takes up a leader of this group who ends up creating an identity along with the followers. In their work, the identity could be used to solve many problems, such as collective action problems, coordination issues, and so on.

I feel Mutts could be located in the theoretical framework of how identities are produced. Think about caste-based Mutts. There are fantastic accounts of a Japanese anthropologist who came to Karnataka, learned Kannada, and when she speaks to the new-age Mutts — and just to give a brief history, the Lingayats are the ones who pioneered this model of Mutts, but many castes eventually start imitating this model (inherently, it's quite useful to have a Mutt like this) — all of them told her that the goal to do so is to unify people, to create an identity of oneness. So this is embedded in the process of Mutts: to create an identity for caste groupings, which can eventually be leveraged to meet ends of some kind.

What I find interesting is that it brings in some aspects of club goods. For instance, if you have to participate in this identity creation, there is necessarily some individual preferences that you give up. Perhaps I vote the way my group thinks or asks me to vote. I participate in certain kinds of rallies. Caste groupings end up giving some of their donations to the Mutts. So there is an individual cost to pay to be part of this group. But ultimately, this identity helps them reach a lot more goals that they have created for themselves.

In the modern day, I would set apart two different time frames — and this is of interest from my paper as well. Some of the dominant castes have had a long history of having Mutts. Particularly, Brahmin Mutts tend to be more associated with the temple, and let's say Vedic learning and Sanskrit becomes a part of that. But Lingayat Mutts somewhat are supposed to be the opposite — their Mutts genuinely do not have temples in most cases, because that was the original philosophy of Lingayat Mutts. And Vokkaligas — that's the other major caste group in Karnataka — they tend to have Mutts as well because of how successful Lingayat Mutts become in running, for instance, free hostels, schools, and so on.

Later on, after the 1990s, a lot of other castes which now want to start bargaining with the modern state of Karnataka — any kind of representation, it could be bureaucracy, it could be the political parties — they start imitating this institutional setup. And virtually all major caste groupings in Karnataka have their own collection of Mutts. So the modern-day setup is quite interesting: there is a market of entire Mutts, so to speak, in terms of economics. All of them have different levels of strictness or commitment towards religion, but more so they use it as a fantastic enforcer of collective action.

五、Mutt 之间的竞争：非宗教服务的多重市场

Shruti: Since it's a marketplace, there's also competition, right? Between them, which is sort of brokered by the kinds of philanthropic and charitable services that they provide and the kinds of donations they can attract. So it's multiple different markets that they are trying to operate in.

Kishan: Absolutely. And I think this is where I would also like to reference my supervisor's work — Shriya's work — on religious organizations competing on non-religious services. How do we differentiate in a typical Hotelling model from other organizations? I start getting into giving them beyond just satisfying the religious beliefs and religious services. I perhaps give them free meals, or provision of education, free hostels, hospitals in some cases — as far as even enforcing contracts in some cases.

Shruti: A crucial question of contract enforcement, for instance, may become simpler because Mutts end up coordinating this kind of action.

Kishan: All of these services offer a bouquet of things for people who follow these Mutts, and it's an interesting mix of creation of identity along with offering all of these services to their constituents.

Shruti: Shriya was actually on the podcast — she was a very early guest, and she talked about exactly this paper of hers on the podcast. We'll throw in a link for that.

六、教育：Mutt 与基督教、伊斯兰教机构的比较

Shruti: Now that we have a pretty good setup, I want to come specifically to education, because these are also set up originally as somewhat educational institutions, coming from the monastic tradition. And you are also specifically studying educational institutions in Karnataka as a big part of your paper.

Now when I go back and think about the economics of religion and how it treats education, there is an interesting tension there, depending on which religion we're talking about, and the effect can go either way.

One possibility is that these missionary- or Mutt-like institutions are sort of complementing secular education, oftentimes providing secular education in addition to a religious education. You see this most with missionaries, and now, as you point out, in the case of some Mutts. The economics of religion scholars who have studied Muslim equivalents of missionaries or Mutts — basically madrasas or some of these Sufi-tradition institutions — often find the opposite effect: that it ends up being a substitute for a secular education through the religious education that is provided.

So how do Hindu Mutts specifically in Karnataka fit into this literature? Because I think you're the first person to study the Hindu institutions when it comes to this very large literature on the economics of religion and provision of education.

Kishan: Absolutely, well put. The direction runs in either way, and it's so interesting that it cannot even be attributed to a religion per se.

For instance, in some cases, Catholic missionaries — say in France — there's a fantastic paper by Mara Squicciarini: during the Second Industrial Revolution, she finds that the presence of Catholic schools in education actually impact downstream literacy rates to go down. In many other cases where Jesuits and Catholic missionaries go — even including in India — we notice a large uptake of literacy rates and even downstream economic development.

And as you've correctly noted, even in the case of Pakistan, a great work by Mirza and Malik, they show how shrines in Pakistan essentially substitute for secular education. They use a large shock to show that over time, high exposure to these shrines actually reduce the literacy rates in Pakistan.

Hindu Mutts, interestingly — I would like to quote an example. When I was going through these papers, I came across this fantastic ethnographer from Chicago called Aditya Sood. He was a student of Sheldon Pollock. He came to study Mutts in Karnataka as a Sanskritist. He came to study Mutts because he thought he could learn more of how Sanskrit education is delivered in Hindu Mutts, and much to his surprise, he came to do this work and he realized almost all education in these Hindu Mutts tend to be either in Kannada or English — the vernacular languages — and the education delivered mostly was secular education.

This is what makes Mutts, in a way, stand out quite a bit. There is a very interesting historical aspect to this. The role of the princely state of Mysore was involved in this, mostly because most of the government jobs at one point were largely dominated by Brahmins. And early 20th-century setting up of Lingayat Mutts wanted to also come into this kind of space. So they start getting some patronage by the princely state of Mysore — so much so that you have, for the first few Chief Ministers who would come to rule Karnataka, some of them actually came from these Mutt-run institutions. One notable example is B.D. Jatti, who became actually the acting President of India — he came from one of these Mutt-run hostels.

So they have a long history of actually dispensing education through secular means — secular education — and this has been a standout feature. And hence the results in my paper kind of show that they complement and improve the delivery of secondary education schools, senior secondary education schools, and sometimes even colleges.

Anecdotally, some of these Mutts — just to name the Siddaganga Mutt in Tumkur — they run over 150 education institutions. Most people probably would not even be aware of the size and scale through which they function. This includes multiple universities, medical schools, engineering colleges.

The key feature, from my point of view, is that where it becomes interesting is: the autonomy to run these Mutts was given fully to the organization itself. That allows sort of the manager or the guru to dispense with the assets that they have collected for whatever they think is the best use. It could be a school hostel in the 1920s, where it could be an engineering college in the 2000s. So they would have the incentives to respond to the changing scenario. And that I think was one of the dominant reasons why in my paper, at least, I find that education institutions go up, and that in a way pushes the structural transformation of the economy.

七、法律与监管：为何 Mutt 被豁免？

Shruti: This is really hard to study, right? You've given us the simple version of the story of how these Mutts have actually operated. But the Mutt as an institution itself — it's religious, but it's also educational, it's also charitable, it plays a political function. And then there is, of course, the modern law and regulation, which interfaces with this. And I'm talking about both the modern law and regulation that governs how these Mutt organizations are run, and also modern law and regulation on how educational institutions in the secular side are run.

How would you conceptualize the Mutt as an institution from the point of view of the modern legal institution? You've kind of hinted at it a couple of times — that they were allowed to run them autonomously — but that's quite different from the historical setting. Can you walk us through, in the instance of Karnataka, what is this regulatory regime that they are really under? And then we can parse out the effects.

Kishan: Perfect. The way to understand the regulation of temples and religious institutions generally — especially for Hindu religious institutions — is where they were left to the devices of state governments to take a call on this. Most of the states in southern India, where most of these temples and associated Hindu religious organizations work at scale, inherit Tamil Nadu's laws on HRCE — the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act.

Notably, what happens in Karnataka is: they borrow the same, but they explicitly mention that the Mutts are kept outside of this, and they say so in the law. And interestingly, in 2013, the Karnataka High Court strikes down the law saying, "We don't understand why this particular institution is kept out of purview of the regulation." But the Karnataka Legislative Assembly — again, irrespective of political parties, everybody supports this, just to show how important they are politically — repromulgate the Act. They bring back the Act again, keeping the Mutts outside of this. It's a legislatively conscious decision to keep them out.

Shruti: In terms of context, this is very different, because in India, different religious institutions actually fall under almost different regulatory regimes. Historically, the view has been that there is a lot more state interference in how a Hindu temple is run versus how other minority institutions are run. And this is a very interesting example where you're talking about a majority religion, but because of a certain kind of statutory or regulatory structure, you find that there is far less state interference overall. Which is the second part of what you're saying — which allows them to adapt.

But allowing them to adapt goes both ways. Sometimes Mutts can do a lot of good; sometimes they also go the other way. We hear lots of stories, not just in Mutts but in various places, about embezzlement of money or mishandling of public funds and abusing certain religious norms. And largely these Mutts have been kept out of that state supervision — and you find that that has some incredibly positive effects, at least in the state of Karnataka. Sorry, I just wanted to set that up, because I think most people don't know to what extent we regulate religious institutions in India.

Kishan: That's absolutely well put. The personal conviction that I've had when I'm doing this kind of work is that free organizations are better than not free. This is in a way almost unanimous in the literature on the economics of regulation of religious organizations.

But yeah, I think temples continue to be regulated. The main idea being cross-subsidy — for instance, in Karnataka we have about 35,000 temples. All of them come under the state-run regime. And the issue with that is, in my opinion, there is very little incentive for these temples and the people who run the temples to do anything innovative. And that, in my opinion, causes a big problem. For instance, how do you respond to modern challenges like mental health, teenage issues with drug abuse — specifically given that we have literature that shows religion plays an important role, including papers by Shriya? Daniel Hungerman shows these "deaths of despair" — people who are severely abusing drugs and alcohol have the best successes when they go to a church program.

In that way, I think religious temples in India are severely constrained, and Mutts, specifically Hindu Mutts in Karnataka, offer a sort of a welcome change. And that's probably the only institution we can study at scale in India to produce any kind of evidence. So if somebody tomorrow wants to lay down a basis for whether any institutions need to be free or not, I would recommend we need to have some kind of impact study like this. It so happens that I had, in my case, an interesting example of Mutts, which has longstanding history, and it helped quite a bit.

八、数据构建：如何测量 Mutt 的影响？

Shruti: Coming back to my original question: it's really hard to measure the different things that you're looking at — there's a religious impact, an educational impact, a political impact, and so on. So how do you actually lay that out in Karnataka? And what kind of data are you even able to look at? I imagine you have to stitch together lots of different data in addition to the data that you put together on Mutts.

Kishan: Absolutely. Because of the nature of Mutts — or generally temples and Hindu religion — it's very hard to find one point registry for finding the list of all of these Mutts. I know this because I tried. I tried the first possible solution to get this going, but eventually I realized that exercise is futile and I couldn't do it.

Let me put this out in three different tranches of work.

Tranche 1: Building the Mutt dataset. The first was actually to have a dataset on Mutts, and specifically for my interest, these had to be existing before the 1990s (because that's when the shocks end up hitting the economy). So what I did was to use the Google Search API to go to every village and figure out Mutts — or different variants of Mutts — that are actually located on Google. In many cases, it won't work because people may end up missing very small Mutts. In my case, I don't have a problem with it; I patently want large and influential Mutts. So I built a large dataset, and there's a big problem with lots of Mutts coming over, but I deduplicate it quite a bit and used a lot of filters so that I retain genuinely ones that I can manually verify existed before 1990s — in most cases a few decades preceding the national shock of 1990s, in many cases many centuries, because they have a long tradition of having these Mutts.

Tranche 2: Combining with administrative data. Once the geotag locations of all of these Mutts are there, I need to combine them with an administrative dataset to claim if they have any impact either on economic outcomes or on public amenities. Here, a wonderful gift for the entire research community in development economics is the dataset called SHRUG — the Socioeconomic High-resolution Rural Urban Geographic dataset. The idea here is: lots of boundaries keep changing in the Indian census over multiple rounds. They fix these boundaries and essentially makes it comparable over time. So I build a panel dataset using this for the census.

Tranche 3: Economic, population, and political data. I use the economic census — and this is not a survey, we have every economic non-farm activity actually picked up in this. For that, I have four different years that I get: 1990, 1998, 2005, and 2013. Similarly for population census, where I get schooling data, I have 1991, 2001, and 2011. So combining all these three datasets — and of course the fourth one being the political dataset, which is a bit more richer because it goes from 1978 until 2013 — I combine all of this to then see: areas which have higher density of Mutts versus areas which have lower density of Mutts, do they start changing after the national shock of economic liberalization arrives?

And just to flag this, this national liberalization shock has got nothing to do with the location of Mutts or anything to do with Mutts. So it's a truly exogenous shock.

Shruti: Yeah, it was a balance of payments crisis. We've documented this pretty well. I don't think you have that kind of endogeneity problem.

Kishan: I agree. So when that happens, crucially what happens is the returns to non-farm activity improve quite a bit. And that's where I feel Mutts start to kick in. They've created these assets, they have large amounts of land, education institutions, and they also liaise with the government. It's a routine activity for these heads of these Mutts to submit their wish list to the Karnataka government to provision more schools.

So I find that over time, schooling improves after 1991 in areas where Mutts are more densely located than not. The first thing that I find in the economic census is that quite a bit of manufacturing goes up. Interestingly, it happens with a lag. If anything, in 1998 — which is after the reforms have happened — my control and treatment, or rather the high-density Mutt areas, actually have lower non-farm employment than areas with lesser Mutt density. But over time, the areas which are exposed to higher Mutt density really improve quite a bit.

My sense is that it comes from the education institutions going up — and it in fact doubles over time per capita. This mechanism, I think, has some bite also because this is how some of the other people who have documented Christian missionaries' work also notice the same, and also a very similar gap as well in terms of it takes about 10 years for these schools to come up and then you notice the improvement in the economic outcomes. So that's the larger structural transformation, which I think the Mutts end up having some kind of impact on.

九、机制细节：教育之外，还有信用与信息网络

Shruti: The mechanism that you find is twofold, right? One mechanism is: they have been placed under charitable institutions and trusts, as opposed to religious institutions. So they have greater autonomy, which means they're able to deploy their capital much better — both their human capital and their physical capital and assets. But a second layer of that is very specific to education: they decide to invest in education services. And this is not just charitable schools for poor kids — our typical sort of understanding of what some of these religious institutions run, like they'll feed the poor, they will provide cataract operations for poor people, and they'll also start a primary or a secondary school for young girls from poor families. These are actually colleges that then turn into proper engineering colleges — people are getting computer science degrees at these places.

So is that the appropriate mechanism — that because they are able to be more autonomous in their deployment of capital, they can actually adjust to the demands? And being that close to Bangalore and post-1991, given that the biggest demand is for engineers in that area, that's sort of the direction in which they go in? Or is the story just too simple and too convenient?

Kishan: I would like to agree with you largely. I just do want to add a couple of clarifications. In the analysis, I leave out urban areas and specifically Bangalore, because it's so easy to get confounded with the presence of large cities. As you know, service sector tends to agglomerate quite a bit around Bangalore. So when I break down the results that I have in the economic census, a lot of this actually turns up in manufacturing. So you're absolutely right — it's not just schools, but also people who go to colleges, senior secondary schools, and so on, end up enrolling themselves in manufacturing sector.

What happens interestingly — just to rule this out — is: there is no uptake or severe difference in the government jobs. So it's not a simple story of these governments just want to appease Mutts and they end up provisioning more government jobs. That doesn't happen. It so happens that it shows up in manufacturing, which makes me think — unfortunately my data can't fully prove this — that there are other things beyond also just the education story.

It's also that these Mutts become, in a way, congregations of information networks. There are anecdotal evidence of credit lending happening through these organizations. Some of the largest non-bank financial organizations are actually run by these Mutts, and it's not surprising because information about credibility becomes common knowledge through these organizations — because people know each other quite well. And the other aspect is of course that in parts of these places, they actually end up dispute-adjudicating.

Shruti: A crucial question of contract enforcement.

Kishan: Again, I find this very interesting, and I think they will add more complexity to the work. It's much harder to say that with the data that I have right now. I suppose a follow-up work with some kind of survey of where people are getting this kind of credit will actually add a lot more depth to this. But yes, I agree with you — the headline is that education institutions improve, and of course we see an uptake in manufacturing. But I do think, just based on anecdotal evidence and possible economic explanation, there is credit networks and information networks also playing the role.

Shruti: If I were to tell the simpler version of that same story, it's — whether you tell it through credit networks or through educational institutions — structural transformation requires resources to go to their highest valued use. And that needs to happen relatively swiftly in a fast-growing economy. And basically, these Mutts are able to maneuver that, or at least catalyze that, if not directly maneuver it. Is that the better version of the underlying mechanism?

Kishan: Absolutely, I would completely agree. Just corroborating this thinking: we do have evidence from other parts of India where caste networks really improve the kind of occupational choices — Kaivan Munshi and others, they work quite a bit on it. So I think this is what's happening in this case as well.

十、Konkani 与 Tulu 少数族群的角色

Shruti: One follow-up question: Karnataka is not just the hub in India of Mutt-led institutions within the educational — Mutt-led educational institutions — but it's also overall the hub of educational institutions. And this comes with a long history. You could start with South Canara and everything that happened there with their credit networks, TMA Pai and all the educational institutions. But that comes through a slightly different constitutional mechanism, which is linguistic minorities.

In India, we like to interfere with all sorts of things — the government can interfere with lots of institutions. But then we carve out these interesting exceptions, and educational institutions that are run by minorities overall, and particularly linguistic minorities, are protected under Article 30 of the Indian Constitution. So you have a lot of these Tulu-speaking (which is technically a minority language) that set up these educational institutions, which incidentally don't teach Tulu — they are actually teaching engineering or medicine or something else.

So how much of the overall effect of education uptake is coming from that effect, versus from the overall effect of Mutts providing education institutions?

Kishan: No doubt. I think specifically the areas that you have named have been largely driven by probably Konkanis and Tulus. There have been pioneers in setting up of education institutions, banks. I mean, there are like four or five nationalized banks coming from a small district in Karnataka. So it's quite exceptional.

I do think, though, we do have such minorities elsewhere in India — for instance, let's say Parsis in Maharashtra or Gujarat. But the true success, in my opinion, seems to me that the organizational setup or the blueprint that the Mutt gives helps propagate this effect elsewhere.

In fact, even the first property — I mean, you're an expert on this — the Shirur Mutt case happens to be a Mutt again. And they have a fantastic history of eight Mutts in Udupi, self-governed since 1522. They sort of have a tradition of changing who governs the temple. There's a lot of rule enforcement that happens as a collective rather than run by the state.

But overall, this blueprint somehow transported across different parts of the Karnataka state and ensured that on average, I think the whole state has these institutions spread out quite a bit.

But I do agree — I think it's a fascinating study to understand how the Tulus and Konkanis have had their own role. And also, the princely state of Mysore has given quite a bit of patronage to revolutionary kind of thinking for their time period. And it could be a study of its own to understand how the British colonial legacy — direct rule versus through these kinds of princely states — end up generating these kind of heterogeneous outcomes.

But long story: my claim, I think, is that the organizational design and subsequent autonomy granted to these Mutts made it more immutable and it transports across the state.

Shruti: So I guess the economist version of my question would be: are you able to isolate districts which have greater proximity or exposure to these, say, Konkani or Tulu set-up educational institutions versus Mutt set-up educational institutions and see any difference? Or are they all just clustered together in a way that it's very difficult to parse out?

Kishan: Great question. I think I'm a bit handicapped by the census data that we have from Indian government. In 2011, the best distinction we can make is whether an educational institution was private or if it was government-run. Going back to 2001 or 1991, we can't even say as much. So to set these institutions apart, the most we can do is geographical separation. But within a sub-district or a village, it's very hard to say what actually that is. And because we need a panel of data before the shock and after, it's much harder to separate these things out.

What I can say though is: on an average, this is what happens, and underneath there could be many mechanisms including what you said working beneath the headline number.

Shruti: What is a good way of thinking about this non-farm employment result? Should we think about it as just broader structural transformation after 1991? Or should we think about education playing a very specific role? I guess what I'm asking is: do we see evidence of schools that train mechanics or electricians or a particular kind of industrial work, as opposed to schools that may provide the more general K-through-12 education?

Kishan: Absolutely. Having some kind of data on trade schools might help quite a bit. At this point, I have to rely on anecdotal evidence to say that this could, or evidence given by ethnographers and anthropologists. And I would very much encourage people who are listening — young researchers also — to do more on this, because it's just a handful of people who worked on this space right now.

Because of the census data that we have, it's hard to say whether it's driven by trade schools or not. It's just an aggregate number of what education per capita overall looks like. Largely, I think one extension that I am thinking about is trying to combine with other datasets that we have to see specifically what types of industry actually is driving this beyond just manufacturing, services, or government jobs. But it's a nightmare of its own in terms of combining all of this data together to make it comparable. And also going back 40 years, I think, is the even harder part. More recently, you have slightly better data now.

十一、政治竞争：Mutt 不是票仓，而是摇摆制造者

Shruti: In the end, we've talked a fair bit about the structural transformation and the education piece of the puzzle. You look at one more major area within this paper, which is looking at what greater exposure to these Mutt institutions does to political competition. Does it increase political competition or decrease?

I imagine that your fundamental mechanism is that they have very strong identity formation in these areas, and a lot of the caste and religious and linguistic identity also plays into political competition — and they might be able to broker, in some sense, what happens in that political marketplace.

So what do you find, and how do you actually study this kind of question to figure out if there's greater or lesser political competition?

Kishan: No, I think I was fascinated by this question myself, because this usually tends to dominate the news cycle around Mutts — specifically in the kind of political involvement that they end up taking.

What I found out actually did surprise me. The Mutt areas don't really end up supporting just one party. And it depends quite a bit on election cycle to election cycle. They are pretty much on the swing margins, which makes them even more important to be appeased of some sort. And I think they're well aware of this fact, and hence they use it to the fullest. So they have a fantastic bargaining chip.

In terms of their role in the paper that I show, it's less than a percentage point, but if you notice, Indian assembly elections have very small margins.

Shruti: Yeah, that's a non-trivial number.

Kishan: Exactly, and it's very precisely estimated as well. So Mutts have a unique role in making the electoral politics more competitive. It could be to meet their own end goals of any kind that they have, but inevitably they end up making it more competitive. And I think this is the key mechanism — that one can say that the electoral democracy becomes more accountable in a way to the people through Mutts. Because it's of course much harder to talk to individual constituents, and Mutts end up aggregating this kind of information and preferences over time. And one could have theoretically — it could have gone either way.

What I find interesting is the post-90s phenomena of expansion of Mutts, and there is clear government patronage to some of these Mutts. For instance, many governments — including the BJP government, which first came in Karnataka in 2008 — explicitly started making budgetary allocation for instance during flood recovery and so on. So it's a very complex political economy between the state and the Mutt system entirely. And again, it goes beyond any particular party. All of them try to appease them, and their support sometimes makes a big difference in the electoral outcomes.

十二、对印度教民族主义先验的颠覆

Shruti: This is such a lovely result, in the sense that: what are our priors when we just watch the news or read the news? It is that if there is a wave of majoritarianism, or in this case Hindu nationalism, you would imagine these Mutts brokering that particular side. Or there's going to be a wave and you would imagine there's going to be less political competition in these areas, because they're basically byproducts of the majority religion. So the more you have a sort of political Hindu nationalist wave, the less competition we should see.

And what you find is in fact exactly the opposite. And even more specifically within that result, the resources are scarce and political allocation of resources is not going directly to the Mutt — but it's going towards announcing a new factory, flood relief, or setting up a new college, or putting in a new port, or something like that. Which means that the original point where we started — which is they broker a particular kind of club good or philanthropic collective action good — is also now interfacing with the politics of Karnataka.

Kishan: Absolutely, and I completely agree with the characterization that you've made.

Shruti: Well, I would hope so, because I got it from your paper.

Kishan: An interesting counterfactual, or rather the comparable result, comes from Indonesia. For instance, where you had extensive land reforms in the 1960s, but the Waqf properties end up being exempt from that. So a large amount of land ends up getting deposited in those places, and mosques get built there — eventually explains the role of Islamism overall in Indonesia.

It's hard to have a unilateral understanding of Mutts that way. They tend to be a lot more dynamic. And perhaps this also speaks to the results where Timur Kuran says that ossification of any kind of assets under a religious organization end up making them sort of less relevant. But Mutts are, as you characterize, quite different. They will probably go and do these things with whomsoever offers them a good deal for their constituents and where they're located. It so happens they care about education, they care about hospitals, they care about factories being located near where they are.

So the crucial difference between — or rather the crucial start to understanding — these Hindu institutions, at least in the case of Hindu Mutts, is: they tend to want and care for secular education and secular goods, rather than them being a substitute for secular goods overall.

十三、与 Punjab 的 Deras 比较；Guru 为何不下场参选

Shruti: I think here you're also quite clearly showing that the political representatives are to some extent in competition with Mutt representatives. They are both in some sense competing for influence and patronage, and the Mutts seem to be better at delivering what the local community wants. That's the direct point of competition. So either the political patronage has to align with the Mutt, or take their chances and maybe have a close election or lose the election.

Kishan: Absolutely. The only other work that I have seen in India in recent days — and I think Kartikeya was also on your podcast — Avantika and Kartikeya put together this dataset on Deras in Punjab. And they show sort of similar outcomes where all politicians end up taking the blessings of these Dera gurus and people who had Deras. And despite Deras being a much smaller entity compared to a Karnataka Mutt — and also newer, less sticky norms. I mean, Karnataka Mutts have like 400-year tradition in some cases of how they're going to appoint the next person and so on.

Shruti: And some of the Deras play a little fast and loose with the institutional accountability.

Kishan: Exactly. And compared to that, in this case it happens to be even more credible, even more dynamic, and a lot more politically embedded than the Deras. So you're right — a lot of political leaders do end up taking the blessings of these Mutts. And often the kind of news you end up seeing in the news cycle is: certain leaders of these Mutts end up lobbying for a candidate to get a ministerial berth. That's the kind of news that gets dominated. But behind it, there is a large stateness of the whole Mutt system complex. And it's quite hard to in a way veto their preferences, because you never know — the next elections can end up being counterproductive to the party.

Shruti: My favorite anecdote on this is: when the Ayodhya temple was built and the consecration and the puja happened, there were actually a lot of Hindu Mutt leaders — not the small ones, like all the major ones which have had a thousand-year history — who were quite unhappy, because they said that what is basically a religious ceremony and a sacred ceremony has been completely politicized, and is going to be — there's going to be a political winner, so to speak, who is actually going to preside over this what should be a religious ceremony. So you can see that sense of competition between political influence and religious influence even at that highest level, when you would, as a prior, imagine that their incentives are largely aligned.

Kishan: Absolutely. And one key difference that I have noticed — and I could be wrong in this — is: the Mutt leaders in Karnataka seldom themselves get into politics, as opposed to say the larger North Indian politics where you often see religious leaders becoming themselves political candidates.

Shruti: Yeah, like Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh.

Kishan: Indeed. And I think that is quite important for them to reinforce their credibility over time. The more worldly somebody seems, the harder it is for them to run this large institution. And that's been one of the exceptional results that I have anecdotally noticed in Karnataka.

结语

Shruti: This was such a pleasure to read your paper. It was absolutely fascinating. I feel like I don't get to read about economics of religion in India, which is such a shame, because it's the most fantastic petri dish to study pretty much every kind of religion, religious sect, religious practice, and so on. So it was fascinating to read this. And thank you so much for coming on the show and sharing this with us.

Kishan: Thank you so much. It's a tough field to be in, specifically working on economics of religion. But I think we'll be getting there step by step. Thanks a lot for having me.

Ideas of India is produced by the Mercatus Center at George Mason University. If you enjoy this podcast, please subscribe on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app. Help us grow by giving us a rating and leaving a review. Follow us on Twitter at @srajagopalan and @IdeasOfIndia. Also check out our initiative commemorating 30 years of India's market reforms at the1991project.com.

item.description:
## 一、最意想不到的结构性发现：MUT 其实是"反瓦合夫（Waqf）"的罕见样本
真正令人震惊的，不是 MUT 推动了结构转型，而是**它逃过了宗教资产的"僵化诅咒"**。Timur Kuran 的经典论断是：伊斯兰世界之所以在现代化中落后，很大程度上来自瓦合夫——宗教信托一旦设立就无法随时代变更用途，1000 年前为抄经房准备的地产永远只能抄经。印度尼西亚 1960 年代的土改豁免瓦合夫，结果宗教资产沉淀最终催生了伊斯兰主义政治。
Karnataka 的 MUT 走出了完全相反的路径：**1920 年代拿来办免费宿舍的那块地，2000 年代可以变成工程学院；明天还能变成医院或创投基金**。关键不是"自由"二字本身，而是**决策权交给一个独身、无子嗣继承、具有宗教威望的 Guru 个人**——这个制度安排意外地解决了宗教资产的委托—代理与跨期灵活性问题。你会发现这个结构在跨领域中有一个精确对应物：**现代主权财富基金的"独立治理 + 使命弹性"**。挪威 GPFG、新加坡淡马锡追求的治理蓝图，Karnataka 的 Lingayat 其实在 400 年前就无意中达到了。
