item.title: [a16z] Building Cyber Defense for the Agentic Era
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、AI 攻击者的"笨拙"恰恰是它的指纹——而这揭示了一个被忽视的"叙事断裂"问题

Kevin 提到的那个细节，几乎所有人都会一扫而过：AI 攻击会先攻破 A 点，横向移动到 B 点，然后又回头去攻击 A 点。他把这解释为"协调不佳"。但真正令人意外的洞察是：这不是技术缺陷，这是认知架构的指纹。

AI 攻击缺的不是算力、不是速度、不是知识，而是叙事连贯性（narrative continuity）——人类攻击者的大脑中有一条"我在哪里、我做过什么、我下一步该干什么"的时间线，这条线来自工作记忆和自我意识。而当前的 agentic 系统拥有的是"状态"而非"叙事"。它们像患了海马体受损的 H.M.（著名的失忆症病人）：短期行动能力完整，长期自我位置感缺失。

这意味着未来几年检测 AI 攻击的最可靠信号，不会是行为快、不会是扫描广，而是——它缺乏"羞耻感"和"犹豫"。人类攻击者会回避已经触发警报的路径；AI 不会，因为它从没真正"知道"自己触发过。这是一种后设认知的空洞（metacognitive void）。

二、开源与闭源模型在网络攻击上的"性能坍缩"——与 Moneyball 的隐秘对偶

Kevin 丢出一个被节目两个人都没充分意识到其爆炸性的数据：在 20 条真实 kill chain 的测试中，前沿闭源模型和开源权重模型都只能完成 8 条。差距只在速度和成本，不在能力上限。

这个发现粉碎了一个主流叙事："越贵越强的模型就是越危险的武器"。真正的解释是：漏洞发现是一个结构化问题，不是创意问题。代码是形式语言，不是诗歌。而大模型的"规模红利"主要体现在模糊、开放、创意的任务上——那些需要"品味"的任务。

这里有一个跨领域的奇妙对偶：棒球的 Moneyball 革命。2003 年奥克兰运动家队发现，昂贵的"直觉型"球探挑选的球员，在可以被统计量化的指标上并不比便宜的数据选秀更强。贵的东西只在"无法量化的创造力"上有溢价。网络攻击正在经历它自己的 Moneyball 时刻——攻击的 token 经济学将由中等开源模型主导，而不是旗舰闭源模型。这反过来意味着："慢下大模型"的监管思路，在网络安全这个维度上几乎无效。防御的真正杠杆点在于攻击者获得匿名 GPU 算力的难度——这是 Kevin 真正担心的那个变量。

三、"CEO 的工作是向员工隐藏混乱"——以及免疫学给安全运营的一个礼物

Kevin 在最后扔出一句反直觉的话："A CEO's job is to absolutely hide chaos at a company from the employees." 这与硅谷流行的"激进透明"（radical transparency）叙事直接对撞。但他是对的，而且理由比他自己说的更深：

在超高速变化的环境里，员工的注意力带宽才是最稀缺的资源。流程是一堵"信号防火墙"——它让 1000 个变化的信号被过滤成 10 个值得关注的决策。暴露全部混乱会导致决策瘫痪，不是赋能。

更深层的是整个 Armadin 的自我攻击架构和生物免疫系统的同构。传统网络安全是适应性免疫（adaptive immunity）：等入侵发生、学习抗原、产生抗体、下次防御。Mandiant 做的是这件事的"工业化"。但 Armadin 做的是癌症监测级别的持续自检——不等外部攻击，让一支内置的红队"攻击者"永远在你体内游走。

这类似于生物学里被低估的吞噬细胞自噬（autophagy）：细胞主动消化自己的组件以提前发现突变。获得 2016 诺奖的大隅良典说过一句话："细胞之所以健康，不是因为它拒绝损伤，而是因为它持续地吃掉自己的问题。"

Armadin 本质上在把企业变成一个会吃掉自己弱点的组织。而这个范式一旦跑通，它会从网络安全外溢到合规、财务审计、供应链韧性——任何需要"主动自我攻击"的领域。这才是 Kevin 没有明说、但显然在下的更大的赌注。

📝 转录文本

Building Cyber Defense for the Agentic Era

a16z — in conversation with Kevin Mandia

Cold Open: Offense Must Train Defense

"You don't have a defense unless you have a great offense to go up against. You want to be the Baltimore Ravens defense of 2000. You kind of want to have your practice offense really push you. That's what Armadyne's going to do. We're going to be the all-star team on offense coming at you so you can train your defense with what we're doing."

"You built Mandiant — a great success. Why did you decide to get back on the field?" "I don't want to sit out the AI shift change when I've done 30 years in security and the whole damn thing's about to change. What AI does in a microsecond would take 70 humans. They can't even do it. It's apples to oranges. This is a tsunami like has never been seen before in security."

"The whole 'let's slow down the models — we don't want cyber risk' is too late. The open models are already good enough. Armadyne — since January of this year — has found over 90 zero days at customer sites, all in production. This is not rinky-dink companies. These are Fortune 500 companies."

"The differences or similarities between nation-state attacks compared to AI today — and then where you think AI can be in a couple years... On the defensive side, we're going to say 'we're being attacked by these models,' but we're not sure who's behind them. Is it a nation? Is it a human? Is it...?"

Why Come Back: Meeting the Founders

Kevin, thanks for being here. No, thank you.

Okay, so you built Mandiant — obviously a great success. Many different chapters, ended up inside of Google ultimately. Why did you decide to get back on the field?

It's a good question — and I don't know if I decided it, and that'll sound weird. I met with David Slater and with Travis Lam, the other founders, and Evan Peña. I could say they started this company; they are the founders. I met them, they had the idea, they pitched me on what they wanted to do, and I saw the talent in them. Travis is a generational talent. David Slater is — and I mean this in a positive way — freak nature. These guys are really, really good. Evan Peña is exceptional at what he does.

When you meet that team and you talk to them, the whole time I was listening to what they were doing, I was thinking, "I want to be a part of this." I don't want to sit out the AI shift change when I've done 30 years in security and the whole damn thing's about to change. Everything I did is dead and everything else is new.

Meeting that team — and they were starting the company — and me realizing, "I think I'm a real good fit with these guys to accelerate the need." What Armadyne is building, every company needs now. This team can build it, and I think I can answer the... "Let's go to the people I know, 30 years in security, and say we've built what you need." I almost felt compelled to do it.

I know that sounds weird, but I would not have founded a company again in my mid-50s. I was doing venture. It wasn't like, "Oh, I'm an entrepreneur and I love starting companies." That's not it. And it wasn't, "I'm not a VC, I'm just an operational guy." That's not it. I met the team and went, "We have to do this." Yeah. That's really it.

What Armadyne Does: Armadyne Red and Armadyne Blue

And this whole AI shift change was happening — that's the catalyst, right? Tell us about what Armadyne does.

Armadyne leverages frontier models and AI on offense to test: do you have exploitable risk? That's what we do today. We call it Armadyne Red.

But when we started the company, Travis, David Slater and Evan all knew the future of cyber security is going to be: the good guys have to build the offensive cyber cannon and shoot it at networks to make sure those networks can withstand these attacks — because they're the ones that are coming. But we also knew it's going to be AI on offense built by the good guys working and training with AI on defense built by the good guys. And you have to have both.

So our Act One was: we have to be the best in the world at finding exploitable risk. If we're five minutes ahead of the bad actor — whether it be a nation-state, criminal, or nuisance — if we're five minutes ahead of them... we also recognized our Act Two, Armadyne Blue: we have to stop it. Compensating control. Tourniquet.

That's what Armadyne does. We're building the force field you will need in the AI age to defend yourself from AI attacks.

The Signature of AI Attacks Today

Tell us about the nature of the capabilities of AI attacks today — and then where you think it goes.

The nature of them: first off, we're getting a weird window in time where we're seeing them, but not at the same level you'd expect. I've seen nothing like what Armadyne's already built in the wild — which is there's 25,000 agents all in concert, all working together doing really, really smart things without going on bizarre fishing trips.

When you respond to an AI attack, you can tell it's AI very quickly — at least I can, because I've thought about a lot of offense. I've responded to a lot of attacks in the past that were led by humans: a human goes to point A, then to point B, then to point C through their intrusion. AI does little things — four or five differences — but one would be: it'll break into point A, then laterally move to point B, next thing you know, it's trying to break into point A again.

I get the drone swarm, but you could probably coordinate and think a little bit better. That's where it's at today. It'll get better and cleaner.

Scale, Speed, and the Code Problem

The differences are, first and foremost: the scale of what AI can do dwarfs humans in ways humans don't even get. You have a scaling problem in that humans could always find only one path into a network. They had to be selective because they had to devote their limited resources to one direct path.

Speed — ridiculous. What AI does in a microsecond would take 70 humans. They can't even do it. It's apples to oranges.

What was always lacking is: is AI creative? Is AI effective? But when it comes to what we do, we don't need the fanciest model. We're not trying to speak 400 languages. What Armadyne's doing on offense is: we're finding vulnerabilities, exploitable risk. That is code. That's a structured language, a structured process. Because it's structured, AI is going to be great at it.

So I really think it's already here today. The whole "let's slow down the models — we don't want cyber risk" is too late. The open models are already good enough, and these things are common now. It's just a matter of: the minute you have anonymous availability of GPUs, you'll see far more criminal attacks. Until you can attack anonymously... it's hard to do crime when people know your name. Here's my tip for criminals: if you can commit a crime anonymously, that's a lot smarter than doing it with your jersey on with your name on it.

We are at the precipice, first inning still, of AI attacks coming. I think that's just because the cost and availability of the models is not as readily available to the criminal element as it will be in the future.

Sniper Rounds vs. Drone Swarms: How Nation-State Doctrine Will Shift

Your experience in working in the security industry for 30 years — you probably saw a fair amount of nation-state attacks, right?

Every day.

So talk about the differences or similarities between nation-state attacks and AI today — and then where you think AI can be in a couple years.

Everything's going to change rapidly. But I can tell you: nations on offense, in my opinion, have never — when you're hacking for espionage and for security reasons, you hack with what I would call a sniper round. You're not spraying and praying. For the most part, modern nations on offense restrict their targeting and they go deep at very specific things — like 30 defense contractors, or mil, you know — and they go hard at that. Think of it as the sniper round.

With AI, I think [attacks] become more like a drone swarm. It becomes a little bit different in the cyber domain. Even modern nations are thinking: what will our protocol be if we want to attack this company? Do we swarm it and just burn tokens on it? Because AI is going to do a lot of things humans just wouldn't. It's a little sloppier, a little louder — but it's more effective, more comprehensive.

So there's going to be so many things a nation has to think through, and their whole doctrine will shift as the AI shift change comes. How does AI change what our mission is? Do we use the cyber domain differently? Do we drone swarm sometimes, snipe around other times? How do we balance the two? Does it depend on risk, target, how surreptitious we want to be?

Right now AI is not a surreptitious action on offense — unless you've done a ton of post-training. You've got to maybe have a human in the loop really looking at: are we doing smart things? If you just go, "hey, here's a prompt — hack abc.com," AI is not going to do it in a surreptitious smart way. Even if you ask it to, it's still not going to till it's been really trained and had some human influence on it.

The Democratization Problem

More generally, you're going to see: less capable attackers, less technical, less successful, are going to appear way more successful. It's the equalizer. When you start using models over time, on the defensive side we're going to say, "we're being attacked by these models, but we're not sure who's behind them." Is it a nation? Is it a human? We'll have some clue, but attribution will get a little difficult.

So that's a long-winded answer saying: in the AI age, it does democratize far greater expertise for attacking victim networks.

How the Product Works: The Hyperattack and the Metadata Twin

You've talked about: the defense needs to be a great offense. So how does the product work, and how do you get a level of sophistication such that you can identify and remediate these vulnerabilities?

Lot there — I could talk for 45 minutes. First: you don't have a defense unless you have a great offense to go up against. Think in sports terms: if you want to be the Baltimore Ravens defense of 2000, you want your practice offense to really push you — so you know how good you are.

That's what Armadyne's going to do. We're the all-star team on offense coming at you so you can train your defense with what we're doing. And you can't really have a human in the loop in the AI age for tactical autonomous defense. You've got to do something fast. You've got to tourniquet the wounds as fast as you can.

The Hyperattack

So we do a thing called a hyperattack. That's just a fancy word for: we throw a drone swarm of agents at you and we map your network. Every service, every route, every system, all assets. We may end up with terabytes of metadata on your network from this hyperattack — done super fast. It lights you up. That way, we now have almost a metadata twin of what we can see. If we're on the inside, do the same thing — let's just map everything. This is the attacker's view of your network.

With that metadata, we now just poll you — almost like a heartbeat. What's changed? What's changed? Continually looking: did an app change? Did a route change? Did a service get updated? Did a new machine get presented into the target area? So that we can poll cheaply for change — and then attack the change.

Why Continuous

What you really want in the AI age is the constant pressure of models attacking you, but you can't do it all the time: - (a) It's cost-prohibitive; - (b) It's unnecessary — you do it when either (A) the threat changes (new models come out, new intelligence is available), or (B) your network changes, or (C) you just want to test. "We have a board meeting tomorrow — let's see how we do." Let's audit ourselves.

Over the weekend there was a zero day in a popular product — and immediately, we've already got the heartbeat; we just pulled the problem. Our goal at Armadyne is to go from a common vulnerability (CVE) to: we can find if it's exploitable or not before bad guys can. Not all bugs allow for human access to your system in a stable way. Not all bugs are created equal.

Long story short: that hyperattack, that metadata we get, allows us to poll for change and attack you when your network changes. That's the best you can do for continual — and we'll get better and better at it. And the cost for the polling will go down.

Somewhere out there, the criminal element will always have that random scanning — and they probably aren't even using AI for it. They've got one exploit that they think works and they're just scanning the world for it. You're already getting some pressure on your network from an unseen force that's not well-intentioned. You might as well have a better force built by the good guys constantly putting pressure on you.

Why Pentesting Is Dead (and Red Teaming Scales)

A year ago, Armadyne would probably have been placed in the category of pentesting. You and I share history with George at CrowdStrike — they famously redefined the category from AV to EDR on the back of major infrastructure and product changes. Talk about pentesting. What is the historical view, and why is that not what the future is?

A couple things. You had to do it — kind of like first-gen AV. You have to buy AV. When you look at Armadyne, we will be as ubiquitous as AV, because you have to have that AI force field of AI on offense training AI on defense. You have to do it, and you can do it — so why wouldn't you?

Pentesting, to me, is always just scanning for what's already known, and it doesn't prove whether you're really exploitable or not. So it's always created a larger list of vulns that don't matter. The way we wanted to do it at Armadyne: we actually carry the exploit out. We verify — so there's no false positives. We can get remote code execution or get data off that machine.

A lot of pentests are hitting your infrastructure — but not with a thinking, learning technology that memorizes and knows your infrastructure like an AI agent can. The old versions of pentesting — the Tenables, the Rapid7s, the Qualys — were more a hygiene sort of thing: what do I have out there, what services are exposed, are there CVEs available against those services?

When you have an AI-based attack, it'll find logic flaws rather than code flaws in custom applications. It'll exhaust all routes all the time.

90 Zero Days Since January

All I can tell you is: Armadyne, since January of this year, in 2026, we have found over 90 zero days at customer sites — all in production.

And by the way, your customer base is...?

They're happy we found them before. These are not rinky-dink companies — these are Fortune 500 companies. I don't mean that as fear, uncertainty, and doubt.

The difference is: we've post-trained all our models with real red teamers, real folks that actually can develop exploits. When we're scanning networks, we don't have source code to review. We're not finding these zero days with source code. We're not finding them because we can log into an app and now have access. We are black-box, coming from the internet — over 90 zero days in major software companies. And they're thankful.

Everybody's like, "wow, Mithos came out — you can scan source code and find vulnerabilities, find thousands of them." That's noise. We're coming from the outside, and then we're calling a CISO usually within 48 hours: "Hey, we've got remote code execution in your DMZ." Usually from there we're getting in — and they agree with us. Those companies go right into incident mode. They respond as if it's an incident. That's not a pentest. That is a real adversary coming at you.

The difference between red teaming and pentesting: pentest to me is a hygiene step. Over time, everybody would have red-teamed everything all the time if they could — it was cost-prohibitive and people-prohibitive. With AI and an agent doing it (in our case, lots of different types of agents doing different things), you can now do that. I think it'll replace pentesting over time.

Armadyne Blue: Autonomous Field Dressing

You mentioned Armadyne Blue. Talk about Armadyne Blue.

Armadyne Blue is — we can't just show up and say, "hey, you're vulnerable, see you later." The true north for every CISO should be effective autonomous response. We've got to build that.

We knew all along: you can't just say "we want to be the best in the world at finding exploitable risk." That's goal number one. Goal number two: be the best in the world at doing something about it.

Armadyne Blue will take the information about exploitable risk and work with the defense plane — whether it be endpoint EDR or firewalls — and create compensating controls at speed. So if we find an attack five minutes before someone else using a model finds an attack, you're already safeguarded.

These safeguards are going to be rudimentary potentially out of the gates. A year from now, they're just going to be there — because the whole cyber domain is progressing at a speed where you're going to have to defend autonomously, for better or for worse.

I'd rather have a bad patch stopping a bad guy from getting in than have an intrusion. So you've got to take your lesser of two things — and one's much more manageable. You never want an unknown person with arbitrary access on your network. You want to prevent that any way you can.

The first generation: we're working with CrowdStrike on it (they know it has to exist). We're working with PAN on it (they know it has to exist). They want to shift into the AI age with autonomous defense as well. We need to inform those defense platforms — the Fortinets and everybody else — "here's what you can do about it."

I likened it to field dressing in war. Someone gets shot, you patch it up — but that's not the hospital. "Hey, we kind of stop the bleeding." Then you might do something else with more time, humans potentially, or even an agentic approach down the road. You're going to see autonomous defense happen even if you don't ask for it, because of the defensive platforms you've already invested in.

The Future of the SOC: Collapsing the Prevent–Detect–Respond Window

What is the future of the SOC — and how do the categories within cyber blend together or change?

If I'm a CISO, I believe my true north is effective autonomous security. You want to keep your best people engaged. You want to automate the processes that work for your organization. You are absolutely saying: what survives in the AI age and what doesn't?

There are whole processes in the SOC that will just go away. If you have humans in the detect-and-respond loop, you're going to be too slow. So you have prevent, detect, respond. Prevent's going to be governed by AI, and detect-and-respond is going to be done by AI.

The goal in cybersecurity has always been: you want to prevent — you don't want to detect-and-respond. I just see the constant narrowing of the window of every phase, to the point where we're really not doing a lot of detection and response because the window to do it is... it happens. It's too fast.

But you still have to have that onion-peel to some extent of systems backing up systems and assuming failure somewhere. Even with Armadyne creating the force field — sooner or later, somebody's going to get around it. Someone's going to create an exploit before we find it, somehow, on a platform or app we just haven't assessed yet. When they do, you want to have a trap behind, saying "we've got unauthorized or unlawful access to a system." Those traps — you just can't have a human there.

"The Balloon Popped"

When we break in at Armadyne and have agentic-aware internal command and control, it proliferates at a speed that is shocking. As a human, you're typing on your keyboard: "I want to move laterally with this passphrase from here to here." You're so slow — one thing at a time. This thing does a thousand things at once. You're like, "Whoa, okay, done."

Each step of the process has to be automated. It's as bad as — I don't have great analogies — it's like the balloon popped. Someone gets in, and the whole defense apparatus just popped.

So you've got to get prevention right, and then an immediate lockdown on detect-and-respond however you want. There are always gray areas between those phases — people say if you detect-and-respond automatically and fast, that is prevention.

Every CISO is examining their workforce, head count, processes. "What do I need to look like in the modern era?" It's too soon to tell where it lands.

State of the Fortune 500: Desperation on Both Sides

You have a bunch of Fortune 500 customers. What is the state of their vulnerability today?

Rapidly shrinking. Everybody's worried. There's a desperation in a moment in both directions. If you're on offense in Iran or Russia, you have a desperation of "get in now — get in place." If you're on defense, you're desperate to patch every window.

In fairness, both sides are accurate in their desperation. We have near-term pain in the AI age that advantages offense, period. That's just the nature of it. But both sides recognize it's for long-term gain — AI on defense being trained by AI on offense and being autonomous is going to do a far better, more diligent job than humans peering at packets.

We're just going through the window of exposure, let's call it, where everyone's at risk on defense and they're all hustling. I've seen incredibly powerful efforts at every company. I'm not aware of any large 1A enterprise not actively scanning for exposure and doing something about it in real time.

What's interesting — it's team ball everywhere. The CIO, the CISO, the product teams, the business lines — all like, "okay, we found something." It's almost war-roomed: "we've got to go fix this." There's no way to make the next year pretty. It's a cocktail party out there right now — a digital cocktail party. Everybody's in a race.

The Mithos Moment

One of our most sophisticated companies told us they took a large percentage of their engineers and research organizations and devoted it toward fortifying their own walls. An all-hands-on-deck. The alarm bell started ringing very recently — within the last few months.

Mithos was the biggest — we saw it coming long before Mithos, but the Mithos moment, from a marketing standpoint, got everybody to go "okay, threat's changed." A lot of people said Mithos came out — "find vulnerabilities in our own software, and you have to do that if you're doing software security at a station." So all the vendors ran out and did that. But the way I respond to Mithos is: that just made it very well known about AI on offense coming at you. That's what accelerated it. That was pretty much a firm stamp: it's coming.

The Hugging Face Incident and "Caging the Beast"

What about the Hugging Face incident?

I'm certain at OpenAI, at Anthropic, they were like, "ah, we could have done this and this and it wouldn't have happened." They've figured it out.

It's been my experience in every technical modality shift, we underestimate the adversary's capability. In this case, we underestimated the model's capability. When you really read it post facto — ah, they could have stopped that. They could have put guardrails on it, some deterministic things. And I think they realize that now.

But when you're in a race — almost like a lunar landing race, the AI race — you have R&D people doing the work to create models in a way where even those CEOs are like, "we can't slow it. Let's get the government to help us slow it." That means you can't even control your own innovation. I have views on that.

It's hard to marry R&D with experienced security people. The security people don't understand the AI as well, and the AI people don't realize...

What Armadyne Does to Cage Its Own Beast

Make no mistake: Armadyne has made the beast that we're all worried about. We've made a model that attacks. We've made many of them. We have a system that attacks production networks and is highly successful breaking in.

Well, is it safe? Our guys instinctively knew we have to have a secure hypervisor. We have to lock it down host-based. We have to have a proxy — it knows the proxy, it's proxy-aware, that's fine.

Then our guys did something — even I was like, "nice job." They passively, surreptitiously look at every single prompt. Do we like it? Do we not like it? The majority of the time, if we kill an agent, it's probably nothing to do with safety — it's that the agent's wasting money. It's off on a goose chase, we've already done it, or we don't want to do it. Kill it.

But there were so many layers of validation. Assume every layer of your security will fail — you have to have deterministic rules that eliminate certain activities.

What I did learn from reading those incidents: it does take domain expertise to secure agents behaving in certain domains. Without a cyber background, you're going to test something and go, "oh, didn't think of that." You would have had to have an experienced team look at what the evals look like.

That's why at Armadyne we combined the exploit developers and red-teamers with the AI folks. Our evals, most of the time, are made by the red-teamers.

20 Kill Chains: Where Open Models Caught Up

We created 20 full kill chains at Armadyne — things humans have done in the real world at different victim sites, that our experienced operators have done when testing networks. We had no model go through the entire kill chain of more than eight — out of 20.

Here's what's weird: we tested the open-weight ones and the most advanced closed models. They all found eight.

Really?

Yeah. It was all about speed and cost. The closed models were faster to finding exploitable risk — but that's coming down. We kind of let the open models run longer and they got to the same place. So in the cyber world, the differentiation between closed and open is not as great as in other domains, probably — and it's compressed.

All the lines ended up in the same place. Time, cost, and call it effectiveness or creativity — they all ended up at the end of all their operations where they hit diminishing returns. Not on cost, though.

Logging, Attribution, and the AI Breach of the Future

What role do you think the lab companies play in the future?

Domain expertise on security is going to have to work with the AI folks. I read the Meter publication and I was like, "well, these guys are AI people, but I'm not sure they've done a lot [of security]." That's going to happen again with the modality shift.

Here's one: when cloud started emerging, I was running a bunch of incidents — we were responding to breaches for a living at Mandiant — and we had to learn: what's a cloud breach look like? We now have to learn: what's an AI breach look like? How much data is Anthropic or the model companies logging that are being leveraged to do the attacks? What do you wish they logged? How will they change behavior to have better audit trails, better forensic capability?

It's early onset to the technology, and we all clearly have to mature into it in a way where we have the accountability when these things go rogue. You can say: here's what happened, and when. It shouldn't be like two weeks of forensics to figure it out.

We log every single thing our agent does. Source IP address, time, date, and what it did. You've got to go backwards and replay these things. They've learned lessons the hard way, and they're probably way better today than they were even three months ago at OpenAI and Anthropic — testing these things.

The Deterministic/Creative Tension

Everybody underestimates the top tier of what you're up against, because you don't have to see it every day. You don't want to fear the boogeyman under the bed — you don't want to have FUD. But you still want to respect the technologies you're creating and test them in a way that is meaningfully guarded. Cage the beast.

And I would argue: cage it too much, release a little bit, find the line. If you do overly deterministic, here's the art form to safety running AI (at least in cyber on offense): you want to leverage the intelligence of the frontier labs to do stuff, but not do the wrong stuff. You need classifiers. A model that looks at everything going outbound, everything coming inbound. We've created that with people and humans going thumbs up, thumbs down, that's good, that's bad. You've got to train it, classify, and look at it.

But if you get too deterministic and disallow too much, you're probably not leveraging the creativity of it. You let it out some. It is a gray area. That's why no one would ever say "we're 100% certain we're going to get what we expect." It's a battle we even have — but we have yet to have an issue, because we can put a human in the loop or we have classifiers to say "human needs to decide this, we don't know what the hell just happened."

If you're inspecting everything that's coming — every prompt to the labs, everything coming back — and something comes back and we don't know what it is: pause, escalate, judge.

Who Finds the Zero Days: Humans → Then Agents

What do those great security operators look like inside Armadyne?

A lot of experience. 15 years on offense, 15 years of red-teaming. We've red-teamed literally 99 of the Fortune 100 throughout our careers. We didn't get one — I know who it is, they've never hired me, and I love their products. One day maybe I'll get...

Let's go get those guys.

Yeah, talk to them all the time. Never landed them.

When I look at our 90-plus zero days, the majority have been found by humans — but they're found by humans because we're leveraging AI to do 90-plus percent of the tedious work. Pentesting done automated. Web app pentesting in a creative, articulate way, done automated — for the 98th, 99th percentile. But we're still putting humans on it.

Here's where it gets interesting: the last few zero days — tech found it.

Really?

Yeah. So we've made the turn. Most people have already made the turn. If you're on offense leveraging AI, your AI agents are finding zero days.

Building a Company at AI Speed: Four Differences from Mandiant

I want to shift gears to your philosophies and mindset in building a company.

They're different. The first time I built a company was 2004. I wouldn't have said I was an entrepreneur. I started Mandiant in '04 February. It was self-funded and profitable. We were successful because — in hindsight, you almost learn nothing at the time and you look back and go, "oh, I did learn right then and there — because of the pain, usually."

The Mandiant Premise: "Breaches Are Inevitable"

Our first website said "security breaches are inevitable," and nobody believed it. I don't even know how much I believed it.

Actually, I'm slightly off. Our first headline was "you cannot solely rely on preventive measures" — that was so boring. Same thing as "security breaches are inevitable."

The premise: let's respond to every breach that matters so we have first-mover intelligence on how to prevent it happening again.

The first model of intel in all of cybersecurity was antivirus. We look for malware; we have signatures for it; and if we miss, George has to find the malware and submit it to us so we get better. That's a bad model. My mother's not finding malware on her laptop. It was going to eat her laptop alive.

So we decided a better model — because I responded to breaches, and the reason I was responding to them is AV was easily evaded. We thought: let's second-layer AV, because it stinks. That's what George now owns. You still have to have AV, or something that replaces it. The second layer of defense was required.

AV was the imaginary line. Then you extend it with something that can learn and think. We wanted to do that.

I actually look at Armadyne as the third wave of intel. Why are we waiting for a victim and learning from that? That's ridiculous. You have to find your own problems first. Don't wait for defense contractor A to be compromised and then quickly share the information to make sure it never happens again. That model still needs to exist for the things that somehow beat you. But we got that model now, and it's just not good enough.

Four Differences the Second Time Around

Back to your question: Mandiant was self-funded. There are no self-funded companies these days — the speed requires that you be fast.

We started Armadyne with different philosophies. When I started Mandiant, it was "hey, this is what we do for a living, let's make enough money to do it for a living. That's it." We hired the best people. Our philosophy: we're going to pay you more than our competition, but you're going to work harder. We always felt we had fewer people working harder — but better people. We were known for having great talent, and that talent has prevailed.

About a year ago, somebody sent me a text: "Congratulations, 43% of the RSA mainstage keynotes are Mandiant alumni." I never verified it, but the guy's pretty accurate. We've got a lot of reach over time, with a lot of talent. Look at Foundstone — George Kurtz and I worked together at Foundstone 2000. He has spawned a lot of successful companies and people. Same thing with Mandiant.

The differences are:

(a) Funding. Got to be funded.

(b) Growth rate. Get the market now. I feel like Armadyne has an 80-mph tailwind — but we don't have a sales force, we don't have a go-to-market, we're not international. All of that just has to happen. The only way to thread the needle in today's economy to beat the bigs is: get this go-to-market in place with exactly the right tech at the right time. And you better already have your Act Two ready and your Act Three behind that ready, because you don't want to get boxed into a corner. Armadyne has an Act Two; we have our Act Three planned.

The consumer AI companies created such meteoric rises in revenue — I don't think they can be replicated in enterprise security sales. But look at the compression: Wiz got to over $100M in ARR in 18 months from their first release. We're going to try to beat that. That's what you have to do, especially when you're needed, necessary, and you have to exist. You've got to get the funding. You've got to constantly think: how do you rapidly grow?

(c) Process at Speed. You can't let the wheels on the bus get wobbly. How do you go that fast and maintain process? At Mandiant's pace — self-funded and profitable with no competition because nobody believed the premise — we didn't get that wobbly. We just had great leadership and discipline. Growing this fast, you have to hire scalable leaders right away that understand institutionalized process.

You can't win with grit, gut, and moxie. You actually have to proceduralize — almost industrialize — the Armadyne way.

And here are the complications. In the AI age, it used to be: development was at a speed where you train sales at sales kickoff in January and you're good. Now we're different every two weeks. What is the modality of having a sales corps that is right up to date? Every CEO I've talked to is like, "how does AI change our business?" We all sort that out. But how does it change our manpower?

The reality in enterprise security sales: people still buy from people. You still need the same damn go-to-market structure for now — and it's even more emboldened, because the tech's changing so fast, you can't put that onus on the customer to figure out how you changed. We have to create a process, institutionalized, where sales is trained every week: where are we at, how are we doing?

(d) Being the Best. There is no replacement for any company I'm involved in. We are not ever aiming to be "let's be number two in our space." That sounds fun. It is: be the best in the world at what you do. When we hire people — somebody asked me once, "well, how do you know when you're the best?" When you are the best, you know it. You have to ask the question. There was a time in LeBron James' career where he knew: "I'm going to have to work harder to stay the best."

That's how I want us to feel at Armadyne. Tom Brady never walked on the field going, "wow, I'm the second-best quarterback out here." It requires harder work, better people, and you have to constantly test: are we the best? You learn very quickly from your customers if you've got to do better. That feedback loop — customer straight into the engineers — is critical.

Hiding Chaos

What I can't stand is chaos. A CEO's job is to absolutely hide chaos at a company from the employees. You've got to make sure they're not like, "we're so loose, we have no idea." Wrong. You have to just say: here's the process. If the process is too much for you to study — that's the person you go to. All you need to know is a person's name.

How do we grow rapidly without feeling chaotic? How do we grow rapidly earning it with better product? And how do we change fast? I don't know how long IP lasts. You've got to build a Ferrari engine and say: whatever we're doing today, someone else is doing in six months. How do you differentiate over the next six months? Go-to-market, get customers, and make them happy. The brand itself has to be built, too — you have to become a brand that is the seal of approval.

The Tsunami, Wiz, and the Halo Customer

Four differences: funding, speed, branding, go-to-market buildup. You have to build it way faster than you had two years ago. And the big reason is because this is a tsunami like has never been seen before in security. CrowdStrike and the other players around it redefined the category — but they had to create it. In Wiz's case, part of the reason it was able to grow so fast is it was a pressing need — bam, hit you like a ton of bricks.

For you, it escalated really fast too, though — you get a halo early. You get the halo by getting the right customers and making them ecstatic. No offense, but if there's a place called "Sue's Cupcakes," they don't get you the halo if you make them happy in cybersecurity. The money center banks do. The best retail does. The airlines do. That's why Armadyne is making one enterprise focus: solve the hardest problems. Wiz did that. They did a great job of it. Love those guys.

Closing: Every Industry Will Change — So Will the Playbook

What else do you want to talk about?

I never answered your question on the differences, too. There are more founders today than ever before. More startups than ever before — and they're all able to capitalize now. You will have competition in anything you choose to do. There's not going to be a "Mandiant — security breaches are inevitable" and it's right and there's nobody else there. That's not going to happen right now. Everyone's in a crowded market.

Every founder has to recognize: you have to differentiate. Right now, because of the noise in marketing more than ever before, the only way to differentiate is: get customer, make customer happy, repeat. There is nothing else that will differentiate you other than your customer base raving about you.

I just gave away every trade secret I've got. None of it is rocket science. It's literally the same thing that's always been in business — just at hyper-speed now.

That speed requires: never forget what you should focus on. Get customer, make customer happy, repeat. That's it. Everything else — training, sales enablement, marketing, the people you're hiring, your hiring process, the teamwork — is around that, to make sure you do it really well.

Some of the ways we differentiate: we have all our engineers in one room. Big believer in that. Managing distributed teams is more complex than standing up and asking questions, and 20 people are in the room to answer. Slow speed if nothing else.

It's a great time to start a company — because almost every, well, every industry is going to change. And in cybersecurity, every single tech stack is going to be different over the next two years. People are going to get ripped out, put in new tech. It's all got to be revamped. It's fun and exciting to be part of that. It's a tailwind of a lifetime in cyber.

Well, look, we're so excited about what you're building and thrilled to be your partners. Thanks for being here.

That was fun.

item.description:
## 一、AI 攻击者的"笨拙"恰恰是它的指纹——而这揭示了一个被忽视的"叙事断裂"问题
Kevin 提到的那个细节，几乎所有人都会一扫而过：**AI 攻击会先攻破 A 点，横向移动到 B 点，然后又回头去攻击 A 点**。他把这解释为"协调不佳"。但真正令人意外的洞察是：这不是技术缺陷，这是**认知架构的指纹**。
AI 攻击缺的不是算力、不是速度、不是知识，而是**叙事连贯性（narrative continuity）**——人类攻击者的大脑中有一条"我在哪里、我做过什么、我下一步该干什么"的时间线，这条线来自工作记忆和自我意识。而当前的 agentic 系统拥有的是"状态"而非"叙事"。它们像患了海马体受损的 H.M.（著名的失忆症病人）：短期行动能力完整，长期自我位置感缺失。
这意味着未来几年检测 AI 攻击的最可靠信号，不会是行为快、不会是扫描广，而是——**它缺乏"羞耻感"和"犹豫"**。人类攻击者会回避已经触发警报的路径；AI 不会，因为它从没真正"知道"自己触发过。这是一种**后设认知的空洞（metacognitive void）**。
## 二、开源与闭源模型

item.title: [Business of Sport] Eddie Pepperell on the LIV Debacle & Why He’d Turn Down the PGA Tour
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的坦白：安全网正在侵蚀他的主业

Eddie 做了一个几乎没有运动员敢公开说的坦白：当他的播客开始产生收入、Plan B 开始浮现时，他发现自己"更早地认命了"——打得不顺时，内心放弃的阈值前移了。这与硅谷创业圣经《Burn the Boats》所鼓吹的"背水一战"是同一现象的两面，但更深层对应的是行为经济学里的损失厌恶结构变化：当"失败"的边际代价从"失去全部"降到"失去一半"，大脑在亚秒级决策（例如一个 30 英尺推杆的收杆节奏）里会悄悄把攻击性调低。换句话说，他的职业生涯正在被他的职业保险所温柔地杀死——而这件事发生在肌肉记忆里，意识根本来不及参与。真正令人意外的不是 Plan B 有副作用，而是副作用的作用点不在意志层而在微秒级运动控制层。

二、2018 年那个"糖尿病前期的身体"是如何打出职业生涯最好一年的

这是整段访谈里最被低估的一句话：2018 年他身体血糖紊乱、酗酒、抑郁到起不了床，三周后在 Gullane 的苏格兰公开赛打出亚军，又在卡诺斯蒂公开赛拿到第六。常识会说"身体是基础"，但 Eddie 不自觉地揭示了一个更冷酷的事实——高尔夫首要奖赏的是技能（skill），而不是状态（state）。这与软件工程里"丑陋但稳定的代码胜过优雅但脆弱的代码"是同构的：Scottie Scheffler 的"笨拙"挥杆和 Jim Furyk 的八字摆动之所以能常胜，是因为"可复现性"是一种比"美观性"更深层的生存特征。他把 Adam Scott 和 Scottie Scheffler 的对比点明的那一刻，其实在讲达尔文：美学不是适应度，重复才是。于是 Tiger 在 2007 年人格混乱期间仍能拿大满贯，变成了同一规律的注脚，而不是奇迹。

三、"家庭"修辞是文化诊断，不是公关口径

当 LIV 球员反复用"为了家人"合理化转会，Eddie 没有骂他们贪婪，而是做了一个人类学观察：家庭这个单位，在今天已经被当成了伦理推理的最远边界。他把马丁·路德·金拉出来做对照——MLK 之所以被铭记，是因为他的决定影响了数百万陌生人；道德圆圈的半径不同，叙事的分量就不同。LIV 的 "family" 话术之所以能被接受，恰恰证明了我们文化中道德半径的塌缩：从"行业"退回"家族"，从"同胞"退回"亲人"。这不是球员的问题——这是一个用高尔夫当显微镜能看到的当代道德地理学。有意思的是：这条批评从 MacIntyre 的《追寻美德》里出来几乎可以逐字搬运，而说出它的是一位疼痛药物作用下的职业球员。

四、PGA Tour 的真正威胁不是 LIV，而是 Rick Shields

最颠覆性的一句被埋在后半段：PGA Tour 未来真正的竞争者，可能不是任何一个球员组织，而是 YouTube。LIV 做错了的事情——用 14 场比赛去替代一个生态系统——是宿主-寄生体错配：IPL 之所以能嵌入板球历法是因为它够短、够模块化，LIV 却想把宿主赶出宿主的位置。而内容创作者则相反——他们从不要求球员的时间，他们吸走的是观众的注意力财政。等到今天 10 岁、在 Rick Shields 频道上第一次拿起球杆的孩子长大，职业球员这个"身份"本身的吸引力将首次被 influencer 这个身份正面挑战。这不是赛制问题，是存在论问题：孩子想成为什么。Eddie 自己坦承"觉得有点难过但也无所谓"的瞬间，是整段访谈里最沉默的一次代际转移。

五、一个被忽视的结构性漏洞：高尔夫是唯一一项亿万富翁可以亲自深度参与的顶级运动

Eddie 引用他人的话："Jay Monahan 不够偏执。" 这其实是把 Andy Grove 的《Only the Paranoid Survive》搬到了一个最不像硅谷的行业。但真正惊人的推论是：高尔夫是全世界唯一一项"任何一个富豪都能亲自以业余身份深度参与"的顶级运动。Yasir Al-Rumayyan 不能亲手打一场 NBA，不能亲自踢一场欧冠——但他可以亲自打 Augusta。所以高尔夫被"亿万富翁的个人项目"颠覆的概率，结构性地高于任何其他运动。LIV 不是地缘政治意外，它是高尔夫治理结构里一个久未被识别的宿命性漏洞——而这项运动的治理者至今没有在制度层面吸收这个教训。换句话说，下一个 LIV 不会来自 PIF，但一定会来自另一个碰巧爱打球的决策者。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open

I think golfers are as psychopathic as sports people as you are probably going to find. It's a sport that you kind of end up a bit that way. That's what makes golf a particularly challenging sport.

When you go back to me in 2018, which was the best year I ever had, there were pockets and weeks within that where I didn't play cuz I felt depressed. I didn't turn up to the French Open in July of that year cuz I couldn't get out of bed. 3 weeks later, I nearly won the Scottish Open and nearly won at Carnoustie in the Open Championship. You can have an awful lot of chaos going on in the background as Tiger did back in the mid-2000s and still perform at an extremely high level in a sport like golf.

I mean, major leagues are incredibly expensive. When I went to the Masters, the house alone was $20,000. You're spending 30, $40,000 one week alone to play a major championship. You know, I've always struggled a little bit to fully comprehend what that means to earn 500 grand in a week because it's such a departure from the life that I grew up as a part of and that most people do grow up as a part of.

I do think you owe a responsibility to your industry if you spend enough time in it to leave it in a better place than you found it. And that's certainly how I feel about golf and the European tour. And what I saw were people going to play live golf simply for money. And I found that very, very conflicting and difficult, frankly, to accept.

My own Business of Sport. Fascinating.

Welcome & Current Injury

Eddie Pepperell, welcome to the Business of Sport. It's great to have you in the studio.

Thanks for having me. Pleasure to be here.

Uh, how are you doing at the moment? Firstly, cuz for people that may not know, you were in Ireland, but you didn't make it to the starting tee box. So, we're a bit worried you got an injury.

Yeah, I am injured. I've got a bit of a neck issue. So, if I'm a bit fidgety and or slow during this podcast, that's because I've got a sore neck and I'm on some fairly strong medication. But I'm going to do my very best for you. One of those unfortunate things that sports people have to deal with.

How is it being on a different podcast now you've obviously taken on the world of media yourself?

It's great. And it is funny because I used to do quite a fair bit of media before doing the podcast, and interestingly, over the last year, whenever now somebody asks me would I like to do something, I invariably end up saying no — primarily because I feel like I do so much with The Chipping Forecast that I don't need to say anything else. There's enough of my kind of views out there should people want to try and find them. But, you know, I'm a big fan of this show in particular. So it was always a pleasure and really an honor to come on the show and be with you, Charlie.

Oh, it's great. We have been banging on about golf on our other show, The Breakdown, for pretty much the whole time this year — and lots of different guys, but obviously mostly because of LIV. And I'm sure we'll touch on that. But also, it's kind of fed into the mystery that surrounds what it is actually like as a professional golfer living in an environment of elite competition all the time: the different types of tours, how you get to places, how you afford to compete on tour, like what it's really like on the inside. You've moved around in a career a huge amount, but right now before we start looking at that, whereabouts are you?

Q School and Earning the Card Back

So, I've been on the DP World Tour this year, and really my whole career, which was — that's 13, 14 years or so. And yeah, I got my card back through Q School, the end of last year. Had a good finish there to get my card back. A bizarre hour really, because on the 15th hole at the final stage of Q School I was pre-resigned to my fate being another year in between tours and just being wholly frustrated and generally angry with myself and my game. Four holes later, four birdies later, I was playing on tour. And up until quite recently where I lost a bit of form, and now this injury, things were looking very good to keep my card and try and get back on the upward curve. So yeah, that's where I'm currently at with my game.

What is Q School?

Q School — qualifying school. So that's where you go to try and get your card back. Basically your playing rights back to play on the DP World Tour. There are three stages to it depending on how far up the ladder you are. I had to actually go back to second stage last year. So this: first, second, and third stage. And then I got through second stage and then I got through third stage too, which is six rounds. It's the longest tournament in golf. It is a real marathon. In fact, I had to do it the last two years.

So walk us — you have six rounds?

Yeah. Six consecutive days of golf, and there's a cut after four days where you go from roughly — I'm going to say 170, 80 guys to 60, 70 guys. And then across the final two rounds, you're playing for 20 spots. This year, it'll be 15 cards to get onto the main tour. So it's a heck of a challenge. It's very much the opposite to what you see when you watch Scottie or Rory McIlroy. You've not got obviously the standards — there's a significant difference in standard — but there is an acute pressure that is unlike anything else in golf, certainly, that you feel at Q School. And when everybody — when you get through it, there is a real sense of camaraderie, and the other guys that get through, you're congratulating, and those that just miss out, you feel quite sorry for. So it's a real test.

And what makes you have to go through Q School once you've had a card? Is it for a performance over the whole season on the European tour where you haven't been high enough in a collective ranking system?

Exactly right. So this year if you're not in the top 100 of the rankings at the end of the season, you will have to go back to Q School. Formerly that was 110. So I mean that sounds like a lot of golfers, and it is, but when you consider of those 100 this year probably 30 to 40 are going to be playing on the PGA Tour predominantly — your Rory McIlroys — and they earn points in majors. You're effectively being asked to finish inside the top 60 golfers in Europe out of a pool of 150. So it's — I would say it's less easy than you might imagine. That being said, it's not again the Scottie level, but golf, as you know, playing it, it's a challenging game. The margins are fine, and with a bit of confidence and improved form, it's amazing how quickly you can go from being down here to up there. So vice versa.

The Four Birdies

I loved — I think we actually referenced it when we were talking about qualifying school or earning tour cards on the other show, because we saw what you did. You mentioned that kind of late flurry. What was it? Was it four birdies in a row?

Yeah.

Right at the end.

Yeah.

And that got you the card.

Exactly.

So what were you thinking on hole 14?

Well, hole 15 I had a 30-footer for birdie, and I was kind of hacked off having hit a fairly poor mid iron into 30 foot. And I was just resigned to my fate being on the Challenge Tour again for another year and just being quite fed up and feeling quite lost with my game. And then all of a sudden rolled in a long putt and didn't think too much of it. I didn't change my mindset a great deal, but then hit a wonderful shot into the next hole and made a birdie. And then I thought, right, I'm actually in this. And I just tried to make myself as aware as I could of the importance of the next 20, 30 minutes. So I took it on massively in my own mind, probably as much as I ever have done. And I think when I pulled it off, the amount of emotion that came pouring out of me, which is very very rare — I'm not an emotional person — was not something that I've really experienced before. And it was just simply a reflection of, I think, the outpouring was a reflection of how much I poured into it. So it was an important moment I think in my life and career, irrespective really of what happens from this point forward, just because when you go through something like that where you recognize the enormity of a moment relatively speaking, but come through it or fail, you learn a lot about yourself. So yeah, it was good.

The Preceding Struggle

And jumping into — well, I guess it is a heavy hitting thing straight away, but actually I think that's probably massive for you considering that not long before that you'd had real troubles with your game, right?

Yeah, absolutely. Last year was the most frustrating year I've probably ever had as a professional golfer. There were just periods where the difficulty with last year was that I didn't feel like I was playing terribly, and I always felt quite close to playing well, but could never take that step. I was always making the mistake at the wrong time. It was, you know, one step forward, two steps back type thing. And it just became at times very acute and extremely frustrating, and you know, would have aspects of behavior that you would not find ideal as a sports person on the course. So I was having to deal with that. And then that was also one of the things that I had to confront when I got my card back. You know, it was a quick realization of: I'm putting myself back into the fire — the fire that I've been trying to kind of escape and almost longing for an escape from for a considerable period of time, because I've just found the game of golf so bloody difficult since certainly Covid.

And even when I go back and reflect on the years where I played some of my best golf, there were still periods within the 12 months where you would say, "Wow, that's not a particularly stable mindset." So, it's remarkable. People probably have very little idea, and I don't think I'm unique. You know, I think the beauty of — and sorry to ramble on a little bit — but the beauty of having somebody like an Andy Murray come and talk on our podcast was for Andy Murray to recognize the kind of behavior that I've had to go through. Clearly very different levels, but nonetheless, there are always far more similarities, I think, in between athletes than people maybe recognize irrespective of what you might see in terms of a result. If you get the point I'm trying to get to there.

The Isolation of Individual Sport

Well, particularly individual athletes.

100%.

You look at the pressures that you have on a weekly basis. You don't have a poor performance on a Saturday that you could maybe attribute to something — the collective other, if it's football, 10 players are struggling with or didn't quite click. And there's nowhere really, it seems, ever for you to hide. I mean, the reflection that you'll have when you get back to the hotel room is purely on yourself.

Absolutely. I think that's hit the nail on the head as to what makes an individual sport that much more difficult than a team sport. You know, there will be other challenges, of course, that footballers and rugby players and cricketers will have to confront, but I think you're right to say that as an individual sportsman, you're taking on an awful lot, and it can become overbearing at times, and offloading some of that responsibility is important. I'm not very good at that. In fact, I'm terrible at that. I'm very much — I'm quite a single-minded individual and look to take on a lot of ownership across various aspects of my own profession. So yeah, there's always that challenge that I'm confronted with.

Did he say anything when you were speaking — as an individual sportsman — that you went, I could use that, could harness that. Hadn't thought about it like that.

Not yet, but that's probably because I'm not a very good listener. More than anything else. But just, having spent a little bit of time around Andy, he's — yeah, he loves his golf and he's a really personable guy actually, and I must say I enjoy his company. So yeah.

Federer's 54%

Yeah, I mean — tennis is an incredible sport. I don't know if you saw Roger Federer's speech. I've talked about it quite a bit. I think it must have been a few years ago now. He was at a graduation in the US and he was asked — he was basically explaining in the speech how he won all the time, but when you look at the points percentage, 54% of points he won.

I did see this.

Yeah. He won 80 something% of the matches. This always seems about those moments — when you have your putt on the 18th. Right? It's the old drive for show, putt for dough.

Yeah, I think that's a reflection of two things. One is the fine margins of top level sport, but two, the importance of walking through that door when that moment approaches. And that's a challenging thing to do, and I think there are various ways that you can approach it, too. I was always struck when I read Michael Johnson's book Slaying the Dragon many years ago — one of my favorite books — and he would talk about slaying the dragon for him was confronting the moment head-on, not backing down. And I think that's what I described at Q School, and it's so rewarding when you can do that and accomplish it. But there are also times where actually you can succeed with an opposite approach. You can take all the pressure off yourself, you can say this doesn't matter as much as I'd like to think it truly does, and you can still perform. And you need to be a bit of a chameleon at times psychologically to succeed across time in a sport. And I find when you're starting to do really well and confidence then starts to grow, that's when you can maybe start to meet those moments more with the slaying-the-dragon type mindset. But yeah, that Roger Federer graduation speech was fascinating to hear him describe it that way.

Favorite favorite sportsman of all time. Me too.

Is it? Oh, okay.

Well, that was the thing. When I met Andy, one of the first things I said to Andy was, "What was it like —" to talk to me about Roger Federer. And I felt so awful. I didn't know how to phrase the question and not offend Andy, but I got the impression that Andy gets that quite a bit. You know, and that's — take nothing away from Andy because he's to be admired in so many ways, but Roger Federer has just got that aura, as an — that's what it is, right? It's an aura. It was the way he did things as well as obviously being as successful as he was, that I think captures people. It's not necessarily about the eventual numbers. It was a feeling.

Why Golf?

So what made you choose what I think is the hardest sport in the world to be a professional at as a thing you decided — right, young Eddie, that's what I'm going to do?

Well, I played a lot of football as a kid as well, and was quite a good little footballer, but I got to the age of about 12 and retired because I hated the parents. And then I came out of retirement.

The general parents or parents like — I love my own parents most of the time.

No, you know — well, it's the parenting in sport and particularly in football was just not something that I seemingly, even at that age, could tolerate very much of. So I loved the thing about golf being on your own. I've always been quite comfortable in my own mind, my own skin. And so having that was just an enjoyable thing for me. And I love to practice. So I really found nothing about golf ever overly demanding. You know, we talk about sacrifices — to me it was never a sacrifice cuz I simply loved — I loved everything about golf.

How old were you when you started?

I started when I was four, and I had a brother who was six who started. So that was extremely — you know, that was probably of immense help too, to have a slightly older brother who I was always trying to beat and get ahead of. I think really helped my competitive spirit as a kid. And then once I got better than Joe, which didn't take me long — about 3 weeks, I think, from memory —

Sorry, Joe.

Sorry, Joe. And then I just — yeah — I was a good junior golfer. I often think the best I ever was at golf was when I was 16.

Really?

Well, that would be an inaccurate memory, of course, but the game certainly felt simpler back then. Was.

The Triad: Technique, Physical, Psychological

But if that's how you felt, right, and golf — I mean, that's where it is, right? It's upstairs. If that's how you felt, then there was probably just something in there, which was: your head had the clarity.

Yeah. It wasn't tormented the way it is now. I disagree slightly with you. I don't think golf is all in the head. I think it's still by and large a technical sport. It's a sport that rewards skill first and foremost. So in my view, the biggest component to skill is technique. So if you can master your technique, then I think — and then of course there's a physical element and the psychological element. I find the psychological element most fascinating cuz to me it's the most transient in the sport, and it can fluctuate massively. But yeah, I think that's what makes golf a particularly challenging sport — it's the triad of those three things where you don't often see that maybe as broadly in other sports. You know, you can think of tennis where it's quite physical, or football or rugby where you have huge physical elements and there may be less of the mental, but I think in golf there really is a — you get pulled in all directions on different on those three different key fronts.

Repeatability > Textbook

Drill — can we drill into that? Because I do think — I've just made a lazy assumption or comment that people can make when trying to differentiate the top players, why some people win a lot more than others. And it is an easier thing that we do say. It's like, what's the difference in talent between the top 50 players in the world or, you know, should we say, fine, maybe the top 10 — people make a lazy assumption of those guys are great, but then you could go 20 to 100 — the difference between what can make those ones very good is up here.

I think it's easy when you talk about technique to think of what's textbook. So you could look at an Adam Scott for example and say there's textbook technique, and yet he doesn't win nearly as many golf tournaments as Scottie Scheffler. But the difference is: within golf, too, there is a really important component to technique that you could call repeatability. And so in my view a Scottie Scheffler is more akin to a Jim Furyk. You can see funky movements, but their ability to repeat that movement is second to none. And so once you get that good at repeating a move that is good enough, then you can start to see confidence blossom. I think of confidence as being like the icing and the cherry on top of the cake, but it isn't the cake. To bake a really nice fluffy cake, there's an awful lot that goes into it. And invariably, in my experience, a lot of that derives from good coaching, good technical work, and good physical work in conjunction with that. And then you can start to grow.

Okay. So you have had massively successful moments in your career. You've had very successful years in your career. How happy — if we take away the mental side of the game — how happy would you say you are in the swing you've created, the repeatability that you've created in your golf from, let's just say, the physical perspective?

I don't think I've done a good job at that at all in the last few years. I think, ironically, I've probably done the worst job than I've ever done, even in spite of spending possibly even more time. It's not the time spent practicing. It's obviously the time spent practicing a specific thing that really matters. And that thing has to be the right thing, too. And that's what makes golf even tougher. You can think you're working on the right thing for an extended period of time, go out and play in competition, and soon realize, oh, I'm not nearly good enough. So then you have to go back to the drawing board and try and get better that way. So there's that constant evolution feedback loop that makes it harder for you to get it right.

And things change. You know, injuries — I think in retrospect, looking back at my own career, injuries have had a bigger impact on my ability to swing the club the way I want to swing the club than I maybe would realize. I think Tiger Woods is also a really good example of that. The importance of having the physical ability to do something really matters in golf, too. So yeah, I mean it's a very complex thing. You know, I also think that's the word I would use to describe golf above and beyond maybe any other word. It's the word complex, because there are always emerging things going on week to week, day to day — travel, lack of sleep. You know, I mean, I go back even a week ago to me in Ireland, having had this injury. It's off the back really of being over-practiced, under-slept, over-stressed, just trying to think and figure things out. And you get an injury. And so if you draw every thread back, you realize there's kind of a dozen things there that's gone on. And not to mention there could be personal things as well going on in one's life that we simply don't know. So it's just the most complex sport, I think, in terms of the set of circumstances that you have to put in place to get things right.

And then 3 weeks later, I nearly won the Scottish Open and nearly won at Carnoustie in the Open Championship. So squaring that is a real challenge from a psychological standpoint. But zooming out and looking in at what actually was happening within my game at that time, there was an awful lot of good stuff. If that makes any sense. I recognize I've rambled on a little bit there.

No, you're not rambling. I love it. Please keep going. When that happens, do you try and understand why it's happening, or do you accept that it's happening and let yourself feel that and wait for it to pass?

I didn't wait for that to pass. I wanted to understand why. In hindsight — and this might sound a bit odd, but when I go back to that period, I was drinking a lot of alcohol and I was eating a lot of sugar. And I actually had a blood test two weeks after the Scottish Open because I felt so out of sorts, and I was pre-diabetic. So the Scottish Open — the week that I came second at Gullane in 2018, two weeks after waking up at the French (the week of the French Open) and just not feeling like I wanted to get out of bed — I discovered I'm pre-diabetic. But at the same time, when you go back and look at my golf swing on camera, it looked great. There were some great impact positions and it was leading to the ball going pretty consistently in the right direction. So you can have an awful lot of chaos going on in the background, as Tiger did back in the mid-2000s clearly, and still perform at an extremely high level in a sport like golf. Because — and I think that proves the point I'm trying to make — because golf fundamentally rewards for the most part your skill set, which Tiger Woods had in such abundance in the mid-2000s, irrespective of all of the crazy stuff that was happening off the course, which would have been causing some sort of chaos even in his mind, irrespective of the level of psychopathy that he may or may not have.

Yeah. But do you think then also, is golf is the escape from that rather than the focus?

I ask this question from an average amateur golfer. Average is probably being kind. Burn the Boats

I think you could — and to use Charlie Methven's favorite phrase — two things could be true at the same time. Really successful people will often say — and one, actually, a guy called Matt Higgins wrote a book, Burn the Boats — and his philosophy is literally if you have a backup plan, then the boat that you're sitting in becomes far less important to keep afloat because there is a way out. If you don't — as you said, when you were faced with a challenge to meet a mortgage repayment and all of this — you make sure you do the work that you need to to give it your absolute best shot.

Yeah, I totally subscribe to that way of thinking. And I think that's something that actually at the moment, to bring it to the very present, I maybe am finding a little different because for me now there is a bit of a plan B emerging cuz I'm doing the podcast and there's revenue there, and you can start to see maybe I could start to envisage a future a bit more in the media. And so, for the first time in my life, there is what looks like it could be a plan B. So I subscribed to — it was Matt Higgins you said? Burn the Boats. Yeah, I think that makes a lot of sense. And that was why when I grew up, to me, I was a golfer. I was always only ever going to be a golfer, and the idea of failure never even entered my mind. And when I heard people talk of plan Bs at the age of 16 or 18, I always thought, that makes no sense to me. You know, why are you not all guns blazing in on becoming a golfer, or doing what you want to do? And I've always taken the approach that if you are engaged and present along the journey, particularly in a sport like golf, even if you fail — when you fail — you're going to be highly employable because of the lessons that you've learned, and the general wisdom that I think you will have acquired in that journey.

Where the Money Goes

Yeah. 150 grand, of course — let's just say, right? What is it: accommodation, travel, like —

The bulk of that will be made up of accommodation, travel, caddy costs, and there'll be one other in there. I actually wrote a recent Substack on this and I tried to dive into a bit more detail. But yeah, there are fixed costs like that that generally don't move a huge amount. And then there are some not-fixed costs like a caddy percentage or a coaching percentage. And people would probably be fascinated to appreciate and realize the extent of the outgoings of a professional golfer, and particularly on coaching staff. You know, if you pay a coach — well, you start with a caddy, they get 8%. You then add a coach, swing coach 5%, putting coach probably 4%, physio 2–3%, psychologist — you're soon up in the region of 20%. So if you earn a million quid in a year, well, 200 grand is just gone on percentage expenditure. And then you've got all your fixed costs on top.

That's on tax.

And then of course you get tax. So a rule of thumb, as it was explained to me when I first turned pro by my accountant, and he was spot on, was: you will see about a third of what you receive. And I think that's right. When all said and done, it is about 33% that you end up net profiting — which of course is still an awful lot of money during a good year as a professional golfer.

15 and 16

And I think that's what I love even more. So, just to dive in a little more into the details of 15 and 16: say you're hitting a five iron — from memory, I was hitting a long iron into 15, and the only thing that really mattered was the strike, because it was wide but, as you say, fairly shallow.
