item.description:
### 一、最反直觉的坦白：安全网正在侵蚀他的主业
Eddie 做了一个几乎没有运动员敢公开说的坦白：当他的播客开始产生收入、Plan B 开始浮现时，他发现自己"更早地认命了"——打得不顺时，内心放弃的阈值前移了。这与硅谷创业圣经《Burn the Boats》所鼓吹的"背水一战"是同一现象的两面，但更深层对应的是行为经济学里的**损失厌恶结构变化**：当"失败"的边际代价从"失去全部"降到"失去一半"，大脑在亚秒级决策（例如一个 30 英尺推杆的收杆节奏）里会悄悄把攻击性调低。换句话说，他的职业生涯正在被他的职业保险所温柔地杀死——而这件事发生在肌肉记忆里，意识根本来不及参与。真正令人意外的不是 Plan B 有副作用，而是副作用的作用点不在意志层而在**微秒级运动控制层**。
### 二、2018 年那个"糖尿病前期的身体"是如何打出职业生涯最好一年的
这是整段访谈里最被低估的一句话：2018 年他身体血糖紊乱、酗酒、抑郁到起不了床，三周后在 Gullane 的苏格兰公开赛打出亚军，又在卡诺斯蒂公开赛拿到第六。常识会说"身体是基础"，但 Eddie 不自觉地揭示了一个更冷酷

item.title: [Sequoia Capital] Google's AI Infrastructure Chief, Amin Vahdat, on the Physics & Economics of Frontier AI
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的发现：这不是"芯片战争"，而是"同步性危机"

真正令人意外的洞察藏在Vahdat对"goodput"的定义里。表面上，所有人都在谈论FLOPS、TPU vs GPU、谁的芯片更强。但Vahdat透露了一个被所有人忽略的真相——在10万颗加速器规模下，每小时都会有东西坏掉，而真正的瓶颈不是"算得多快"，而是"如何在不可避免的局部故障中维持全局同步"。

这与我们对AI基础设施的直觉完全相反。我们以为AI数据中心是"更多更快的芯片"，但它实际上是一座被迫以微秒精度跳集体芭蕾的失败管理系统。一颗芯片打喷嚏，10万颗兄弟姐妹就得集体回滚检查点——这意味着"算力"的真正敌人不是物理学，而是概率论。规模越大，恰好所有组件同时正常工作的概率越趋近于零。

一个让我震撼的跨领域连接：这与同步大型管弦乐团的失败模式完全同构。一个首席小提琴手走神，整支乐队必须停下来。所以Google真正在做的不是"造超算"，而是发明一种可以让一万人同时演奏贝多芬第九、而且其中任意一人随时倒下都不影响演出的新型指挥学。TPU不是乐器，是让这种演出成为可能的新型乐理。

二、隐藏模式：Google正在复刻互联网协议战争的胜利公式——但很少有人意识到

Vahdat顺口提到了IP协议为什么打败竞争对手——"因为它是沙漏的窄腰"。这句话被埋在采访中段，但它是整个Google AI战略的罗塞塔石碑。

注意他的动作组合： - 开源JAX，但也支持PyTorch - 卖GPU，也卖TPU
- 推动光开关标准，但不锁死硬件 - 甚至愿意把本地发电"回馈电网"

这不是"做好人"，这是精心计算的协议级战争。Google看懂了一件竞争对手还没完全领会的事：在一个即将经历爆炸性扩张的生态里，占据"窄腰"位置的收益远超占据"顶端"位置。IP协议的发明者没赚到钱，但建立了整个互联网。谁定义了AI基础设施的"沙漏窄腰"——是模型框架、是加速器接口、还是数据中心互联协议——谁就是下一个二十年的隐形税收者。

出人意料的推论：Google开源JAX、支持PyTorch不是防守，是攻击。因为一旦JAX在协议层固化为"标准之一"，TPU的生态位就自动合法化了。这是用标准化武器对抗CUDA垄断——不是打破它，是让它变得不再必要。

三、最被低估的洞察：电力正在改写"公司"的定义本身

Vahdat承认power是"唯一的根本约束"。但真正惊人的是他顺口描述的解决方案——Google开始像电力公司一样思考，并在"最热的两周"把电卖回电网。

这里发生了一件没人注意到的事：超大规模AI公司正在悄悄异变成准公用事业实体。Google不再是"从PG&E买电的客户"，而是电网的协同调度伙伴。他们规划自己的发电、承担输电线路升级成本、在高峰时成为电网的供应商。

跨领域连接：这与19世纪末钢铁巨头为了保证煤炭供应而买下整个铁路系统的历史模式惊人相似——卡内基不是想做铁路生意，但煤炭成了瓶颈，所以铁路成了"外部化失败的内部化解决方案"。

但有个更深的扭曲：芯片6年折旧 vs 数据中心25-30年寿命 vs 电网基础设施50年寿命——这三个时间尺度被硬塞进同一个资本决策里。Vahdat轻描淡写地说"我们规划未来5代芯片"，但真正的意思是：Google正在被迫成为一家需要同时在月度、年度、十年、半世纪四个时间尺度上做协调决策的实体。这种时间尺度的叠加，在人类商业史上只有极少数组织承担过——罗马教廷、英国东印度公司、以及现在的超大规模AI公司。

一个让人脊背发凉的推论：如果电力真的是根本约束，而电力规划的时间常数是20年+，那么今天的TPU v8决策实际上已经锁定了2040年代的AI能力分布。这不是技术决策，这是地缘-能源-算力三位一体的提前宣誓。

📝 转录文本

开场：芯片特化的艺术

In hardware, as you know, there is this opportunity where the more you specialize to a particular workload, the less flexible it is — the faster, the more power efficient the hardware is going to be. So it is this art, and it's this projection of what are you designing to and how persistent is that workload. In other words, if it's going to go away after a month or two months or three months, even if it's big for those three months, you got a really narrow window to intercept it. So it has to be somewhat durable, and you have to be able to project exactly what win you can get for specializing to it.

Host: Thrilled to welcome Amin Vahdat to the show. Amin, thank you for joining us for today.

Amin: It's really exciting to be here. I'm really looking forward to it.

人类历史上最大的资本支出建设

Host: I am very excited for today's topic because we are in the middle of the biggest capex buildout in human history. You are in the middle of it. Google alone is expected to spend more than $200 billion on capex this year, most of which is going into building data centers. You're at the center of it all. You were named the head of Google's AI Infra at the end of last year. So you are the man spearheading the efforts of one of the most capital intensive buildouts in human history, and so I am really excited to get into it with you today.

Amin: It's a huge year for sure, of course, across the industry including at Google. Really, I don't think we've ever seen anything like this, honestly — certainly not at Google, but as you said, I think in the history of humanity in terms of the buildout and the pace of transformation. Really unbelievable.

什么是AI数据中心？

Host: Before we get into it, maybe just a crash course for the audience. What is an AI data center and how is it different from a non-AI data center?

Amin: It's a very good question, in that AI data center and a non-AI data center do have a lot of similarities actually, and they're not radically different. It consists of concrete, an enclosure, electrical yards, mechanical yards, cooling. You have row after row of power being distributed. There's a huge amount of network infrastructure there — in other words, we connect large amounts of computes to one another. A fair amount of storage infrastructure goes in there.

I think the big difference that we're seeing with AI infrastructure is specialization. In the past, when we're building a data center, it really is a 20, 25, 30-year building investment, and we're thinking about how it's going to be evolving over that period. You might have servers go into it, networking, storage, some accelerators — GPUs, TPUs, whatever they might be — but it's a 25, 30-year planning horizon. The lifetime of the hardware might be six years, so many generations that we have to plan for.

An AI data center oftentimes is going to be more purpose-built. We are oftentimes co-designing the building with the hardware that might go into it. We might be saying, you know what, actually we're not going to put a lot of storage into this building. Why? Because a storage rack might have 10, 20, 30, 40 kilowatts of power. You put that next to a TPU rack or a GPU rack that easily is hitting hundreds of kilowatts today — people are talking about megawatts in the next few years.

Designing a building that might take 30 storage racks in a row versus one or two AI racks in that same row — very very different design. Just think of it in terms of the size, in terms of the power and how that would be distributed across the building, etc. Networking would be the same. The amount of networking that you would need for a storage rack is tiny — especially if it's hard drives — compared to an AI rack. So if you're trying to make it fully fungible, you'll probably make it too big and too overbuilt — fungible over certainly a 30-year period.

An AI data center likely is going to be much more purpose-built, co-designed with the hardware, even to the point of cooling and power distribution. A lot more co-optimization.

美学时刻：Ineffable的集群

Host: You all delivered a big Vera Rubin cluster to one of my portfolio companies, Ineffable Intelligence, and I saw the photographs of it as it went out. That is a thing of beauty.

Amin: It is.

Host: I mean, that's one of those things where, similar to looking at the biggest construction projects in human history, you look at that data center and it's like, wow, that is a monument to what mankind can do.

Amin: We got a nice picture of it, and this is just a couple of racks. The cabling, the fiber distribution for it is really — I mean, beauty is in the eye of the beholder, but for folks like me and probably yourself and others in the audience as well, it is a thing of beauty. We put this picture up on social media. People love the fact that Ineffable — they're huge fans of what they're doing, fantastic team — got a lot of attention. Okay, great rack for Ineffable. But actually, people just loved seeing the pictures of the fiber and the fractal nature of the fiber. One of the most popular posts that we've ever had actually was around that.

Host: Yeah, I had goosebumps seeing the picture.

衡量标准：从FLOPS到Goodput

Host: How do you measure and hold yourselves accountable in the middle of this big buildout? We were talking right before the show about how FLOPS is a vanity metric and you prefer an alternate metric. Can you say more?

Amin: One thing to note is that whether it's FLOPS or pick your other favorite chip-centric metric, these are in theory. In other words, under some conditions for whatever chip you have, this is the maximum amount of FLOPS that you can deliver. What we really care about in the end is what's the performance delivered by workload. That's what we're looking at. And relatively rarely is that performance determined by a single chip. It's FLOPS, HBM, SRAM capacity, etc. — those are all super important — but it might be how 2, 4, 8, 16, a thousand, 10,000 more of these chips composed together with not just the accelerators (TPUs or GPUs) but then the CPUs that might feed them the data, the network that connects them all together.

So what is the workload that you're running and what is the performance of that workload? One measure that is interesting is what's your FLOPS utilization. For a particular workload, if you have in theory a teraflop or a petaflop capable, what fraction of that are you delivering?

Host: Now, that's a measure of goodput. What is goodput?

Amin: You can think of throughput, which is a well-known term — that's the throughput that is possible. But now let's consider some other considerations. What is the slowdown of the workload? Other aspects really hit our reliability.

In terms of how we hold ourselves accountable: if we have a chip failing for a synchronous workload — and many of these workloads, whether training or serving or agentic workloads, are synchronous — there's many components working together simultaneously. If you have a thousand, 10,000, 100,000 of these components working together simultaneously and they really need to coordinate at microsecond or millisecond granularity, one of them fails and it might actually bring the whole thing to a stop. Everyone is counting on everyone else to do their part of the job in order to come up with the answer to a really tough question. One of them stops — now we have to figure out what happened, which one stopped, what's a checkpoint that we have of the computation at some previous state in time, how do we restore that checkpoint, how do we restart. Worst case, we have to restart from the beginning. That would be really bad, but that can happen in certain cases, especially on the inference side.

The point here is that if you now have to go back and redo a bunch of computation, if you have to pause and wait to figure out what happened for the failure, all that work is work — it's not actually helping you get the answer. In terms of working out a problem on paper: step one, step two, step three, step four. If you have to go back to step one because you made a mistake, yes, you're still doing work. That's throughput. But what is the goodput in delivering your answer? It's basically the total amount of time it took you to solve the problem. That's what matters.

So how do we hold ourselves accountable? It's delivered goodput, not theoretical benchmark throughput or goodness in theory — but actually for a workload for real failure conditions, what's happening? And the unfortunate reality is that at a 100,000 accelerator scale —

Host: I was going to say at that scale, something's failing all the time, right?

Amin: All the time. And each one of these chips is a wonder of nature. They're at the very bleeding edge of what's possible to manufacture. To me, it's stunning. Now actually these chips aren't just one chip, they're packages made up in many cases of two, four, eight, maybe more chiplets that are composing together. And then of course HBM off to the side, network connectivity, maybe things like co-packaged optics. No criticism — lots of things can fail. If you've got 100,000 of them, something is going to fail. You have to be prepared for that. Detect it in near real time. Recover from it in near real time.

The telemetry problem is massive. It's like finding a needle in the haystack continuously across certainly seconds and minutes, but for some of these jobs, hours and days and even weeks — just continuous and online. How we hold ourselves accountable is: what's the goodput that we deliver for the workloads that actually matter in the data center.

Host: Is goodput a Google term or an industry term?

Amin: It's a Google term, but I think more and more people across the industry are starting to pick it up.

Host: And just to calibrate me — at 100,000 accelerator scale, is it going to fail once a minute, once a day? How?

Amin: 100,000 accelerators — it is definitely going to be at that scale multiple times a day, and perhaps depending on the exact configuration, multiple times an hour, something is going to fail.

Host: And what are the most common failure reasons?

Amin: This is the problem — if there were a common failure reason, we'd have figured it out and fixed it. It is a long tail of constant discovery. Whenever we have a new product being introduced, there's going to be something that hits us. In many cases, frankly, because it's at the very bleeding edge, it might be network related — how we connect these things together at super high speed. That might be something to do with the hardware. Those things we work through.

But a lot of the issues could be software. The chip might be capable of a certain level of FLOPS, but if you have a compiler bug, a runtime bug, a model issue, operating system issue — it doesn't matter, that's going to impact the end-to-end system performance. You might have perfect hardware, fully reliable, but then you might have software issues that hurt you.

参考技术栈与定制化

Host: Is there a standard reference stack from the accelerator companies — from Nvidia or from the TPU team — of "here is the optimal system to build around our accelerators and as long as you build to that system you're good"? Or how much of your own data center design do you have to do above and beyond what the semiconductor companies give you?

Amin: There's a reference stack. Nvidia is an incredible whole-systems company — they're obviously a semiconductor company, but they're not just a semiconductor company. They give you a really really strong reference stack. Most of our customers leverage that reference stack, but many also specialize. They might find that for their particular use case, they have an optimization opportunity or something different that they need to do. Similarly for the TPU side, we have a reference stack and most people will leverage that; many will specialize it as well though.

容量翻倍目标：每六个月

Host: In terms of overall capacity, you've told your teams that Google has to roughly double the serving capacity every six months or so. Is that right?

Amin: To be clear, this is in terms of effective available capacity. The way we look at it is from a serving perspective — it's token generation capability. And this is where I would say it's a combination of software and hardware. The hardware might have some inherent level of FLOPS, but what I'm saying is not necessarily that you have to double the number of FLOPS every six months. That's one path. You have to double the capability of that hardware to generate tokens every six months. And as much or more of that is going to come from software as it is from hardware. It could be a model optimization that delivers that, a runtime optimization that delivers that. It's really probably going to be dozens or hundreds of individual optimizations that are just landing again and again and again to make it all possible. But yes, the rate of capacity improvement is incredible.

Host: We've had a few years of data center buildout now and a few years of model progress and software progress. What has been the empirical breakdown of how much capacity increase — as measured by intelligence per watt — has come from the silicon itself versus the models versus other software and any other kind of big components?

Amin: I don't have the exact breakdown, but I would say that in our experience, most of the benefits come from model-side improvements in terms of intelligence per watt. And by the way, intelligence per watt is a fantastic metric. For us, it's also goodput per watt, and we can come back to why the watts need to be the denominator. Goodput could well be a measure of the intelligence delivered per watt — goodput is a workload-specific metric.

But I would say most of the gains often come from the model side, software system quite a bit — because they're able to actually make sure that the hardware that you have is being used effectively. And then the hardware — it is pretty stunning. We're living in a world right now where 2x or more year-over-year performance improvements is absolutely possible. The hardware does support it. It is, if you want, a free multiplier — not free, but everyone else above it can count on it in terms of that being a multiplier that lifts everyone else up year-over-year.

TPU项目的演进

Host: I'd love to talk a bit about the TPU program and co-design. Google started building custom silicon more than a decade ago. It was a contrarian call at the time. How has the TPU program evolved?

Amin: Quite a lot. When the program started in 2013, it was really a contrarian call. It's hard to put yourself back into the moment. 2013 conventional wisdom — all the smartest, wisest people would say, you don't build a custom-built accelerator for a single workload. Why? Because Moore's law is there, doubling of performance every 18 or 24 months. You get to leverage standard programming models, your C++ code, Java, Python, whatever it might be.

Host: Like the bitter lesson of chips.

Amin: Yes, exactly. Like the bitter lesson of chips is that specialization never wins. But in this particular case, we had this one application — or a few, a small number of them — that would benefit tremendously and that would require an unimaginable amount of general purpose CPU to support. So really in 2013, it was a bet, and there were quite a few people even within the company who were not sure that it would work out. It turned out to be a massively successful bet.

The first chip was all about inference. The second chip was — hey, actually we can take the same idea and build a training chip. From there it got picked up for more and more use cases. Around the time the second chip came out, transformers were invented. This was a major moment and that actually completely shifted the TPU program. We of course learned that recommender systems could run really well on the TPUs, and so ads and related use cases came along.

So I would say that change and evolution has been one of expansion in scope and impact. It started with a really impactful use case of a couple of applications for inference serving — this was language translation primarily and voice recognition — to then training, to then transformers, recommender systems, and continuing to generalize as the GenAI moment took hold, to ever larger, ever more scalable systems as well.

芯片的专用化边界

Host: You mentioned the moment the transformer came through being a major moment. The TPU was a specific architecture, but it wasn't specific to the transformer. How do you straddle the fine line of how specific you want your chip to be for the workload?

Amin: This is a great question. It really comes down to the applicability of the chip to a particular workload. We've been thinking about this for every generation. Would we further specialize? The question that we were facing two years ago or a little bit more was: in 2026, should we have two chips or one? We could have one chip that could do inference and training simultaneously and do both quite well, or we could have two chips — one further specialized for inference and a second further specialized for training.

This analysis and this work led to the release of two chips this year: 8I for inference, 8T for training. What we realized is that it wasn't the case necessarily a couple years ago, but by 2026 we saw inference and serving really taking off. Having a chip that would be significantly faster for serving — that we thought might be 30, 40, 50, 60% of the market in its lifetime — started making a lot of sense for us. Relative to if we projected inference to be 2% or 5% of the market, even if that specialized chip is 2x faster it might not make sense — because you'd actually go for the one general-purpose chip that's not fully optimized, but that's okay because you now have the uniformity.

It does come down to a calculus question: would you further specialize? How big is that workload? How big is that workload projected to be in a couple of three, four years? Is this a sustained growth for a particular workload? In hardware, as you know, there is this opportunity where the more you specialize to a particular workload, the less flexible it is, the faster and more power efficient the hardware is going to be. So it is this art, this projection of what are you designing to and how persistent is that workload. If it's going to go away after a month or two or three, even if it's big for those three months, you got a really narrow window to intercept it. So it has to be somewhat durable, and you have to be able to project exactly what win you can get for specializing to it.

Host: So the rough tradeoff is there's a large fixed cost to support a new program, and you basically have to think that there's going to be enough demand for that specific program to justify the cost.

Amin: Exactly. And to some extent, for example, for our 8I and 8T chips, both chips can do the other workload. This is also key. If 8I could only do inference and had zero performance for training, and vice versa — that would have also been a key limitation. We would have to predict ahead of time over a six-year lifetime exactly how much we need of each. In this case, it was nice because both chips are better at what they're specialized for, but if you had leftover capacity in one place or the other, both can actually do the other's job. Depending on the specialization you do, you might get so specialized that you actually limit yourself from being flexible, fungible.

Host: The rough tradeoff is kind of size of program on the other end. So much of the modern AI market is transformer-based. To ask a provocative question, why not just burn the transformer architecture into the chip?

Amin: It's transformer-based, but then the next level of question would be — transformers in the end are about vector and matrix multiply operations and a softmax. So there's a range of essentially linear algebra primitives. We have those, and others do as well, roughly baked into the hardware. It's all transformer-based, but then your model architecture is: how many layers do you have, how do you go through the layers, how do you go across the layers, for each dimension what exact shape of matrices and vectors are you applying. You could go further and specialize to not just the transformer but your model — that's the next level of specialization. I think there are a number of companies out there that are thinking about that. It's a very interesting direction as well.

TPU vs GPU：客户视角

Host: At this point in time, do your customers view TPU and GPU as roughly fungible equivalents, or is there a certain set of problems that is better suited for one or the other?

Amin: There's for sure a better set of problems that are better suited for one or the other. GPUs are more general purpose than TPUs — that is clear. There are incredible products at Google and Google Cloud. We sell a lot of GPUs. We use GPUs internally. But it really comes down to the specifics of your problem. There is overlap between the two, but our customers then evaluate their workload and evaluate their options. What we like to do at Google is give our customers choice — we want to have the right solution for their needs and provide the solution that best meets their needs for them.

代码-硬件协同设计：利弊

Host: What is the case for code design — from the chip to the network to the software — and what is the case against co-design?

Amin: There are huge optimization opportunities with co-design. If you have an N-layer stack and you want to be able to pick and choose whatever component you want — let's say you're running across many clouds or many pieces of hardware, many pieces of software — you could design abstraction layers that would basically say "I can run on any hardware, I can run on any software, I can run on any network topology, any amount of network that you give me no problem, and my system is going to be fully adaptive." Now you have a great capability. You can move anywhere. New capacity becomes available overnight — you're up and running because you've designed your system that way to actually be able to take advantage of anything. You have not hardcoded or specialized at all to anyone's particular infrastructure.

Downside is you probably leave a lot of performance on the table if you become fully fungible, fully flexible to anybody's hardware, software, network, storage, compute stack. The case for co-designing is: between each one of those layers, there's a big impedance mismatch if you try to get full generality. There might be 10%, 20%, 2x across each of these layers. You start multiplying those optimization opportunities through and all of a sudden you're left with a big end-to-end opportunity in terms of intelligence per watt or goodput per watt that you can leverage — all the way down to power delivery and power availability, software optimizations, etc.

Pros: you can run anywhere, anytime, you have no lock-in. Cons: you're leaving significant amount of performance on the table.

Host: My understanding is that if you take OpenAI and Anthropic — OpenAI was kind of primarily building on a homogeneous compute stack and Anthropic was building on a roughly more heterogeneous compute stack. Do you think that's part of the reason that code design is part of the reason why they converged on what is rumored to be very different architectures for their models?

Amin: I can't speculate. I don't want to speculate in terms of what OpenAI and Anthropic are doing. It's one possibility. But without knowing the details of what they're doing, I would imagine that there could be many reasons for why they wind up with different architectures.

与DeepMind的协作

Host: What about for Google then? I'm curious what the working relationship looks like between your team and DeepMind. Who's in the room at what stage of model development, and how are you making decisions together on co-design?

Amin: It's one of the most fun and frankly gratifying parts of being at Google — the opportunity to work really shoulder-to-shoulder with the DeepMind team in terms of co-design of our hardware and models. There's a third element in that we also get to extend that with the consumer services and cloud. I'll put that aside for a moment.

With respect to DeepMind, it really is a deep partnership. From the past, I can give you examples where they have come up with model optimizations — let's say to transformers or to particular math that they might want to do — and we might have a chip in progress, not quite done, but then they say, "Oh my gosh, if we had hardware support for this, our end-to-end training or serving might get significantly faster, more efficient. What would it take to actually now change our hardware definition that we might be an execution on to accommodate?"

This then leads to our engineers and researchers getting together intensely in the same room for a few days, a week, two weeks saying, "Okay, yes we can do this. More likely, we couldn't quite do what you wanted, but we can do this other thing. And then maybe you can change your model architecture in this other direction that gives you 98%, that gives us 90% of what we were looking for. And yes, we can then go back and intercept the hardware. Or we can say — you know what, we're going to delay the tape out by a week or two weeks because wow, for this level of benefit, it's totally worth it."

Similarly, when we're projecting our roadmap out, we have many generations of chips essentially in progress at any point in time: - Chips that are in production - Chips we're working on getting into production (back from the manufacturer, we're debugging them) - Chips in implementation that are about to tape out - Chips in design phase - Chips in concept phase

So it's really this five-six stage, many-year pipeline from in-production to in-your-mind. The collaboration with DeepMind for in-production is significant because we get to work together in maximizing delivered intelligence or delivered goodput per watt. We also get to collaborate deeply on the chips that are just about to tape out — we can intercept and make changes to the chip literally the chip architecture in flight, which would be somewhere between hard and impossible to do if we were working across company boundaries. Not impossible, but harder.

For the chips in design, we have many architectures we can evaluate together. We can ask our colleagues in DeepMind: where do you see model architectures going in two, three years' time? Here's the pareto of things that we can do, here's the pareto of where model architecture is going. We have deep and significant simulation infrastructures that can predict how workloads are going to map to different hardware architectures.

It really isn't that the teams are working separately. It's same building, same rooms many times. Deep daily interaction. I talk to Koray or Demis multiple times a week. It really is a super fun aspect of the work.

Host: That's awesome. And eventually their models will help with chip design.

Amin: We're using Gemini to design hardware for future Geminis as well.

硬件与软件的时间尺度错配

Host: I want to come back to that a little bit later on the collaboration itself. Is there an impedance mismatch still of just — I figure the cycle times are probably just slower when you're dealing with hardware than your DeepMind folks get to deal with on the software side. And I figure your planning cycles are much further ahead. How much room do you actually have to adjust?

Amin: For sure, we are planning hardware two, three, four, five years in advance. No question. We talked about TPU 8I and 8T that we announced just now, but you can imagine that 9, 10 and maybe some others are in concept execution. They might be years out. If you're working with model architecture, by default you're not going to be thinking years out.

But I think this is also the great thing about how the company has grown up together. Google Research, DeepMind, transformers being invented — all of this was happening in these overlapping rooms. There's a whole generation of researchers who've grown accustomed to being able to influence the hardware and knowing that the hardware is operating on multi-year cycles. They also know that if they have a small tweak that's going to deliver 1% or 0.5% for a chip that's about to tape out, they're probably not going to come to us — they know enough to know that it's not like software where you can just do a change list and it's going to ship to production in two weeks. Stopping a tape out is a big deal. But if they've got a really good opportunity, we're absolutely going to work together to figure out if we can get it in there.

The hardware does lift all the tides. Significant portions of the DeepMind team — and we're so grateful for it, it's an amazing team — are thinking about how do I influence the roadmap, because it's actually a pipeline. The idea I had two years ago is in production now and it's helping all the workloads at Google go faster. That's a good feeling.

Host: Totally. It seems like an impossible task though — to predict in five years what workloads will be most common and what algorithmic breakthroughs will have occurred.

Amin: I hear you that it would seem like an impossible task, but here's the awesome thing — and actually we're working on writing this in great detail — the stunning thing is that the TPU architecture at a medium level of detail hasn't really changed since TPU v1. One way to look at it is the instruction set architecture for a CPU. You've got loads, stores, adds, subtracts, branches — and yet what has the software on top of it done over that period of time?

Same thing with TPUs. We have some fundamental instructions and fundamental primitives. Of course we've extended it — it's not like the instruction set hasn't gotten changed at all — but the primitives are there in terms of specializing: numeric, very large matrix multiply units, a sparse core that manages vector operations and scatter-gather operations, etc. There's five or six things that really define it — load, remote-load-store. We can read and write remote memory through our ICI network. The fundamentals have been there and they've extended just to many generations of models, many generations of even deep neural network algorithms and model structures.

长时程智能体：新的工作负载形态

Host: Speaking of shifting workloads, it seems like one of the biggest changes in workloads over the last year — I think it really started at the beginning of this calendar year — was the rise of the long-horizon agent. I would guess that's a very different shape of workload than kind of the quick-turn LLM conversations of years past. What does that mean in terms of data center needs?

Amin: There are two huge aspects to this.

One is: it's no longer human-to-accelerator interaction. When you are typing a prompt on a web browser or on your phone, in response to your prompt there's going to be a bunch of work that happens, but then when the response comes back, you've got to read it, think about it, and then maybe you have a follow-up. That's multiple seconds of interaction time. Now in Deep Horizon Agents, there's no human in the loop that is going to naturally rate-limit how quickly requests are going to go to the model. What went from seconds, maybe tens of seconds in interaction time, is now going into perhaps milliseconds — as soon as I get a response back, I can parse it, I can reason about it perhaps a bit, and figure out what my next request is going to be.

Big change two: all that reasoning and parsing is going to probably happen on a CPU. And that CPU is then going to have to think about — okay, what other state do I need to go gather before making my next prompt back into the model? I've learned something from this response, I'm going to take another step, but I actually need to go grab some context — maybe from DRAM local to me, maybe from someone else's DRAM on another CPU, maybe on SSD or on HDD somewhere else. A huge amount of orchestration has to take place.

So the design actually is changing pretty significantly where the demand for accelerated compute is going up, but the demand for CPU and networking and storage — the traditional data center CPU — is also going through the roof.

Host: Does that mean you're putting more CPUs alongside your GPU racks then?

Amin: This is the key question. Going back to specialization: if we start putting lots of CPU racks next to the GPUs and TPUs, that means we can't fully specialize to the density and network requirements of a TPU rack relative to a CPU rack. TPU rack is going to be more dense than a CPU rack. It's probably going to need more networking. Our building design is going to change.

Another option is to maintain your uniformity. Put your TPUs or your GPUs all in one building and the building next door, but maybe put your CPUs in another, and the hard drives have to be in another building on the other side because they have yet another set of requirements. Now you need networking between these buildings at a pretty significant level. Once you leave a building, the networking complexity goes up significantly — from a reliability perspective, from a cost perspective, latency goes up probably acceptably but still — you might go to hundreds of microseconds potentially more with queuing between the components. So the considerations do change in pretty interesting ways.

Host: Your job is hard.

Amin: It's fun.

网络技术：光学交换的前沿

Host: What's happening on the networking side? I've heard that Google's always been at the forefront of the newest in networking, including optical. Can you say a word on the state of optical networking?

Amin: At Google — this was probably 15, 16 years ago — we were among the first to bring essentially what's called wavelength division multiplexing, where you could put multiple signals on a single fiber within the data center. We leveraged that for all of our communication between racks. At the same time, we introduced a technology along with the wavelength division multiplexing called optical circuit switching.

Essentially what optical circuit switching does, in contrast with traditional electrical packet switching, is it transmits and moves data entirely in the optical domain. In a packet switch, you would take a packet that has a header, look at it in the electrical domain, figure out where the packet is headed in its header. It might have an IP address that says, "Okay, for that destination, look up in a table, what ports do I forward it along?" Billions, perhaps trillions of packets coming through at super high speed per second, you're forwarding them along.

Optical circuit switching says: I'm not touching these bits in the electrical domain. What I'm going to do is figure out, for an input port, which output port to send the light to. There's multiple ways to do this. The one that we started with is called MEMS switches — micro electrical motors that basically control mirrors in 3D. We can programmatically take a box that might have 128 ports, 256 ports, some number like that, and configure every input port for a fiber that comes into it, map it to an output port, and then change the rotation of mirrors where the light literally shines down on these mirrors and gets reflected to the right output port.

Initially, the reason we did this was twofold: 1. Create locality between groups of racks. Let's say I had a compute cluster and a storage cluster, both in support of search. We knew these two clusters would talk to each other a lot. So we would configure the mirrors to create shortcuts purely optically between those two clusters. 2. Expand and contract the network without moving any fiber. The optical circuit switch would allow you to reconfigure the spine of the network without a human having to do anything other than a controller that would manage that.

Now fast forward to TPUs. A TPU has a torus topology that connects all the TPUs to one another directly. One of the things we can do is if we have a TPU rack that fails, we can replace it with another TPU rack without moving any fiber. Essentially, we have a spare rack available at all times, and when a rack fails, we redirect the light to that new rack — and that can be done in milliseconds.

Host: Why do you have the fiber at all then, as opposed to fully free space?

Amin: Very good question. Attenuation loss and the bandwidth would drop dramatically. Furthermore, across the range of a very large building, aiming everything without the benefit of fiber to connect it all together in 3D would be challenging to possibly impossible. We've talked about it — there have been some really interesting discussions — but yes, it's mostly in fiber. When they hit the optical circuit switch, essentially the light then literally shines down on these tiny chips. That's one big direction of networking. Networking is exploding in terms of its capabilities and need, frankly, in the data center.

Host: So cool. We could have an entire conversation on that. Even going back to the picture from Ineffable, it was all the cables that caught everybody's eyes.

Amin: Exactly. And those cables eventually, some of them wind up at optical circuit switches in our data centers.

电力：根本约束

Host: Okay. I want to flip to talking about power. You've been talking about goodput per watt and other units per watt. Makes me think "per watt" means power is kind of the binding constraint or the scarce constraint or the expensive constraint in some way.

Amin: I get asked this question — what is the biggest constraint that we face? The reality is there is no single biggest constraint. They're all constraints. They're all super hard. They shift continuously. But if I had to answer fundamentally, I would say that power is the single most fundamental constraint that we face. Like, everything else seems like we know how to solve them and it's a question of solving them over some period of time. Power — yeah, I think the way that you put it is really nice. It's a binding long-term issue. Nuclear is going to abundant clean energy, which would solve a lot of problems for sure when that happens — and at scale, still unknown.

Host: How does it work in practice? You're standing up a new data center, it needs a gigawatt of power. I imagine you can't just call PG&E and say, "Hey, please send a gigawatt of power." What does provisioning power actually look like, and are you having to actually vertically integrate all the way down to doing your own turbines, or how do you solve the power bottleneck?

Amin: Our preferred model at Google is always to be utility-connected, to be grid-connected. So it's the equivalent of calling —

Host: Oh, so you can't just call PG&E?

Amin: Exactly. You very politely call your favorite utility wherever it is that your data center is, and of course you give them many years of notice. If we're talking about a gigawatt scale, it's not something that you can say "Hey, I need a gigawatt tomorrow — when can you start billing me?" It's something that we co-plan together.

For us, it's something that we also take very seriously from the perspective of ensuring that when we work with these utilities — the costs of putting that infrastructure in place — we could get into a long conversation just on this topic. We cover those costs because with the way that billing works, it actually could be that by the act of the utility building out capacity for us, let's say other people's rates could go up in theory. What we ensure is that let's say the transmission lines that have to be built, upgraded, additional utility base stations etc., that we pay for those as well.

It is a long planning process. It can absolutely be the case that let's say we need a gigawatt in — I'll make up a date — 2028, and the utility can get us a gigawatt in 2029 but can get us let's say 700 megawatts in 2028. Now we might be left with a question of how do we cover those 300 megawatts. One answer is just wait. Another answer is to say okay, would we figure out how we generate some subset of that power ourselves, maybe with solar cells or with batteries as a backup, from other sources?

Then we again work with the utility. It might also be a combination where we might maintain some power generation local and have the capability, even when the utility comes online fully at the gigawatt scale, where we could actually provide power back to the grid. Having that when they need it as well — there might be the two weeks of the year, maybe the hottest two weeks, where there's a huge amount of residential demand. If we have some local generation, we can provide that back to the grid.

Host: Why is your preference to work with the utilities as opposed to vertically integrate yourselves?

Amin: The main reason is flexibility and uplift on both sides. Statistical multiplexing — or the law of large numbers. If we need to have a gigawatt of power with 99.99% plus reliability, it probably means we have to build two gigawatts of power. At 99.99 or 99.999 you have to have one-plus-one redundancy. That gets expensive. Making sure that's going to be ideally a clean energy source probably right next to our data center can also be challenging.

If we partner with the utility — maybe we have some amount that we can bring ourselves, that we can give to the grid when they need it, less that we can take their power. By leveraging that statistical multiplexing over a much larger base, everybody wins. We win, the grid wins, residences win. We prefer that.

In rare cases, we will do it behind the meter, but even then we're doing it under the assumption that we're going to work with the utility — it might be a year later, we want to be connected to the grid. It's an uplift for us; it's an uplift for the grid.

数据中心规模的艺术

Host: Makes sense. How do you decide how big to make a data center?

Amin: That's an art and a source of significant debate. 10-plus years ago, 15 years ago, big debate at Google — should we just put everything into one data center? Back then it was going to be a gigawatt.

Host: Simpler times.

Amin: Different times. 10, 15 years ago we're going to have a gigawatt data center. One obvious concern there is single point of failure. If you're looking at things from a 30-year perspective, that's a huge concern.

On the other hand, if you're talking about training workloads today, bigger is better. From a networking perspective, you want to have things concentrated in as small a distance as possible. But then again — two issues: single point of failure, but then also power availability. While a gigawatt was huge 10 or 15 years ago but imaginable, there's no way anywhere in the country or the world we're going to get the total requirements of Google built in in one place. It's just not going to be possible.

Now what's the optimum size? We have models for this, simulators etc. It also depends — look, in some places we're going to be at the edge of the network, we're going to be in-country, that might be tens of megawatts. We actually partner with ISPs that might be a rack — literally it could be a rack. This is a training cluster — okay, maybe that's going to be closer to a gigawatt. Some other sites might be hundreds of megawatts.

训练vs推理：集群生命周期

Host: I'd love to understand how you think about the portfolio life cycle management. My guess would be that the biggest, newest clusters are used for training the latest frontier model, and then you kind of recycle the older stuff and run inference on it. Is that a fair framework? Are you also standing up inference-specific clusters? How does that all work?

Amin: Very reasonable framework. Makes a lot of sense. But I would say that the demand for inference is such that we can't just rely on older training clusters that are no longer being fully used, just for training, as the basis for inference.

Also, if you think about it, we might centralize again in a particular year into a small number of large sites our training clusters. There is benefit to keeping the network distance between them small. So wherever they're located in the world, they're probably going to be on the same continent or even in the same portion of a continent in a particular year. Now you might be left with not enough serving capacity on the other continents. Then we have to go build specialized inference elsewhere across the world.

Your intuition is spot on but not wholly. Here are the training clusters — yes, probably they're going to be used for serving in some number of years. But we're also having to build the serving clusters as well.

Host: Are your serving clusters different than the training clusters? Are they smaller? Are they cheaper per megawatt?

Amin: Not necessarily cheaper actually, because for serving there is more need to co-locate compute, networking, and storage. That then gets to the inability to specialize. For training you have this big density, uniform deployment. For serving you're going to have the mix of storage, compute, and accelerators.

Furthermore — a very interesting aspect — for serving you actually don't want to have too much in one place. You want to be serving your workloads from all over the planet. We wind up having individual model endpoints, and that actually can be variations of models. We have to spread these models out across the world, also accounting for locality. They will be smaller. They'll actually be less vertically integrated probably on the inference side.

芯片的使用寿命

Host: Super interesting. So if you made a data center five years ago, state-of-the-art accelerator five years ago was very different, vastly less efficient than the ones being made today. Do you actually go back and swap out the chips in those old data centers? And this kind of relates to there's been an ongoing debate of what is the actual useful life of a chip?

Amin: I've been on record of saying this — one of my more... I was surprised by how much pickup this had — I said that our seven and eight year-old TPUs are still at 100% utilization.

Host: Wow. I think I saw this. I think that was —

Amin: I didn't mean for it to be a meaningful statement, but it was a meaningful statement apparently. Our older TPUs, GPUs — but our older TPUs — are seeing significant utilization. We do replace them in the end. Depreciation lifetime is approximately six years. Once they're fully depreciated, and given the power efficiency of newer generations, it does make sense to replace and upgrade them. It's not that we replace the chips — but it's really the systems.

In other words, we think in terms of pods. A TPU 8 pod might be 9,600 chips and it might be 140-something, 152 racks. We would say, okay, we're going to pull out that pod and we're going to replace it with a TPU 12 or 13 or 14 pod. It might not be a perfect fit — the new pod's footprint might not be a perfect fit for the old pod's vacancy. We just have to account for that, figure out how we would retrofit. We can't plan that because we don't know what that many generations of TPUs are going to be. So then it's again a bit of an art, actually hard work, figuring out how we would decom and then replace as quickly as possible with new TPUs.

开放标准的信念

Host: You've written publicly about open standards. Can you say a word on that?

Amin: We talked about this interoperability question. While we support vertical integration and we make it possible to extract just as much performance as you want, for us it's really important to not force lock-in and not force a sort of walled garden in terms of how the system works end-to-end.

One example: at Google we've developed a model development framework called JAX. We like it a lot, we think it's really really good, we use it extensively internally. Many of our customers like PyTorch. One thing we could say is, "Hey, if you want to run on TPUs, you got to use JAX, it's the best." I'm being facetious. Or we could say, "Look, if you like JAX, we like JAX, you can use it. But if you like PyTorch, we have Torch-TPU where your unmodified models can run."

We've seen this throughout history with many examples. I've used the example of IP. Why did the internet protocol win? There were actually many competing protocols to IP. This is ancient history in the 70s and early 80s. Why did IP win? Because it was an open standard and it was this narrow waist to the hourglass where anything could run on top in terms of software, and anything could run underneath it in terms of hardware. Open standard, interoperable — anyone who brought IP could plug into a router port and become part of the internet like that. It was beautiful, and that's what allowed the internet to explode in its growth and reach across the world.

We really do believe in those open standards in terms of plug-in points. If you want to plug in something highly specialized, you can. If you think you've got a better thing to plug into our framework, you absolutely can. But we want to really support open standards, ideally open source around it as well.

Host: It's too big and too important of a buildout to be any one vendor's closed proprietary stack.

Amin: We really believe that. And it's got to be one of choice — that's also why for example we fully support and have TPUs, GPUs, other accelerators.

AI改变日常工作

Host: How has day-to-day life for your team changed with AI? Where is it changing your function the most?

Amin: The easiest answer is on the software engineering side. This has been documented externally quite a bit. We at Google and my team are using it to great effect in terms of our software development capabilities, but also frankly test rollouts, even helping with design.

On the hardware side — which has maybe gotten less external coverage — also significant change. My hardware engineers — I was just looking at the numbers earlier today in fact — are using AI (if we take token counts, not the best metric, but still a metric) as much as the software engineers are. Productivity has gone up. Time from design kickoff to tape out is shrinking. Time for bring-up is shrinking.

Other, maybe less expected changes: how we do data center design has changed significantly. How we evaluate — you mentioned, hey do we do a gigawatt building or 100 megawatt campus or 200 megawatt campus. In the past, this would be very detailed, very spreadsheet-driven, human-driven processes. And it still is to some extent. But there's a lot of AI now involved that really streamlines the process in terms of planning and development as well.

Host: Like reasoning models?

Amin: I wouldn't say quite yet reasoning models. It's not replacing human judgment, but it's making it much easier to bring the necessary information together in one place and put the right information in front of the humans making the decisions.

收尾一：轨道数据中心

Host: Okay, I'm going to bring us home with two kind of out-there, fun questions. Question number one: orbital data centers. I've seen that Google is thinking about this quite seriously. Does the fact that people are seriously running the numbers on orbital compute mean that there are kind of serious binding constraints on Earth? And what do you think of orbital data centers?

Amin: It's an exciting direction. We are actually pursuing it, and we've referred to it with no tongue-in-cheek as a moonshot — one of our big efforts that we're excited about investing in.

It goes back to the earlier part of the conversation where you raised, I think correctly, that in terms of fundamental constraints, energy and energy production is a key challenge. Bottom line, from a fundamentals perspective: in space, you have something like 40% more power available because of lack of attenuation in the atmosphere. In other words, just more solar capacity — what, 1.4x.

But in a sun-synchronous orbit, you have 98 to 100% coverage of sunlight on your solar cells, relative to 28, 30, maybe 35% on land. Just this enormous amount of power. You take the 1.4x and you take the 3 to 4x in terms of number of hours per day. You remove batteries more or less from the equation. Now you have the potential for something that can really — and of course carbon-free — lots of benefits, lots of challenges.

Okay, now what about cooling? Naively you might think cooling in space is easier. It's actually harder. Reliability — we talked about how these things fail sometimes. Repairs become harder, not impossible, but harder in space.

Host: Robots up there with the cluster?

Amin: Exactly. Perhaps there'll be this model, a promising direction. Redundancy will probably be your friend. Your prior question on free space optics is now going to become reality. We're probably not going to be stringing fiber between these components. It will actually be free space, and we're going to have the lasers pointing at the receivers and calibrating in real time. There are no showstoppers here. No fundamental showstoppers.

收尾二：2036年的前沿超算

Host: Last question. I've had this image of the Ineffable big supercomputer that you built them in my head this whole time. So here's a question: 10 years from now, what will the most frontier supercomputer look like?

Amin: Oh my gosh. 10 years is right at that edge where — I would say in all sincerity, probably some people are thinking about what the 2036 computer looks like. We might have a few thinking that far ahead. But wow, the cone of uncertainty there is way way too wide.

If you look at the trends: the level of integration is going to be tremendous. We saw the beautiful fiber and the VR200 racks that we put together for Ineffable. My guess is it's going to be more integrated — less fiber. I won't say no fiber in 2036, but I think probably from a rack perspective, the rack will look much more tightly integrated, and the amount of fiber there'll be — maybe a small fiber bundle coming out of the rack.

One view from a modular manufacturing perspective: these racks in 2036 are likely going to be manufactured centrally. Whether they have 72, 144, 288, or probably more — 576 — pick your favorite multiple of GPUs (since we're talking about the Ineffable case, but same for TPUs) — deeply integrated into a rack. Would a rack be multiple megawatts? We don't know exactly how, but 2036, we get to imagine — things could be multiple megawatts in a single rack. Now you bring water, you bring power, you bring fiber. You wheel that rack in, you plug those three things in, and you're off to the races.

Host: Okay, so it's not going to be like a big alien orb then up in space by 2036?

Amin: I wouldn't say that it's not possible for 2036 for it to be directly launched into space and then maybe taken by a robotic arm at some space station and then plugged into the right module. Yeah, maybe that for 2036.

结束语

Host: Fun to think about. I really enjoyed this conversation. This is the most intense, biggest capex buildout in history, but I also think it's a technology revolution that is a thing of beauty. I think you have such a grasp over the beauty of the technology and the binding constraints and how to balance this all. Google is in good hands. Thank you for taking the time to share what you're doing.

Amin: Ton of fun. We get to live through this and we get to define it. So thank you very much. This is a great conversation.

Host: Thank you.

Amin: Yeah. Thanks.

## 一、最反直觉的发现：这不是"芯片战争"，而是"同步性危机"
真正令人意外的洞察藏在Vahdat对"goodput"的定义里。表面上，所有人都在谈论FLOPS、TPU vs GPU、谁的芯片更强。但Vahdat透露了一个被所有人忽略的真相——**在10万颗加速器规模下，每小时都会有东西坏掉，而真正的瓶颈不是"算得多快"，而是"如何在不可避免的局部故障中维持全局同步"**。
这与我们对AI基础设施的直觉完全相反。我们以为AI数据中心是"更多更快的芯片"，但它实际上是**一座被迫以微秒精度跳集体芭蕾的失败管理系统**。一颗芯片打喷嚏，10万颗兄弟姐妹就得集体回滚检查点——这意味着"算力"的真正敌人不是物理学，而是**概率论**。规模越大，恰好所有组件同时正常工作的概率越趋近于零。
一个让我震撼的跨领域连接：这与**同步大型管弦乐团的失败模式**完全同构。一个首席小提琴手走神，整支乐队必须停下来。所以Google真正在做的不是"造超算"，而是**发明一种可以让一万人同时演奏贝多芬第九、而且其中任意一人随时倒下都不影响演出的新型指挥学**。TPU不是乐器，是**让这种演出成为可能的新

item.title: [Invest Like The Best] Why Every AI Lab Will Become a Biotech Company | Andrew Huberman
item.dc:creator: Invest Like The Best
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被忽视的范式转移：AI公司的"身体化转向"

第一层：Huberman 真正说的不是预测，而是在泄露一个战略秘密

表面上看，这期对话最抓眼球的是那句"每个AI实验室都会变成生物科技公司"。但更深的洞察在于：他实际上在描述一个"计算基质的终极迁移"。

硅基计算有一个无法克服的瓶颈——它永远在"隔墙模拟"大脑。而真正的下一步不是让AI更像大脑，而是让大脑的 I/O 带宽追上AI的输出速率。这里有个几乎没人指出的反讽：我们一直以为AI的瓶颈是算力，但当算力过剩时，瓶颈反而变成了"把结果传回人类"的物理通道。人类的眼睛、耳朵、手指——这些 Shannon 意义上的低带宽接口——正在成为AI价值释放的真正瓶颈。所以Meta、OpenAI、Anthropic 投资神经接口不是扩张，而是救赎自己的 ROI。

第二层：出人意料的跨领域连接——"睡眠入门"和"大语言模型的温度参数"是同一个东西

Huberman 讲的"关闭思维三步法"（关思绪 → 降心率 → 忘肢体位置），其工程学本质和 LLM 的 temperature/top-p 调节惊人一致：

  • 关思绪 = 降低预测熵（brain 本质是预测机器，关掉即禁用生成）
  • 呼气拉长 = 降低系统 clock rate（RSA 调节心率等同于降低推理频率）
  • 忘记本体感觉 = 关闭 input embedding（propriception 是身体对自我的持续"token化"）

这三步合起来，就是把大脑这个"持续运行的 LLM"切换到低温推理 → 关机状态。所以真正的入睡技能，和"让一个过热的服务器优雅降级"是同一个控制论问题。这解释了为什么你高强度工作日需要4小时才能入睡：你的大脑运行在高 temperature + 高 context load 下，没有一个优雅的 cooldown 协议。

第三层：那个让人脊背发凉的"记忆乱序激活"实验，暗藏了关于"你是谁"的颠覆性暗示

Huberman 提到的 Tonegawa / Mayford 实验结论——神经元被同时激活（而非按原顺序）仍能产生同样的行为——这个发现被神经科学界刻意回避是有原因的：

它意味着"时间性"可能不是记忆的本体，而只是记忆的调用接口。换句话说，你的网球发球动作、你童年某个夏天的气味、你对一个人的爱——它们可能并不"按顺序"存在于你脑中，而是以某种无时间的激活图谱存在。你以为的"回忆的流动感"，可能只是大脑为了让体验连贯而生成的后处理动画。

这个发现与一个看似毫无关联的领域深刻共振：Transformer 架构的"位置编码"。LLM 本来没有时间概念，位置编码是人为注入的；大脑可能也是如此——时间不是神经活动的内在属性，是叠加上去的"显示层"。

第四层：藏在"健康人格"叙事下的权力转移

Huberman 对"健康话语场正在崩塌"的抱怨背后，有一个他没明说但很重要的观察：健康影响力行业正在经历与"内容农场"同样的生命周期。他描述的"晒腹肌 → 自称自然 → 粉丝"的三步公式，和早期SEO内容农场的"关键词堆砌 → 排名 → 流量"是同构的。

真正的洞察是：当一个话语场的"进入门槛接近零"时，权力必然在两个极端重新集结——要么是极致的娱乐性人格（Bryan Johnson 式），要么是回归机构权威（博士+MD组合）。中间地带会被挤空。他对此的焦虑，本质是意识到自己处于那个即将消失的中间带。

让人意外的结论：你应该把 Huberman 的睡眠建议当作神经接口技术的"过渡协议"

这期访谈真正的隐藏结构是：所有当下的"健康干预"都是在为未来的"可注射神经通道"做数据训练。冷水澡、咖啡因、长呼气、晨光——这些是我们目前能够访问大脑状态的低分辨率 API。而他讲的"病毒注射 + 超声激活"路径，是同一套接口的高分辨率版本。

所以 Huberman 的真正商业模式不是健康教育，是在为未来20年的神经接口消费者建立"自我监测素养"。他在教人们习惯测量自己——这是任何直接写入大脑的技术能够被接受的前置条件。他自己也许意识到这一点，也许没有。但这才是他的工作在历史上的真正坐标。

📝 转录文本

AI 实验室的生物科技转向：一个大胆预测

I'll go on record saying this. Anyone who thinks that Meta, Open AI, Anthropic, anyone that thinks that those are LLM AI companies is perhaps going to be surprised at this prediction. Every single one of those is going to be a biotech company. They're all interested in the brain. You talk to any of those guys, they may not have formal training in it, but they understand a lot of neuroscience, and they will all tell you the goal is to be able to read and write from your brain non-invasively.

带宽瓶颈：从世界追不上天才，到天才被自身能量限制

There's a very interesting thing happening that relates to a piece of your work which I I haven't seen you talk about as much and so maybe it's a fun place to begin which is that it feels like we're now bandwidth limited on the most talented people's ability to do work. Like it used to be that the rest of the world couldn't keep up with the most talented people and so they would get frustrated that no one was moving as fast or as efficiently as they were.

There seems to be something flipping which is actually some of these people would earn a really high return if they could generate more energy, maintain more energy, not burn out. I heard this from several great entrepreneurs this summer that there's this expectation that the real greats kind of like I think maybe Elon has just gotten into everyone's head that the real greats are going to run multiple companies and and there's just this like this technology unlocks so much potential for the most talented people and so it seems like an actual bottleneck is like these people's energy and I'd be curious in your in all your research and and and study what you've learned about the component parts of this like generating energy maintaining it clean versus dirty fuel, long-term performance, like all of these things are fascinating and I think actually important to the degree of progress.

And so I would love you to just riff on on all that for a while with the caveat that you know Elon represents the apex of being able to do multiple huge things uh simultaneously and I don't think he has any peers in that in that regard. In fact, one of the best multi-billionaire investors from the Bay Area who may have gone to Stanford and may have been part of the PayPal early team has asked me, we're friends, um, how is it that Elon does this? I'm like, I I can't tell you

like physiologically.

生理学的诚实自评：你需要多少睡眠？

Physiologically, I mean, there are examples throughout history of people who seem to require less sleep. They just have more energy. And most people can get their energy up. There are a lot of healthy ways to do that now. And I think now we've undergone this huge shift whereby everyone understands you have to sleep eventually and you have to know your own sleep requirements. So to delude oneself into thinking you only need four or five hours because Elon only needs four or five hours, that's that's ridiculous. We know where that leads.

So I think a an honest self assessment about how much sleep one actually needs to perform well and perhaps best and what you can get by on you know if you can't get that that's an important thing to understand but most people know like for me it's 7 hours I feel great eight I'm probably puts me into the day a little bit groggy six I can manage just fine for one day or or a sleepless night I'm good two nights like that of four to zero hours of sleep and I'm cratered and I Most people are similar.

What's really changed is that we have effective healthy ways to build our energy up. We know to sleep. We can talk about exercise, caffeine. Some people are using nicotine. Yes, it's addictive. It raises blood pressure, but it does put people into that, you know, focused but relaxed mode. I always say if you really want the benefits of nicotine, don't use it very often. If you want the actual cognitive enhancing effects or the focus enhancing effects, then you have to not be a chronic user and then you know spike your system with nicotine at low amounts every once in a while.

内在状态与"额外一档"：有些人天生有更多能量

But setting Elon aside is the with the understanding that he represents that ex extreme uh in terms of energy and and sleep requirements being very low. I think what's really happening now is people are hopefully doing this self assessment. Like I would hope people would have an honest conversation about themselves and say, you know, at this point in my life with or without without kids, at this stage of my company, at this stage of my career, whatever it is, at this age, how much sleep do I need in order to feel awesome, good enough, or it's not enough? And I think most people know that. Okay, so that's step number one.

The next one is something most people don't ever talk about, which is some people actually just have more energy, right? they can focus for long long periods of time. They have a ton of energy to run. They have a ton of energy to then go work. But what we never ask is what is that person's internal state. So I know people that can do all of that, but they're kind of redlinining and they're using a lot of stimulants to do it or they're not using stimulants to do it, but they're redlinining and then at night they're having a hard time switching it off and so they're not resetting their system.

Some people, however, are these like wake up at 4:00 a.m., work out, handle business, deal with family, go off to work, back to business, come home, and they pivot and task switch really fast. I don't think these things are necessarily stable features throughout our entire life. But whenever, you know, it seems to be a lot of young guys come up to me and they're like, "What should I do?" The Oracle said it best, like know thyself. You really have to be honest with yourself about what you need in order to do something for a long period of time.

Now that said, I do recall working 80 even 100 hour weeks in graduate school and that served me well. I mean eventually led me to tenure at Stanford etc. I do think that for the if you can pull it off I think from zero to maybe first four years of starting a company or if you're in medical school you know the goal is don't die get as much as done as you can and don't impair yourself with an injury or chronic disease and then you start to pivot into okay how you know we don't really define this thing optimization then it's how can I insert kind of components of rest along the way maybe during the day or across the week or the month that really allow me to access my, you know, my best levels of focus and creativity.

But I'd be naive and I'd be lying if I said, "Okay, you know, somebody's starting a company in the AI realm in the Bay Area or elsewhere these days, you're going to sit them down. You go, listen, you really need 8 hours of sleep. You got to do your resistance training. You should do some breath work." Like, no, none of that. What they should determine is how much energy they actually have. And you've met these people, right? Occasionally you'll run into, you know, like a Jimmy Ivine or a um there's some of the I've met some of the folks doing AI at Meta um and they just seem to have an extra gear. Some people have this extra gear.

入睡的三要素：关思绪、慢心率、忘记肢体位置

Now, there's one other component we can we can deep dive into any of these that nobody talks about and that's the ability to switch off your thoughts, your planning, and your concerns at the end of your day and drop into sleep.

Yeah. Can we go deeper in that one? Because the the to be very selfish about it, like if I was to self diagnose, the biggest problem I have is downshifting. Like so sometimes where it'll take four like literally four hours to go from a crazy exciting awesome day to literally even be able to fall asleep or just like stop the mind and if I could bestow myself with any gift it would be what you're describing. So what what is the research there of how to do that?

There are a couple of prerequisites for sleep. There are a bunch of don'ts. So obviously you don't want to drink caffeine too late. Um you know being under too much bright light late late in the day can make it difficult but a lot of us can't control that. um alcohol, cannabis, these things impair the quality of your sleep, help you get to sleep. We all know that by now.

But in terms of being able to turn your thoughts off, this is a very very difficult thing for people um for, you know, good reasons, right? The brain wants to think, plan, remember, and organize itself around what's coming next because such a huge aspect of brain function is prediction of what's happening next.

So, first requirement, turn your thoughts off. Second requirement is slow your heart rate down. Okay, so that's purely of body. And then third is you need to forget about the position of your limbs in space.

第一步：关闭思维——把注意力从思考移向纯感知

Okay, so let's work through each one systematically. For the first one, turning your thoughts off is a skill. It's a skill. How what do you do? Okay, we can think, we can predict, we can remember, but we also can get into pure sensation. And that's the gateway to turning off your thoughts.

Okay. And this doesn't come from eastern tradition per se. Although there this has been discussed for a long time in those traditions, but there's a neuroscience correlate to all of this of course and we can talk about those. So how do you do that? You have to focus on pure sensation. So you start focusing on the surface of your body. If you can detect your heart rate, some people are very good at what's called interosception. can actually get pretty accurate measurements of their heart rate just without, you know, pressing on a on a vein or artery and they're just listening to their own breathing. They're listening to the sounds in the room. They're bringing their conscious awareness just to the body and it generally helps and this relates to the second thing to slow the heart rate down by just doing long exhales.

Now, this might sound very woo, but I want to be very clear this is not meditation because meditation has you do something very different. Meditation has you focus all of your attention on your breathing or all of your attention on, you know, some region behind your forehead or your hands or whatever. In this sort of practice, what you do is you actually migrate your attention to your feet, to your legs, to your breathing, to sounds in the room, then back again. Now, this might sound really squishy, but you're moving away from thinking and planning to pure sensation and perception. And you're literally bringing your perception into the present. Remember, this is one door in front of turning off your thoughts.

第二步：通过长呼气降低心率（呼吸性窦性心律不齐）

To actually turn off your thoughts, your heart rate actually has to drop a certain amount. Those long exhales drop your heart rate through something called respiratory sinus arrhythmia. Arrhythmia makes it sound dangerous or bad, but it's actually very good. As you're breathing, the size of your heart is literally changing based on the amount of space it has because the movement of the diaphragm and the filling of the lungs. And when we inhale, our heart rate actually speeds up a bit. When we exhale, the heart actually gets a little bit smaller volume-wise and the blood therefore that's in it moves a little bit quicker per unit volume and the brain sends a signal to slow the heart down.

So when you exhale, you're slowing the heart rate down through this thing that we call the vagus nerve. So, if you want to slow your heart rate down anytime in waking to de-stress or just bring your level of activation down or if you want to fall asleep, it really helps to do some long exhales until lungs are empty and then just passive inhales. Normally, when we're really activated, we're doing a lot of inhaling. We're passively exhaling.

第三步：忘记肢体位置——摇摆、眼动与新一代眼罩

And then the last piece is to be able to turn off your perception of your limbs relative to you. This thing that we call propriception. And there are two ways to Well, there are three ways to do this. Okay, one is old school, everyone accepts it. One is pretty wacky sounding and then there's a new technology that's coming out that I wish I had developed that I think is going to make people more comfortable with the second one.

So here here goes. So there, believe it or not, there have been studies of what puts babies to sleep and what puts adults to sleep without pharmarmacology. And it turns out that the rocking pacing that we do with babies at a certain rate, parents figure this out on their own, puts them to sleep. Turns out that you can build, and they've done this for studies, a bed that rocks at a certain frequency and adults will fall asleep very quickly. What it has to do with is the fact that when you're moving side to side, your eyes are generating under your closed eyelids compensatory eye movements. Our our eye movements all the time are communicating through our brain stem to our cerebellum to control balance and propriception. So when people are rocked this way, somehow they fall asleep more quickly. That's interesting actually. And the frequency that at which that works best and fastest is known.

Now I don't have a rocking bed. I don't know anyone large enough to rock me and hold me. And if they did, I'm not sure I'd feel comfortable with that. Can't imagine you would either. So there are two ways to approach this. One is something that looks kind of wacky but works, which is to mimic the eye movements under closed eyelids that help you forget about your limb position. I've been talking about this a lot in public education recently, and I confess it makes me feel really weird as a neuroscientist. So I'm going to just preface this by saying please don't just put the part out into the world about the eye movement thing without just allowing me to first say that this confuses the circuit between for the ficinados these direction selective cells in the retina the accessory optic nuclei of the brain stem and the cerebellum and you forget about body position and basically what you do is under closed eyelids you move your eyes to one side then the other slowly or fast doesn't really matter then up then down you can roll them counterclockwise and clockwise you can do a long exit But really what you're doing is confusing this system.

The reason I got so interested in this and the reason I went to the literature on rocking of babies and adults to fall asleep is because a group out of MIT approached me and they said, "We'd like you to try this eye mask." The eyes are two pieces of brain. They're just not in the cranial vault, which makes them unusual in terms of parts of brain. And so the eyes are an amazing gateway to the rest of the brain. Everyone knows about eye masks to get the darkness out. These guys have developed eye masks that measure rapid eye movement because right now your your whoop, your aura, your eight sleep. They're not measuring REM directly. This can measure REM directly, but they designed this mask specifically to make people fall asleep faster. Like I want that thing.

So I got to try it and it works very well in the daytime or at night. And what does it do? It generates these slow back and forth up and down eye movements through a like small amount of stimulation behind your ears because it turns out you can access the extraocular muscles well enough from that location. So just an eye mask with some straps. You sometimes feel a little bit of the stimulation and you're out and then once REM sleep starts it actually helps amplify those the REM stage. You get much more REM. So I wish I had a stake in this company. I don't. These technologies are about I would say 7 to 12 months from release. I'm super excited about them.

从睡眠监测到清醒状态的神经调控

I'm also super excited about the fact that people can just do this on their own and obviously babies get rocked. You could do you know the non-mask tool approach or you could use the mask. I will say and I don't want to take us too far off course but for those interested in emerging technologies and AI in particular neural technologies I do think that in sleep reading from and writing to the brain is going to be a huge area but of course I'm most interested or I should say also interested in reading from and writing to the nervous system in waking states.

You could imagine like within 12 months to a year of the release of the technology that I just described, you could imagine somebody developing eyeglasses like this that are stimulating some component of the autonomic nervous system so that I'm exceptionally focused at certain times a day and then when I'm walking home, I'm sort of in a slightly more relaxed state to capture some more of that energy. We're going to start shifting brain states into focus into modes for learning and we're going to start doing it with technologies. Right now we're doing cold showers, caffeine exercise. We're doing inhale emphasized breathing versus exhale emphasized breathing to get more alert or calm. If you think about it, all breathing exercises can be summarized as inhale emphasized or exhale emphasized.

So yes, we can do that stuff deliberately, but you can imagine that pretty soon there will be non-invasive stimulation devices that will allow people to do this, but it will start in sleep because we're all kind of comfortable with the idea now of measuring our physiology in sleep little bit in waking states, but this is where this is going.

So to return to this in sequence, you need to learn to turn your thoughts off. You need to forget about your body position and and slow your heart rate down. # 一个被忽视的范式转移：AI公司的"身体化转向"
## 第一层：Huberman 真正说的不是预测，而是在泄露一个战略秘密
表面上看，这期对话最抓眼球的是那句"每个AI实验室都会变成生物科技公司"。但更深的洞察在于：**他实际上在描述一个"计算基质的终极迁移"**。
硅基计算有一个无法克服的瓶颈——它永远在"隔墙模拟"大脑。而真正的下一步不是让AI更像大脑，而是让大脑的 I/O 带宽追上AI的输出速率。这里有个几乎没人指出的反讽：**我们一直以为AI的瓶颈是算力，但当算力过剩时，瓶颈反而变成了"把结果传回人类"的物理通道**。人类的眼睛、耳朵、手指——这些 Shannon 意义上的低带宽接口——正在成为AI价值释放的真正瓶颈。所以Meta、OpenAI、Anthropic 投资神经接口不是扩张，而是**救赎自己的 ROI**。
## 第二层：出人意料的跨领域连接——"睡眠入门"和"大语言模型的温度参数"是同一个东西
Huberman 讲的"关闭思维三步法"（关思绪 → 降心率 → 忘肢体位置），其工程学本质和 LLM 的 temperature/top-p 调节惊人一致：
