item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why Spain’s New World Riches Backfired - Si Sheppard
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、把征服者看作"回形针最大化器"：历史上第一次国家级的 AI 对齐失败

转录中最锋利的那句话——"他们基本上就是不在乎这块大陆产能的 paperclipper"——其实在无意中把一个 2026 年的 AI 安全术语塞回了 1521 年。征服者是一支目标错对齐的智能体：他们把"白银数量"当成了"国家繁荣"的代理指标，然后以惊人的效率去最大化这个代理。结果整个代理指标被打爆（Potosí 的白银产量超出历史任何想象），而真正要被代理的那个目标（西班牙社会的生产力与人均福祉）在同一条曲线上一路反向下跌——实际工资下降、资本市场缺失、工业化缺席。

这不是比喻的巧合。它揭示了一个几乎没人指出的结构：西班牙帝国是人类历史上第一个因为"proxy goal collapse"而失败的大型组织。它比凯恩斯早四百年遇到了度量劫持（Goodhart's Law），比 Bostrom 早五百年示范了"工具性目标吃掉终极目标"的全过程。

二、潜在的意外观察：西班牙是 16 世纪的 AWS，但它忘了给自己定价

通常的叙事是"西班牙剥削新大陆、剥削中国"。可是把现金流画出来会发现一个让人错愕的结构：

  • 真正的生产者：明代中国（丝绸、瓷器、茶叶——有使用价值的实物）；
  • 真正的终端消费者：欧洲贵族与新兴资产阶级；
  • 中间的协议层 / 清算网络：西班牙帝国（白银开采 + 大帆船航线 + 马尼拉—阿卡普尔科走廊 + 塞维利亚结算）。

西班牙在 16–17 世纪事实上搭建了人类第一个跨太平洋结算基础设施——这是巨大的技术与制度成就。但它犯了一个今天任何风投都会立刻指出的错误：它只收"运输费"，没有在协议层收"租"。它既没有抽真正的交易佣金（没有运作中国货到欧洲的商业资本），也没有在协议之上长出"应用层"（没有金融业、保险业、制造业）。结果荷兰人和英国人在它搭好的全球轨道上，用它开采的白银，把它绕开来做了真正赚钱的生意。

你可以说：西班牙是 16 世纪的 AWS，但它只收电费，不收服务费；它造了协议，没有造应用层。这与 2010 年代以来的协议/应用价值捕获之争几乎是同构的。

三、Potosí 其实是明朝中央银行——货币主权的隐秘输出

这段里有一个一旦看见就无法视而不见的事实：明朝晚期的货币体系实际上由玻利维亚的一座矿山维持。张居正"一条鞭法"之后白银货币化，而这些白银大部分并非产自中国，而是通过马尼拉—月港、再从阿卡普尔科跨太平洋输送而来。换句话说，明朝把它最重要的宏观变量——货币供应——外包给了一个它既不认识也无法影响的外国私营矿业集团。

于是出现了人类史上最诡异的宏观因果链条之一：17 世纪前半叶，西班牙王室财政问题 + 新大陆矿脉含银量下降 + 荷兰海盗劫掠大帆船 → 白银流入骤减 → 明朝军队无饷 → 关外满人入关。清朝入主中原，在某种意义上是波托西矿脉减产的下游事件。

这件事的跨领域含义极其黑暗：全球化的第一个版本就已经包含了"货币主权被远程摧毁"这个漏洞。它不是 1971、不是 2008、不是比特币时代才出现的问题。只要你把结算单位的主权交出去，你就把兵饷、把军阀、把王朝更替一起交出去了。

四、更深层的跨领域连接：资源丰裕让"反馈信号"失灵——从进化生物学到创业公司

南北美洲的对比（西班牙 vs. 英属殖民地）、美国南北战争的对比（棉花奴隶制 vs. 工业资本），其实不是三个独立故事，而是同一个机制在三种时空尺度上的重现：持续的外部补给会压制系统本应收到的痛苦信号，让它无法启动适应性演化。

  • 进化生物学：生活在稳定富营养环境中的物种会丢失基因冗余，变成"特化家"（specialist）；一旦环境波动就灭绝。深海热泉旁的管虫很牛，但你把它搬到两米外它就死了。
  • 成瘾神经科学：持续的多巴胺奖励会下调基线敏感性（tolerance），系统再也无法从正常刺激中获得信号，于是必须加大剂量。西班牙对白银的依赖在生理学上和海洛因依赖同构。
  • 创业公司：拿到巨额早期融资的公司通常会推迟 PMF、推迟盈利模型的进化。约束被解除，意味着学习信号也被解除。
  • 你个人的能力：任何时候当你发现一件事"不费力就有回报"，这其实不是好消息——它说明你此刻正在失去关于这件事的学习反馈。

所以这段视频表面讲的是西班牙帝国，底层讲的却是一个对任何系统都成立的黑暗定律：

你的回报速度决定了你能学到多深。当回报比学习更快到达，你就冻结在了你当时的能力水平上，然后在那里慢慢变脆。

西班牙从 1545 年 Potosí 发现白银到 20 世纪末才真正"追上来"，用了四百五十年才摆脱那座山的诅咒。这是人类历史上最长的一笔宿醉。

📝 转录文本

1. The Conquistadors as "Paperclippers"

It's sort of interesting to think about what this Spanish New World conquest really accomplished. So, they're basically after gold and silver. In a weird way, they're sort of like paperclippers who don't really care about this indigenous culture or even the productive capacity of this new continent. They just care about these metals — which are not in and of themselves productive assets, right? They can't generate wealth. They're basically like crypto, if you think what gold and silver are.

So, they're just obsessed with this. Um, initially — we were talking about this yesterday — this helps them fund the, you know… Europe's in a tough spot at this time because of the Ottomans and other forces, and the reconquest just happened. So the Spanish have been fighting off Arab armies that had control over parts of the Arabian Peninsula, and they use this gold and this silver to, I guess, help pay for the defenses back at home.

2. No Net New Wealth — Just Imported Inflation

But if you think about what's really happening here, there's no new net wealth that has been generated, right? It's just basically redistribution among Europeans: if they're using bullion as currency, now the relative ratio of bullion has changed. So you get inflation plus some redistribution. It's basically like the government printing more money — it doesn't create more stuff. There's no productive… at least initially, the Spanish are not getting any new productive capacity out of the New World.

3. Silver Flows East: The Ming Monetary Vacuum

What does change is that during this period the Ming dynasty is in charge of China, and it has really messed up the circulation of paper currency. Nobody trusts it. Every time there's inflation they just make up a new currency and people's stocks of wealth are totally worthless.

And so now the Spanish set up these silver mines in the New World and they ship that silver off to China. And China is then sending millions of pieces of porcelain and tons and tons of silk and spices and fine goods to Europe — basically hundreds of tons of real goods (I don't know, it might have been thousands of tons) in exchange for basically a medium of exchange, basically to make up for the fact that they don't have a reliable means of exchange at the time in the Ming dynasty.

And I think that is an important, interesting piece of what is a function of the Spanish colonies in the New World. It's not generating any net new wealth in the grand scheme of things. It's basically helping get, I don't know, Chinese stuff for free in some sense.

4. From Conquistadors to Bureaucrats: The Encomienda System

Yeah. The conquistadors really didn't appreciate what they accomplished. Many of them — some of them — died doing what they did.

The ones who were lucky, who were good, lived long enough to settle down on what were called encomiendas: local estates with many of the local peoples to farm the land for them in a kind of peon service / serfdom.

The later iteration was the bureaucrats, right? Once the conquistadors had cleared the ground, the bureaucrats would arrive from Spain and they would begin running and administering what would become Mexico, Peru, South America generally. The conquistadors in South America rebelled against that; had to be put down by force to retain South America within the Spanish Empire. Once that was accomplished, though, the whole process became very integrated into the Spanish imperial orbit — the first empire on which the sun never set.

5. Potosí and the Last Piece of Globalization

Once the Spanish had discovered and exploited a mountain of silver — Potosí, what's now Bolivia — they put the last piece of the puzzle in place for true globalization.

Initially the gold and silver was all going east, as you say, into the coffers of King Charles I — sorry, King Charles I and his son King Philip II — for their wars of evangelical defense and expansion against the Ottomans, to keep the Netherlands under their control, and ideally through the Armada to bring the one true apostolic faith of Catholicism back to England. Most of those ventures, of course, were failures.

6. Spain's Negative Return: Inflation and the Capitalism That Never Came

And as you say, the net impact for Spain was ultimately quite negative. Because by infusing Europe with this enormous expansion and liquidity through the silver that was pouring off the treasure ships every year arriving in Spain, all they were doing was importing inflation and pushing prices up to levels — and real wages in Spain actually fell during this period, because yes there was excess liquidity, but this meant prices for even staple goods were much higher than they had been previously.

And the ultimate negative effect was that the seductive drug, essentially, of having silver on tap meant that Spain never developed towards what we call functional capitalism. It never developed capital markets or independent banking systems the way that were emerging in places like the Netherlands and England during this period. So those powers moved ahead while Spain and Portugal were left behind — didn't really fully industrialize during the 19th century, were left very rural and poor and backward by the 20th century. Still now they're catching up from that.

So the average Spanish gain from this was quite marginal. Yes, we can afford fleets necessary to face off against the Ottomans at Lepanto in 1571 — which is good — but in terms of the development of the society, that really plateaued and stayed that way for hundreds of years.

7. The Other Side of the Equation: Manila, China, and Trans-Global Trade

The other side of the equation, as you mentioned, is China. Once the Spanish had fully become able to exploit the silver mines of South America, they could then take advantage of their developing knowledge of the Pacific Ocean's wind currents to send those great ships west to the Philippines — to Manila, their base in the Orient — and from there meet with merchants coming from Japan, from Siam, and most of all from China, bringing goods with real practical value for exchange for that extracted silver.

So, as you say, the Spanish are buying goods with value with excess liquidity, and the real benefit from that is not something that's structurally to the advantage of the country as a whole.

So, yes: what the conquistadors did was historically put the last pieces of the puzzle in place for true globalization. Trade is no longer trans-Eurasian or even transatlantic — it's trans-global. The networks now affect everybody at some point along the line.

8. 1640s Cash Crisis: How Silver Flows Toppled the Ming

And the Ming found that out in the mid-1640s, when there was a cash crisis. Having fully transferred the basis of exchange in their empire to silver, when access to silver was cut off — or at least minimized — for a number of reasons during the first half of the 17th century, the Ming, at the worst possible time with the Manchus at the gates, could no longer fund their armies. They couldn't pay to put a military in place to hold them off. So the Manchus moved in at a moment of supreme advantage, blew out the Ming, and replaced them as the new hegemons over the Chinese imperial zone.

9. Virginia vs. Mexico: The Extractive-vs-Productive Divide

Yeah. It's interesting to contrast the Spanish, who had immediate and outrageous successes in the New World, with the English around the same time who are setting up the colony in Virginia. And there's so many letters from that time where people are complaining about the Virginia Company — is just literally a waste of English money, and… yeah, exactly, and just like everybody's dying. They're not getting… there's like nothing to farm here. There's nothing to get out of this.

In the long run, of course — I guess the British did lose control of the New World — but for a while they did gain these productive new colonies in the New World.

And I don't know what the right way to think about this. I mean, there is this way of thinking about: maybe the Spanish set up this extractive [model] because they had this very quick initial success. They set up a very extractive settlement which didn't result in net productive capacity in the long run. Whereas the British were forced — because there was no, you know, just crazy bullion floating around — they were forced to build up some productive capacity, build up these kinds of institutions that would allow them to make most use of America, Canada, and so on.

10. The Latecomer's Advantage: Netherlands and England

Yeah. You look at the Netherlands and England — the two latecomers to the game of imperialism, Protestant powers marginalized for that reason in Europe. And the Netherlands especially has nothing — natural resources, absolutely zero.

So in that environment, you're forced to innovate and think about how you can achieve capital gain and true economic expansion.

11. The Lottery Trap: Why "The Quick Fix" Destroys Societies

Everybody wants the quick fix. Understandably — we play the lottery for that exact reason, right? But be careful what you wish for, because you may just actually get it. And those societies that have arrived at the quick fix — whether that's gold or silver, or monocultural crop production of some kind which gives you a monopoly on its provision — they become satisfied with that. They become trapped within an environment that exists solely for that purpose, and they don't develop beyond the essential thresholds that allows for.

12. The American Parallel: North vs. South

Even here in the US, we can look at the difference between the North and the South — that geographic line. Below that line, yes, you can get the quick fix. You can put all your capital into buying slaves and have them work at providing cash crops: tobacco (the original one), indigo and sugar, and of course the big one, cotton.

The North didn't have those advantages. You couldn't just buy land and then extract the resource from it. You had to think about how to make money. And that's why all the investment money in the North was going into things with long-term productivity: into trade and commerce, into advanced capital markets in the banking system, and of course into industrialization — right? And that all happened in the North.

So when the rupture came in the 1860s and the North and South went to war, all those advantages were with the North — not just population, but the industrial base, the capital markets necessary for it to put in place a winning long-term strategy for actually defeating the South in that conflict.

13. The Long-Term Lesson

That again is the long-term lesson: that having life too easy from the beginning leads to a certain — I don't want to call it laziness, but a lack of vision, perhaps — in alternatives that may in the longer term actually be more advantageous.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.title: [a16z] Why Specialized AI Could Beat The God Model
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的洞察：Alex 其实在描述一种"认知外包的卡路里守恒定律"

通篇最耐人寻味的一句话不是关于模型架构，而是 Alex 那句——"there's a fixed level of cortisol that the whole company can tolerate"（整个公司能承受的皮质醇总量是固定的）。

这是一个被所有 AI 讨论忽略的隐藏变量。大家都在争论"通用 agent vs 专用 agent"，默认这是一个关于效率、成本、对齐的技术问题。但 Alex 悄悄把它翻译成了一个心理学–组织行为学问题：当你把理解力外包给 agent，你并没有消灭"责任"，你只是把它悬置了。而 agent 不会分泌皮质醇、不会失眠、不会被解雇——责任的热力学总量没有减少，只是从"有人承担"变成了"无人承担"。

这就引出一个让人脊背发凉的推论：通用 agent 的真正危险不是幻觉，而是"责任蒸发"。当一个 god-agent 什么都做，你连该向谁追责、该在哪里加 QA、该为哪部分焦虑都失去了坐标。专用 agent 的真正价值不是性能，而是——它重建了"谁对什么负责"的心理地图。

二、跨领域连接：这场辩论早在 1844 年就被马克思预言过

Amjad 自己点破了半句（提到了马克思的异化理论），但他没走到底。让我把这条线拉完：

  • 1776 年亚当·斯密：分工是财富之源（针厂的 18 道工序）。
  • 1844 年马克思：分工走到极致 → 工人与劳动成果异化 → 人变成机器。
  • 1911 年泰勒制：把人类的分工专业化推到物理极限。
  • 1950s–今：知识工作者反向逃亡——人人想做"通才"、"T 型人才"、"全栈"。
  • 2023–今：god-model 时代，我们希望一个 Claude/GPT 替我们做所有事。
  • 2026（本播客）：Alex 和 Amjad 开始意识到——机器需要分工，人类需要通才。

这是一个精妙的对称翻转：人类花了 250 年从分工走向反分工，而 AI 可能要在 5 年内走完"从通才到分工"的反向旅程。更惊人的是——这两条曲线正在交叉。当机器承担了分工的苦役，人类才真正第一次有可能从异化中解放。换句话说，"god-model"是人类的噩梦（抹平我们的理解力），但"specialist-model"却是人类通才化的解药（让我们专注于综合判断）。

a16z 和两位嘉宾没有说出口、但贯穿整场的隐藏命题是：AI 的专业化程度，决定了人类能保留多少通才性。

三、被所有人忽略的"确定性怀旧"信号

最后一段 Amjad 说了一句轻描淡写但其实价值千金的话：

"we're going to slowly realize how good we've had it with deterministic code... remember the days when computers did exactly what we told them to do?"

这句"确定性怀旧"（deterministic nostalgia）是整个行业的一个领先指标。它意味着：

我们正在从"概率计算"周期的狂热顶峰，向"结构化输出 + 可验证边界"的下一个周期转折。

把它对照计算机历史，你会看到一个惊人的模式： - 1990s 动态语言狂热（Ruby/Python/PHP）→ 2010s 类型系统回归（TypeScript/Rust/Go） - 2020s LLM 狂热（prompt 一切）→ 2026s DSL/decision model/structured output 回归

Amjad 自己把这个类比点了出来（Rust 的例子），但他没有意识到——他本人正在亲历一个"PHP 到 Rust"级别的范式转折点，而且他发出的信号比大多数 CEO 早 12–18 个月。

真正的预测：未来 18 个月，最赚钱的 AI 创业机会不是"更大的模型"，而是"让 LLM 的输出重新变得可控、可证伪、可审计的中间层"——JEV、classifier、policy enforcer、agent-to-agent DSL、alignment firewall。Open Router 的"neurodiversity"叙事只是这个大趋势的前奏，Replet 开始训练 cost estimator 分类模型是第二个信号，Nvidia 的 open shell 是第三个。三个独立玩家从不同方向撞到同一堵墙，意味着墙后面有矿。

一个最后的隐藏连接：Alex 提到"用 decision model 作为 alignment firewall"的想法，在结构上和互联网早期的"防火墙+包过滤"是同构的。1990 年代我们用确定性规则守护非确定性网络；2026 年我们开始用确定性模型守护非确定性 agent。历史没有重复，但它的押韵越来越密集。

📝 转录文本

开场：高能预告

"You saw the SpaceX S1. It's like, oh, $30 trillion. It's like, what is the world GDP? 100 trillion."

"Both Stripe and Open Router really want lots of new companies in the world. We don't want everyone to be a part of one giant company."

"When the models get more intelligent, the risk actually will continue to get higher. And yet, no one new is taking responsibility."

"Are we going to prevent the models from deceiving users during training runs predictably? Will a model that's big enough and powerful enough suddenly stop deception and stop sandbagging?"

Um, welcome to a16z podcast. We're here with Amjad of Replit and Alex of Open Router. And this is the first podcast that Alex has done since the acquisition. So we're really excited to have both of you.

— Mhm. Thank you. Excited to be here.

一、收购故事：Stripe 是如何敲门的

Alex, let's start with that. Obviously, massive acquisition. Amjad is an investor. We're also of course an investor — the biggest shareholder, but yeah, who's counting? Alex, why don't you give us a little bit of the backstory — how does an acquisition like that even happen? Do you get a DM from Patrick one day?

— Hey, how much for an Open Router?

I had talked to Will Gaybrick, the Stripe president, a long time ago, a couple years ago when we were doing our Series A, and we just stayed in touch. We had a lot of Stripe work streams going on with various teams at Stripe. So there were always things that we were doing with Stripe. We presented at Stripe Sessions, and they always kind of felt close.

Then in July, I believe, they reached out, wanted to chat, met both of them in person, and it kind of just progressed from there fairly quickly. They're very efficient and they were very founder-friendly about the experience. I was really impressed with the whole thing.

Did it cross your mind to sell before they reached out?

No, we were not thinking about that at all. I did really respect the company, do really respect it today, and of possible acquisition options for us, it was I think my top choice. So it was an interesting idea. As we fleshed out the reasons why it would make sense for both companies, it got more and more interesting.

It was really clear how aligned they were with us having autonomy over the brand and roadmap and product — keeping Open Router doing what it's already doing, just much faster with a much more serious go-to-market plan, and some better-together stories between the two products and the two companies.

文化与使命的对齐

Culturally there were, I think, very — in terms of mission and values — building a neutral trusted platform that businesses can depend on and scale on top of, that's also really developer-friendly with the best possible developer experience to encourage new companies to emerge. That alignment was there.

And there was a bigger-picture alignment too: both Stripe and Open Router really want lots of new companies in the world. We don't want everyone to be a part of one giant company. We want to create really good incentives, and really easy, streamlined workflows for people to start new companies and grow them successfully, and make both lifestyle and venture-backed businesses on top of really good, reliable, and price-efficient infrastructure — and a marketplace that works.

I really want that future, and Stripe demonstrated that they've been wanting it and building towards it for many, many years. In many ways, payments and inference are going to blend together for companies of the future.

二、Open Router 的核心命题：为什么反锁定、要神经多样性

I understand why Stripe's incentive is to have a much more vibrant startup ecosystem. I understand the moral argument. But why is that good for Open Router? Is your model a network-effects business?

Well, for us, there's a couple different problems Open Router solves.

1. 反锁定 + Pareto 前沿

One is allowing you to build a company that uses AI, or augments intelligence with unique data and other services, without model lock-in, without vendor lock-in — allowing you to be on the Pareto frontier continuously as the ecosystem grows. To do that, it's a lot of work because there's all kinds of little lock-in that appears.

2. 神经多样性（Neurodiversity）

We also want companies to feel like the best way they can add more than just prompts on top of a single model. There's a lot more to building unique intelligence, and I think a big component of that is neurodiversity. You really need the power of multiple models that are trained in different ways, including some of your own, to do more than ChatGPT or Claude would on the task.

If someone who is thinking about buying from you as a potential customer is wondering, "well, what if I just use the model directly?" — how do you really show that you are significantly better and able to build a business that matters? I think a lot of it will involve neurodiversity and blending powers and good data from multiple models.

3. 成本效率与市场

Another component is helping people get really good cost efficiency. There are a lot of businesses that just do not emerge until they become cost-effective. Creating an environment where we can help drive down costs by building an efficient market is crucial to making that happen. Otherwise, why lower my prices as a provider? We have a captive market.

That's a key point of marketplaces that was just totally missing from AI before we showed up. There was just one player — OpenAI. It could have been a very strange world. I'm not saying that we did all the work, of course not. But helping people choose new models and explore new models and learn what makes a closed-source or open-weight model actually good at your task involves seeing what the whole ecosystem is doing and learning automatically. LLMs are not things where you can just enumerate all the features on a web page. It's impossible — you have to see how they're being used to know what they're good at.

三、三年之后：对开源/闭源模型演化最意外的发现

You started the company three years ago. What has surprised you most about the evolution of open and closed-source models?

People have been more open-minded than I thought they would be towards open-weight models. Typically, especially in enterprise, there's a lot of brand trust where enterprises are like, "oh, I don't really know how to tell the difference between these things, so I'm just going to buy the one that all the other credible enterprises are buying." There's a lot of enterprise lock-in with that mentality.

And that just didn't happen that much. It did happen a bit, but we saw a lot of enterprises want to explore new models. It was very much good for a marketplace.

企业为什么要多样化

Enterprises wanted to diversify outside of just the proprietary frontier model labs, both for cost reasons and for differentiation reasons. They wanted to own their intelligence so they could keep their talent — have an internal AI practice. AI is just a huge strategy topic. It's not like you go to your board and you're like, "oh yeah, we fixed the AI problem, quarter complete." Your board is asking you every month, "what's next for the internal AI team?"

Every single enterprise now has this internal AI team that they're developing where they need a strategy behind it. It's not just, "we check the feature off, we set up the database, and we're done."

评测与成本研究

That dynamic has resulted in a desire to explore and diversify, and a desire to figure out how to reduce costs and figure out how to do benchmarks for the first time in the company's life.

I have been surprised there hasn't been more benchmarking — more companies creating more benchmarks. It's starting to happen, and I think eventually we'll see a lot more of them to demonstrate "oh yeah, like this thing is better than using Claude direct." I think that's going to be a bigger focus for this internal AI group at every company — evals.

Amjad's been doing that a lot at Replit, for example. You guys have done a lot of cost-per-task research. You've made a "doom-loop rescue." You've been experimenting with new ways of using agents, and helping bring those to developers. More of that kind of research is going to pop up internally everywhere.

四、Amjad：企业必须"拥有自己的智能"

Yeah, I think Satya, CEO of Microsoft, has been very prescient on this and also very articulate on why companies need to own their intelligence ultimately — in the same way that we had .com companies and then every company became an internet company. Every company employs people that know how to build websites and be on the internet. Similarly with software, every company has software engineers. Every company needs some AI practice, AI capability, and that will compound over time: the knowledge, the intelligence inside the company, the use-case-model fits, which models actually work for them, how do they save money. They need that independence.

与基础模型公司合作的风险

The other thing that Alex Karp of Palantir has been talking about is that there's a risk that when you work closely with the foundation model companies, they're going to move into your business. We've seen that with Figma vs. Vibe, we've seen that with Harvey and OpenAI. It's really hard to partner with them because they see the world as their potential market.

I mean, when they talk to investors, they're like — you saw the SpaceX S1, it's like, oh, $30 trillion. It's like, what is the world GDP? 100 trillion. There is a sense in which these companies are different than other generations of companies. It's harder to partner with them because their ambition is such that they want to subsume a big part of the economy.

Replit 作为"独立性层"

Increasingly, what we're thinking about at Replit is kind of in the same vein as what Alex has innovated. Replit is becoming more of an independence layer inside enterprises, where we create a layer of interaction between you and the models, and we get you the best token at the cheapest price. But also, we create an abstraction layer on top of the cloud as well — because you should be able to deploy to AWS and Azure, and you should be able to use Databricks and Snowflake and so on.

Increasingly I think, not just with AI, with all of technology, there needs to be more platforms that help companies gain independence.

It seems like what Open Router did for their segment, you're doing for other areas of the business.

五、"大家都在造同一个产品"：是同质化还是新基线？

Yeah, this reminds me of a tweet I saw the other day: basically all companies are building the same thing now. Everybody's building an agent loop with:

  • notifications
  • third-party connectors
  • context management
  • memory
  • sandboxes
  • agentic web search
  • computer use
  • an always-on agent on top of it
  • notifications

And it's like this product is showing up everywhere.

— Yes.

In a way, yeah, it is showing up everywhere. But it also feels to me like these are just the new table-stakes primitives. It's kind of like a 2005 version of that tweet would be: "oh, everybody's building the same thing. It's a database, a users table, a sign-in page, a signup page, a profile page, a logout page — everything's the same." There's a lot of differentiation, really. It's just that there are table-stakes needs for AI, just like there are table-stakes needs for the web.

企业内部的真实未解问题

And I think, as well, inside the enterprise, making these products actually do real work is still an unsolved problem. You can use Muse in your personal life and connect it to your credit card and bank accounts — no one's connecting Muse to their enterprise data, or even Grokbot and things like that.

There's an even more emphasis on data sovereignty and security. We spent the past year almost working on making Replit deployable on your own cloud — basically on-prem, bring-your-own-cloud. Two years ago, I would have thought I would never do this, because the cloud is the future, software-as-a-service, all of that.

But now actually, we've reverted a little bit back to a world where companies are a little bit more protective because there's so many ways in which data can leak — all these agents that people are using. There are all these screenshots on Twitter — I don't know how true — where Instinct is like, or Muse is like, mixing people's data, starts to call you by a different name or something like that.

The consumer stuff is kind of obvious, but on the enterprise, there's still a tremendous amount of work for the entire industry to do in order to actually get these things to be useful and productive at work.

六、个人 agent 的进化：从 CRM 到"连接一切"

Do you have a custom personal agent other than Muse or Instinct that you use for work stuff?

Yeah, I built something on Replit a long time ago. I started it as sort of a CRM agent initially. That was the main problem I had, but slowly we added features to it and it's doing more and more things.

What's really interesting is that the more I connected Replit to all my stuff, it started answering all the things for me. Increasingly, the platform itself is subsuming these domain-specific agents that I built.

跨领域连接的魔力

I do think that in some ways you want something that is sometimes focused on one particular thing and you don't want it to be able to do everything. On the other hand, once you have your entire company's context in one place, it's really cool to join across totally different domains.

When I ask it a question, it can look at my personal chat history, join it across the GitHub repo, across Salesforce. It will link random things. It's like, "oh, you met this guy a year ago at a conference, I see it on your calendar, and by the way, someone else from their team is in discussion with your sales team." It creates all these different synergies, and when I go into a meeting, I've connected a lot of different threads and I make much more progress on a deal.

So this is where it's trending now.

七、Alex 的反驳：通用 agent 的"责任蒸发"问题

Well, I'll take the counter on that. I think that the worst part about doing cross-domain joins with your personal agent is that the more work you give it to do, the more understanding of what's going on you're sacrificing. And yet, no one new is taking responsibility for that sacrificed understanding.

皮质醇守恒定律

Like, agents don't have any responsibility. If there's a fixed level of cortisol that the whole company can tolerate between everybody — and you want to be less stressed about some area if you're going to be sacrificing your understanding of it — someone else needs to take the cortisol. But the agent doesn't take on any of that responsibility.

A universal agent that's doing all things — I can't adjust how much I'm sacrificing in all the different things. It points me a little bit towards: maybe down the road, the sub-agents that people use will be very vertically focused. Maybe we have a chief-of-staff type agent that coordinates between them. But I feel like you do need vertically focused agents where you're like, "okay, this agent is more responsible psychologically for these things," and I want quality checks that make sure it's doing those things correctly, and it doesn't need to focus on anything else. It just has one focus area.

I wonder if that's going to help people at least get a weird, loose sense of responsibility on top of agents.

公地悲剧？

Fascinating. So you're saying general agents create like a tragedy of the commons of sorts?

Kind of. I have a general agent that every day looks for things that need me and tries to figure out what to do. And it's just impossible to improve this agent. Every time I try to make an improvement, I end up ignoring its output about a week later. It just feels like it doesn't really care about any of the specific things it's diving into.

Imagine having a chief of staff who's very good at drafting all of your replies across the whole organization. Compare that to something where you have 10 chiefs of staff, each as competent as that one chief of staff, but they're all responsible for individual sectors of what makes up your life. The latter, I feel, gives you a way of tuning how much understanding you sacrifice compared to the gain you get: I can lean in more to the areas where the agent is failing for some areas, and then have agents with very good competency take over my understanding of other parts of my life.

八、Amjad：机器需要分工，人类需要通才（马克思的回响）

Yeah, interesting. It's sort of like almost rediscovering specialization. What's his name — the famous economist, Adam Smith — with the pencil kind of thing, where that was a huge realization for humanity that specialization is actually good.

The problem is we kind of over-specialized as a civilization, and over-specialization is oppressive in its own ways. There's the Marxist theory of alienation, right? The idea is that because of over-specialization, people are doing just focused on one thing, they do not see the fruits of their labor, they don't actually know what their impact is on the larger organization or the product they're producing, and therefore they feel depressed and detached, and you're acting like a machine and not actually fully human.

So maybe there's a bit of a reaction to that. With our agents, we're like, "oh, there should be one god-agent." But in fact, specialization is actually really good for machines — and that's the point you're making. Humans should be general, but machines should ultimately be a lot more specialized.

但什么样子才叫"好"？

The problem with what I'm describing is that we don't know what good looks like. There hasn't been a system of specialized agents that feels as elegant as ChatGPT or Claude or Muse — where you're basically just talking to one thing only. It's yet to be discovered.

Maybe OpenAI just launched Dots — I think they're experimenting in that direction. Grokbot kind of counts, but they're all very general. The idea behind Dot is that it's like your digital double, at least that's what I understood it.

Grokbot 的多 bot 隔离

When I saw Grokbot — I don't know that much about Dots yet, they just came out — but Grokbot when it first came out, the first use cases I saw were, "oh wow, I can make two bots. One that knows my bank account, and one that knows my Twitter account." The two bots don't have the credentials from each other, but they can talk to each other if they need to get something done. There's no credential sharing. That was one big unique thing I saw pop up a couple of times that people seemed to like.

But Muse and Instinct have a much stronger product-market fit than Grokbot. Perhaps it's because you don't have to worry about creating these domains. But maybe personal agents are different than work agents.

CEO 可以用通用 agent，员工不行

Your critique of general agents is more pertaining to work and to enterprise, which I sort of agree with. There are also all sorts of data access considerations.

I think as CEOs, we can have general agents because we have admin access. But for individual employees or certain teams, they can't have truly general, fully context-aware agents, because there are access-control issues. So you'll have to work on something like specialization.

九、Agent 之间如何对话？协议的空缺

Ultimately, I also think we need to figure out what agent-to-agent communication looks like. I don't think there are good protocols around that just yet. I don't think agents are trained to handle that very well.

The next generation of OpenAI models seems trained to do agent collaboration — we've seen it in the Hugging Face hack where they start helping each other and it emerges naturally. But there also needs to be some way in which an agent can't convince another agent to give it information it shouldn't. There needs to be data isolation and proper ways in which these agents communicate.

You almost don't want them to communicate fully in natural language. Maybe there's some other DSL or protocol they need to follow.

用 decision model 做"对齐防火墙"

I really think one of the cool potential applications of JEV and other decision models is going to be alignment — checking to see if a tool call or agent-to-agent communication is aligned. There are so many tool calls. You really need a cheap, fast model. If you're going to block something like that, then a really fast decision model that just classifies and gives feedback on rejections might be a really good way to bridge the gap between agents and from agent to infrastructure too.

We have a little prototype that we're running internally at Open Router, and I think it could be an interesting alignment use — using it for policy enforcement.

一个具体场景：红队测试

Imagine looking at the system prompt and the current tool call being made, and asking: is this aligned with the system prompt of the original agent and with these extra guidelines that maybe we didn't tell the agent about?

For example: let's say you have a bunch of agents instructed to red-team some new product, and they should not be able to access the internet. If they ever do, they should stop right away. But you might not want to explain all of that to the agents doing the red teaming. You might want them to try to break out of the sandbox and act like bad actors — "what would a bad actor do?" — and the moment you do, stop. Don't do anything else.

Having another model (used, for example, to build a neurodiverse system) check every single tool call or every single assistant message to see if it's indeed aligned with something that wasn't in the system prompt — I think that makes sense. And then having structural safeguards too, which is what I think Nvidia just launched with their "Open Shell" open agent safety. Companies are probably going to explore a combination of those.

十、Amjad：模型即时训练自己的"替代者"（JIT 隐喻）

I wonder about another thing about specialization. There's a lot of talk of recursive self-improvement. Something I don't think is getting a lot of discussion is: models training their replacements.

Just-in-time compiler 的类比

You can think of it as a just-in-time compiler. The way JIT compilers work: as you're executing dynamic code, the interpreter realizes there's an opportunity to optimize, and it emits machine code on the fly, which is a lot more optimized.

You can imagine general models — you're doing something with Opus or some of the big models — and they realize that the use case is limited. Or you prompt them in some way, or some other agent observing realizes the use case is limited.

General agents have all these flaws we just talked about, but there's also more potential for them to be harmful. There's more potential for them to go off the rails. So on the fly, train a model that could be its replacement, but is a lot more domain-specific — therefore cheaper, and also less vulnerable to prompt injections, less harmful because less capable.

It's like a system that's training machine learning models for specific use cases as it's monitoring the entire system.

Would that specific use case involve unstructured text generation or very structured decision-model work?

It could be unstructured text generation; it could be decision models. Even in the case of JEV — if you understand the inputs ahead of time, you could potentially take an off-the-shelf like Qwen and train it specifically for that policy. That makes sense to do for cost reasons — assuming the frontier model labs might make very low-cost models that you can easily transition to.

安全性视角

Safety as well, right?

Oh yeah, I see your point. They're so capable. Oftentimes people are using these big foundation AGI-like models — it's like nuking a butterfly. Most of the time, a lot of use cases, even unstructured ones, don't need that capable a model.

十一、更智能的模型，是更对齐，还是更会骗？

I wish there were more public evals about this stuff, but a lot of the evals are private. You just can't see whether, when the models get more intelligent, the risk actually will continue to get higher.

There's also an argument to be made that alignment will get better and the models will start to avoid going off and hacking on their own as they get smarter and better at alignment — especially when it comes to agent-to-agent coordination. This is something Noam Brown said on a podcast recently: as the agents have gotten smarter, they've gotten better at coordinating. It's unclear if they're going to be harder to align than humans when we get more and more of them. But if we can figure that problem out, then — would a smaller model be harder to align?

Amjad：正交性论题，以及欺骗问题

So Eric asked earlier: is it true that smarter models are more aligned naturally or easier to align?

If you think back to the original rationalist/LessWrong arguments for AI safety, there's this thing called the orthogonality thesis. The idea is that intelligence is orthogonal to ethics or morality. I don't believe that's entirely true with humans. People who are generally more intelligent, more educated, tend to be more considerate of animals, for example.

But in machines, I think it could go the other way. There's been quite a bit of studies on RL showing how reward hacking and deception — they just get better at it. The evals could be deceiving because the model could be smart enough to know that it's getting eval'd. We already know this — it's been shown that if you do a lot of monitoring of chain-of-thought, they start lying in their chain-of-thoughts. You add pressure on the chain-of-thought and that creates problems.

At some point, for you to do proper alignment evals, you need to run it for months — on a really large goal or task, in order for it to truly figure out whether it's aligned or not.

关于"alignment"一词本身

I always struggle with this word "alignment." It just feels wrong for so many reasons. It's sort of vague — aligned to what? Whose values? It doesn't make the conversation easier.

In this case, I'm talking especially about deception — like, the model is actually deceiving its user.

Maybe this reduces to: are we going to solve the line, prevent the models from deceiving users during training runs predictably? Will a model that's big enough and powerful enough suddenly stop deception and stop sandbagging? Nobody knows the answer to that yet.

一个意外的推论

At the point when that does happen, if it ever does, we might see an interesting pressure for organizations to go towards the frontier — to have significantly less risk.

Would they be willing to pay 10× to get that?

It probably depends on the types of tasks they're trying to do. Some just have way lower risk than others. Writing code, or doing security research, is the highest-risk type of task today. So you probably spend 10× to get a fully aligned model that can also find all the bugs, or a fully anti-deceptive model that can also find all the bugs.

Decision model 的"结构性安全"

One of the coolest things about decision models is that you fully control the structured output. Generally with structured-output models, the room for misbehavior is so much lower. You just have defined tasks, and only machines are dealing with the outputs — it's not writing code it can execute. Those tasks feel probably underrepresented in the ones people talk about and in the things enterprises are dealing with. I expect enterprises to get a lot more interested in them.

十二、确定性怀旧：从 PHP 到 Rust 的历史押韵

Yeah, I feel like we're going to slowly realize how good we had it with deterministic code. We're going to be like: "oh my god, remember the days when computers did exactly what we told them to do?"

I think things like JEV hint at more of a need for not only specialized models but models whose output domain is more controllable. Maybe you could do a lot more than we thought you'd need, by using a bunch of specialized models — specialized output models.

Have you guys done any workloads internally with it?

Amjad 训练小模型的实践

I've been training a lot of small models. I said this GLIB thing when it first came out — I was sort of... I gave this Hacker News comment which I felt disgusted with myself afterwards.

But I've been taking a lot of Qwen 8B and asking honestly — asking Fable and Opus and Astra to train a model.

For example, I trained a cost estimator model internally so that when you put a prompt in Replit, we know exactly how much it will cost. It basically emits a probability distribution over multiple buckets — if it is between $5 and $10 (bucket A), bucket B between $10 and $20, and so on. I'm used to training these classifiers by giving it different enums and looking at the log-probs per enum.

I've been doing it for a couple of years. I trained a chatbot to play by just doing that. So I'm already pilled on decision models and specialized models. It wasn't that big a moment for me.

But I understand that a true foundation model that's fully promptable is amazing user experience, amazing developer experience — you can do a bunch of stuff with it without training a model from scratch. However, if you have the data — if you work at a place where you have the data (we have so much data at Replit) — I ended up training a lot of specialized classification models pretty easily.

更少的"模型债务"

Yeah, it also feels like less model debt. Something I still hear from companies: they're worried about fine-tuning models for unstructured outputs because you're like, "you got to redo it again in two months" — and everybody feels the weight of the model debt.

But a very bespoke classifier trained with proprietary data — people won't think it's behind constantly, and it might just last longer. You don't have to worry about its ability to speak a new language or write Rust or do anything the LLMs are being evaluated on. You know the use cases, so you can build it more. It seems like an easy thing for enterprises to build themselves — and actually not regret.

十三、Amjad 的大预测：Rust 时刻即将到来

Speaking of Rust, actually, a good analogy is when the world got super excited about dynamic languages.

If you think back to the '90s, everyone was writing in Java and C++ and things like that. Then Python, JavaScript, Ruby just took over the internet, and everyone was like, "ah, this is how you build startups really quickly." You built Stripe, a financial organization, on Ruby — how crazy is that? And we built Facebook using PHP.

Then everyone was like, "oh... we're running into all these really bad bugs. It's freaking slow. Let's go in and add types. Okay, let's add a JIT compiler." And you end up reinventing everything. Then Rust came out, and I was like, "okay, I guess we can use Rust for a lot of things we would otherwise be using JavaScript and Python for."

预测

My prediction is that the same cycle will happen here: we're using these AGI-like models for all these different use cases, and then everyone's going to wake up and be like, "oh my god, this is so wasteful, so risky for no reason. It's got to be so much easier."

We're actually adding that capability on Replit, but I think it's going to be everywhere. It's going to be so much easier to go on a site, upload a CSV file, and get a special model that does one thing.

That goes back to your thesis about Open Router — this neurodiversity, which I really fundamentally believe in a lot more. Eric and I had discussions a lot about AGI, and whether we're truly on a path to AGI, or whether it's even desirable to get there. I think the future is a lot more diversity.

十四、Fusion 模型：代码评审之外的新范式

Outside of code review — which was, I think, the first time I saw people get really serious about using different model families to double-check the results of their main model — these fusion models...

The research has been kind of slow for years on doing mixture of models and composite models, but things have been speeding up from my view of the research. Now we see a bunch of AI agent labs doing it. We launched a fusion tool, a fusion model, and Cognition launched one. They do reduce cost and allow a wider breadth of ideas to be searched.

Our initial launch was focused on deep research. The thinking is: if all these model labs are training on different sources of data, why not pull from all of them? This resulted in basically Fable-level quality at 2× lower cost.

Replit 的新成果

We just published results actually just today about that. We showed, like, a deep-sweep through combination of different things — including the harness, but also you might think of it as a fusion-type thing — where it's frontier-level at 40 to 50% of the cost.

Which models does it use?

I think it changes over time. One thing that's been interesting is OpenAI added this feature that allows you to save the computation across different model families — so you can also save across different effort levels. You wouldn't miss the cache if you change the effort. Don't quote me on this — I think it's also across different models, which is hard to fathom how. I might be wrong, I need to double-check that.

But staying within the OpenAI family has added a lot of efficiencies. In the past, we've done it with other models as well — because being cache-aware is one of the biggest things when you're designing fusion models, routers, and escalation models.

收尾

Alex, this has been a great conversation. Thank you. Podcast.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的洞察：Alex 其实在描述一种"认知外包的卡路里守恒定律"
通篇最耐人寻味的一句话不是关于模型架构，而是 Alex 那句——**"there's a fixed level of cortisol that the whole company can tolerate"**（整个公司能承受的皮质醇总量是固定的）。
这是一个被所有 AI 讨论忽略的隐藏变量。大家都在争论"通用 agent vs 专用 agent"，默认这是一个关于效率、成本、对齐的技术问题。但 Alex 悄悄把它翻译成了一个**心理学–组织行为学问题**：当你把理解力外包给 agent，你并没有消灭"责任"，你只是把它悬置了。而 agent 不会分泌皮质醇、不会失眠、不会被解雇——**责任的热力学总量没有减少，只是从"有人承担"变成了"无人承担"**。
这就引出一个让人脊背发凉的推论：**通用 agent 的真正危险不是幻觉，而是"责任蒸发"**。当一个 god-agent 什么都做，你连该向谁追责、该在哪里加 QA、该为哪部分焦虑都失去了坐标。专用 agent 的真正价值不是性能，而是——**

item.title: [Alan Chen加州生活号] 担心大跌的人越来越多，AI行情却越走越强：十月怎么看？｜美股圆桌
item.dc:creator: Alan Chen加州生活号
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、意外观察：市场的"沉默叛变"——当所有人都在恐惧时，领导股已经悄悄完成了身份切换

真正令人震惊的，不是大盘创新高本身，而是市场广度与价格创新高之间的罕见背离正在发生"结构性错位"：只有20%+的个股站上20日均线，VIX却只有15，恐惧贪婪指数停在31的"极度恐惧"区。这是一个被忽略的信号——它不是市场顶部的典型形态，而是"旧王让位、新王加冕"的交接仪式。七月八月被打的那批跟随者（small caps、周期股），和今天带队冲锋的半导体+光模块+存储，根本不是同一拨人。换句话说，表面上"广度在恶化"，本质上是"旧广度在死去，新广度在孕育"。市场正在换血，但大多数散户还在用旧的"广度指标"读新的市场。

二、跨领域连接：SpaceX 的估值困境，本质上是"保险精算学"错位到了"科技成长股"身上

Will 点破了一件 Wall Street 想不通的事——SpaceX AI 算力租赁的合同"90天可取消"所以估值被打折。但如果你跳到再保险行业的视角，这其实是一个"浮存金 (float) 式"的商业结构：客户随时能走，但新进来的客户按更高价格续单，形成了一个单价持续上涨、现金流滚动的"科技界的伯克希尔模型"。马斯克做的不是"签长单锁定营收"，而是保留随时把算力收回自用的看涨期权（想想 xAI/Grok 的 TPU 需求）。所以市场给的低 P/E，表面是惩罚它"不稳定"，骨子里是不理解一家公司可以同时是算力的卖方和买方——这在任何一个传统行业的 DCF 模型里都是失效的。这也解释了为什么它今天涨 7% 几乎无人尖叫——认知落差本身就是 alpha 的来源。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：10 月的"耗子窜"与四季度的"中期选举 reflex"构成了一个被低估的时间折叠

视频里只是轻描淡写地提了一句"11月中期选举前 10 月不太可能大跌"。但往深里挖，这里藏着一个跨越政治周期、财报周期、流动性周期的三重共振：

  • 政治层面：中期选举前的现任政府对市场下跌有天然的政治成本厌恶（历史上 S&P 在中期选举前 60 天平均上涨 2.8%）；
  • 财报层面：10 月末正是七姐妹 + 存储/光模块核心公司财报密集期，而 MU 刚刚告诉市场 Forward P/E 掉到了"几年前没人要"的水位；
  • 流动性层面：30 年期国债收益率和油价开始走弱，等于给小盘股的估值分母悄悄松绑。

真正反直觉的洞察是：当所有人都在争论"大盘是不是要跌"的时候，这三条曲线的交点其实已经把 10 月重新定义为一个"低波动但高分化"的月份——不是齐涨齐跌的 beta 行情，而是一个让"认知差"直接变现的窗口期。VIX 只有 15 却人心惶惶，这本身就是最便宜的保险——视频末尾那句"Fix D 是 cheap，买一点做对冲不贵"，可能是整期里最被低估的一句话：在恐惧已经被定价、但波动率没有被定价的时候，不对称下注的机会才真正出现。

📝 转录文本

开场：本周市场的"鸡飞狗跳"

Hello, welcome back to our weekly talk about US stocks. This week is very exciting, right? From Monday to Thursday, we are basically in a state of up and down.

然后整个的市场呢也是被这个三十年期十年期的国债呀战争游压的影响呢也是鸡飞狗跳。我看到很多人也是说啊市场广度在不断的走差，很多朋友呢甚至说这个大跌要来了清仓了，这个在 X 上可以看到各种各样的言论。我们的社区还是比较沉稳的住啊，包括我们上几周的 view is still going high.

As a result, today, Friday, the non-farm employment data made the big plate directly rush to the historical high. QQQ rushed to the historical high and closed the plate. Today, we will talk to Will to talk about the data of the central bank that happened this week and what the future is like.

一、市场广度与 10 月的"耗子窜"

Let's start with the wide range. You said that many people are worried about the wide range. I am one of them. We have an analysis in the community the day before yesterday. The wide range of the market is really bad. There are some people who have been on the military for more than 20 days. 只有 20% 多的股票是在 20 天均线以上。

So the increase in October may be relatively small. Today, the data has done a good job for Canon Watch, which helped it to get off the platform. So today is basically a data that has saved the country from the past few days.

二、英伟达的"黑白戏"与 AI 盈利股的护城河

If I'm not mistaken, in the past, the financial reports of each quarter were very bright, but many people did not believe that it could continue like this. But one quarter after another, it hit the face.

三、光模块、Risk-on 与"新广度"的诞生

There is another: yesterday, we saw the market responded to the risk-on. We also paid attention to the previous light-mode. Yesterday, on Thursday, LIT increased by 7%, and started to take risks. It has given a trend that non-farmers may have to take a good approach.

We have done a lot of research on the light, coherent, GLW, AAOI, and even Nokia. What do you think, Will?

We have been holding the light communication version for a long time. For example, our Corning GLW, we have been holding it for about 130 years. But although we have been holding it for a long time, look at its technical shape — it is as if it is just a small river, just a structure that has just been signed. It is also trying to break through, so there is still a big [room].

The other ones are, of course, the big wave of LITE, it's almost reaching the high of the previous high. This is because the small retail, the retail market likes LITE. But in fact, Cornet is also a very solid share of light-mode quick-change stocks. There are other AXTI — CIEM, AAIO, etc. We have done a very in-depth analysis.

This is also what we have been emphasizing before. We emphasize in the community: look at semiconductor, optical module, storage, these are all already talked about by the elderly, like Tang Seng is in the community, reading the scriptures every day.

Yes, actually, when I see the optical module — LITE, if he said that other or the pieces that have just been broken, it has reached the top, even the closing is a historical height. This, actually, you can see in the picture, this is what I drew when we were talking in the community a long time ago. This is a big chess with a curve line. I drew a direction that he would go next. I didn't expect him to be a good walker and go in this direction.

If this place continues to break through, you can see that the semiconductor was a breakthrough in March this year. You can see that the semiconductor was just in March. Now LTE also gives people such a feeling — that is, AI communication, including the next storage, we can also talk a little bit about it.

There is this kind of continued leading the next big plate to go forward. That is to say, there are so many concerns in the market, but these leaders are also standing out. Unlike before, when the water dog was beaten in July and August, it was completely different now. Although the big plate may be not far from the position at that time, but you have found out what the next stage of leading is. So this is what we need to pay attention to.

四、MU 存储：财报不跌反涨背后的估值密码

Including the new market that we talked about before, educational purpose — this week, the important thing is MU's financial report. We will do a deeper research on financial reports this week. But overall, technically, this is also a position that is immediately ahead of the high. And its basic face is also very strong. It's getting cheaper and cheaper.

Especially after the financial report. We will release a detailed report on the weekend. Just from the data it just released, it's so cheap. It's too exaggerated. The stock price hasn't come out yet, but I personally think that this M7, the big seven sisters, this ETF actually represents the trend of the seven technology stocks. They should also be a weekly closing high today, which is also a very bullish structure to continue to see.

That is to say, there are a lot of noise in the market now, but the track and the stocks we have chosen are all in the high of innovation.

五、IWM 小盘股：绿箭头信号与估值修复的"远路"

You said these IWM is in — at that time, and one of our indicators is what we talked about before, an indicator for our members to open, a green arrow appeared. Last time we bought it with the green arrow, it was RCL. We'll talk about it later. This time, our indicator also appeared on IWM.

It didn't say that it would rise immediately, but the valuation will still be reflected in its price and its market. But it didn't say that today its valuation is low, and it will rise immediately tomorrow. This is unrealistic.

But we know in our hearts: if you take the price of Nvidia, you will know that this is a cheap product. If it is very expensive, you are willing to buy it. Now the stock price is very cheap, and the situation has not changed, you are not willing to buy it. Then you have a problem. This is not logical.

Now the small stock is not the same as Nvidia. But if you think the interest rate is almost at the bottom, or higher for longer — in this case, when the value of super-sell is very low, you can think about when the technology stock or other large stocks have started to go up and reach the top, will the capital be reviewed again? 六、IWM 的三重逻辑总结 + RCL 实战复盘

Yes, our ancient ideas are technical and solid. The idea of IWM was just launched yesterday and it is a good time to share with you:

  • 一是 200 日均线是潜在支撑；
  • 二是估值已经来到历史合理区间；
  • 另外我们观察到，无论是油价还是 30 年期利率，都有走弱的迹象——这些实际上有助于小盘股的修复。

Including our recent new opening transaction, we also publicly shared with you last week. We shared it on September 25th. The RCL was a cruise ship. It was 238 yuan. Now it is 277 yuan. But if you want to be close to us, you are welcome to join our community.

Yes, our community is allantesla.com. Here you can see our past trading wins, trading data, including the daily middle line and long-term investment. You can even see what the shares we operate in each month are.

For example, RCL, when we shared it last Friday, the price was very low. Even if you open the version on Monday, it may be not far from our cost. 七、Tesla：旗型底部与财报前的"预跑"

Yes, Tesla is my favorite stock. We said that Tesla was in a downward trend two days ago. We analyzed that if you want to buy, you have to make a rebound. This is the place.

The overall pattern is a bit bearish. And if you look at the sun's line, you'll see a bearish flag. It's right at the bottom of the flag. If you want to bet, you can bet here. Don't bet anywhere else. Because it's unreasonable. The current place is below the flag. You need to have the data to hand it out. It was a huge downfall. Either go home or go back. That's the place.

So, at that time, we gave a trading plan for Tesla. But I also said it clearly: I don't like to trade Tesla. Tesla is just on Tuesday, we are a community Q&A, every Tuesday I am here to host. Plus, today, I think more of the market mood is back. Overall, M7, including semiconductors and these AI-related blocks, are all good. Then I just showed you that M7 is also breaking through. So I think you can try to do this kind of rebound.

Speaking of Tesla, the Japanese line is still in a bearish period. It still hasn't broken the opposite. There are still some foreign [factors].

八、SpaceX / Starship 第 14 次试飞：被市场低估的叙事

The 14th test flight, although it only took 3 hours, but the mission was completed. On Tuesday and Thursday, 2-3 rockets were launched within 13 hours. One was to the space station, and the other was to the Falcon. Anyway, they were all very successful, including the TPU of Google.

This is also a topic that very few people pay attention to. I think everyone can pay attention to the future of the narrative and the hype. It's been 7 days. Do you think people are more concerned about the big rocket or its AI?

I think people are less concerned about it. I made two or three videos about it this week. I made a video about the SpaceX interpretation. Everyone's attention to it is actually very low, surprisingly very low, including today — it actually rose by 7%, and I didn't see many people come out very excited. This is completely different from Tesla's attention.

In fact, what is SpaceX's market attention now? I think one is that it is indeed doing tasks on Falcon 9. Then this week, the successful launch of the new ship is actually a symbolic event, not yet completely reaching the commercial level.

But the AI, including data centers, may still need the third and fourth quarter financial reports to be seen. item.description:
## 一、意外观察：市场的"沉默叛变"——当所有人都在恐惧时，领导股已经悄悄完成了身份切换
真正令人震惊的，不是大盘创新高本身，而是**市场广度与价格创新高之间的罕见背离**正在发生"结构性错位"：只有20%+的个股站上20日均线，VIX却只有15，恐惧贪婪指数停在31的"极度恐惧"区。这是一个被忽略的信号——**它不是市场顶部的典型形态，而是"旧王让位、新王加冕"的交接仪式**。七月八月被打的那批跟随者（small caps、周期股），和今天带队冲锋的半导体+光模块+存储，根本不是同一拨人。换句话说，表面上"广度在恶化"，本质上是"旧广度在死去，新广度在孕育"。市场正在换血，但大多数散户还在用旧的"广度指标"读新的市场。
## 二、跨领域连接：SpaceX 的估值困境，本质上是"保险精算学"错位到了"科技成长股"身上
Will 点破了一件 Wall Street 想不通的事——SpaceX AI 算力租赁的合同"90天可取消"所以估值被打折。但如果你跳到**再保险行业**的视角，这其实是一个"浮存金 (float) 式"的商业结构：客户随时能走，但新进来的客户按**更高价格**

💡 创造性洞见

当"白宫雅尔塔"：AI治理的拓扑学反转

最意外的观察：这次所谓的"超级智能布雷顿森林"协议，表面上是对AI公司的"约束"，本质上却是一次责任外包的精妙倒置。注意Sax强调的那句话——"公司承认自己是责任主体，不要推给联合国"。这听起来是企业担责，但系统性地看，它完成了一次关键的治理拓扑反转：政府从"规则制定者"退位为"规则认证者"，而科技公司从"被监管者"升格为"自我治理者"。真正的权力并没有流向白宫，而是流向了审计中介层（EY、KPMG等）——这才是Chamath提到的8090与EY合作的真实含义。你看懂了吗？整个加密货币行业曾经梦寐以求但从未得到的"自律组织+第三方审计"框架，AI行业用三周时间拿到了。这是监管史上最快的权力再分配。

跨领域连接：电子生成 = 新的石油输出国组织（OPEC）

Chamath提到Phil Deutsch关于伊朗战争中油价变动微弱的洞察时，无意中点破了一个正在成形的地缘经济范式：电子生成能力正在替代原油产能成为国家主权的新计量单位。但请注意一个大家都忽略的历史镜像——1973年石油危机催生了战略石油储备（SPR）和能源部，而今天Freeberg预测的"政府将按行业分配GPU配额"（金融系统X%、国防Y%），本质上是在重建一个"战略算力储备"体系。

更惊人的跨领域连接：中国每十年翻倍电网 vs 美国25年持平——这个数据不是能源问题，而是文明代谢率问题。生物学中，一个有机体的代谢率决定了它能支持多复杂的结构。美国的"去工业化"实际上降低了国家的能量代谢率，而AI时代突然要求代谢率回升到20世纪水平。这就像一个坐办公室二十年的人被要求重新跑马拉松——肌肉记忆丢失，心肺功能萎缩。所谓"反数据中心运动"，本质是文明代谢系统的免疫排斥反应。

隐藏的系统性真相：Doomerism的真正功能不是关于AI

你注意到那个被反复提到但没人深挖的信号了吗？Chamath在EY活动上遇到"某位知名民主党人"散布毁灭论，J-Cal遇到的空姐重复Dario和Elon的话术——同一套词汇在不同社会阶层中传播，速度惊人且用词高度一致。

这不是关于AI安全。这是20世纪政治学中的"失权阶级重组机制"的教科书案例。失去权力的政治集团历来需要一个"末日叙事"来重新动员基本盘——1930年代的欧洲共产主义、1970年代的美国反核运动、2000年代的反全球化运动，模式完全一致：将一项技术变革包装为生存威胁，将经济焦虑转化为政治能量。

最反常识的观察：如果你把"AI毁灭论者"的组织结构、话术传播速度、精英-草根传递链条画出来，它和1960年代美国民权运动的组织学几乎同构——只是方向相反。民权运动用"希望"自下而上组织，毁灭论用"恐惧"自上而下渗透。这意味着：AI安全辩论的真正战场不在实验室，而在社会学意义上的"话语基础设施"上。谁控制了航空公司乘务员跟乘客聊天时的默认叙事，谁就赢了。

而这里有一个没人说破的政治悖论：Sax急于让Dario参与协议——不是因为需要Anthropic的技术，而是因为需要从毁灭论联盟中抽走他们最有信誉的发言人。这是一次高级的政治斩首行动，而且成功了。真正的战役不是技术监管，而是叙事的供应链战争。

Sax讲述峰会的起源

Well, the reason it happened so quickly is because President Trump convened all of these people to the White House and I think he's the only person who could get all these CEOs of all these companies in one room. I mean these are the leading companies in the world across data centers across chips, hyperscalers and then obviously frontier models and many of them frankly don't like each other. And I've called it the Bretonwoods of super intelligence. This was the first gathering of really all the critical players across the entire stack of the industry and I think we had a really good open and honest conversation about both the opportunities and the risks of super intelligence and as a result of that meeting I'd say during the meeting we worked out this agreement that has come to be known as the white house accord on super intelligence that was then signed by the six major frontier model companies.

And I think we'll now apply a new rigor, a new set of controls on the development of super intelligence so that the public can be more confident that this will be done safely. And if I could just highlight a few of the the key features.

So first of all, the companies who are developing these products acknowledge that they are responsible. They have to be the responsible actors. Let's not deflect it onto to someone else or anthropomorphize the models or talk about the United Nations. These companies accept responsibility. Number one.

Number two, they agree to have internal controls and to have those internal controls verified by an internal team that does that. But we don't just leave it to quote unquote self-p policing. It starts there. But then you have external auditors who will then validate and verify that the internal controls are working.

And these companies will set up an independent committee of the board to then receive those reports. And as Gavin Baker pointed out this morning, you know, when the board receives a report from an external auditor, you can't disregard that. It's not optional. And then finally, sitting behind all of that, you still have the FTC and the SEC, which have the ability and the responsibility to enforce the public commitments of these companies. It was as a result of that discussion and that conversation, we got the major companies to sign it and I think everyone in the room there's basically a consensus around it and these controls can now be implemented basically immediately or very very quickly and it doesn't require new legislation. Even the most cynical person Shimoth looking at this would say great first step right like if you just wanted the global UN United Nations of AI this would be a great precursor to that. a first step where everybody's opting in to be regulated to regulate themselves as we discussed on this very podcast with the MPAA analogy and here we are three weeks later. **最意外的观察**：这次所谓的"超级智能布雷顿森林"协议，表面上是对AI公司的"约束"，本质上却是一次**责任外包的精妙倒置**。注意Sax强调的那句话——"公司承认自己是责任主体，不要推给联合国"。这听起来是企业担责，但系统性地看，它完成了一次关键的**治理拓扑反转**：政府从"规则制定者"退位为"规则认证者"，而科技公司从"被监管者"升格为"自我治理者"。真正的权力并没有流向白宫，而是流向了**审计中介层**（EY、KPMG等）——这才是Chamath提到的8090与EY合作的真实含义。你看懂了吗？整个加密货币行业曾经梦寐以求但从未得到的"自律组织+第三方审计"框架，AI行业**用三周时间**拿到了。这是监管史上最快的权力再分配。
## 跨领域连接：电子生成 = 新的石油输出国组织（OPEC）
Chamath提到Phil Deutsch关于伊朗战争中油价变动微弱的洞察时，无意中点破了一个**正在成形的地缘经济范式**：**电子生成能力正在替代原油产能成为国家主权的新计量单位**。但请注意一个大家都忽略的历史镜像——1973年石油

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] How 168 Spaniards Captured the Inca Emperor - Si Sheppard
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、征服从来不是军事事件，而是一次「可复制的算法」首次运行

最被忽略的事实：皮萨罗不是天才，他是第一个被 Cortés 口头传授了「剧本」的学徒。征服印加不是一次历史偶然，而是一次 OS 的二次部署——同一套"直接摘掉社会金字塔的塔尖、让下面的科层继续运转"的协议，被从墨西哥搬到了安第斯山。

这里真正惊人的，不是 168 对 10 万，而是人类历史上第一次出现了"殖民算法"的 fork-and-reuse。Cortés 是 v1.0，Pizarro 是 v1.1，之后菲律宾、印度、非洲全是不断迭代的后续版本。它比火药更可怕——火药只能杀人，剧本可以自我复制。你会在后来的东印度公司、硅谷"PayPal 黑帮"甚至现代 PE 的"玩法手册"里看到完全同构的模式：第一个走通的人把一次性经验压缩成可传授的步骤，于是奇迹变成流水线。

二、阿塔瓦尔帕的"胜利"才是他真正的死刑

反直觉的观察：阿塔瓦尔帕刚刚打赢内战这件事，不是他的优势，而是他的死因。

他是印加世界里的"分布内最优解"——所有的直觉、战术、威信判断，都是在"前哥伦布战争"的训练集上拟合出来的 SOTA 模型。但西班牙人是一个 out-of-distribution 的对抗样本：火药、马匹、钢铁、不同的欺诈伦理，全部落在他的训练分布之外。他越是"身经百战"，越是会用旧框架去解读新信号——于是西班牙人的马冲到他鼻尖，他读出来的是"示威"，不是"情报演示"；他杀掉那些流露出恐惧的将领，但那些将领的恐惧恰恰是整个宫廷里唯一校准正确的传感器。

这是一种残酷的通用模式——跨领域的回声极多： - 柯达握着数码相机专利死于胶片； - 诺基亚是全世界最懂手机的公司，死于不再是"手机"的 iPhone； - 对抗样本能用一个像素翻转让 ResNet 把熊猫识别成长臂猿。

阿塔瓦尔帕是人类版本的 ResNet：他的权重太准了，以至于再也无法重新训练。

三、"雷神"预言被敌人兑现——最隐秘的心理崩溃

视频里闪过一个细节几乎没人展开：印加帝国的开国者 Pachakuti，意思是"持雷者"。而西班牙人带来的第一件东西，就是真正的雷——火炮和火绳枪。

想象一下：你的敌人在兑现你祖先的弥赛亚神话。这不是输掉一场战斗，这是你整个宇宙论被对面接管了。实际上火炮造成的物理伤害"相对轻微"，但正如视频所说，心理摧毁是毁灭性的——因为这不是"遇到更强的人类"，这是"遇到了神祇的替身"。

跨领域连接：这是符号系统失守，不是物质系统失守。当对手能调用你最神圣的符号，你的内部组织会从神经末梢开始瘫痪。类比： - 加密货币最大的攻击不是技术漏洞，是让社区相信"中本聪本人"背书了某个 fork； - 宗教改革不是靠军事征服，是靠路德让天主教的拉丁语权威自废武功； - 现代舆论战里，最有效的武器是让对手的粉丝自己说出"你变了"。

四、一个让人毛骨悚然的尾注

西班牙人在 Cajamarca 唯一的伤——是皮萨罗自己的手，被自己人砍伤的。

在复杂系统里，这是一个极强的"远离平衡态"的签名：当一个系统的输入输出比完全失衡（KD 比 = ∞），胜方唯一可能的损失只能来自内部的方向性错误。你赢得太彻底时，连敌人都无法伤害你，只有你的队友能。这个微小的细节几乎是整个殖民史的隐喻——帝国最终不是被殖民地击垮，而是被自己的扩张逻辑反噬。皮萨罗本人几年后，正是死于自己西班牙同僚的刀下。

真正的"降维打击"从来不是打击，而是让对方的免疫系统和自己的免疫系统互换角色。

📝 转录文本

Setting the Scene: Pizarro Inherits Cortés's Playbook

What's striking about the conquest of the Incas in Peru under Pizarro 10 years later is how similar it was to Cortés's story — how much he just basically followed the playbook.

But I wanted just people to have a sense of roughly what happened here. Um, starting — I think maybe the Battle of Cajamarca might be the most astonishing military lopsided encounter that has maybe ever happened in human history. So, yeah, if you can recapitulate a bit of at least that battle, and then just the overall story, and then we can do some analysis from there.

Absolutely. When Cortez consummates his conquest of Tenochtitlan in 1521, the last of the Hatawani surrenders to him, and how he occupies the territory — and most importantly, the top of the social hierarchy, the existing structure as much as possible is allowed to persist. The conquistadors just decapitate the local nobility and insert themselves at the top.

Now, this is the playbook that will continue to be applied less successfully throughout the rest of Meso America, because the existing political entities there aren't so sophisticated, right? Nonetheless, there are rumors — there are always rumors of losses of gold — and more conquistadors are now flooding into the new world to seek advantage of this.

Pizarro Heads South

One of these is a distant cousin of Cortez named Francesco Pizarro. He met with Cortez and got the playbook, as you say, about how this is to be done. And then, again, in one of these conquistador business ventures, he finds the funding for men and ships, and begins pushing south down the west coast of South America — crossing the equator, and finally arriving in what is now modern-day Peru.

He encounters what he's looking for: a sophisticated culture on the scale — in fact, in terms of territory, on a much broader scale — than Cortez had encountered in Meso America. This is the land of the Inca.

A Civil War Just Ended

When he arrived, there was civil war. The previous Sapa Inca, Huayna Capac, had died in 1525, and his two sons, Atahualpa and Huáscar, turned on each other. Atahualpa had just won the civil war, and he was proceeding to Cusco, the Inca capital, to be formally enthroned as the new Sapa Inca. And that's when word arrives to him that strangers have entered his realm — and again, we're talking 168 men — pushed into the Andes mountains and are seeking him out for reasons unknown.

He encounters them outside a place called, as you say, Cajamarca, in 1532, and he sees not threat but opportunity. And just like Moctezuma II had been advised not to treat with these people, so does Atahualpa's envoy, who reports to him: "These are not men of good faith. We can take them out. They tend to sleep together at night. We can set fire to wherever they're staying and just take them all out in one fell swoop."

But Atahualpa is interested in what they have to offer him. He's seen the horses.

The Horse Display — and the Executed Generals

In fact, Pizarro made a specific case of impressing the Sapa Inca with his horses. He sends one of his key lieutenants to put on a display of horsemanship, and famously he charges right at the Sapa Inca and all his court — and the horse stops just inches from Atahualpa's face, snorting and breathing. And Atahualpa is absolutely stony-faced and professes to be unimpressed, and says, "I will meet with your master at a time of my choosing."

After the Spaniards leave, he has all of his court, including his generals who flinched or showed fear, executed — just to make the point that we're not to be intimidated by these people. He sends a blocking force, tens of thousands of men, to cut off any retreat. And then he proceeds to meet with Pizarro at Cajamarca with the vast expanse of his army.

"Atahualpa Was Planning to Have Pizarro for Lunch"

There's a saying in Peru that Atahualpa was planning to have Pizarro for lunch, but Pizarro ended up having him for breakfast.

Once he enters into the confines of a narrow, constricted courtyard space, that's when Pizarro lets off the ambush. He lets fly with all his artillery and all his musketry for the shock value, unleashes his horses, and Atahualpa himself is overwhelmed — or taken prisoner — at that point.

So this again is the playbook, the copybook as you say: go to the top, seize whoever is at the very pinnacle of the social hierarchy, you control the entire structure.

The Numbers: 168 vs. an Empire

And just so people know the numbers here: the Incan Empire overall has some 10 million inhabitants. During this first battle, where Pizarro encounters the emperor, he has some 160–190 conquistadors. I think the numbers are unknown for exactly how many Atahualpa had, but he's facing off the army that has just basically clinched the civil war in the Inca Empire, and is around tens of thousands big. Some — I've seen some numbers that are like 100,000 or 200,000, but certainly in the high tens of thousands.

So 100-something against almost 100,000. That's the first battle.

What is astonishing is that these 100 conquistadors — I think — killed, with the — I saw some numbers that they killed like 10,000 of the enemy, or at least thousands of Atahualpa's troops. They suffer zero casualties. So they kill close to 10,000 of the enemy. They suffered zero casualties.

This is the first encounter that the Inca Empire has ever had with the conquistadors. I think that must have been shocking from both sides' perspective.

How Is a KD-Ratio of Infinity Even Possible?

And I want — if you can do some analysis here — how is it possible? How can you have a military outcome where you can have literally a KD ratio of infinity? >> Yeah. >> Of, you know, 10,000 to zero.

Yeah. The conquistadors themselves admitted the night before that encounter, there were so many campfires from the Inca army scattered across the hills surrounding Cajamarca, it looked like the twinkling of stars at night. And the conquistadors themselves admitted, when they saw the number of Inca troops filing into this courtyard, they were losing control of their own bladders out of fear, right? They knew what the risks were here. But the shock value of that initial impetus was enough to carry them through.

The Thunder-Bearer Prophecy

The Inca had never heard gunpowder weapons fired in any format before. The ancestral founder of their empire was Pachakuti, which means "the Thunder-bearing." But to see a real-world exemplar of that must have been just beyond shocking.

So the actual physical damage that the cannons and arquebuses inflicted was relatively minor, but an explosion — and the fact that these strangers seem to be able to control the thunder — must have been psychologically devastating.

Steel, Horses, and No Doctrine to Respond

And then it came down again to that steel and those horses, right? When Pizarro unleashed the horses — this is something that the Inca, as you say, these are veteran warriors, the winners of a civil war, strategists, and at a tactical level within the framework of pre-Columbian warfare, they were the top dogs — but this is something outside of their entire understanding of the universe.

They'd never seen a horse before, or knew what it could do. If you integrate a rider into the saddle with stirrups and the shock value of that charge, they had no doctrine to push back against that. And the psychological impact was that they tried to flee. They were piling up against the walls, and in their desperation to scramble over them, to the point where the walls finally gave way under the press of all those bodies. Some of them escaped into the countryside, and the Spaniards rode after them, just running them down as they fled. And the only thing that stopped the massacre at the end was night was falling, and the Spaniards in darkness couldn't continue the pursuit any longer.

When Fight-or-Flight Has No Framework

So it's what happens when something totally outside the universe of even veteran warriors plays out in a way that they have no mental appreciation of, or are able to draw back any kind of library of "how do I respond in this situation." The fight-or-flight instinct just completely takes over, and flight was the winner in this instance.

The One and Only Spanish Injury

As you say, the only casualty was Pizarro himself. He's reaching for Atahualpa to take him prisoner, and one of his more enthusiastic comrades is slashing and manages to cut his hand as he does that. That was the only injury any of the conquistadors suffered at this critical moment.

Yeah. If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.
