item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最大的反直觉：他们卖的不是"自动化"，是"主权"

表面上 Gumloop 是 agent builder，但真正让 Shopify、Instacart 这类公司签单的，是一个被低估的词——"agentic sovereignty"（代理主权）。

注意 Max 说的那句被低估的话："当那些实验室带着八位数合同来找我们、而我们已经全部用了他们的方案时，我们有能力说走就走。"

这揭示了一个隐秘的商业模式转换：Gumloop 本质上在卖"对冲工具"，而不是生产力工具。它的核心价值主张不是"让 AI 替你干活"，而是"让你永远不被任何单一 AI 实验室绑架"。这就是为什么他们的定价模仿 OpenRouter——token at cost——因为他们在把自己定位成"AI 时代的瑞士"而非"AI 时代的 SaaS"。

这就解释了一个数据之谜：为什么他们的首要买家不是业务负责人，而是 IT leader？因为 IT leader 买的从来就不是功能，是可撤回性（reversibility）。

二、跨领域连接：Gumloop 走的是"核武器时代的裁军逻辑"

这里有个意外的类比——Gumloop 正在复刻冷战时期的"不扩散条约"商业模式。

冷战时期最赚钱的不是生产核武器的国家，而是提供核查、仲裁、中立托管的瑞士。Gumloop 做的事情惊人相似： - 实验室（OpenAI、Anthropic）= 超级大国 - 大型企业客户 = 中等国家，不想被任何大国单独绑定 - Gumloop = 瑞士银行 + 日内瓦公约 + IAEA 核查员

Max 说"model layer 会被商品化，实验室会去抢客户的生意"——这不是预测，这是挑动恐惧的销售话术。而他们"deploy in your own cloud, you own the database"的定位，几乎是直接从 1970 年代 Swift 银行间清算系统的中立性叙事里 copy 过来的。

第二个让人意外的跨界映射：他们的"customer-success-powered growth"其实是传教士模式（missionary model）。那个 Instacart 的 power user——最后被他们招聘——这不是"销售"，这是"改宗（conversion）"。他们的真正销售漏斗不是 marketing funnel，而是 early Christianity 的网络传播机制：一个狂热信徒 → 内部布道 → 跨公司迁移时携带信仰 → 新据点。

这就是为什么 Max 说"我接了 1100 个客户电话"——那不是销售，那是神学院训练，训练自己辨认"谁会成为下一个使徒"。

三、最隐蔽的系统性真相：他们的"小团队哲学"正在悄悄崩塌，而这是好事

Rahul 说过一句轻描淡写但极其危险的话："我们当初想做 10 人独角兽，现在 50 人了。"

但真正的洞见藏在 Max 说的那个 "multiplier metric" 里——他优化的不是绝对团队规模，而是"客户以为我们有多大 ÷ 我们实际有多大"的比值。

这是一个被 YC 文化系统性低估的指标。

绝大多数创始人用两个指标自我麻醉： - "我们多精益"（头数） - "我们营收多少"（美元）

而 Max 发明了一个更深的指标：感知杠杆率（perceived leverage ratio）。这个指标的狡猾之处在于——它直接量化了信息不对称作为商业资产的大小。当客户以为你是 300 人、你其实 50 人时，你在谈判桌上拥有的不是"效率"，而是"隐藏的产能"作为心理武器。

这里的跨领域连接：这个指标在军事学里有个名字，叫 "force projection ratio"——投射力量相对实际兵力的放大系数。拿破仑、以色列国防军、华为早期的研发组织，都在这个比值上做文章。它从来不是"精益"的问题，而是"让对手误判你的实际能力"的战略问题。

而 AI 时代的创业，第一次让这个比值可以被软件系统性放大——因为 agent 让 50 个人显得像 300 个人不再是演戏，而是客观事实。

这意味着一个让大多数 YC 创始人没想到的推论：团队规模不再是信号（signal），而是噪音（noise）。未来十年，"我们只有 X 人"会从骄傲的标志变成暴露弱点的失误——因为它暴露了你真实的产能上限，让竞争对手精准定价你的反击能力。

Max 正在走出"小而美"的 YC 教条，进入下一代的"不透明杠杆"游戏。而这，可能是整个访谈里最被低估的信号。

📝 转录文本

[music]

【开场介绍】

Today I'm here with Max and Rahul from Gumloop. Um, thanks for coming back to IC.

Thank you for having us.

I'm really excited for this conversation. You guys are one of the most successful yet kind of unknown companies uh from Win24. Tell us what Gumloop is.

Gumloop's the agent builder that a lot of companies like Shopify and Gusto and Instacart uh use so that everyone can build agents and share them across the business while it can manage and control that data.

So kind of like the holy grail of agents — like this is what everyone is talking about, what they want to actually build. Like this is probably one of the more common applications I guess we get from Twice today, but you actually built it, and you're deployed in like many of the biggest companies.

Yeah, it's definitely a crowded space because it feels like obvious that someone has to solve this problem. There's definitely a bunch of players that are doing a good job, but we're just trying to be one of the leaders.

【从 AgentHub 到 Gumloop：早期演变】

And you applied to IC for uh winter 24, uh you called AgentHub at the time.

And then I switched to Gumloop.

Yeah. Um, what was this product when you applied?

Yeah, it is ironic that we called ourselves AgentHub back then because now we are an agent hub. Uh, but there was a bunch of — everyone thought we were a real estate agent company because agents weren't common back then. But we were a workflow automation platform. Same mission of like automating tasks, but the models weren't good enough back then. So we just made a visual builder, and people could define their workflow step by step. And then we added agents, and that was kind of like the hockey stick moment where anyone could build it on the platform and usage kind of skyrocketed. But same mission since the beginning.

【Gumloop 怎么用】

How does Gumloop work? Like, how would you actually use it?

Yeah. So basically you can go onto the platform and then create an agent, um, and add —

How do you create it?

You create an agent in the onboarding, but you can also just click the "create agent" button, and then you're presented with the kind of standard chat interface. Then you have a set of connectors that you can pick and choose — all the apps that you work with. Um, you can start talking to the agent right away to get work done, or you can add the agent to your Slack workspace, Microsoft Teams — uh, wherever you work, we kind of bring the agents to you.

What's some good examples of common agents that people make once they have your UI?

They tend to be team-specific. So the sales team at pretty much all of our customers, for example, will have a sales agent that's connected to their call recording software, their CRM, a bunch of enrichment tools, web search tools. And it has a bunch of skills for how they like to do business and how they want to manage opportunities and analyze calls. It becomes like a coworker for the sales team that the sales team uses and relies on. So they're pinging it in Slack every day. They're CC'ing it on email threads. They're having it set up next steps, clean, dedupe accounts — like all of the tedious work that a salesperson would be doing. They built an agent to do that for them. And it's like their little co-pilot.

Does it replace the software tools that they're currently using, or is it kind of interacting with them? Like, how does it work with say Salesforce or something like that?

Yeah, we like to be the connector between all of your tools. Uh, so sometimes it actually does replace vertical SaaS you might have procured. For a lot of our customers, they're canceling contracts to just use an agent instead. But oftentimes we're like the gum — we like to say — between your different data connectors. So you're using all the tools that you love, but you're bringing them into one place and giving it to this alien little co-pilot that can just do stuff for you in the background.

A lot of companies are developing internal tooling. Their own engineering teams are building agents, and we kind of fit right into that ecosystem as well. We provide a pretty robust SDK and API. So pretty much anything you can do through the UI in Gumloop, you can do via API or SDK. And we have hundreds of integrations exposed via MCP servers. And so a lot of our customers are building internal tooling and infrastructure using Gumloop as a base layer for their AI.

【模型变好的那一刻：从工作流到真正的 agent】

And it seemed like you were one of those companies where basically you had this idea before models were good, and once models got good, this product just got infinitely better. Is that what happened?

Yeah, I think that was definitely one of the strategies at first — which was: the models were not good enough to make agents work, and so we kind of met the models where they were. And that's why we started with this workflow builder and kind of minimized the use of AI, and just had it in the key area that it needed to be used for in a giant workflow. Everything else was standard infrastructure that made things actually reliable and economical at a point where the models weren't good enough. But now models are good enough to automate tasks completely end-to-end. So you don't really need this workflow manually built out — the agent can just do it by itself.

【早期用户与企业客户的转折】

Who were the first users? What were they building?

There was an initial wave of PLG growth. So like individuals, indie hackers, people just having really tedious tasks before AI could really automate anything.

Solo?

Solo. Yeah, exactly. Like I think during our YC interview, the use case we quoted was someone transcribing their Dungeons & Dragons session. Uh, that was innovative at the time — the fact that they could talk for two hours and then have a transcript and send it around to the attendees. They were using a Gumloop workflow for that. But then little use cases like that — and then all of a sudden we had business users. Like, I remember this Australian health tech company was using us to automate a lot of their research just by pulling from the web and regulating that data and putting it in certain places.

And then we realized the enterprise customers are willing to pay a lot more. Their problems are a lot more serious, um, and the value we provide them is just so much deeper.

How did that realization come about?

Slowly over time. I think we always wanted to be the PLG tool that your mom would use and that your coworker would be using. But we just saw — when you were giving the pitch to different people — like the people who have a thousand employees and they need a layer to help them all automate, and they deeply need security and observability and access control and all of the boring stuff behind automation — their eyebrows raised higher than —

But I'm assuming you didn't get to that pitch right away. There was some step function to get there. What was that like?

I think I took 1,100 customer calls the first year. Uh, I was like top 0.1% of Cal.com users. And it was iterative — like every call you'd kind of hone in on what is getting someone excited, what makes them nod their head. And it all trends towards what we've built now, which is the enterprise platform.

And when the product wasn't good back then, we really had to be super involved with customers and help them to get something into a working state, right? So we were very familiar with their use cases and exactly what they were doing. And a lot of these solopreneurs or consulting-type people — it was just really hard to make things work for them. And even when we did make things work for them, it wasn't generating that much value. But when we saw, you know, like this Australian health tech firm — when we made their use case work and we saw how much money it was making them and saving them — we were like, okay, this is obviously the natural direction of things. But I don't think it was super clear at the beginning.

【第一个企业客户：Instacart】

Instacart was your first real enterprise. How did that happen?

We had one power user there who was obsessed with Gumloop and started bringing us — he brought us into a Slack channel and then he was kind of selling the tool for us internally, starting all these threads. Because he was the one teaching everyone at Instacart how to use AI tools and how to automate tasks. He was using every tool in the market to show people how to be more efficient, because he saw the light of what AI was capable of before most people.

Um, and then we ended up hiring him as one of our first employees, and he helped us understand what enterprise sales means and how to talk to a procurement team and how to price —

What a champion was.

Exactly. How to identify a champion. And then that led to our next logo and next logo. And then people at these big companies go to other companies, and if they love your tool enough, they'll bring it with them. So we just had this natural growth that happened in the early days.

Were you the best product? Were you the first product? Like, how did you get a foothold in big tech companies that other companies don't have?

I think for the workflow automation builder, we genuinely were the best product. We were by far the easiest product to use, and our product allowed you to do things that you couldn't do on other platforms. And um — Aaron, who's our head of community and education, has taught a bunch of these no-code tools. And the one thing that he always said to us was: the reason that Gumloop is so capable is because you guys did not know what any other product in your space did or looked like, and we kind of built things from first principles. And so the way our thing worked was just a little different than anything else, and it made it so much more powerful. And we realized quickly why other tools don't work that way — because it's actually really hard. The problems we were solving were really hard.

【企业级需求：那些"无聊"但关键的功能】

Yeah. Tell us about these things. So when you sell to a big enterprise, there are things that they require that small companies don't. For someone who's watching this and wants to sell to enterprise, what are those things specifically?

Yeah, I think stuff like role-based access control, SCIM, SAML, um, audit logging — all that type of stuff.

Why do big companies ask for that?

There's just so much at stake when you're a large company. Like, you're a publicly traded establishment that has sensitive data and all these requirements and restrictions with what you can do. So you need to make sure that if you're going to give 10,000 people at your company a tool, they're only able to do the things you want them to be able to do. And certain users — it gets infinitely detailed. Like, these 500 users need to be able to do these 10 things. These users are actually an outsourced team that shouldn't have access to any data; we need them to have restrictions on their accounts. We need to use our own API keys. We need to host it in our own cloud. We need to have audit logging for every tool. We need to have APIs to get that into our data lake. Like, it never ends.

But that's the value we have to create before the end user can have that wonderful moment of like, "oh, I connected data and it just worked." There's so much depth before they can use it.

Yeah, it can be frustrating sometimes because they want to disable so much functionality that we worked so hard to build. But uh, yeah, I guess that's what it takes. And then when they warm up to us, we just enable more and more things.

How did you figure out what all these things are, and what they need? Because you can't show up and be like, "Oh, we don't have these things, let's go build them." I'm assuming you have to figure it out —

It's just conversations with customers. Like, hundreds of conversations. And you get a sense after building for a while of what feels directionally correct when they're asking for a feature and what you should just ignore. Most of the time, everything that our big companies are asking for is something other big companies would want at some point. So we build it.

And I think the level of care you have and the speed at which you respond to them — the amount you feel like a partner to them, and the speed that you ship what they want — it really makes a difference.

【模板、工作坊与"冷启动"问题】

One of the things I've noticed with companies — and I remember we had these conversations early on — is if you have a tool that can do anything, people don't really know where to start.

Yeah.

How have you solved that today, and what are the most common things that people use your tool to do?

Yeah, that's a good question. So, I remember when we met you for the first time, when you saw the product, the first thing that you said was: "You guys need templates — pre-built use cases to show people what to do." And then we came back the next week with three different templates. And then you were basically like, "Guys, that's not what I meant. You need like a hundred of these things." And so we built this really large template gallery.

We kind of do similar stuff like that today — we have use case pages with pre-built agents, and that gives people an idea. Case studies help. We do workshops with companies and we're like, "Tell us if you could wave a magic wand — what would you automate?" We get 20 hands raised and then we'll help them all automate their own things, and then that sparks more ideas.

You handhold companies through the onboarding process to build out the initial —

Sometimes they come to us with like 10 ideas and they're like, "I already did five. These are five more. I need these features shipped before I can do that." And we're like, "Okay, consider it done." But sometimes it requires fully inspiring a team.

【创始故事：温哥华的 AI 会议】

Let's go back to earlier, prior to doing YC. How did you guys meet and decide to start a company together?

There was an AI conference going on in Vancouver, and I was presenting what I was working on at the time — which was a personalized AI tutor for students. And Max was presenting an early version of Gumloop, and what he was building sounded really cool. It sounded really promising. I thought it had real potential to work. And so I basically asked him if he needed a co-founder.

Well actually, he said there's a couple caveats to this story. One: the "conference" is a very generous term — it was like 30 people in a room just talking about AI, right when the GPT API came out. Basically, my co-founder had quit that morning. The guy I was working with, who I met on YC co-founder matching. And he was like, "This idea won't work. I need someone more senior." Like, this whole laundry list of reasons. I believe the "no," but not the "why" — I learned that after working with YC.

But I went to this meetup to take my mind off things, because I was so distraught. I'm like, "I'm screwed." Basically, there's a bunch of other things that happened in the background that made me more screwed at the time.

Rahul was demoing with his co-founder. And that person ended up joining as our founding engineer like a year later. But the whole video of us interacting for the first time is captured on my Twitter. I was like, "My co-founder quit this morning, I'm looking for another one." And then the next person to speak is Rahul asking about GPT functions —

Yeah, which had just come out that day. And he's like, "Have you considered those?" And I'm like, "No, I don't even know what that is."

But it was very serendipitous. And then we got drinks the next day and he came with his laptop that was duct-taped together — [laughter] — with a Google Doc of 50 questions. Because the product was open source at the time, so he read all the code before AI could just answer questions about a codebase. And he had very detailed questions about the framework that I had built. So I was like, "This guy's pretty serious."

And then we worked in the co-working space together for like a month.

And you were both in Vancouver?

Yeah. In Canada.

【申请 YC】

And then from there to applying to YC?

Yeah. I think we always wanted to apply to YC. Max knew way more about it. He had applied to YC three times in the past. I had never applied to YC, but we knew what YC was.

I'd applied with very different ideas previously. And I'm actually thankful in hindsight I didn't get in, because it would have put me down the wrong path — working on ideas that weren't the right fit. But yeah, this was my fourth time applying. And we worked in a co-working space for 12 hours a day, every day, for a month and a half, I think, until we applied to YC.

And at that point we had people who loved the product — a very small number of people who loved the product — but they got value out of it. And we got lucky and interviewed.

【AI-native 公司的真相：第二章】

At YC we've released something called uh, Quota Master recently — it's open source. We've built our internal company brand at YC. I'm like, "This is the biggest software tool we ever launched at YC internally." Like, I use it all the time. And I'm assuming that your customers are kind of like this — it might be the biggest thing that they ever see internally in terms of productivity.

However, it's just hard to get people to start using things. I imagine that you also built up this knowledge in how to basically make a company AI-native that others don't have. And this is sort of at the top of the list of every management team right now: "How do I get my company to become AI-native?" Talk about that — this is the holy grail again, the transformation of AI.

I think that was the first chapter. We definitely built up a lot of expertise around making a company AI-native and use AI for as much as you can. And then there's the second chapter that comes immediately after that where you're like, "Okay, they're using it for too much, and we need to actually govern and moderate and make sure it's being used in a productive way." So we've gone through — I think we've built expertise in both.

But tricks for making your company AI-native: bringing agents to where they're already doing work has been the biggest unlock for us. If you have to go to yet another platform and use the AI system there, there's friction. But if you bring it to the platform they're already spending eight hours of their day in, you — they'll natively adopt the tool.

Bringing it to a place where you can see other people use agents and see how they use agents — that's one of the things that Gumloop does really well compared to a lot of other agent platforms: this aspect of collaboration, sharing agents, multiple people talking to the same agent — that multiplayer portion of it. Being able to see how your coworker who does literally the exact same job as you interacts with an agent in a public Slack channel naturally lends yourself to using agents in that way.

【Gumloop 内部怎么用 Gumloop：Heimdoll 的故事】

Can you talk about how you use Gumloop internally at Gumloop?

Yeah, I think everyone on every team uses it for everything. The first breakthrough agent that changed the way we work was this one we call Heimdoll, which is connected to every single data source at the company. And it has a Slack channel that was just "ask Heimdoll" originally, but now it's in every single channel across the entire company. And you can ask it anything — like, "Get me all the users that signed up yesterday morning that are in this time zone, that have this role, and aren't in this certain —" It'll work for 20 minutes and get you that answer. We don't need a data analyst. We just have Heimdoll answering every customer-related question.

And then that spawned a bunch of ideas. The sales team went off in their direction, and they have Sales Loop which automates everything in the sales process so they can just focus on talking to customers. Our customer success team has Success Loop — the health score of every single customer is diligently tracked, they get notifications if anything's ever going wrong, if any usage is skyrocketing or dipping. Everything that they were spending their time monitoring is handled for them.

Our education lead — we have cohorts every two weeks where he teaches hundreds of people how to build agents. The entire process is automated: people signing up, the follow-ups, even the editing of the videos when they demo on Fridays and show their agents — fully automated — so that the clips get sent to those customers and they can share it around their companies.

【PMF 的瞬间】

Throughout this process, was there a moment when you felt "we have PMF, this is working"? Was there something very visceral that you remember, or was this more gradual?

I think there's been a bunch of moments like that. But I remember the first one felt like our first conscious thought about whether this is something that people actually want — when they were using our initial workflow builder, early early days. And it was awful. But they were using it anyways. And we're like, "I've built a lot of bad software before that no one used, and for some reason people were spending five hours of their afternoon building a workflow on our platform." We're like, "Oh, this is actually so painful for people that they're willing to put up with how bad this is." That feeling of "wow, people are really investing their time" has hit us every couple months.

Yeah, I think when we realized that certain users were spending 8 hours a day, 10 hours a day using Gumloop — building stuff, automating their entire jobs or the job of their entire team — that was big. When we realized our users are spending way more hours than we are in Gumloop building stuff. And some of them know how to use the platform better than we do in some ways.

I think for me one of the big moments was the first day we launched at Shopify. Because it was kind of like we basically just went out to 4,000 people on the same day —

I think it was 8,000 people.

8,000 people on the same day — they just got access in one day. Just seeing people pick up and use the tool and play around — it was a super cool moment. People were just figuring things out, and we didn't have to — I think before then, it was a lot of sitting down with customers and building stuff out for them, a lot of handholding. But then people just started building stuff on their own, which was cool.

【怎么拿下 Shopify】

How did you get Shopify? I remember Toby writing the AI-native sort of manifesto. It sounds like there couldn't be a better customer than them.

It was actually one of the word-of-mouth customers. Someone from Instacart had influence at Shopify and just put it on their radar. And then they evaluated the tool. They rolled out a bunch of tools the same week — different automation tools — and they just saw what stuck. And then they ended up investing in Gumloop after, because they really liked the rollout. And they've been a great partner since.

【定价演变：从 $20/月到 token at cost】

What percent of employees of these companies are using Gumloop on a daily/weekly basis?

It varies a ton by company. Sometimes it's extremely concentrated usage with one team — everyone using agents to automate this one function. Sometimes it's wall-to-wall deployments with light usage on some teams and deep usage on others. Sometimes people are using Gumloop but they don't even realize it — they're getting all these reports so they can do their job better, or the prep for a customer call, but it's all Gumloop in the background. So completely different patterns at every company.

But for the most part, everyone has access. We never charge per seat. I never want someone to second-guess whether they should be using this tool or not. It's just usage-based. So whoever wants to start automating can just turn to Gumloop and figure it out.

That's not how you got started though. When did you switch to usage-based pricing?

Initially it was seat-based. We had a limit on the team plan for seats.

How did pricing develop over the years?

When we first started, we had a $20/month plan and a $40/month plan. That's what we went into YC with. We picked those numbers because ChatGPT had something similar, and that was all we knew — products that we liked to use were in that price range. But we quickly realized our pricing was way too low, and that the value we were providing business customers especially was far greater than what we were charging. So we basically doubled our pricing three times during the batch but kept the same plans. At first we just included a set amount of usage, but then we started a credit-based system. But our recent pricing model is even completely different.

Yeah, it's still credits but it's very transparent. We sell tokens at cost, we sell the compute at cost, and the APIs at cost. And then we charge an orchestration fee on top of it. Very similar to OpenRouter.

It just feels like if you're going to be in this "build versus buy" debate, to be considered a tool that is in the "build" camp — when people say they're going to build something internally, they're going to use Vercel, they're going to use Cloudflare, they're going to use these pieces of infrastructure that help people build — the pricing being transparent is such an important part of being in that group.

Most of our customers are deploying it in their own cloud. It feels like internal infrastructure, and it could be part of that build camp. But if you have opaque pricing, that'll never happen — you'll always be the enemy. So we changed our pricing recently to be very clear about where Gumloop's value is and what our margin is. And it's totally agnostic — if somebody wants to use Claude, or has an agreement with OpenAI, or wants to route everything through their Braintrust or their Amazon Bedrock proxy, they can totally do that using Gumloop as well.

【投资人会议 & 融资经验】

What's an investor meeting like for you today? Is it just a demo?

I learned pretty quickly that with a tool like ours, showing the value with a demo is 100 times more impactful than just talking about what we do. Even in this discussion now, people are probably rolling their eyes when we're like, "Yeah, we automate work and it's so amazing." They're like, "Yeah, everyone does." But if you see it working, you start to believe it. So now I exclusively just open the product and show people what it can do, or give them access so they can start using it. That speaks way louder than a pitch deck.

You raised three rounds of funding — First Round, then Nexus, then Benchmark. Talk a little about how they all came around, and what you've learned about fundraising.

The first round with First Round was the most — that's the only time we actually fundraised. We did the whole process, like what YC helps you get set up to do — a week of meetings and talking to every VC. Extremely tiring. And I think they were the best possible firm we could have went with — they've been amazing partners.

It's very similar to dating, I guess — I don't know what analogy to use. But building the company and gaining traction is the most important thing you can do. It's not about tricking an investor to think your company's cool, or having a better pitch deck than someone else. They will always follow your company and try to invest if you're showing that you're changing the way people work or having some impact in the market.

So our other two rounds were preempted. We didn't raise, we didn't make a deck. We just kept building. And I think the fact that we didn't need the money, and we're going to succeed regardless, is what makes someone want to invest.

【加拿大创始人 vs. 搬去 SF】

What's the experience of being a Canadian founder moving to San Francisco? I remember there was some tweetstorm about this — advice to Canadian founders who either want to stay in Canada or might want to move here. What comes to mind?

You can absolutely stay in Canada. We have an office in Canada. We employ a ton of Canadians. I think we're going to be going back to Canada at some point. So I don't think it's "you must move to SF" like a lot of people say.

Our approach was: we had every odd stacked against us. We still do. And we want to succeed by any means necessary. So if there was a half-a-percent better chance that we might meet a customer or someone we want to hire in San Francisco because they happen to be down the street — like Instacart was a block away from our initial office — we were going to do that. But I think you can 100% stay in Canada and build a generational company there. There's a lot of great Canadians who are comfortable and happy and they don't want to leave the country. You can hire them, and you have an advantage in that market for hiring.

What are the best hubs — most ambitious or best engineering talent right now?

It's just where more people are. Yeah. Vancouver and Toronto, I think, in Canada.

Montreal too.

Montreal as well. Yeah. [laughter]

【团队规模的哲学：10 人独角兽的梦想与现实】

How big is the company right now?

Between 45 and 50.

It's interesting, because there's the sort of people were like, "I'm trying to keep the team small." You've been trying to do that, but it's going really well. So it seems like you are still small for the traction you have, but still now this is a big company.

Yeah. Our initial plan was we were going to be a 10-person billion-dollar company. That's what I put out on Twitter, because we raised our Series A when it was Rahul and I and two interns. So we thought — I think we were a little cocky — that we can just keep it super lean. But then we discovered enterprise sales, and [laughter] just how much support a large company needs.

It became obvious that the more people we have, the better. So we're still trying to stay super lean. The — I like to refer to this multiplier where I'll ask a customer who's onboarding, "How big do you think our team is?" And they're like, "250 people, 300 people." And I'm like, "No, we're only 50, or 30." The multiplier of how big they think we are to how big we really are is kind of what I'm optimizing for now — less so the actual objective headcount, because I think we're hamstringing ourselves a little bit by being only 10 people. The 11th person adds a ton of value.

【现在的瓶颈 & 招聘】

What constrains success for the company right now? Is it that models are still not perfect the way they need to be? What will be additional unlocks in the future?

People don't know about us. That's one big thing. I have calls with customers almost every single day where they're inbound or they heard about us through a friend, and then I actually show them the tool, and they're kind of shocked at how much it can do. We're trying to fix that so that more people know we exist and how much work we can automate. That's one problem.

The other one is we just don't have enough people — as ironic as that sounds based on the small team thing. There's like a hundred things that our customers are asking us for that we could be building right now. But we're very thoughtful about who we hire and whether they're a good fit for the company. So we've been hiring more slowly than the average company. But we're hiring engineers, designers, AEs, customer success.

【卖给企业的愿景：任务理解者才应该是自动化者】

If I was someone who's never used anything like this, and I'm AI-curious and I work for a big enterprise — what's the vision that you would sell me on? How could I run my company differently?

I think the main thesis is: the people who understand the tasks should be the ones automating them.

The anti-pattern we've seen over the last couple years is: you might have a marketing ops team that has something extremely tedious and cumbersome that you're losing tons of revenue by not doing. They're going to hire people to solve it, or they're going to write a spec doc of the problem they want solved with an agent or AI, and they're going to give that to an engineering team, or they're going to give that to a consultant who's going to charge them a crazy amount of money. And they're going to go through this loop of "not quite right" feedback meetings, and you'll get something half-baked.

The people who really deeply understand a task should be the ones just transferring what they understand into an agent to automate it. And the hard part is — the biggest blocker is — a tool that they can understand. Now we're at the point that anyone can build an agent; that's relatively solved. And then the meta-problem behind it is: do they have access to the right data, the permissions — has IT let them do this sort of thing?

So we're secretly catering to IT teams with all the features we build first. If they give the green light, then anyone can automate hundreds of hours of work and scale their output. But it being onboard — that comes from leadership. A company like Shopify is so AI-native that they're going to clear the way to make sure this is possible. Whereas a large health tech company in Europe — they're going to have more rigidity, an IT team saying no to everything, and you have to work through that to get the unlock of automation.

【反直觉：AI 不是替代人，是让每个人变成管理者】

A lot of people pitching AI tools for companies are basically saying "this tool will automate this work, and therefore fewer people." It sounds like you actually are describing something that's the complete opposite — where everyone basically instantly has more people and does more. Talk about that.

Yeah, part of it is this future world in which everybody is a manager, and we're all overseeing agents and having agents do work for us. That seems to be what we're trending towards. So the way we see it is: you don't necessarily need fewer people, but the people that you have can do a lot more.

We see that within our engineering organization at Gumloop as well. We have 8 core engineers working on the product — that includes myself — and everyone's able to do the work of 5 people basically, using agents.

【最难的挑战：Agent 的真正边界】

What are the hardest challenges that you guys are facing right now? For someone thinking about joining Gumloop — what would they work on?

A lot of the stuff that the labs are dealing with as well — the biggest challenges the labs are facing at the application layer. Which is: how do you get the most out of the agents and the models in their current form? How do you get them to do real work? How do you get them to do long-running tasks that take multiple hours? How do you get them to use computers and browsers efficiently?

A lot of the appeal of working at a company like Gumloop is that you're really at the frontier and pushing the limits of what's possible to do with AI and the current models. I think that's really exciting for people, especially people that are at a more traditional company.

There's — every feature that people think we should build, and that we start building, comes with a hundred features underneath them that are secretly the hard part. Browser automation is something we're working on. But then, okay, if people can automate with browsers with agents in the cloud and on their local desktop — how does it make sure that they're not going to certain websites, or that it's not doing anything nefarious, or that they're able to watch back a session recording? And then they'll ask, "How do I watch back 5,000 session recordings and understand what agents are doing in aggregate? How do I make sure it's efficient from a cost perspective?" Everything that comes with those features is the hard part. So we have to think of the whole picture when we're deploying it in a company. There's so many little edges to every feature that we need great engineers to work on.

【与实验室的关系：瑞士定位】

What's the dynamic with the labs? You mentioned in the past that your customers already have relationships with the labs, and some of them have competing products. I'm assuming co-workers in this world as well.

Totally. Yeah, there's a ton of competition. I think we exist in this sweet spot in between the labs where we're kind of like the Switzerland between the labs. You can use your inference from wherever, and that becomes quite appealing to an IT leader or any leader at a company. When you're like, "I can build agents across the business without being locked into one of these vendors — when a better model comes out next week on Twitter and everyone's going crazy over it, I can one-click switch to that inference provider." And then when those companies try to approach us with an 8-figure contract and we're all using their solution and we can't go anywhere, we actually have the ability to walk now to a different inference provider.

And the idea that you own your agents — the "agentic sovereignty" — you deploy it in your cloud, you own the database where the traces are stored, you own the full integration stack. You're owning your agentic future. That becomes quite enticing. Especially as — I think the model layer will get commoditized, and the labs will need to generate revenue in other places, and they're going to go after their customers' businesses. We've already seen that with a few of our customers who had the labs come up with direct competitors against them, and they're kind of burned by that experience. Most companies will probably face that in the future. So owning your agents is quite important.

【前沿模型的选择权】

Do your customers need frontier models?

Yeah, I think so. For many of their tasks. They need the choice for sure. Because some things are so complex — like you're informing the CEO about a growth function that is going to be in the board deck next week — it would be better to use the most qualified model you possibly can. But then you're running a support use case 80,000 times an hour — using the cheapest model in the market will actually make a difference in your revenue.

And I think that's a key thing — you do want the choice because not all use cases need frontier intelligence. So giving people the option to switch down and switch up — and having that control at the organizational level, so admins and people in the know can force people to use certain models, or force certain teams and certain use cases to use certain models. Because if given the choice, probably every individual employee is just going to use Frontier Intelligence because there's no limit and like who cares, right? But if you give the people that actually know what they're doing the ability to enforce different things, we find that works out better for everyone. It's cheaper and faster for the end user, and for the company it's also more efficient.

【销售漏斗的秘密：IT leader 是真正的买家】

Typically there's one buyer for each product category, one product. But it sounds like in this case it could still be a bit bottom-up where someone actually discovers this. How does it bubble up to the decision maker?

It's like a riddle every time. It's different. We're definitely forming more of a pattern. But the person that bubbles up to, and the person that gets most excited, is normally an IT leader — the person responsible with the AI rollout and security of the fact that everyone's using 80 different tools and the data is going everywhere, and they need to kind of wrangle all of that. They tend to be the person we were most excited to meet, because their eyes kind of light up when they see our feature set.

And then they're the ones unblocking the sales team to do sales-related use cases, and the customer success team to do their use cases, because they're giving them access to all the internal data. But yeah, it tends to bubble up to them. And sometimes it starts with an individual who found us on Twitter or saw our post on LinkedIn, and then they showed it to their manager, they showed it to their manager, we gave them a pilot. They showed they generated 3x more revenue with a small sales team, for example, in a week, than they did the three months prior.

Can you give a pilot to them without getting to the decision-maker?

We have to talk to IT to get the pilot working, right? That's the hard part. It's something we're learning and figuring out over time still. But it's not super helpful to have a pilot and then they can't connect any of their tools. We kind of made that mistake in the past. The number of connections that you have access to is directly correlated to how good your experience is using the product.

【搬到 SF：Before & After】

How important was it for you guys to move to San Francisco?

I think it was pretty critical.

Yeah [laughter]. It gave us instant validation —

Internal or external validation?

Maybe a little bit of internal validation, but mainly external validation — that people would take our call. Before that, we were just two guys with laptops being like, "Yeah, we're automating work," and no one cared. It gave us a jump-start to just start building momentum, and then a lot of guidance for how to harness that momentum into something bigger. So it definitely was a before-and-after moment for us.

【个人动力：对平庸的恐惧】

You've always seemed to me very self-motivated. Tell us more about that.

I think it's a fear of mediocrity. I'm just terrified that I'll look back in 30 years and realize I wasted an opportunity.

I don't know where that comes from, but what motivates you?

I think when I was working at Amazon out of university, my goal was to get a job at a big tech company. And I was like, "Oh man, if I do this, I'm going to be set for life." And so I went and did that. And within like a week, I was like, "I cannot do this for the rest of my life. There's no way I can work here." Because things were just moving so slowly, and I felt like what we shipped with a team of 10 people, I could do with my buddy on a weekend, you know what I mean? And so I had to be in an environment where we were working at a fast pace and just shipping things quickly. That's what motivated me.

【结尾】

Awesome. Thank you so much for coming and speaking to us. This was a really good conversation.

Thank you. Appreciate it. Thanks.

[music]

item.description:
## 一、最大的反直觉：他们卖的不是"自动化"，是"主权"
表面上 Gumloop 是 agent builder，但真正让 Shopify、Instacart 这类公司签单的，是一个被低估的词——**"agentic sovereignty"（代理主权）**。
注意 Max 说的那句被低估的话："当那些实验室带着八位数合同来找我们、而我们已经全部用了他们的方案时，我们**有能力说走就走**。"
这揭示了一个隐秘的商业模式转换：**Gumloop 本质上在卖"对冲工具"**，而不是生产力工具。它的核心价值主张不是"让 AI 替你干活"，而是"**让你永远不被任何单一 AI 实验室绑架**"。这就是为什么他们的定价模仿 OpenRouter——token at cost——因为他们在把自己定位成"**AI 时代的瑞士**"而非"AI 时代的 SaaS"。
这就解释了一个数据之谜：为什么他们的首要买家不是业务负责人，而是 **IT leader**？因为 IT leader 买的从来就不是功能，是**可撤回性（reversibility）**。
## 二、跨领域连接：Gumloo

item.title: [Business of Sport] Manchester City: The Verdict
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个让人意外的角度

1. 曼城的"原罪"不是作弊，而是买错了俱乐部

主流叙事把这个故事讲成"沙漠石油贵族入侵英超、腐蚀公平竞争"。但如果你把时间轴拨回 2008 年 9 月 1 日，会发现一个几乎没人点破的反转：曼苏尔买曼城时，欧洲足坛还没有财政公平法案。换句话说，他是基于"花钱买冠军合法"的旧世界规则买入的一个中游资产。两年之后，游戏规则突然改了——而且是其他俱乐部专门为了压制他而改的。

这就形成了一个商业心理学的经典陷阱：被困住的赢家心态（trapped winner syndrome）。你不是在赌场输了钱，你是赢了钱之后被告知规则改了、钱不许带走。这种时刻，人更容易做出极端决策，因为"沉没成本 + 身份羞辱"的双重压力远超理性。曼城高管在 2011-12 之间做出"系统性撒谎"的选择，并不是贪婪，而是被困住的尊严——一个国家主权层级的身份绝不能接受"重新变回中游球队"。

2. 跨领域连接：这是一场典型的"合规套利 → 合规崩塌"叙事，和加密货币 FTX 的脚本完全一致

把曼城换成 FTX，你会惊讶地发现剧本几乎逐字相同： - 新玩家进入一个监管尚未成形的高增长行业 - 用真金白银 + 虚构账本同时撬动增长 - 利用"规则还在追赶创新"的空窗期建立不可逆的既成事实 - 当监管终于到位，选择"双倍下注否认"而非认罪求情 - 最终由一个事后追溯建立的独立机构（独立委员会 / 独立财务监管官）终结游戏

更惊人的是，萨姆·班克曼-弗里德和曼城主席 Al Mubarak 的辩护逻辑同构："你们看不到的那部分证据才是真相。" 这是所有"后真相式辩护"的共同句式——它不是在反驳证据，而是在否认证据的可知性，让对方陷入认识论的陷阱。Charlie 用了一个精准的词：gaslighting（煤气灯操纵）。这不是法律辩护，这是心理战术。

3. 真正的系统性真相：英超的罚则其实已经"自动执行"了，不需要任何人下判决

这是最反直觉的洞察——曼城的沉没已经在数学上既成事实，剩下的只是时间。看看这个结构：

2026 年 11 月 2 日 - 2027 年 2 月 27 日 独立足球监管官（IFR）法定的"重新申请期"
法律框架 直接移植自金融服务业的"适格人员测试"
对"知悉或鲁莽地提供虚假信息"的处理 强制禁业
曼城 114 项罪名中落入"严重类别"的 68 项

换句话说，议会在 2023 年通过足球治理法案时，就已经不知不觉地把曼城判决了——只是没有人在当时意识到。独立委员会和 IFR 这两条独立的时间线像两艘航船，各自航行了三年，直到 2026 年 10 月才在同一个坐标点交汇。这是一种无主体设计的制度共振（institutional resonance without designer），类似于金融市场里的"闪电崩盘"——没有谁按下按钮，但所有机制同时触发。

斯塔默首相今天早上说"曼城老板走了我会很遗憾"——这句话之所以让 Charlie 气炸，不仅因为政治越界，更因为它暴露了一个更深的事实：连首相都没搞懂自己的政府已经自动把判决执行了。他以为这还是可以讨价还价的政治议题，但其实游戏结束已经写在法条里了。

元层面的洞见：这个案子最终将成为一个研究案例——不是关于足球作弊，而是关于国家主权在跨国规则体系中的"面子不可退缩性"如何成为战略盲点。中东主权基金在未来十年会反复复盘这个样本：当你用一个国家的尊严去持有一个受规制资产时，你就把自己变成了一个不能道歉的玩家。而在现代合规体系里，不能道歉就意味着不能生存。

So, we're not going to say anything other than somebody who is fit and proper to run a football club should at least be able to clear the hurdle of running a financial services business in this country.

不适格的后果

And specifically, it makes provision for what happens if the IFR doesn't think you're a fit and proper person. Confiscates your club, sells it for you, passes on the proceeds.

Where did this happen before, Charlie? Well, Chelsea, Chelsea, but I want to be very — But I want to be very clear here. Exactly. Because people have said, "Well, couldn't the government just do this?" Well, the government passed their power to that to their own body. Exactly. Because the difference of Chelsea was they handed geopolitical sanctions against Roman Abramovich, which forced the sale of Chelsea basically through the freezing of assets across Russians in the UK.

Right now, it's — let's be quite clear because I'm going to come on to our prime minister in a moment. Right? The independent football regulator is a creation of the government as an arms-length body independent of the government which regulates football. And this is how regulators work because the idea is that politicians should not be able to influence week to week, month, year to year regulation of industries because that might lead to positions of personal conflict and so on and so forth, favoritism, whatever it might be.

关键时间窗口：2026 年 11 月 - 2027 年 2 月

Now, it so happens that the application process for this new regime runs from November the 2nd, 2026, exactly 1 month from today, to February 27th, 2027. So there is a 4-month process during which all current owners and directors have to file their applications to be fit and proper owners and directors to the football regulator who then determines whether or not you are fit and proper to run a football club in time for the 2027-28 season.

Right? So all of this process was in place before any of this happened. This has all been put through the House of Commons, put through the House of Lords. It's on the statute books. It's law. It's law. It's not what do I feel like today.

首相的失态

Which made it absolutely dumbfounding that our prime minister came out this morning and said, "Oh, I'd be really sorry to see the the guys from Abu Dhabi go because I had a few nice times with him in Manchester."

Unbelievable. I mean, literally unbelievable. This is a guy, an Everton fan, our prime minister, who when Everton were under sanctioned by the Premier League said, "I don't think this is fair. This makes the case for why we need an independent football regulator who can't be influenced in that way." We then have an independent football regulator and the prime minister then tries to influence the the independent football.

Unbelievable. Yeah. I mean, just just as we've been recording, Downing Street has actually released a written statement to try and clarify and clarify — I rode back from — Yeah. Um — what did that statement say, Charlie?

Uh what the one the one the one that came out yesterday? No, the one that they've just put out trying to row back on — Burnham's — prime minister made clear this is serious and no one is above the rules. Uh it's an independent process should be allowed to run its course etc.

Yeah, the prime minister did not make that — very very loosely. I mean you know the specific words he said yesterday were I would be really concerned to lose them i.e. the city owners. They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester — shock. Obviously the building of Manchester City and the global into the global force that it is.

Pablo Escobar 比喻

It's quite unbelievable. I mean it's sorry I just I just want to pin this one cuz this this this made me spitting mad. Burnham says that because they helped build some buildings in Manchester that they fundamentally he himself as the sovereign head of his majesty's government in this country that he would be sad to see them go. Well, I'm sorry Mr. Burnham. Pablo Escobar built hospitals in Colombia. Does that mean say that he doesn't deserve to go down? What are you talking about?

That's literally but it it reveals kind of you know the uncomfortable truth really that he's talking about here which is that yeah you you know come and invest in our countries. Do you need to abide by all of our rules? Ah well.

国家主权持有俱乐部的根本矛盾

And that's you know that that's really what is now looked if you're looking at decentralization devolution whatever we want which is part of the broader political landscape that we're in right now the most powerful export of the UK — of England let's call it — Premier League right? Well one of them anyway.

If you are to go around the country and you're talking globally about the value of a Manchester or a Liverpool or these cities, the football club sits incredibly high up on the reasons why internationally those cities are known and relevant. If you're looking to attract investment into those places, the football club is highly likely to play a part in that.

Now, if you're going to invest in them, just like City have done with the training facilities and the infrastructure around it, the value to the region is going to be significant that extends far beyond football.

That's a that's a power, right? It's a good thing. It's a good reason to go and attract international investment and it's going to be the it's not coming from governments. It's not coming from local councils. So attracting that foreign investment is good.

But it doesn't but to to suggest that that means you don't have to comply with the regulations is so dangerous whether he meant it or not. The point is he's come out and again he's trying to have a conversation about something that he really just shouldn't be having a conversation because as he's as saying this is the government you know I am arms length away from here. This is not my position.

But you know what the challenge is here Charlie and this comes back to the conversation that we have to have regularly and previously you know people have their opinions on it but it's the nation state ownership of football clubs what's the biggest challenge that you know supposedly is faced beyond football here. Well the 25 billion trade relationship that you have with the UAE is under threat. You have Etihad who is sitting here threatening action against decisions that are made in the UK. You have um Burnham coming out talking like this. If there was ever evidence that the that a nation state shouldn't own a football club like this, this is it.

IFR 的法律义务分级

Very good, Charlie. Very very good. I I totally agree with you. I I just want to just finish this how the um under the legislation how the IFR has to judge this, right? Because he's lifted — they've lifted the FCA regulation.

So the duty on somebody to prove themselves, right? So the people that we're talking about here are either owners who hold more than 25% of a football club. Yeah. Or people and directors of significant influence. Right? So what we're talking about here is Sheikh Mansour, Khaldoon Al Mubarak and Ferran Soriano. That's what we're talking about here. These are the guys we're talking about the top three right are all held within that either owning more than 25% or people and directors of significant influence.

The judgment on what their duty is to be able to prove that they're fit and proper people — they have a duty and this is lifted from the FCA this is not something which has been put on post this verdict this is stuff that's already there: 1. A duty to report with accuracy and completeness. 2. A duty to correct. 3. Incomplete reports count as unreceived.

Now, there are then three levels of breaking, a breach, right?

  • One of which is by mistake. There are sanctions in place for that within the financial services industry and we've seen it in the football industry, right? It's being applied in the same way.
  • The next level down from that is making the mistake but then cooperating and being holding your hands up.
  • The next level down from that, which is the worst level, is knowingly or recklessly giving false information.

That is the very worst thing that you can do as a financial services director. And football has lifted the same terminology, the same thing, right? And that is termed in the FCA to be a criminal offense potentially, most obviously a criminal defense may offense. Maybe it might from time to time not be for one reason other and it results very specifically in individual bans from being able to be involved with a financial services business. That is the specific sanction, right?

So having taken lifted the financial services legislation into football legislation quite rightly in my in my view these are social institutions you absolutely should be held to the same account as someone who runs a financial services company.

So fundamentally under the legislation the independent football regulator has no avenue to grant a license to operate this club to the current ownership and directors. Yeah.

Under the legislation there is no avenue. There is no way. There is no wiggle room under the legal statute book. This is not one guy at his own discretion. This is the statute book. He has no avenue to offer them a license.

68 of the charges basically fall into that severe category if you're saying the failure to provide accurate financial information and failure to provide accurate player and manager financials. So a huge number of those charges would fall into that severe category. But don't forget also then the categorization of how you breach it. So if you breach it knowingly with recklessness, then the sanction is even worse.

九、过渡期的实操困境

So Charlie, let's round this round this kind of back then to where a lot of people are talking now. Um because what I think everyone's confused is well it's twofold. How long is this really going to take? We've kind of touched on it to to get to the resolution. What do we do while we're trying to get there? Because in the meantime, the season goes on, right? These dire— you know these people are still going to be sitting in that club making decisions the owners are still going to be there the fans are still turning up in st— or not turning up in stadiums sit at Anfield in 10 days well in 8 days time 9 days time.

为什么不可能"正常运营"

Okay, right I I totally get you and at this conference I've just come from this was the one of the biggest sources of debate amongst current and former executives of football clubs was leaving aside anything the IFR will have to do and as I said it's optional. He's going to have to ban them.

Even just pragmatically, it's it's going to become impossible for them to operate that football club. When you actually start to think about the week to week, month to month of running a football club once you've been found guilty of that level of misbehavior, what is going to be the situation at every single match?

And I know it sounds trivial, but it's not. You are basically asking your employees to conduct their work whilst being booed and abused every single week.

内部管理崩塌

When it comes to dealing with current and future potential employees, so any kind of disciplinary process that you might think you have internally, the employee says, "Why should I listen to you? You've been found guilty of every trick in the book. Why would I pay any attention to you — you have no moral authority whatsoever."

When it comes to signing new players with the level of uncertainty that exists over this whole situation. Well, um, so what do you think is going to happen? Well, I'm not sure. I mean, we could get relegated three divisions or we could get relegated one division. Not really sure at the moment, frankly. In fact, the ownership might not even be here. Do you know what I think? I think my player will be okay at Anfield.

So, all of those conversations straight out the door. Any players who are coming towards the end of their contract, you start to enter into a new discussion. Oh, by the way, we might be under a total registration embargo, so we might not we might not be able to complete this discussion. Cy, okay, I might might start going speaking to to Barcelona then if that's okay.

Like, you cannot operate a football club when this has been proven against you. It's not practical. It's not pragmatic. So, they are in denial. They're living in denial at the moment by thinking that they can carry on as normal.

清退所有权是唯一出路

If the — does the removal of ownership cure a lot of those issues? Yes, of course.

So, so that so that if we're coming if we're trying to pull a lot of our thoughts together, right, the biggest thing really to happen here is the removal of the — is the removal of the owner. Correct. Absolutely right.

All the other things are within the normal framework of what happens when a club has been found guilty of indiscretions. Right. They happen to other clubs on a very regular basis. Sad to say it's what it is a grand scale. This is a very specific problem by which on a both a pragmatic level, a moral level and a governance level in terms of the football, the the independent football regulators own rule book, these people will not be able to operate this club. And therefore, it's in everybody's interest, including theirs, I have to say, that they remove themselves from the situation as quickly as possible because it's it's just going to be so difficult to operate that football club. Once once these things have been proven against you.

So I I think yeah that's that's my conclusion fundamentally is that by all means throw the rule book at them. I'm very against inventing a new rule book. This thing about let's relegate them four division. I don't like that.

But also it doesn't in in whose interest is that? It's not in the interest of the league where they get relegated and it's not in the Premier League. It's fans of other clubs wanting to see blood on the carpet. Wouldn't it be funny if dot dot dot? I don't like that kind of thing. None of this is funny. No, it's not funny.

十、英超品牌与国家声誉

And I think probably one last thing that we should discuss is what it means for the brand of the Premier League. Yeah. Right. Um because there's no doubt and I don't think anyone doubts that Serie A took an absolute hammering as a brand from the Calciopoli scandal. And I guess from here on we're in making the best of a bad job territory.

Yeah. Right. The most damaging thing from here on in, the Premier League is, as you said earlier on, one of Britain's most valuable exports culturally and even economically to a degree. What we want to see here is quick resolution, right? We don't want to see this whole thing drag on for months and years. That will make everything worse and worse and worse and worse.

最优方案：外交斡旋，静悄悄退出

We need quick resolution. And what that probably means is actually at diplomatic level a quiet word saying before the football regulator has to do his thing. Why don't you go quietly? Why don't you go quietly? The club that you leave behind will take the punishments maybe other than the fine. Whoever it is who comes in and buys that club will have to accept the fact that the club might have to pay out compensation to Liverpool and Arsenal and Co and this type of stuff.

You walk away, we'll sell the club for you, right? Yeah. And we'll send you the check. That is the best way out for everybody here. If they carry on down the route they're currently going on here, it's going to get really messy and really unpleasant and much worse for them.

And I don't see it as a moment for joy. I don't rather like you actually. I don't see it as a a good thing. I see it now as demonstrating that as a country and as a football jurisdiction when there is wrongdoing it gets dealt with swiftly efficiently and effectively — which is which is really one the brand is the brand value of the Premier League — and and of the country let's face it you know if it if it were to be perceived by other parts of the world that basically as long as you build a few buildings somewhere you can break all the laws which would normally apply to British citizens but don't apply the foreign citizens. That's not that's not a good look. That's a terrible look.

结语：曼城该如何自处

Yeah. Cool. I mean, you can go on and on. I think that does it.

And and I think actually the good news for our Substack members is we're going to is that we are going to go on and on. We are going to keep on disc— we're going to do a bit of gossip over on Substack. Um which obviously a much smaller audience, much more intimate audience where we can talk a little bit more about what we really think about these things.

All we've been trying to do here is lay out the facts. Yeah. Right. I I deliberately mentioned earlier on the mitigating factors as to why I thought they they come to this decision. Right? So just to try and gain some understanding, but what we've laid out are simply the facts. This is what's happened. Yeah. And this is the rule book and these are the sanctions and this is what needs to happen next. Not because we hate anybody. It's not because we are favoring this club or that club, whatever it might be. These are the facts.

No, it's actually the opposite. We love football and we love the product and what's funny is maybe a bad result against another team. That's something you sit here and laugh at. This is not funny. This is not good for any.

Do you know what Chaz, I think even from Man City's point of view, the sooner as a club and as a fan base that they can actually rebase themselves and say, "Do you know what? Okay, that was a period in time. We've got some really great memories from what happened, but obviously they're tainted somewhat. But now we're still a great club and we always were like, okay, maybe we are a mid-table club, you know, but that's fine." Yeah. Right. We can now get back to being not the brand front for a Middle Eastern country. We can now get back to actually being a proper football club.

Yeah. Brilliant. Well, worth the wait, Charlie. I enjoyed it a lot. Thank you so much. Look forward to keeping it going. Thanks a lot.

item.description:
## 三个让人意外的角度
### 1. 曼城的"原罪"不是作弊，而是买错了俱乐部
主流叙事把这个故事讲成"沙漠石油贵族入侵英超、腐蚀公平竞争"。但如果你把时间轴拨回 2008 年 9 月 1 日，会发现一个几乎没人点破的反转：**曼苏尔买曼城时，欧洲足坛还没有财政公平法案**。换句话说，他是基于"花钱买冠军合法"的旧世界规则买入的一个中游资产。两年之后，游戏规则突然改了——而且是其他俱乐部**专门为了压制他**而改的。
这就形成了一个商业心理学的经典陷阱：**被困住的赢家心态（trapped winner syndrome）**。你不是在赌场输了钱，你是赢了钱之后被告知规则改了、钱不许带走。这种时刻，人更容易做出极端决策，因为"沉没成本 + 身份羞辱"的双重压力远超理性。曼城高管在 2011-12 之间做出"系统性撒谎"的选择，并不是贪婪，而是**被困住的尊严**——一个国家主权层级的身份绝不能接受"重新变回中游球队"。
### 2. 跨领域连接：这是一场典型的"合规套利 → 合规崩塌"叙事，和加密货币 FTX 的脚本完全一致
把曼城换成 FTX，你会惊讶地发现剧本几乎逐字相

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、这位"比特币多头"其实悄悄投降了——而他自己没意识到

孔剑平最意外的一句话不是"革命刚刚开始"，而是那个比喻："比特币是过去十年的月亮，但太阳升起后月亮就看不见了。"

这是一位在Bitcoin Conference 立下"百万美金是起点"旗帜的人，在一年之后把 BTC 从主角贬成了"背景光源"。更有意思的是他给出的资产配置——50-70% AI 股票 + 30% 数字货币——这不是比特币信仰者的仓位，这是 AI 多头顺便拿点 BTC 当对冲的仓位。他嘴上说长期看好，身体已经转向了。

这揭示了一个比特币叙事中的隐藏裂缝：比特币最大的敌人从来不是监管，而是"更性感的新叙事"。当资本注意力被 AI 虹吸，连核心布道者都开始用"月亮"自我安慰时，这个资产面临的是比熊市更危险的东西——相关性坍塌。

二、"台积电股价提前一年见顶"背后的时间悖论——这是一条可跨到航运、油轮、半导体历史的规律

他说台积电只能满足 70% 的 GPU 需求，产能限制决定了未来三五年持续增长，但股价可能在增长见顶前一年就提前见顶。

这不是技术分析，这是一条周期性产业的通用规律，而且发生过很多次：

  • 1980s 油轮：航运业老兵经历过暴跌 PTSD，拒绝扩张，造成 2003-2008 结构性短缺，但 BDI 指数在实物短缺最严重前就已见顶
  • 2018 芯片周期：三星、台积电的 CapEx 犹豫导致 2020-2022 全球缺芯，但半导体股票早在 2021 年 Q4 就见顶
  • 今天的 GPU 供应链：孔剑平亲口说了关键——"产业链老人经历过太多周期，看过太多尸体，所以保守"

这里有一个被忽视的洞察：产业老兵的"创伤后保守"本身是一种宏观稀缺性制造机。他们活下来的方式正是让下一代继续短缺的方式。这不是产能问题，这是代际记忆的金融化。

三、最反直觉的发现：中国开源模型拯救了软件公司，而不是毁灭它们

这是整场访谈最像"啊哈"时刻的部分，但主持人没追问下去。

常识叙事是："AI 会取代所有软件公司"。孔剑平给出了相反的因果链：

  • 闭源模型价格高 → 软件公司成本结构被挤压 → 真正的死神是闭源，不是 AI
  • 开源模型价格降 10-100 倍 → 节省的差价由云厂、软件商、客户、模型方四方瓜分 → 软件公司重新获得毛利空间

这里有一个跨领域连接非常震撼：这和心理咨询师 vs ChatGPT 的护城河是同一个结构。

心理咨询师的壁垒不是知识——ChatGPT 知道的心理学理论更多。壁垒是情绪价值的分发通道。同理，B 端软件公司的壁垒不是算法——而是对无数细分 B 端用户的 workflow、合同条款、历史数据的占有。大模型公司永远碰不到那层最后一公里。

所以 AI 革命的真正受益者不是"AI 公司"，而是"旧渠道 + 新算力"的结合体——它们像是继承了燃油车经销商网络的电动车公司。

四、隐藏的终极洞察：AI 为什么会选比特币而不是稳定币存钱

他说："AI 雇人挖金子，人把金子搬走了，AI 找不回来；但 AI 存比特币比人更能守住。"

这句话被包装成一个段子，但里面藏着一个产权革命的预言：

  • 稳定币 = 支付中介（人类法律系统的延伸）
  • 比特币 = AI 能独立行使所有权的第一类资产

人类资产体系的所有权本质上依赖人类暴力机器（法院、警察、合同执行）。AI 没有身体、没有法律人格，它无法真正拥有股票、房产、黄金。比特币是迄今为止唯一一种 AI 用密钥就能完整主张所有权的资产。

当 AI 产生 AI、AI 开始需要为自己攒钱时——比特币不是加密货币，它是"非人类主体的第一桶金"。这才是比特币十年后真正的 utility，而不是"数字黄金"。

📝 转录文本

台積電股價恐提前見頂？算力危機全面爆發

嘉賓：Jack Kong 孔劍平（Nano Labs） 節目：邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain

開場：中國芯片依舊是"紙板箱項目"

In China, chips are still a project of cardboards. Because the card can't get in. But China's open source model is growing fast. So it requires a lot of computing power. So in China, chips are the biggest growth space.

一、一年之後，百萬美金起點論還成立嗎？

主持人：大家應該還記得孔博士，Nano Labs 的孔博士去年在 Bitcoin Conference 的時候說比特幣超過100萬美金才是起點。今天，一年後的今天，你還這樣相信嗎？

孔劍平：我覺得過去一年這個挑戰的確比以往更多了。對，但我覺得還是依然非常看好比特幣的一個長期前景。

主持人：但如果說現在一般人想要讓整個家庭是很舒服的，他應該要……

孔劍平：I think in the past 10 years, Bitcoin has been a moon. Um... yes, when the sun rises, the moon and the stars are not visible anymore. So I think in the next three to five years, the development speed of AI will still be very fast. At this time, other assets, including Bitcoin, will definitely be affected by this. As a family configuration...

二、AI 革命該投哪一層？——"運氣 + 熟悉領域"原則

主持人：There are many different levels of technology revolution in AI. For example, there is a hardware-related investment in Nano Labs. AI has electricity and other different levels. How should people decide which one to invest in?

孔劍平：I think investment is mainly based on luck. Most people can't predict what the future will be.

For example, a few months ago, you might think that the capital spending of cloud companies is very high. This is too low and the asset load rate is very high. In the past month, cloud companies have suddenly become good assets. Because its GPU recovery can be extended, and the rent can be increased. Anyway, the more capital you spent in the past, the more cards you bought, the more the credit you got.

So the trend has been changing. But overall, it's about the direction of the technological revolution. At this time, you actually have to be in your familiar position. Continue to do certain things, maybe your success rate will increase. But if you jump differently, keep jumping, in all the areas you are not familiar with, if you keep jumping, it may be difficult for him to enjoy this wealth and prosperity.

主持人：You mean to say that choose one layer to study and then invest in that layer. Don't want to take a little bit of everything, right?

孔劍平：Yes, yes, yes. Although everyone makes money by luck, but on the basis of luck, you may still have to add some understanding of this industry and some judgments of the future trend of this industry.

三、AI 泡沫？孔劍平：革命才剛剛開始

主持人：For example, the stock price fell a while ago. I just want to know what your judgment is.

孔劍平：My judgment is that the revolution has just begun.

主持人：The revolution has just begun, but the value of American AI stocks is very high. 大家在想，OpenAI 會不會是 AI 泡沫的雷曼兄弟，會爆掉，估值太高，你覺得呢？

孔劍平：我覺得這看階段。如果這是一個AI革命的爆發的初期，那這種情況會有一些企業會爆掉，但大部分頭部的企業還是能活下來。

But if this is a late revolution, it's like the last three or five years of China's real estate — many companies will report it, many AI companies will report it, including because of the guarantee of various kinds of credit receipts, it may form a continuous problem. But I personally judge that this is still early. It has enough space to deal with these risks.

主持人：Is it because they have produced enough income?

孔劍平：一是 AI 的使用、AI 的生產力在整個人類社會中仍然非常低。二是我們看到 Anthropic 這類公司的收入已經可以實現利潤。許多雲公司也已經實現了利潤。

Like Amazon's financial report, its entire GPU will be able to return in three years. Like DeepSeek's internal speech by Liang Wenfeng, its GPU will be able to return in ten months. So this is a very healthy investment.

四、中美雙源競爭：閉源 vs 開源的"共生式對撞"

孔劍平：China's AI is also very strong now. I think the Chinese open-source model is developing very fast. The US's B2M model has obvious advantages in all aspects, with a large capital and a lot of experienced technology personnel.

So I think the long term of the future of AI design is a long-term competition between the US B2M model and China's open-air model. But this competition will not consume the other party, but will promote the other party's further growth, because the entire market is growing.

主持人：So you think the US will always be the source of the currency, and China will always be the source of the currency, and these two forces will compete for five years?

孔劍平：Yes, I think in the next three to five years, these two forces will grow together in competition. I'm not saying that because China's model is stronger, the US model will fall. I think it will still develop very quickly.

五、賣鏟子的台積電：產能卡住 70%，但股價會提前見頂

主持人：Can I say that I don't want to guess who will win in the end, so I will invest in people who sell shovels, such as Taiwan's TSMC? Can I?

孔劍平：I think TSMC is a great company. And now, cardboard is actually cardboard TSMC. Because the latest financial report also said that it can only meet 70% of the customer demand because of the production capacity limitation.

這個產能限制來自於台積電和其他上游供應鏈的限制。If TSMC can expand further, it can produce more GPUs for more users. It is clear that TSMC will continue to grow in the next three to five years.

But the stock price may reach the top one year before its growth. Why? This is the second-tier market.

⚡ 廣告插播：MyTrade 交易平台

想要嘗試參與市場，MyTrade 這個投資平台擁有全球四大監管機構的交易牌照，而且商品種類很多——股票、外匯、加密貨幣指數、大宗商品、ETF 都可以交易。

MyTrade 是一個差價合約（CFD）交易平台，用戶不是買賣資產本身，而是在買賣交易價格的變動。它支援信用卡跟 USDT 直接出入金，不用先換成美金再轉帳。交易本身免佣金，點差偏低，槓桿最高可以開到 200 倍。

TradingView 平台裡面還提供很多資訊、新聞跟交易策略可以參考。達成入金和交易條件之後，可以免費得到彭博社一年的新聞網站訂閱。他們也是阿根廷國家足球隊官方贊助商，2025 年獲得了歐洲最可靠經濟商、最佳數字客戶體驗等金融類獎項的肯定。現在有一個頻道專屬的活動……

六、軟件公司為什麼能活下來？——開源模型反而救了他們

主持人：這軟件真的很有趣，因為前一陣子就說 AI 會取代所有軟件，然後現在好像又沒了，這個敘事變得非常快。

孔劍平：對。前段時間是因為這些閉源模型特別強，軟件公司只能採購這些閉源模型為客戶服務，那至少它成本非常高。

而現在中國的開源模型上來以後，開源模型的價格是閉源模型的幾十分之一甚至幾百分之一的價格。The savings of dozens of times the gap was shared by cloud companies, software companies, customers and open source models. At this time, its service price can be lower, and the customer experience can also be lower. 這時候軟件公司有了另一次發展機會。

主持人：But why weren't they threatened before?

孔劍平：They were threatened. Because all their income was taken away by the closed source model. Now the open source model provides software companies 低成本切入大模型服務的機會。

主持人：但作為用戶，我可以直接用 AI 模型，而不去付錢給任何這些軟件公司？

孔劍平：因為 AI 軟件公司更多不是為 C 端用戶直接提供服務，更多是服務 B 端用戶，B 端用戶會有無數的細分需求需要去滿足。

These software companies are originally rooted in these distributed channels and have more data in distributed channels and the needs of distributed channels users. So they know their users better than large model companies.

Just like a psychologist, he can provide emotional value to his users. In fact, you may ask ChatGPT a lot of psychological questions, but when the psychologist tells you, they will give you more emotional value. So more software companies, compared to large model companies, they will also give their users more emotional value.

七、AI 泡沫的警示指標在哪裡？——老兵的保守反而製造結構性短缺

主持人：If the audience is worried about the trend of AI bubbles, what kind of data or what indicators do you think need to be more conservative?

孔劍平：I think...

（關於世代差異）The 90s and 00s were naturally very busy. They didn't care about the price and just wanted to develop. The 50s and 00s went through too many economic cycles and saw too many bodies. So they were relatively conservative. When the market expanded, they didn't care about the price and just went for it.

So at this time, the expansion of these chips, the expansion of the upstream supply chain, 短期內永遠跟不上大模型的發展速度。所以沒有什麼資本支出太多的問題，資本支出很多依然跟不上大模型的增長，以及未來 AI 生產 AI 的增長速度。

現在還是人跟 AI 偶合在生產，未來就是 AI 生產 AI。AI produces AI, but the production power of humans and AI produces humans are different.

主持人：So you are watching the news, CNBC, they are all talking about AI bubbles. You don't feel worried?

孔劍平：No bubbles at all.

主持人：No bubbles at all?

八、AI 芯片的"折舊年齡" vs 真實使用壽命

孔劍平：The age of AI chip recovery is different from the actual age of it. It's like mining back then.

比特幣五年前跌的時候，礦機還能賣；比特幣一年前跌的時候，礦機就必須淘汰。The price of Bitcoin fell 5 years ago, and the mining machines can still be sold. The price of Bitcoin fell 1 year ago, and the mining machines have to be eliminated. Wow.

九、普通投資人如何選到"穿越熊市的公司"？

主持人：How do ordinary investors catch up with these news?

孔劍平：I think it's like having Internet bubble in 2000. But after 2000, cloud computing and Internet applications have seen a rapid growth.

In the past, some traditional companies, such as hardware companies, had problems. But new companies have seen a rapid growth. 它們拿到過上萬倍的回報——but some of them are dead.

主持人：But how do we choose whether this company is able to hold out in the fall?

孔劍平：I think it depends on whether it is in the core position of an industry chain.

In the past, it may be a GPU company, a storage company, a fiber factory. As its growth rate exceeds the high-speed stage, I think it is still in the high-speed growth stage, so don't worry. In the future, it may be the core VAF cloud company.

十、AI 與比特幣：為什麼不是穩定幣？

（關於 AI 自主性與資產安全）AI will be trapped by humans when it creates its own creativity. As an AI, I hired a few people to mine gold, but people moved the gold away. AI can't find it back.

But AI can store Bitcoin better than people. Because it has better encryption methods and better management methods. It can also find better ways to have a loophole. It's definitely better managed than people.

So digital currency is definitely an AI-suitable currency.

主持人：Why not stable currency? Why Bitcoin?

孔劍平：Bitcoin is a wool（原料/本位）. Stable currency is a payment tool. 支付中介。These two are not in conflict.

For example, the daily payment of agents is definitely stable currency. It is not possible to be Bitcoin. But if AI makes money to save money, it can only save Bitcoin.

十一、終極倉位配置：100 萬怎麼分？

主持人：Last question. If the audience has one million now, I don't care what currency it is. How do you distribute it now?

孔劍平： - 50% ~ 70% → AI 相關股票（未來增長空間） - 約 30% → 以比特幣為基礎的數字貨幣

In the future, AI development or digital currency development or AI and digital currency development in common, you can enjoy this red power.

主持人：I really want to hear this. Thank you.

孔劍平：Thank you.
